Ukraine and Europe have little choice but to work with Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:36:03 UTC
15:36:03 KST

Ukraine and Europe have little choice but to work with Trump
Despite growing tensions over Russia, Kyiv and European leaders remain dependent on US military support and diplomatic leverage.
“It’s painful when President [Donald] Trump chooses one side, not our side,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Wednesday. The United States president’s much-discussed diesel deal with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, has become another source of tension between Washington and Ukraine and its European backers.
The reported disruption of Starlink/Starshield services on October 13-14, which wrongfooted Ukraine’s military, has added to those tensions. Service was later restored, and reports that the restrictions were imposed at the White House’s behest to pressure Kyiv remained unconfirmed.
Nevertheless, the two episodes have reinforced the impression of a widening rift between Ukraine and the US. On Friday, Zelensky accused Washington of continuing to throttle Starlink and promising the Russians new concessions.
Obviously, one needs to wait until the dust settles. Trump has tilted towards Moscow before, notably at his August 2025 summit with Putin in Anchorage, Alaska, only to return to conditional support for Ukraine amid Russian intransigence and diplomatic efforts by Kyiv and European leaders. The arrangement under which Europe pays for US weapons delivered to Ukraine is working, and the US continues to share intelligence with Kyiv despite reports that some critical information has been withheld.
The White House has also walked back proposals to recognise Crimea as de jure Russian, floated in its April 2025 peace framework, or to require Kyiv to withdraw from the entirety of its Donbas region. For their part, Ukraine and Europe have continued to go along with Trump’s diplomatic overtures to Moscow, led by his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
The diesel deal itself may yet unravel, given bipartisan opposition in Congress, including from Republican senators. Washington’s latest shift towards Moscow may, therefore, prove less significant than it currently appears.
The above is no reason for complacency on the part of Ukraine and its principal backers in Europe. They have plenty of reasons to worry beyond Trump’s unpredictability.
Chief among them is Putin’s resolve to ramp up the war. Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure are coming under daily attacks from ballistic missiles and upgraded jet-propelled drones while its air defences are struggling. The country is bracing for yet another tough winter. A propaganda war is unfolding in parallel, fuelled by the diesel deal.
Unlike Ukraine, Russia never embraced Trump’s proposal for a partial ceasefire on strikes against energy facilities. Yet Moscow is now portraying Kyiv as the spoiler after Ukrainian attacks resumed, including an attack on a refinery in the city of Ryazan on Thursday which Trump slammed as “a disgrace”.
Fighting has spilled over onto NATO’s eastern flank with ships transporting Ukrainian grain through the Black Sea attacked in Romanian waters. Russia is expanding its hybrid attacks in Europe to disrupt supplies of weapons and ammunition to Ukraine and sway public opinion in key countries such as Germany by sowing fear. In some corners of the European Union, there is a push to re-engage with Moscow. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico confirmed that the Slovak-Russian intergovernmental economic commission would resume work. His Bulgarian counterpart, Rumen Radev, praised Trump’s diesel diplomacy, even as Russian drones carried out strikes near Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast.
Paying for Ukraine is another headache for the Europeans. The 90-billion-euro ($101bn) loan the EU authorised in April might be exhausted well before the end of 2027. Some estimates suggest Kyiv would require an additional 70 billion euros ($79bn) for defence and civilian purposes in 2027.
That threatens to open a can of worms for EU member states, which are already negotiating the bloc’s 2028-2034 budget.
With some calling for deep cuts in spending, the controversial question of whether aid for Ukraine should come from Russian financial assets frozen in Europe is coming back with a vengeance. Trump is meanwhile calling for some of the money to be released.
The squabble comes before several major elections, notably the French presidential election in April and May as well as polls in Spain, Italy and Poland.
Given the fragility in Europe, it is remarkable that diplomatic and financial support for Ukraine has remained rather steady. “This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia’s sanctions,” European Council President Antonio Costa said on Friday while appearing alongside Zelenskyy and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels. “If we fall, 20 million Ukrainians will come to Europe,” Zelensky reminded everyone, “Stay strong, defend our country.”
In the run-up to the summit, the EU opened two clusters in accession talks with Ukraine and imposed a new round of sanctions on Russia. Zelenskyy came to Brussels after talks with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and King Charles III in London on Wednesday.
But there is a limit to how much more the EU and the United Kingdom can do beyond what they are already delivering. They have already replaced the US as the principal international champions of Ukraine and de facto guarantors of its survival as a state. Becoming a member of the EU – or, at the very least, a closely integrated partner like Norway – is the best-case scenario for Kyiv in the long run.
At the same time, Europe lacks the political heft and the military capabilities to substitute for the US in the short term. That is abundantly clear on the battlefield. Although top European intelligence agencies can probably supply Ukrainians with some data, there is no EU alternative to Starlink. Europe cannot deliver enough air-defence systems and interceptors to fend off Russian attacks without US support. Faced with US unreliability, Europe is investing in these capabilities in pursuit of strategic autonomy, but even in the best-case scenario, these efforts will take a decade to bear fruit.
Most crucially, Europeans have little leverage they can use to bring Putin to the negotiating table. Sure, there might be positive incentives in the form of sanctions relief and the restoration of oil and gas flows. But any Russian response is likely to require pressure of some kind. The US has thus far failed to twist Putin’s arm – and under Trump has moved from sticks to carrots, dangling all kinds of “deals” mixing diplomacy and business. Part of the failure is due to the fear of escalation with another nuclear power; part of it is the current US administration’s opportunism. But the bottom line is that there is little reason to expect Europe can do a better job.
In light of all this, both Zelenskyy and the Europeans will probably fall back on the familiar approach: trying to keep Trump onside and smoothing over their differences as much as possible. They are probably hoping and praying that the current White House overture to Russia will fizzle out after the midterm elections. They will also tell Trump that the best way to secure his legacy is to stand firm against Moscow, a position that enjoys support among his fellow Republicans. The strategy is to wait it out: first the winter, then the Trump presidency.

U.S. Osprey fleet gets new flight computers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:35:39 UTC
15:35:39 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Bell Boeing $90.8 million to continue redesigning the V-22 Osprey flight control system, including new flight control computers.
- The upgrade addresses aging electronics, cybersecurity and parts obsolescence for U.S. and Foreign Military Sales Ospreys, with work running through October 2030.
The U.S. Navy has awarded the Bell Boeing joint venture $90.8 million to continue redesigning the V-22 Osprey’s flight control system, including new flight control computers and cockpit interface units for the tiltrotor aircraft flown by the U.S. Marine Corps, U.S. Air Force, U.S. Navy and a foreign customer.
The order, signed on Oct. 15 by Naval Air Systems Command at Patuxent River, Maryland, also covers new test equipment, software, technical documentation and logistics products needed to buy and support the redesigned system later. The U.S. Department of War said the upgrade is meant to deal with aging electronic components, cybersecurity requirements and parts that are no longer being made, so the Osprey fleet can keep flying for the rest of its service life.
The flight control system is the core of the V-22’s fly-by-wire design. Its computers turn pilot inputs into commands for the aircraft’s rotors, wings and engine nacelles, which tilt between helicopter and airplane modes in flight, so the computers have to keep working reliably for the Osprey to fly at all.
Bell Boeing will perform 52% of the work in Ridley Park, Pennsylvania, where Boeing builds the Osprey’s fuselage, and 42% in Mesa, Arizona, with smaller shares in Fort Worth, Texas, where Bell assembles the aircraft, and at other U.S. locations. Work is scheduled to finish in October 2030.
The government obligated about $4.9 million at signing, including roughly $3.1 million in U.S. Air Force research and development funds, $369,250 in U.S. Navy research funds and $1.4 million from the Foreign Military Sales customer. Japan is the only foreign country flying the Osprey, with V-22s in service with its Ground Self-Defense Force, though the contract notice did not name the buyer.
The award, issued as a sole-source order under an existing basic ordering agreement, extends work that began five years ago. In September 2021, the U.S. Navy gave Bell Boeing a $214.4 million order for the redesign and development of the V-22 flight control system, flight control computer and cockpit interface unit, citing functional obsolescence, cybersecurity and parts shortages. That work was due to be completed in June 2026.
The U.S. Marine Corps flies the MV-22B for troop and cargo transport, Air Force Special Operations Command uses the CV-22B for special operations missions, and the U.S. Navy operates the CMV-22B to carry people and supplies to aircraft carriers. The services plan to keep the aircraft in service for decades after production wraps up, which makes replacing electronics that suppliers no longer support a recurring task for the program.
Bell Boeing is expected to complete development of the redesigned flight control system, along with the software and support products needed to field it across the fleet, by October 2030.

06:35:00 UTC

US President Donald Trump denied involvement in reported throttling of Ukraine’s military-grade Starlink satellite communications, asserting that neither he nor American billionaire Elon Musk ordered service limitations on the network.
Trump said the US had not introduced operational curbs on the satellite system and claimed that the network continues to function normally.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I don’t know if it was somebody, because it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump told reporters. “And, as far as I understand, everything is the same as it’s always been.”
Trump’s remarks contradict reporting published by The Telegraph, which cited four sources familiar with the matter stating that Musk directly approached Trump with a proposal to throttle Starlink operations in Ukraine, a recommendation the US president reportedly approved.
According to The Telegraph, Trump’s consent cleared the way for the US Department of Defense to slow Starshield, the specialized military variant of the satellite communications network developed by SpaceX.
The reporting was corroborated by a senior European official alongside two Ukrainian sources.
While Musk publicly denied responsibility on Oct. 14, alleging that “any speed or usage limits” were determined by the US military and the White House, sources cited by the British newspaper indicated that Musk sought to deflect responsibility due to concerns regarding consumer blowback across European markets following severe grid disruptions and civilian casualties in Kyiv.
Putin Doesn’t Want Talks ‘in Any Format,’ Zelensky Says, Urges NATO to Take Drone Threats Seriously
Operational fallout on counter-drone systems and logistics
The conflicting accounts regarding the origin of the service caps follow statements delivered on Friday, Oct. 16, by President Volodymyr Zelensky, who confirmed that Ukraine’s military satellite capabilities had not yet been fully restored.
Speaking at a press conference in Brussels following meetings with EU leaders, Zelensky said that while bandwidth restrictions were gradually easing, Ukrainian forces had not regained the operational parameters required to counter incoming Russian aerial attacks.
“Has the speed been fully restored to what it was before? No. Is the speed being restored now? Yes,” Zelensky told reporters.
Zelensky explained that the restrictions directly compromised Ukraine’s capacity to intercept high-speed, turbojet-powered Shahed loitering munitions deployed against urban centers.
According to the Ukrainian head of state, domestic interceptor drones utilizing satellite links faced artificial velocity caps of approximately 70 km/h (43 mph), while Russian turbojet drones penetrated sovereign airspace at velocities exceeding 400 km/h (249 mph).
“Starlink was not switched off. The speed was reduced,” Zelensky said. “And when the speed was reduced, we were unable to shoot down some of the Shaheds. We were unable to use a tool to protect civilians.”
Zelensky added that the throttling disrupted essential frontline logistics, specifically unmanned aerial supply runs delivering rations, potable water, and medical kits to isolated forward infantry positions that remain inaccessible to conventional wheeled transport under continuous Russian surveillance.
Bilateral contacts
The technological friction comes amid heightened sensitivity regarding Ukraine’s reliance on commercial and military satellite architectures provided by Western contractors.
Zelensky noted that Ukrainian defense officials remain in daily contact with American partners to eliminate remaining bandwidth constraints, mentioning that Kyiv received indications that the White House had contacted SpaceX to instruct the restoration of baseline speeds.
The Starlink controversy coincides with ongoing friction between Washington and Kyiv over battlefield targeting rules.
US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have urged Ukraine to halt long-range drone interdiction strikes on Russian oil refineries, while Trump announced an immediate bilateral “energy ceasefire” following a telephone consultation with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Despite the administration’s stated diplomatic goals, Ukrainian officials have emphasized that degrading communications networks impairs basic tactical defense, leaving municipal centers and civilian life-support systems vulnerable to standoff bombardments.

Annika wins one of Denmark’s biggest music awards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:31:34 UTC
15:31:34 KST

The 21-year-old singer has gone from posting piano videos on TikTok to becoming one of Denmark’s biggest pop stars. On Friday, she received the top prize at DR’s annual P3 Guld music awards.
Danish singer Annika has won P3 Prisen, the main award at one of Denmark’s most prominent annual music events, P3 Guld.
The 21-year-old received the award Friday evening at DR Koncerthuset in Copenhagen, a year after being nominated for the same prize but losing out to Danish band Aphaca.
P3 Guld is the annual music awards show organised by P3, the youth-oriented music and entertainment radio station run by Danish public broadcaster DR.
The event celebrates artists who have made a significant impact on Danish music over the past year, with P3 Prisen regarded as its main award.
Annika, whose full name is Annika Wedderkopp, was selected by a P3 jury ahead of fellow nominees Zar Paulo and producer Anton Westerlin, who is also her boyfriend.
“With an authentic foundation in her own life, Annika creates massive hits about breakups and infatuations, about doubt and a steely belief that everything will naturally work out,” the jury said.
From TikTok to the Danish charts
Annika’s rise has been rapid.
She began by posting videos of herself singing at the piano on TikTok before breaking through with “Knuser hjerter” in 2024.
She followed it with several successful releases, including “Så længe jeg er sexy”, and won P3 Talentet, the event’s talent award, that same year.
Last year, she released her debut album “AW”, which includes “Stolt”, a collaboration with Danish rapper Lamin. She also opened Roskilde Festival’s Orange Stage, the festival’s largest and most prestigious stage.
Previous recipients of P3 Prisen include some of Denmark’s best-known contemporary artists, including The Minds of 99, Tobias Rahim, Artigeardit, Lamin, Tina Dickow and Jada.
Other winners
Several other awards were presented at Friday’s ceremony.
Guldimund and Saveus won P3 Lytterhittet – the listeners’ choice award – for their song “Vil du noget?”.
Zar Paulo received P3 Live, an award recognising an artist who has distinguished themselves on Denmark’s live music scene. The award returned this year after previously being presented in 2001 and 2009.
Danish-Faroese artist Friða Saiya won P3’s Næste, a new award that has replaced P3 Talentet and highlights emerging artists.
Criticism over lack of women
This year’s P3 Guld also faced criticism before the ceremony over the gender balance among its performers.
Twelve men and two women were scheduled to perform during the evening.
Ditte Christiane Jensen, head of editorial at DR Ung, defended the lineup in a written response to Ritzau.
“Talent, creativity and artistic quality are not about gender,” she said.
“This year’s lineup was put together based on the artists and bands that have left a significant mark on the music year and in P3’s universe.”

Trump: Greenland deal biggest real estate deal ever
The US president says he “got it for nothing” after signing a new defence agreement with Denmark and Greenland that expands the American military presence on the island.
US President Donald Trump has described a new defence and security agreement with Denmark and Greenland as potentially “the biggest real estate deal that has ever been made”.
Speaking at a Republican campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia, Trump portrayed the agreement as a major achievement for the United States.
“What do you think of the deal I made on Greenland? Got it for nothing,” Trump told supporters.
“It is probably the biggest real estate deal that has ever been made.”
Trump was campaigning ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3.
His comments come after months of tension over Greenland, an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark. Trump has repeatedly said that the United States wants control and ownership of Greenland, arguing that the island is crucial to American national security.
Two new US military bases
The United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a new security and defence agreement on Greenland at the end of September following lengthy negotiations.
The agreement was signed at the United Nations in New York shortly after Trump addressed the UN General Assembly.
It allows the United States to establish two additional military bases in Greenland.
The US currently operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, which plays an important role in missile warning, space surveillance and Arctic security.
The new agreement also opens the possibility of deploying parts of the planned US Golden Dome missile defence system in Greenland. The system is intended to protect the United States against threats including missiles and drones.
Despite Trump’s description of the agreement as a “real estate deal”, it does not transfer ownership of Greenland to the United States.
Trump’s comments came as Republicans campaign to retain control of Congress in the November midterm elections. Democrats are currently polling more strongly in the race for the House of Representatives, while control of the Senate remains more uncertain.
Republicans currently hold majorities in both chambers.
Source: Ritzau
Denmark’s shift from fossil fuels to electricity is accelerating
Electric cars, heat pumps and electric boilers are driving a sharp increase in the share of Denmark’s energy consumption covered by electricity.
Denmark is becoming increasingly electrified as electric cars, heat pumps and electric boilers replace fossil fuels.
Electricity accounted for 23.4 percent of Denmark’s total energy consumption in 2025, according to figures highlighted by industry organisation Green Power Denmark.
That was an increase of 1.5 percentage points in just one year.
The increase is significant. Between 2016 and 2024, the share of electricity in Denmark’s total energy consumption rose by only 3.8 percentage points.
The acceleration is being driven particularly by the growing number of electric cars and by district heating companies investing in electric boilers and heat pumps.
Kristian Jensen, CEO of Green Power Denmark, says the development will gradually make Denmark less dependent on imported oil and natural gas – and therefore less exposed to international energy prices and geopolitical developments.
“We are freeing ourselves from what is going on in the Middle East and American politics,” Jensen told Ritzau.
“When Danes experience that gasoline, diesel and electricity have become more expensive than they were a year ago, it is because we are still dependent on the price set in the rest of the world.”
Target: 60 percent by 2035
Green Power Denmark wants electricity to account for 60 percent of Denmark’s total energy consumption by 2035.
Reaching that level will require a much faster transition in Danish industry, according to Jensen.
He points to heat pumps as one of the technologies that can help companies replace natural gas with electricity. Iron foundries and food producers, including dairy group Arla, have already demonstrated that large heat pumps can be used in industrial production.
Jensen argues that other companies should follow their example.
“It will not only reduce the companies’ CO2 emissions, it will also reduce energy expenses and thereby improve their competitiveness,” he said.
Figures for Denmark’s electrification rate in 2026 are not yet available, but Green Power Denmark expects the shift towards electricity to continue.

Denmark’s oldest-ever person was a member of the Danish Nazi party
Records show that 112-year-old Kirsten Schwalbe joined Denmark’s Nazi party during the German occupation. She says she did so at her husband’s request and did not sympathise with Nazism.
Kirsten Schwalbe, who this week became the longest-living Dane in recorded history, was a member of Denmark’s Nazi party during the German occupation.
The 112-year-old joined the National Socialist Workers’ Party of Denmark (DNSAP) in August 1941, according to Kristeligt Dagblad.
Her name appears in the Bovrup registry, a record of people who were members of DNSAP. Two historians have independently confirmed to the newspaper that the entry matches Schwalbe’s date of birth and address, although her surname is misspelled as “Schalbe”.
Schwalbe has confirmed that both she and her former husband were members of the party, but says she only joined because her husband urged her to do so.
She rejected the suggestion that she had sided with Nazi Germany.
“Not at all. I barely knew what it was, because I have never taken an interest in politics,” she told TV Midtvest when asked whether she had sympathised with the Nazis.
Schwalbe said she found it unfair that she should have to “pay for it” more than 70 years later, adding that “back then, wives didn’t look into such things”.
Membership does not show level of involvement
DNSAP was founded in 1930 and was strongly inspired by Adolf Hitler’s German Nazi Party, the NSDAP.
But Charlie Krautwald, a historian at the University of Copenhagen, cautioned against drawing conclusions about Schwalbe’s level of involvement from the registry alone.
The record shows that a person joined the party, he told Kristeligt Dagblad, but not why they joined, how long they remained a member or whether they paid membership fees.
A person could therefore appear in the registry without having been active in the party.
TV Midtvest has followed Schwalbe for several years and manages an Instagram account about her life. Two of the broadcaster’s employees have also recently published a book about her.
Her membership of DNSAP had not previously been mentioned. TV Midtvest editor-in-chief Marc Killigren Akselsen told Kristeligt Dagblad that the broadcaster had not known about it.
Schwalbe, who lives in Struer in western Jutland, became the longest-living Dane on record on Wednesday, when she reached the age of 112 years and 218 days.
Source: Ritzau

Lidl has Denmark’s cheapest basket of organic groceries, analysis finds
Lidl offers the lowest prices on a selected basket of organic groceries among seven Danish supermarket chains, according to an analysis by price-monitoring service Madprisluppen.
A basket containing 22 organic products cost 355.20 DKK at Lidl. The same basket cost 449.60 DKK at Meny, the most expensive chain in the comparison.
Madprisluppen said the Lidl basket was 26 percent cheaper than the one at Meny.
“We want to make it easier for Danes to make room for organics in everyday life, and here price plays an important role,” Lidl Denmark purchasing director Peer Sandtner said.
Rema 1000 was the second-cheapest supermarket, with its basket costing only 5 DKK more than Lidl’s.
SuperBrugsen was the second-most expensive, though its total was almost 35 DKK below Meny’s.
The analysis also included Netto, 365discount and Føtex. Prices were recorded from October 9 through October 12.
Products included milk, eggs, vegetables and dry goods. Meat was excluded because Madprisluppen found it difficult to identify comparable products across the chains.
The monitoring service also found that supermarkets carry fewer organic products than they did six years ago. Organic prices have increased, and such products appear in special offers less frequently than non-organic groceries.
Norway to lend 10-meter Viking boat to Danish museum for 10 years
A Norwegian Viking boat will be displayed at Moesgaard Museum near Aarhus under an unusual 10-year loan agreement.
The oak boat is almost 10 meters long and nearly two meters wide. It was among three smaller vessels discovered when archaeologists excavated Norway’s Gokstad ship in 1880.
The Gokstad ship is Norway’s largest preserved Viking ship.
“The boat is a very important cultural treasure from the Viking Age, and it is not an everyday occurrence that we grant permission for such a boat to be taken out of the country,” Kaare Stang of Riksantikvaren, Norway’s cultural heritage authority, said.
The three smaller boats had been chopped into pieces, possibly as part of a burial ritual, according to archaeologists.
The Museum of Cultural History in Norway owns the boat and applied for permission to lend it to Moesgaard Museum for a new exhibition.
Norwegian authorities normally approve loans for no more than three years. Moesgaard Museum must therefore submit a report on the boat’s condition every three years during the loan period.
Stang said Norwegian authorities trusted the Danish museum to protect the boat but emphasized that it must eventually return to Norway.
No arrival date has been announced.
Moesgaard Museum already displays a 6.5-meter Gokstad boat that was used to transport crews and exchange orders between warships.
Copenhagen establishes support groups for parents of children missing school
A new parents’ association has signed a four-year agreement with the City of Copenhagen to establish support groups for families whose children experience prolonged, involuntary school absence.
Such absence is often connected to poor well-being and is considered concerning when a pupil misses at least 20 percent of school for two consecutive quarters. That corresponds to about 10 days per quarter.
The first groups will be funded by Copenhagen and include eight to nine parents who meet approximately once a month, education news outlet Folkeskolen.dk reported.
A family therapist will lead the meetings, with a parent from Forældrekommissionen, or the Parents’ Commission, also participating.
Louise Gielov and Jens Langorn helped establish the association after their family appeared in the Danish public broadcaster DR documentary “Skolens tabte børn,” which showed daily life with children unable to attend school.
The couple received more than 1,000 messages from parents in similar situations after the documentary aired.
The association now has 2,545 members and aims to establish parent groups across Denmark. It also plans to use families’ experiences to promote earlier intervention and broader changes to prevent school absence.
The proportion of pupils with prolonged concerning absence increased from 2.4 percent in the 2019-2020 school year to 5.1 percent in 2024-2025.
The association has also secured 7 million DKK from foundations.
Dane becomes first European participant to receive combined flu and Covid vaccine
A 65-year-old Dane will become the first person in Europe to receive a new combined influenza and Covid-19 vaccine as part of a clinical trial Friday.
The trial will examine whether one injection can protect against both diseases as effectively as, or better than, the two separate vaccines currently used, Danish public broadcaster DR reported.
The first participant will receive the vaccine at Gentofte Hospital.
“We are investigating whether one shot with this new vaccine is just as effective or potentially better than the two shots given today at preventing hospitalizations with influenza and Covid-19,” said Tor Biering-Sørensen, a professor and senior physician at Herlev and Gentofte Hospital who is leading the trial.
About 165,000 Danes have agreed to participate. More than 300,000 people are expected to join over the next two years.
Half of the participants will receive one dose of the combined vaccine. The other half will receive separate influenza and Covid-19 vaccinations.
People age 65 and older in Denmark are automatically invited to receive free vaccinations against both diseases. The Danish Health Authority said about 1.3 million residents received invitations in September.
People with chronic illnesses or other conditions placing them at increased risk are also eligible for the free program.
The vaccines are intended to reduce the risk of severe illness and hospitalization during the winter respiratory infection season.

Archaeologists uncover more than 1,000 graves in Copenhagen park
Archaeologists have excavated more than 1,000 graves containing human remains beneath Hans Tavsens Park in Copenhagen’s Nørrebro district.
The park, located next to Assistens Cemetery, was previously used as a burial ground for Copenhagen’s poorest residents. Victims of the city’s 1853 cholera epidemic are among those buried there.
“We can use it to gain insight into the poor population from this period and Copenhagen’s history,” Museum of Copenhagen archaeologist Olivia Persson told Danish public broadcaster DR.
The excavation is taking place before Hans Tavsens Park and the neighboring Hans Tavsens Gade are redeveloped into a connected green space.
The project will also allow the park to collect water during cloudbursts, helping prevent flooding of nearby roads and basements as Denmark experiences wetter weather.
Construction began in autumn 2025 as part of the City of Copenhagen’s plan for managing extreme rainfall. The redevelopment is expected to be completed in spring 2028.
Most of the remains will be transferred to the University of Copenhagen’s Anthropological Laboratory for storage and examination. Some will undergo additional analysis, while the remainder will be reburied in the park.
Researchers will examine the health of selected individuals. They will also study how the graves were arranged to better understand religious and cultural attitudes toward death among Copenhagen’s poorer population at the time.

Greenland’s parliament unanimously adopted a resolution Thursday directing the government to draft legislation temporarily banning deep-sea mining.
The proposed ban would remain in effect through December 31, 2029, with the possibility of two-year extensions.
Naalakkersuisut, Greenland’s government, supported the considerations behind the resolution. It said it would introduce a bill for the temporary ban during parliament’s spring 2027 session.
The ban must therefore pass as legislation before taking effect.
WWF Greenland, the local branch of the World Wide Fund for Nature, called the decision “an important step in the right direction,” according to AFP.
“With this decision, Greenland has the opportunity to send a strong signal that the protection of the ocean, nature and the Greenlanders’ livelihood must be taken seriously when we face new forms of exploitation of marine resources,” the organization said.
WWF Greenland says deep-sea mining can damage marine ecosystems and biodiversity.
Fishing is the main driver of Greenland’s economy, while hunting remains important to local communities.
The vote came one day after US President Donald Trump said oil, gas and mineral exploration was beginning in Greenland. Greenland’s government subsequently denied the claim. Trump did not mention deep-sea mining.
Greenland suspended new oil and gas exploration permits in 2021. Industrial oil drilling and gas extraction have never been conducted there, according to AFP.
Denmark considers lower temperature rule to allow electric cremation ovens
Denmark’s 20 crematoria could replace oil- and gas-powered ovens with electric models if authorities approve a lower minimum temperature requirement.
The Danish Environmental Protection Agency has proposed reducing the required temperature in cremation ovens’ post-combustion chambers from 800 to 750 degrees Celsius, engineering publication Ingeniøren reported.
The proposed change has been submitted for public consultation.
Electric ovens are expected to reduce both environmental effects and the financial cost of cremations.
Michael Smidemann, chair of the Danish Crematoria Association, said crematoria were interested in replacing their existing ovens.
“The background is a desire to sharpen the green profile, even though it is somewhat mixed how green the electricity we receive actually is,” he told Ingeniøren.
Electric cremation ovens can reach 750 degrees. Requiring them to reach 800 degrees would demand additional heating elements, increasing electricity use and causing heavy wear on the ovens’ brickwork, according to Ingeniøren.
Denmark recorded 58,185 deaths in 2025, according to the Danish Crematoria Association.
Of those who died, 51,252 were cremated, corresponding to 88.1 percent of all deaths.
A cremation typically takes about 90 minutes, according to information from the City of Copenhagen and other sources.

Denmark’s specialized social and education services received 61 percent of the inflation-adjusted growth in municipal service spending from 2018 through 2025.

Specialized services include support for children, young people and adults with particular needs, along with special classes and special education.

“When expenditures in the specialized areas grow, there is less money for the general areas, which also need investments,” AE director Lars Andersen said.
However, the analysis does not establish that the increased specialized spending directly caused cuts elsewhere.
Municipal service funding also covers daycare centers, public schools and elderly care.
The government and Local Government Denmark, the association representing Denmark’s municipalities, have increased the overall spending limit annually since 2018. Their latest agreement raises it by 3.3 billion DKK for 2027.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats has previously acknowledged that rapidly rising specialized social service costs continue to create financial difficulties for some municipalities.

Tiny parasitic wasp discovered in Denmark for the first time
A nature enthusiast searching beneath ferns in a North Zealand forest has identified an insect species never previously recorded in the country.
The discovery was made in mid-September at Gribskov National Nature Park during a bioblitz, a 24-hour event in which participants search for and document wildlife.
Around 70 people took part in the event, organized in collaboration with the Vores Vilde Natur project and biodiversity platform Arter.dk.
Nature educator Lars Holm Hansen discovered the wasp, measuring just a few millimeters, while shaking bracken ferns to examine the insects hiding underneath.
He collected several specimens using an insect aspirator but could not immediately identify them.
After posting a photograph on Arter.dk, he received help from experts who identified the species as Hemiptarsenus ornatus.
“It shows that if you put in a little effort out in the field, you can get lucky, and it is simply worth the effort,” Hansen said.
The Natural History Museum of Denmark confirmed the finding in a press release.
Museum insect curator Lars Vilhelmsen explained that the species has previously been recorded in Germany, Sweden and Norway.
“It has probably been here all along. It is already known from several countries around us, but it is so small that you do not just easily spot it,” Vilhelmsen said.
He added that relatively few people in Denmark study parasitic wasps, meaning many species may remain undocumented.
Hansen, who had participated in six bioblitz events this year, also suggested the insect’s Danish name: smykket dværgsnyltehveps.
He believes Danish names make unfamiliar species easier to discuss and remember.

Full train service between Fredericia and Odense to resume Monday
Full train service between Fredericia and Odense will resume on Monday, Banedanmark announced on Wednesday.
Banedanmark, which operates, maintains and develops Denmark’s state-owned railway network, announced the resumption in a post on the social media platform X.
Earlier on Wednesday, railway operator DSB said in a preliminary announcement that fewer trains would run on the route through Sunday, October 18.
All regional trains on the section have been replaced by buses since Friday, when a fire broke out in a railway relay hut near Aarup, a town on western Funen.
International trains, InterCityLyn express services and InterCity trains have continued to run as normal, but at reduced speeds on parts of the route between Odense and Middelfart or Fredericia.
Signal fault disrupts trains between Copenhagen and Næstved until evening
A signal fault near Kildebrønde in eastern Zealand is disrupting train services between Copenhagen Central Station and Næstved via Køge.
On Wednesday morning, DSB said passengers should expect longer travel times until 1 p.m. But about an hour before that deadline, the railway operator announced that disruptions would continue until 7 p.m., according to its website.
Banedanmark, which operates and maintains Denmark’s state-owned railway network, told DSB that repair work would not take place until Wednesday night, leading into Thursday.
However, a solution has been found that will allow trains to run normally on the affected section after 7 p.m., even though the fault will not yet have been repaired.
Some trains that usually run via Køge Nord are being diverted through Roskilde instead. These services will not stop between Copenhagen Central Station and Ringsted.
Additional replacement buses were introduced between Køge and Næstved on Wednesday morning to ease pressure on train services. The buses stopped running at noon, and DSB is advising passengers to take the S-train from Copenhagen toward Køge. Trains between Køge and Næstved are running once an hour.
Banedanmark told the Danish news agency Ritzau that a severed cable caused the signal fault. DSB advises passengers to check Rejseplanen, Denmark’s public transport journey planner, before setting off.
Meanwhile, fewer trains are running between Odense and Fredericia through Sunday, October 18, according to DSB. The date is provisional, and services could return to normal earlier or later than expected.
All regional trains on the route have been replaced by buses since Friday, following a fire in a railway relay hut near Aarup in western Funen.
International trains, as well as InterCityLyn and InterCity services, are running as normal, but at reduced speeds on some sections of the route.
On Tuesday afternoon, all train traffic between Odense and Fredericia was also halted for a couple of hours after a cable fell onto the tracks and caused a short circuit in the overhead power system.
Three Danish films shortlisted for Europe’s Oscars
Three Danish films have been shortlisted for the European Film Awards, often described as Europe’s equivalent of the Oscars.
The films are the dramas Kvinde ukendt by May el-Toukhy and Gæsten by Mads Mengel, and Sine Plambech’s documentary Rescue, the Danish Film Institute announced on Instagram.
A total of 45 films have been shortlisted in the fiction category.
May el-Toukhy’s Kvinde ukendt has already received international recognition. The drama was selected for the Venice Film Festival in September, where it won the main prize, the Golden Lion. Its lead actress, Mathilde Arcel, was named best actress.
The film has also been selected as Denmark’s entry for the Academy Awards in the Best International Feature Film category.
Set during the liberation of Denmark in May 1945, the drama follows a woman who has worked as a maid in the home of an elderly, respected widower she is now preparing to marry. She struggles to hide the fact that she has had a relationship with a German soldier.
Mads Mengel’s Gæsten has also attracted international attention. In July, the film received two awards at the Karlovy Vary International Film Festival in the Czech Republic.
It won the Special Jury Prize in the festival’s main competition, known as the Crystal Globe Competition, while Mengel was named best director.
The film follows Karl and Emilie, a couple preparing to host a naming ceremony for their son. Their plans are disrupted when an uninvited guest arrives: Karl’s mother, played by Trine Dyrholm, with whom he has not spoken for years.
The third Danish film on the shortlist is Rescue, a documentary by anthropologist Sine Plambech. It had its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival in September.
The documentary follows people fleeing across the Mediterranean and examines how the European Union’s border policies affect the lives and conditions of refugees.
Rescue is one of 15 films shortlisted in the documentary category.
Producers, distributors and other rights holders can submit films for consideration by the European Film Academy. The academy’s board and invited European experts then select films for the shortlist.
Members of the academy, which includes professionals from across the European film industry, watch the shortlisted films and vote to determine the final nominations. They vote again to select the winners once the nominations have been announced.
The final nominations will be announced on November 14. The awards ceremony will take place in Athens, the Greek capital, on January 16.
Danish citizen among three killed in Swiss Alps plane crash
A Danish citizen was among three people killed when a small plane crashed in the Swiss Alps on September 15, according to a report from Denmark’s Accident Investigation Board published on Wednesday.
The other two victims were British citizens, the BBC and other media have previously reported.
The Danish board does not know the age or gender of the Danish citizen, nor whether the person was a passenger or a pilot. It has also not been informed of a possible cause of the crash.
Swiss authorities are responsible for investigating the circumstances of the accident.
The Danish Accident Investigation Board must be notified when a report on the crash is ready. The board said on Wednesday that the authorities have one year to prepare such a report.
The aircraft was a small private plane of the type Cirrus SR22T, according to previous reports by the BBC and Reuters.
Swiss police said in September that the plane had taken off from Lugano and stopped at Sion Airport before crashing near the town of Leukerbad at around 2 p.m. on September 15.
Rescue workers rushed to the scene, Reuters reported. When they arrived, all three people on board had died.
Travelers going between Copenhagen Central Station and Næstved by way of Køge face longer travel times until 1:00 p.m. on Wednesday.
DSB, the Danish national rail operator, announced the problem on its website.
A few trains that usually run on the line through Køge Nord are taking a detour through Roskilde instead. These trains will not make any stops between Copenhagen Central Station and Ringsted.
To help travelers get to their destinations, buses are running between Køge and Næstved to replace the missing train service.
The delay is due to a signal problem at Kildebronde in East Zealand. Banedanmark, the state agency in charge of railway infrastructure, told Ritzau, the Danish news agency, that a severed cable caused the signal failure.
DSB told passengers to check Rejseplanen, the national travel planning service, before leaving home.
Fewer trains were already running between Odense and Fredericia before this latest problem, and that reduction will last through Sunday, October 18.
DSB stated that this date is an estimate, and the issues could end earlier or later than expected.
All regional trains on this route have been replaced by buses since Friday, when a fire started in an equipment hut near the town of Aarup on western Funen.
International trains, along with InterCity and InterCityLyn express trains, are running on their normal schedules, but they must move at lower speeds on parts of the route.
All train traffic between Odense and Fredericia stopped for about two hours on Tuesday afternoon after a cable fell onto the tracks and short-circuited an overhead power line.
Liberal Alliance wants mindset interview for citizenship applicant
A debate in Denmark over a proposed law granting citizenship to 2,055 people has centered on whether the applicants have been checked well enough for anti-democratic opinions.
Liberal Alliance, a political party in Denmark, carried out its own check of the people listed in the citizenship bill. During this review, the party found a woman who had repeatedly praised Hamas and former Hamas leaders Yahya Sinwar and Ismail Haniyeh.
Following the discovery, Liberal Alliance wants the woman called in for an interview with Indfødsretsudvalget, the Naturalization Committee of the Danish parliament.
Alex Vanopslagh, the leader of Liberal Alliance, spoke about the matter to the Danish newspaper Politiken.
“As we see it, it just emphasizes the need to wait to grant more citizenships until a proper screening model is in place, so that we can specifically catch some types who, based on what we can see so far, appear strongly anti-democratic,” he told the newspaper.
Every six months, a new bill is introduced in Folketinget, the Danish parliament, to give people Danish citizenship. This happens after an application process that is often long and detailed. This process was also followed under the previous coalition government in Denmark.
The most recent round of citizenships was scheduled at the same time a parliamentary election was called in the spring. Because of the election, the bill that included citizenship for the 2,055 people was delayed.
The delay gave momentum to demands from opposition parties. They argued that officials must carry out a more thorough review of the people on the list to find out if any of them hold anti-democratic views. Socialdemokratiet, the Danish Social Democratic Party, supported this demand as well.
However, the new government decided to present the citizenship bill before a new screening system was ready. This choice led to a larger debate during the opening of the Danish parliament.
During that debate, Rasmus Stoklund, the political spokesperson for Socialdemokratiet, said that if opposition parties found a person on the bill who had anti-democratic views, they could inform the Naturalization Committee. Liberal Alliance has now acted on that suggestion.
Politiken also spoke with the woman identified by the party. She denied that she supports Hamas or any killings.
“I do not support anyone who kills anyone. Because I do not like anyone killing anyone, regardless of whether they are Israeli, Russian or anything else,” the woman told the newspaper.
She stated that she is ready to attend an interview with the committee to explain her position.
Other political parties have reacted differently to the proposal. Dansk Folkeparti, the Danish People’s Party, supports calling the woman in for an interview.
However, Enhedslisten, the Danish left-wing Red-Green Alliance party, strongly opposes the idea.
“It is deeply concerning that Liberal Alliance now to such an extent wants to begin exercising thought control,” Peder Hvelplund, the citizenship spokesperson for Enhedslisten, told Politiken.
Minister to discuss cyberattack measures with parties
Denmark’s minister for homeland security and emergency preparedness, Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen, says there is a clear need to talk with members of the Danish parliament about how to protect the country against cyberattacks.
Bech-Nielsen belongs to SF (Socialistisk Folkeparti), the Socialist People’s Party, which is a left-wing and green political party in Denmark. She spoke about the situation to the Danish broadcaster TV 2.
“The serious threat assessment and recent events are the reason why I have summoned the parties to a discussion of what initiatives can be set in motion,” she said.
The minister called the political parties in the Danish parliament, to discuss what specific steps Denmark should take to make its digital systems safer. The statement did not say when this meeting will take place.
Her comments came right after Sund & Bælt, the state-owned company in charge of major Danish bridge and tunnel links, announced on Tuesday afternoon that its construction site at Rødbyhavn was hit by what it called a cyber incident.
“Our contractor, FLC, has informed us that they have been subjected to a cyber incident,” said Jens Villemoes, the head of press at Sund & Bælt, in a statement published on the company’s website. FLC stands for Femern Link Contractors, the consortium hired to build the tunnel.
The local newspaper Lolland-Falsters Folketidende described the event as a hacker attack. According to the newspaper, the problems meant that workers were ordered not to connect to Wi-Fi, turn on their computers, or open emails from the contractor.
Large parts of the computer network were shut down. The security guards could not use their digital access systems, and employees were unable to log their working hours in the normal way.
The problems also spread to work on the water. Several ships had to stop moving because they lost access to their digital tools and data. According to the newspaper, these issues first began during the night leading up to Monday.
Bech-Nielsen had actually called for the political meeting before the problems hit the Femern project. That decision came after a recent leak of Danish CPR numbers, which are the personal identification numbers assigned to all citizens in Denmark.
The minister said it is still too early to draw final conclusions about the latest incident, but noted that “the authorities are investigating” it.
Vietnamese president to visit Denmark for three days of engagements
King Frederik and Queen Mary will welcome Vietnamese President To Lam and his wife, Ngo Phuong Ly, for a three-day state visit from October 19 to 21.
The Danish Royal House has published the official program, which includes cultural visits, political meetings and events in Copenhagen.
The presidential couple will arrive at Copenhagen Airport on Monday before joining the Danish royals for a wreath-laying ceremony at Kastellet and a carriage ride to Amalienborg Palace.
Their first day includes visits to Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, a public library, the Court Theatre and the Niels Bohr Institute. A gala banquet at Christiansborg Palace will follow.
On Tuesday, Frederik and To Lam will attend a business conference hosted by Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, Denmark’s main business and employers’ association.
Meanwhile, Ngo Phuong Ly will visit Copenhagen Contemporary to see an exhibition featuring eight artists connected to Greenland.
Queen Mary will later join her for lunch at Gro Spiseri, a rooftop greenhouse restaurant in Østerbro.
To Lam will also meet Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats, while the presidential couple will meet Vietnamese residents in Denmark.
Tuesday concludes with a concert event at the Glyptoteket museum.
On Wednesday, Frederik and To Lam will take a boat tour of Copenhagen Harbour, including views of the Lynetteholm peninsula.
The visit concludes at Amalienborg at 11 a.m.
Denmark and Vietnam mark 55 years of diplomatic relations this year.
Frederik and Mary last visited Vietnam officially in 2022, when they were crown prince and crown princess.
To Lam serves as both Vietnam’s president and general secretary of its ruling Communist Party.
Kirsten Schwalbe becomes Denmark’s oldest person ever at 112
A woman from Struer has set a national longevity record, reaching 112 years and 218 days on Wednesday and surpassing the previous record held by Karla Lindholm Jensen.
Schwalbe also joins the list of Europe’s 10 oldest living people. The world’s oldest living person is Britain’s Ethel Caterham, who is 117.
The previous Danish record holder, Karla Lindholm Jensen from Herning, died in 2020.
Ahead of the milestone, Jyllands-Posten attempted to interview Schwalbe, but she needed a day of rest. Instead, the newspaper spoke with two of her three daughters.
Her daughter Hanne Jensen, 86, described how her mother sometimes struggles to understand that her children are now elderly themselves.
“She knows well enough that we are getting older, but she forgets that we can no longer withstand everything,” Jensen told the newspaper.
Schwalbe was born in Salling in 1914, just months before World War I began, and grew up alongside nine siblings.
She married her first husband in 1938, and the couple had three children.
Despite her age, Schwalbe continues to live in her own home in Struer.
Her life has previously been documented by regional broadcaster TV Midtvest in the television series “Kirstens vilde år,” which airs on TV 2.
Schwalbe has attributed her longevity partly to genetics. Four of her nine siblings also lived beyond 100, she told Berlingske in 2024.
She has also emphasized the importance of maintaining a positive outlook, previously telling TV Midtvest that a person’s mood plays an important role in living a long life.
Government party proposes mandatory helmets for e-bike riders
Rising numbers of serious traffic injuries have prompted Moderaterne, the Moderates, to call for stricter safety rules for people using electric bicycles.
Sten Larsen, the party’s health spokesperson, told regional broadcaster TV2 Østjylland that helmets should become a legal requirement for e-bike riders.
“E-bikes are both heavier and faster than regular bicycles,” Larsen said.
He pointed to an increase in serious injuries and deaths involving electric bicycles as justification for the proposal.
Currently, Denmark does not require helmets for ordinary bicycles or standard e-bikes, whose motors provide assistance at speeds of up to 25 kilometers per hour.
However, helmets are already mandatory for speed pedelecs, which can provide motor assistance up to 45 kilometers per hour.
According to the Danish Road Directorate, 200 e-bike riders were injured in traffic accidents in 2025, including 133 who suffered serious injuries. Another 11 riders died.
The number of seriously injured e-bike riders was the highest recorded in six years.
Larsen wants to discuss the proposed legislation with Transport Minister Signe Munk of Socialistisk Folkeparti, the Socialist People’s Party.
Ritzau sought a comment from Munk, but her ministry said she was unavailable.
Cyklistforbundet, the Danish Cyclists’ Federation, opposes making helmets compulsory, arguing that such a measure could discourage cycling.
“Our purpose is to get more people to cycle. So every measure that pulls in the opposite direction, we will oppose. But we warmly recommend that people use a bicycle helmet,” federation chair Jens Peter Hansen told TV2 Østjylland.
The proposal would introduce a helmet requirement for standard e-bikes, bringing their rules closer to those already applying to faster electric bicycles.
Venstre suggests shifting Danish development aid toward North Africa to address migration
Denmark should maintain its current foreign aid budget but change where the money goes, according to Jacob Jensen, foreign affairs spokesperson for Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party.
Jensen told Ritzau that his party wants to continue spending 0.7 percent of gross national income on development aid annually.
However, he wants more funding directed toward four or five North African countries facing migration pressures toward Europe.
The money would come from aid currently allocated to regions including the Caribbean, South America and Southeast Asia.
Jensen argued that providing education and employment opportunities could discourage young people from attempting dangerous Mediterranean crossings.
“If we can give the typically young men, who alternatively throw themselves into a rubber dinghy across the Mediterranean, a perspective, a job, an education in that area, we can solve many things at once,” he said.
Jensen estimated that between 3 billion and 3.5 billion DKK could be redirected.
However, the regions he identified were already outside Denmark’s ten largest aid recipients in 2025, when the country distributed 22.9 billion DKK in development aid.
Jensen wants to discuss revising Denmark’s development strategy with Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates party.
The government’s proposed aid priorities for 2027 through 2030 already include measures to reduce irregular migration.
Before the general election, Venstre proposed cutting development aid to 0.5 percent of national income to free approximately 6.5 billion DKK for welfare.
That proposal was dropped during government negotiations.
Jensen said the proposed reduction was intended to finance other priorities, not reduce development aid as an objective.
Greenland moves closer to restoring former time zone and ending daylight saving time
Greenland’s three governing parties have agreed to support a proposal that would move the territory back to UTC-3 in 2028, reversing a decision made just a few years ago.
The parties, which hold a majority in Inatsisartut, Greenland’s parliament, announced their position during a debate Tuesday, according to Sermitsiaq.
The proposal would also abolish daylight saving time starting next year.
“We have decided that we should return to UTC-3 on the basis of the many people who have submitted a consultation response,” the governing parties said.
In 2022, Greenland’s parliament approved a move from UTC-3 to UTC-2 to balance the time difference with Europe and the United States. The change took effect in March 2023.
However, the decision has remained controversial, with 4,142 residents signing a petition calling for the previous time zone to return.
Opposition parties Naleraq and Siumut proposed reversing the change in May. The government initially opposed the move but supported ending daylight saving time.
Despite the government’s changed position, Greenlandic leader Jens-Frederik Nielsen of Demokraatit, the Democrats party, warned about potential consequences.
He said the change would increase the time difference with Europe by one hour in winter and two hours in summer.
Nielsen argued that reduced overlap with Danish medical specialists could lead to longer patient waiting times.
He also warned of higher costs for businesses, weaker flight connections with Europe and financial expenses associated with changing the time zone.
The proposal is scheduled for a final parliamentary vote October 21.
All trains between Odense and Fredericia replaced by buses after cable fault
All train services between Odense and Fredericia were suspended Tuesday afternoon after a high-voltage cable fell onto the railway’s overhead power lines.
DSB, Denmark’s national rail operator, said trains between Odense and Holmstrup had come to a complete stop.
Rail replacement buses were being arranged between Odense and Fredericia, with the first expected to begin operating at 3 p.m.
Regional trains on the route had already been replaced by buses since Friday following a fire in a signal hut near Aarup in western Funen.
The latest incident also halted InterCity and InterCityLyn services, which had continued operating at reduced speeds following the fire.
DSB said the high-voltage cable fell during work carried out by an outside party.
“Banedanmark has technicians on the way to remove the cable from the overhead wires,” DSB said.
Banedanmark is the state agency responsible for maintaining Denmark’s railway infrastructure.
Even before Tuesday’s disruption, passengers had been warned to expect longer journey times between Odense and Fredericia through Sunday, October 18, because of damage caused by the signal hut fire.
Greenland cancels 39.8 million DKK in benefit repayment claims
Greenland’s government has cancelled repayment claims totaling 39.8 million DKK against more than 19,000 residents who received excessive employment benefits because of government IT errors.
Naalakkersuisut, Greenland’s government, announced Saturday that recipients would not have to return the overpayments from the Suila-tapit program.
Suila-tapit is an employment tax allowance of up to 1,313 DKK a month for workers earning between 70,000 and 500,000 DKK annually.
The program was introduced on January 1, 2025, to encourage employment and reduce economic inequality.
Errors in the Greenlandic Self-Government’s IT systems caused some residents to receive excessive payments during 2025. The government initially demanded that the money be repaid.
“Some citizens were paid too much without having done anything wrong themselves, and that responsibility does not lie with the individual citizen,” Finance Minister Aqqaluaq B. Egede of Inuit Ataqatigiit said.
Residents who have already repaid the money will receive refunds.
“We cannot turn back time, but we can take responsibility and ensure that citizens do not have to pay for the mistakes made in the system,” Egede said.
The repayment demands had faced public opposition. A large demonstration was planned in Nuuk on Saturday but was cancelled shortly after the government announced it would withdraw the claims.
Danish vehicle register remains offline after authorities detect irregularities
Denmark’s Motor Register has been unavailable for almost 24 hours after authorities detected irregularities following a weekend update.
The Danish Motor Agency, which operates the register, temporarily suspended access after identifying the problem.
“At the present time, we cannot say more about the actual error in the Motor Register,” Deputy Director Claus Holm said in a written statement.
According to the register’s operational status, it has been offline since 2:53 p.m. Monday. The agency has not said when access will be restored but said it is working to resolve the issue.
The ownership transfer app Ejerskifte and the temporary permit app Dagsbevis are also unavailable because they rely on the register.
The Motor Register contains information about all vehicles registered in Denmark. It is used for tasks including registering new vehicles and transferring ownership when cars are bought or sold.
Car dealers normally handle registration when customers purchase new vehicles, but they cannot currently complete the process.
Private buyers and sellers are also unable to transfer vehicle ownership through the system.
New owners normally have four business days to complete the required change of registration.
Cyber incident hits contractor building Fehmarn Belt tunnel
A contractor working on the Fehmarn Belt tunnel project at Rødbyhavn has been affected by a cyber incident.
Femern Link Contractors, known as FLC, informed Sund & Bælt, the Danish state-owned company overseeing major transport infrastructure, about the incident.
“We are in dialogue with FLC about the situation, and at the present time we do not have further information,” Sund & Bælt press director Jens Villemoes said in a statement published on the project’s official website.
According to information obtained by Danish newspaper Lolland-Falsters Folketidende, the incident disabled central systems and significantly affected work on the multibillion-kroner construction project.
Sund & Bælt did not provide details about the systems affected, the extent of the disruption or who may have been responsible.
The Fehmarn Belt tunnel will connect Rødbyhavn in Denmark with Puttgarden in Germany.
Once completed, the journey between the two countries is expected to take seven minutes by train and 10 minutes by car.
Construction began on the Danish side in 2020 and on the German side in 2021.
Copenhagen has far more municipal savings per resident than poorer municipalities
Danish municipalities differ significantly in how much readily available money they hold, according to an analysis by CEPOS, a Danish liberal think tank.
Copenhagen Municipality has the largest liquid holdings per resident, with savings equivalent to 31,685 DKK for each person.
At the other end of the ranking are Hjørring, Sorø, Thisted, Lolland and Aalborg municipalities. Their liquid holdings range from 3,127 DKK to 4,354 DKK per resident.
Liquid holdings can be viewed as municipal savings that have not been allocated to a specific purpose. Municipalities typically use the money to manage ongoing incoming and outgoing payments.
CEPOS said municipalities must always maintain a certain level of liquidity to cover their regular financial obligations.
Local authorities may also build up savings to finance future projects.
More than 500 marine mammals stranded along Danish coasts in 2025
A total of 538 marine mammals were recorded as stranded along Denmark’s coasts in 2025, according to a report from the Danish Environmental Protection Agency’s emergency service for stranded marine mammals.
The animals included 363 harbor seals, 38 grey seals and 137 harbor porpoises.
Most were found dead. Of the harbor seals, 310 were dead when discovered, while 136 of the 137 harbor porpoises were found dead.
The report identified disease, parasites, injuries and weakness as possible reasons for the strandings.
One animal from each of the three groups was recorded as having stranded after becoming caught unintentionally in fishing nets.
More unusual marine mammals were also found along the Danish coastline during 2025. These included a humpback whale and a striped dolphin.
Ambulances get deer whistles to avoid hitting animals
Ambulances and emergency medical vehicles in the North Denmark Region will be equipped with wildlife whistles to reduce the risk of collisions with animals.
The small plastic whistles are mounted outside vehicles and produce a high-frequency sound when air passes through them. The sound is intended to frighten animals away from the road.
“Unfortunately, we have a number of collisions with animals when we drive with emergency signals in forests and natural areas,” the region’s Prehospital Services wrote on Facebook.
“It is dangerous for the people in the car, it delays the driving, and is dangerous for the animals.”
The decision comes as Denmark faces a possible record year for deer collisions.
Dyrenes Beskyttelse, Denmark’s largest animal welfare organization, recorded 8,739 deer collisions during the first nine months of 2026. That compares with 7,994 during the same period in 2025.
The previous annual record was 11,870 collisions in 2025.
The risk of encountering deer is particularly high during autumn and around sunrise and sunset.
However, it remains unclear whether wildlife whistles effectively keep animals away from roads.
Two insurance companies previously gave the devices to motorists as part of separate trials. According to FDM, Denmark’s main car owners’ association, the companies could not reach a clear conclusion about whether the whistles reduced collisions.
Red-Green Alliance seeks 100 million DKK to reduce school costs for families
Denmark’s Red-Green Alliance wants 100 million DKK allocated annually to reduce expenses faced by families with children attending public schools.
Although public education is free, families may still pay for activities and services such as school camps and lunches. The party wants to eliminate those charges, beginning with the most economically vulnerable families.
“When we say we have free education, we actually have it, too,” finance spokesperson Victoria Velasquez said.
The Red-Green Alliance will raise the proposal during negotiations on the government’s 2027 national budget.
The initiative is included in the government platform, but the party wants it implemented in the government’s first budget.
The proposed funding would come from a 900 million DKK reserve set aside for measures negotiated with parties supporting the budget agreement.
The party has not decided whether the money should be paid directly to families or distributed through schools.
One option would be to prioritize the 100 schools where pupils have the lowest academic performance.
The Red-Green Alliance has described the proposal as one of its main demands but has not made it an absolute condition for supporting the budget.
Its other demands include free public transport for young people, free dental care for selected groups and a ban on profits from privately operated welfare services.
DSB warns of longer travel times between Odense and Fredericia
Passengers traveling with Denmark’s national rail operator DSB should expect longer journeys between Odense and Fredericia through Sunday, October 18.
All regional trains on the route have been replaced by rail replacement buses, DSB said Monday.
International trains and DSB’s InterCity and InterCityLyn services are operating but must travel at reduced speeds along parts of the route.
The disruption follows a fire Friday in a relay hut near Aarup in western Funen.
A relay hut is a small trackside building containing electronic equipment used by the railway signaling system. The fire caused signal failures between Middelfart and Odense, creating major disruptions on Funen and affecting train services across Denmark.
Train traffic between Odense and Fredericia was also completely suspended in both directions early Monday after a tree fell onto an overhead power line in western Funen, according to Funen Police.
InterCity and InterCityLyn services resumed at about 6 a.m. Monday.
Regional trains in western Funen remain replaced by buses because of the damage caused by Friday’s fire. Passengers should allow additional time for their journeys until normal operations resume.
Copenhagen apartment prices fall as Aarhus reaches new highs
Apartment prices in Copenhagen fell for the second consecutive month in September, while prices in Aarhus rose sharply.
The average sales price for owner-occupied apartments in Copenhagen Municipality declined by 1.0 percent from August to September, according to housing platform Boligsiden. Prices fell by 0.5 percent the previous month.
Boligsiden housing economist Birgit Daetz said it was the largest monthly decline since March 2024.
“Supply has grown significantly in 2026, and now we see a price drop partly as a consequence of more options and lower demand among buyers,” she said.
Despite the recent decreases, Copenhagen apartment prices remain 15.7 percent higher than one year ago. The average price is now 75,414 DKK per square meter.
In Aarhus Municipality, apartment prices rose by 3.7 percent in September, the third-largest monthly increase since records began in 2011.
The average price reached 50,649 DKK per square meter. This means a 100-square-meter apartment in Aarhus costs more than 5 million DKK on average for the first time.
Prices in Aarhus have increased by 23.3 percent over the past year. Nordea housing economist Lise Nytoft Bergmann called the development “extraordinary” but warned that prices would eventually reach a limit.
Nationwide apartment prices were unchanged in September. Prices for houses and holiday homes increased by 0.3 percent overall.

Trump: Greenland deal biggest real estate deal ever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:31:28 UTC
15:31:28 KST

The US president says he “got it for nothing” after signing a new defence agreement with Denmark and Greenland that expands the American military presence on the island.
US President Donald Trump has described a new defence and security agreement with Denmark and Greenland as potentially “the biggest real estate deal that has ever been made”.
Speaking at a Republican campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia, Trump portrayed the agreement as a major achievement for the United States.
“What do you think of the deal I made on Greenland? Got it for nothing,” Trump told supporters.
“It is probably the biggest real estate deal that has ever been made.”
Trump was campaigning ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3.
His comments come after months of tension over Greenland, an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark. Trump has repeatedly said that the United States wants control and ownership of Greenland, arguing that the island is crucial to American national security.
Two new US military bases
The United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a new security and defence agreement on Greenland at the end of September following lengthy negotiations.
The agreement was signed at the United Nations in New York shortly after Trump addressed the UN General Assembly.
It allows the United States to establish two additional military bases in Greenland.
The US currently operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, which plays an important role in missile warning, space surveillance and Arctic security.
The new agreement also opens the possibility of deploying parts of the planned US Golden Dome missile defence system in Greenland. The system is intended to protect the United States against threats including missiles and drones.
Despite Trump’s description of the agreement as a “real estate deal”, it does not transfer ownership of Greenland to the United States.
Trump’s comments came as Republicans campaign to retain control of Congress in the November midterm elections. Democrats are currently polling more strongly in the race for the House of Representatives, while control of the Senate remains more uncertain.
Republicans currently hold majorities in both chambers.
The 21-year-old singer has gone from posting piano videos on TikTok to becoming one of Denmark’s biggest pop stars. On Friday, she received the top prize at DR’s annual P3 Guld music awards.
Danish singer Annika has won P3 Prisen, the main award at one of Denmark’s most prominent annual music events, P3 Guld.
The 21-year-old received the award Friday evening at DR Koncerthuset in Copenhagen, a year after being nominated for the same prize but losing out to Danish band Aphaca.
P3 Guld is the annual music awards show organised by P3, the youth-oriented music and entertainment radio station run by Danish public broadcaster DR.
The event celebrates artists who have made a significant impact on Danish music over the past year, with P3 Prisen regarded as its main award.
Annika, whose full name is Annika Wedderkopp, was selected by a P3 jury ahead of fellow nominees Zar Paulo and producer Anton Westerlin, who is also her boyfriend.
“With an authentic foundation in her own life, Annika creates massive hits about breakups and infatuations, about doubt and a steely belief that everything will naturally work out,” the jury said.
From TikTok to the Danish charts
Annika’s rise has been rapid.
She began by posting videos of herself singing at the piano on TikTok before breaking through with “Knuser hjerter” in 2024.
She followed it with several successful releases, including “Så længe jeg er sexy”, and won P3 Talentet, the event’s talent award, that same year.
Last year, she released her debut album “AW”, which includes “Stolt”, a collaboration with Danish rapper Lamin. She also opened Roskilde Festival’s Orange Stage, the festival’s largest and most prestigious stage.
Previous recipients of P3 Prisen include some of Denmark’s best-known contemporary artists, including The Minds of 99, Tobias Rahim, Artigeardit, Lamin, Tina Dickow and Jada.
Other winners
Several other awards were presented at Friday’s ceremony.
Guldimund and Saveus won P3 Lytterhittet – the listeners’ choice award – for their song “Vil du noget?”.
Zar Paulo received P3 Live, an award recognising an artist who has distinguished themselves on Denmark’s live music scene. The award returned this year after previously being presented in 2001 and 2009.
Danish-Faroese artist Friða Saiya won P3’s Næste, a new award that has replaced P3 Talentet and highlights emerging artists.
Criticism over lack of women
This year’s P3 Guld also faced criticism before the ceremony over the gender balance among its performers.
Twelve men and two women were scheduled to perform during the evening.
Ditte Christiane Jensen, head of editorial at DR Ung, defended the lineup in a written response to Ritzau.
“Talent, creativity and artistic quality are not about gender,” she said.
“This year’s lineup was put together based on the artists and bands that have left a significant mark on the music year and in P3’s universe.”

The US president says he “got it for nothing” after signing a new defence agreement with Denmark and Greenland that expands the American military presence on the island.
US President Donald Trump has described a new defence and security agreement with Denmark and Greenland as potentially “the biggest real estate deal that has ever been made”.
Speaking at a Republican campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia, Trump portrayed the agreement as a major achievement for the United States.
“What do you think of the deal I made on Greenland? Got it for nothing,” Trump told supporters.

Two new US military bases

It allows the United States to establish two additional military bases in Greenland.
The US currently operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, which plays an important role in missile warning, space surveillance and Arctic security.
The new agreement also opens the possibility of deploying parts of the planned US Golden Dome missile defence system in Greenland. The system is intended to protect the United States against threats including missiles and drones.
Despite Trump’s description of the agreement as a “real estate deal”, it does not transfer ownership of Greenland to the United States.
