Hyundai recalls more than 94,000 vehicles in U.S. over fire risk
Hyundai Motor America is recalling more than 94,000 Hyundai and Genesis vehicles in the United States due to a potential fire hazard linked to overheating power seat motors, Qazinform News Agency cites Yonhap.
According to the U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), the recall affects 94,622 vehicles, including certain 2015-2016 Hyundai Genesis and 2017-2020 Genesis G80 models.
The agency said a faulty power seat control switch could become stuck, causing the front power seat motor to overheat and potentially ignite a fire while the vehicle is either parked or in operation.
As a precaution, owners of affected vehicles have been advised to park outdoors and away from buildings or other vehicles until repairs are completed, as the defect increases the risk of fire-related injuries.
Hyundai is currently developing a remedy for the issue. Notification letters are expected to be mailed to affected vehicle owners beginning Dec. 7, according to U.S. transportation authorities.
Earlier, German automaker Volkswagen is recalling 208,724 vehicles in the US due to a steering system defect, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA).

Oregon school shooting: Police praise 'heroism' of those who intervened to stop more killing

Oregon school shooting: Police hail 'heroism' of those who stepped in
October 17, 2026
Police in the northwestern US state of Oregon have identified a teenage gunman who shot dead four people at a school as a former special needs student there, while praising people who stepped in to stop more killings.
Three children aged 5, 8 and 11 lost their lives in Thursday's rampage, along with a 25-year-old female teacher, before the shooter was shot dead by a father of two pupils at the school, located in the town of Bend.
Another young child and a teacher were also injured in the attack.
Who intervened to prevent more deaths in Oregon?
A man in a vehicle outside the school who was shot at and missed by the 16-year-old gunman was the first to alert police to the danger.
Before they arrived, however, a female teacher tackled the shooter after he had already killed the victims with a pump-action 12-gauge shotgun in the school's special needs classroom.
While the two wrestled with each other, a man identified by family as Kaylub Giamanco, a 36-year-old father of two girls at the school, rushed in with his legally held weapon and shot the gunman dead.
"He heard shooting and saw a teacher involved in a physical altercation with the suspect ... and fired his weapon, striking the suspect multiple times," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz told reporters.
"When someone is willing to risk their own life for others, we recognize that. The teacher who is willing to stand and fight for her children ... incredible. That is true heroism, and we don't see that a lot in society," he said.
Praise from Trump as gun control debate revived
Giamanco's mother told the local branch of Fox News that she was "very proud" and that her son was "an absolute hero."
US President Donald Trump also hailed Giamanco's actions.
"It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," he told reporters.
The shooting in Bend has triggered the usual responses from both sides in the everlasting debate about gun control laws in the US.
The National Rifle Association (NRA), one of the main and most powerful opponents of tighter laws on the possession of weapons by civilians, hailed the actions of the armed bystander.
"Yesterday's terrible act of violence in Oregon serves as another reminder of the importance of a law-abiding armed citizenry," the NRA said in a post on X.
Gun control advocates, however, once more condemned the relative ease with which firearms can be procured in the US, which they see as the main factor in the country's high rate of gun-related deaths compared with most other developed countries.
"America's gun violence crisis is killing our babies. Enough is enough," gun-control group GIFFORDS said.
According to an analysis by the education information portal Education Week, there have been 26 shootings at US schools so far this year that have resulted in injuries or deaths.
More than 360 mass shootings have been recorded across the country this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive.
It defines mass shootings as incidents in which at least four people are shot, excluding the shooter.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — National Taiwan University plans to provide financial assistance to students from low- and middle-income households to cover AI service subscriptions, with the program potentially launching next semester.
As AI becomes more widely used in education, students and faculty face the growing cost of subscription-based tools. Academic research also requires substantial computing resources, according to CNA and Ettoday.
At a university meeting, geography professor Chien Shiuh-shen (簡旭伸) raised concerns about unequal access. He noted that students’ ability to pay for advanced services varies, calling for university-wide licenses to ensure all students can access AI tools regardless of their financial circumstances.
In response, NTU President Chen Wen-chang (陳文章) said AI subscriptions cost about NT$8,000 (US$247) per person annually. With approximately 400 students from low- and middle-income households eligible for assistance, the program is expected to require more than NT$3 million a year.
The university plans to cover the cost through financial aid or a sustainability fund supported by donations from alumni and the public, Chen said. It could begin as early as next semester, once implementation guidelines are finalized.
Separately, Vice President Liao Wan-jiun (廖婉君) proposed a university-wide system for purchasing AI software licenses and subscriptions to improve access for faculty and students.
She added that NTU plans to treat computing resources as basic campus infrastructure because of their importance to academic research. Under the proposed system, the university would allocate computing quotas to individuals and research projects.

France braces for tense day of protests as security concerns take centre stage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:00:58 UTC
15:00:58 KST

The French government is stepping up security measures in anticipation of potential clashes during the 17 October nationwide protests over the cost-of-living crisis, which student groups are also set to join.
The French government and security forces are on high alert ahead of major protests scheduled across France on 17 October. Unions and citizens branding themselves as "yellow vests" will take to the streets to denounce the cost-of-living crisis and rising fuel prices, with large numbers of student protestors also expected to join.
According to a source close to France's Interior Ministry, 500 actions are planned across the country on Saturday, alongside 90 estimated protests. The protests follow four weeks of student demonstrations over a range of issues, including teacher absences, overcrowded classrooms and outdated facilities.
Most student protests have been peaceful, but there have been clashes involving rioters and widespread criticism of alleged police brutality and violence.
Ahead of Saturday's protests, authorities are anticipating possible violence in Paris and other major cities. The source told Euronews that the far-left movement could seek to provoke confrontations with law enforcement and attempt to breach security perimeters along protest routes.
The source also warned that blockades of key transportation routes and essential infrastructure would "not be tolerated."
Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron said on Friday that whilst the right to protest "is fully respected," it "must be accompanied by respect for people and property."
"That is why I call for calm and respect: these rights must be preserved," he said.
Mounting scrutiny of police actions
French law enforcement authorities have faced increasing scrutiny in recent weeks amid several allegations of police violence.
In one case, a 15-year-old schoolboy allegedly lost an eye after being struck by a police rubber bullet. In a separate incident, a 14-year-old reportedly lost his hand after picking up a police stun grenade. The circumstances surrounding both cases remain under investigation.
Following the latter case, France suspended the use of certain types of stun grenades.
Yet, in an interview on Friday, France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that the use of stun grenades would be allowed on 17 October should "serious urban violence" occur on the sidelines of demonstrations, whilst cautioning that stun grenades were "never used when things are going well."
Nuñez told France's Senate on Tuesday that 36 investigations into alleged police violence during student protests had been opened. He said that four of these cases related to mutilating injuries and six to significant injuries, whilst the others were related to alleged blows, insults and reported sexual violence.
There has been speculation that the 17 October demonstration could mark the return of the yellow vest grassroots movement, which emerged in 2018 in reaction to a planned government fuel and diesel tax hike.
For months, yellow vest protestors gathered every weekend to block roundabouts, motorways, and fuel depots across the country, with tense police clashes also occurring.
Meanwhile, the French government is grappling with a major public debt crisis as it attempts to pass a budget containing austerity measures through a hung parliament.
Police union lodges complaint against state for 'endangering lives of others'
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said on Thursday that 937 police officers and gendarmes had been injured since the start of the protests. He also reported injuries among 248 students and 149 teaching staff members, which he said was the highest number of injuries ever recorded by France's Education Ministry.
Lecornu warned that the “secondary school student movement” was transforming into a “wave of urban violence."
Meanwhile, Alliance Police Nationale, one of France's largest police unions, announced in a statement on Tuesday that it would lodge a complaint against the state "for endangering the lives of others."
The union denounced what it qualified as "contradictory orders" given to police officers, who have been "exposed to violence and left at the mercy of public hostility" over the course of secondary school protests.
“After the president’s [French President Emmanuel Macron] expressions of empathy towards rioters and emphasis on dialogue, we are now faced with vague instructions, contradictory orders and superficial public statements!"
"The discrepancy between Laurent Nuñez’s public statements and the verbal instructions passed down through the chain of command has become unbearable," the union said.
The hard-left France Unbowed party has been accused by the government and political opponents of encouraging violence and stoking unrest through inflammatory language.
In a speech delivered on 30 September, the party's leader, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, urged his supporters to "stand up to police brutality," adding that "there will be neither forgetting nor forgiveness for anyone."
He later qualified his comments, stating that he backed peaceful protest methods.

Yemen's Houthis claim responsibility for fresh missile strike on Aden airport
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group claimed responsibility after two missiles struck Aden International Airport Friday, saying they had targeted a weapons depot as well as a military command headquarters. The Aden Security Department said a Yemenia Airways flight bound for Cairo had been preparing for takeoff when the attack took place.
Missiles apparently launched by the Iran-aligned Houthi group struck Yemen's Aden International Airport on Friday, while a Saudi-led military coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile headed for the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key Saudi oil hub that allows exports to avoid the Strait of Hormuz.
The coalition said it had also destroyed two cruise missiles over the Red Sea and three drones in Saudi Arabia's Southern and Riyadh regions. It did not identify the attackers.
In Aden in southern Yemen, two missiles landed on the airport grounds, the Aden Security Department said, blaming the Houthis. It said the incident was the second attack on the facility in less than a week.
In a statement attributed to a military source, the Houthis said an attack targeted "the Saudi forces' command headquarters in the Badr camp in Aden province" as well as a weapons depot.
No casualties were reported. A Yemenia Airways flight bound for Cairo was preparing for takeoff when the missiles landed, the security department said.

Yanbu is a key outlet for Saudi oil exports, allowing the kingdom to ship crude to international markets via the Red Sea, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. The vital waterway has been largely throttled by Iran since the US and Israel launched attacks on the country in February.
With regional tensions and security threats raising concerns over the safety of shipping and tighter global energy supplies, Brent crude oil briefly touched $110 a barrel on Friday for the first time since May.
Saudi Civil Defense authorities issued an alert early on Saturday for Abha in southwestern Saudi Arabia near the Yemeni border before sending an all-clear. Earlier they had issued alerts in the Jazan region and the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait, where such warnings have become frequent since fighting resumed last month.
Also early on Saturday, Houthi-affiliated media reported strikes east of Yemen's northwestern city of Saada. The Saudi-led coalition said it had destroyed two ballistic missile launchers in the area.
Fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government has raised fears of a further deterioration in the country's humanitarian crisis. Aid agencies have warned that conditions are worsening rapidly.
The Yemen conflict has become another front as the Iran war has widened into a regional conflict. The Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014 and forced the internationally recognised government south. A Saudi-led intervention began the following year, leading to years of stalemate before a 2022 truce that held until this year.
The Houthis have repeatedly launched missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia since the conflict reignited following a Saudi strike on Sanaa International Airport in July, with the Iran-allied group targeting airports, oil facilities and other infrastructure.
The group has also targeted sites in government-held parts of Yemen in recent days, including Aden airport and the presidential palace in the interim capital.
A spokesperson for the Houthi-run health ministry said on Friday that 124 civilians had been killed and 327 wounded in what he described as "Saudi aggression" since the escalation began on September 3. Reuters could not independently verify the figures.

Palantir patient data tech rejected by many NHS trusts in England
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:00:24 UTC
15:00:24 KST

NHS organisations that care for millions of people in England are rejecting Palantir’s patient data technology, according to freedom of information responses that reveal health bosses believe they can find better or equal alternatives in many cases.
Some health bodies said the £330m federated data platform (FDP) operated by the controversial US company had made it easier to manage waiting lists and has improved surgery scheduling. But, from Gateshead to Truro, others said they were declining to use it or had carried out trials and reverted to old systems. A Suffolk trust said other systems “supercede” the FDP’s functionality, while Greater Manchester’s care board called the Palantir system “duplicative” and “retrograde”.
The responses come as Andy Burnham’s government faces a crunch decision about whether to exercise a break clause in the seven-year NHS-Palantir deal, which was intended to better integrate the health system’s data to improve clinical accuracy and efficiency. Protests against the US firm’s role have also focused on its other contracts with the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security forces. There is also dispute over evidence for the system’s effectiveness and public concern about the involvement in the NHS of a company cofounded by the tech billionaire Peter Thiel, who said in 2023: “The NHS makes people sick.”
According to more than two dozen FOI responses reviewed by the Guardian, 16 trusts and health boards declared they do not use it, following its introduction in March 2024. They include the University hospitals of North Midlands NHS trust, which said it will not use it primarily because “it does not appear to provide functionality over and above what we have already” and Dorset HealthCare university trust said it “will not be adopting or going live with the FDP”. Humber Teaching NHS foundation trust said: “We have no plans to use it.”
Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS foundation trust said it has used the system but it has “not offered significant improvements on local systems”. Avon and Wiltshire mental health partnership NHS trust said it had yet to find an FDP tool that offered significantly more than its existing capabilities and University hospitals Birmingham NHS foundation trust, which cares for more than 2 million people, said it had no plans to use it, citing “limited expected benefit over existing solutions”. The FOIs were gathered by Medact, a health campaign that opposes Palantir’s role in the NHS, and posted to a public transparency website, WhatDoTheyKnow.
Palantir has previously challenged claims that other software could be just as effective, with its senior vice-president, the former Labour MP Tom Watson, saying last week: “If there are companies that can do it, they would have taken part in free and open competition” to run the FDP.
Watson, a Labour peer and former minister alongside Burnham, was appointed as Palantir’s chief lobbyist last month amid a wave of opposition to the Palantir deal. He warned his former colleagues in Labour not to let “mob rule … lead procurement practices”.
But two parliamentary select committees have urged the government to end Palantir’s contract, including the Commons’ science and technology committee. Martin Wrigley, a Liberal Democrat member of the committee, said the NHS boards’ responses “justify what I have been saying for the last year, which is that Palantir’s system is just not that good”.
“Once again we have proven that centrally dictating a solution to the NHS can’t work,” he said. “We have to get back to developing interoperability so each trust has its own software but with a set of standards for how they interact. Palantir are great sales people but they over-promise and under-deliver.”
Dr Rhiannon Mihranian Osborne, a spokesperson for Medact, said the FOIs showed alternatives existed, a safe transition away from Palantir was possible and “the government has no excuse to extend the contract”.
“Instead of outsourcing key NHS functions to big tech companies, the government must back NHS innovation and the highly skilled NHS data professionals who work alongside doctors and nurses to deliver care in the public interest,” she said.
Palantir accused Medact of “slanted analysis” and of “misleading the public”.
“The FDP is, objectively, a successful programme,” a spokesperson said, adding that its purpose was to provide trusts with tools to draw on depending on their existing capabilities and needs. “It is one of just 20% of major government programmes with a green delivery rating, with ministers stating that it ‘is significantly exceeding its benefits forecast and has exceeded every target’.”
It said NHS trusts, including Chelsea and Westminster, Leicester, Northampton, Bath, North Cumbria, Croydon, Great Western, Dorset, Chesterfield, Ashford and St Peters and Norfolk have publicly praised the FDP.
Palantir also points to NHS data that shows trusts using the FDP have carried out 117,000 additional operations and a 14.3% reduction in discharge delays for long-stay patients. NHS England has, however, had to add a caveat to its statistics, making clear it cannot draw conclusions about cause and effect as other variables have not been controlled for.
The government’s national data guardian for health and social care, Dr Nicola Byrne, this week urged ministers to give substantial weight to the “trust factor” when deciding on Palantir’s fate. More than 44,000 people have filed legal objections to their health data being shared with, stored in or used by the FDP. Byrne, a government-appointed watchdog, said there was evidence “a significant number of local organisations” were reluctant to adopt the FDP including due to concerns about Palantir and “a preference for other solutions”.
Sophie Don, the chief executive of Voror, a patient data company that bid unsuccessfully against Palantir, said: “Of course Palantir isn’t the only company that can do this. It doesn’t surprise me that it is making things harder … If NHS staff are choosing not to use it, it’s a clear sign it’s not creating value. There are many home-grown systems that would release much more value to the NHS than the [Palantir] platform.”
A spokesperson for NHS England said: “137 NHS trusts have now reported benefits from the wide range of tools available on the platform – helping staff join-up and improve care for patients, and work more efficiently.”

A Greece for all seasons: my autumn roadtrip through the Peloponnese
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:00:23 UTC
15:00:23 KST

As I drove across the causeway which links the tiny fortress island of Monemvasia to the south-eastern coast of the Peloponnese, the Aegean sparkling on all sides, I recalled a line by Yiannis Ritsos, one of Greece’s greatest 20th-century poets. Ritsos lived in Monemvasia, in a house that is today a museum on a cobble-stretch by the tawny castle walls. A favourite passage goes: “The voyage is neither a leave-taking nor a home-coming – an ethereal bridge …”
The excuse for my trip to the Peloponnese’s deep south – Messinia, the Mani, and Laconia – fell between those two ideas. My mother has roots in the Peloponnese – a sort-of homecoming that I’ve long wanted to explore – and with the summer over and greedy for an adventure to myself, I set out by car, leaving Kalamata, the leafy port city and gateway to the area, on a coastal road circuit.
Autumn in the Peloponnese is another Greece. Forget the Cycladic white and blue; mountain valleys are carpeted in pine forests and wildflowers, a great stretch of green studded with rustic limestone houses. These villages, relieved by the end of a scorching summer, celebrate boisterous harvest festivals for wines, oranges and chestnuts in Laconia, figs in Messinia, and olives near Kalamata. This is the Greece the diaspora yearns for: the chorio – a word that snaps us back to our relatives and Greek rural life, villages where the air is healthy, eating depends on what is grown metres away, and tavernas are alive with locals rather than tourists. In the shoulder season, the weather is cool enough for long walks along the region’s spectacular trails but, at about 25C, is also still good for swimming.
The two-hour drive to Monemvasia began with the Taygetus pass, winding through villages and cliffside tunnels as golden eagles soared above the firs. On the far side of the Taygetus, the road opened to Mystras, an archaeological Byzantine site stacked up its hillside. I climbed to the Paleologian Palace and its chapels, then descended, hungry, to the village of Parori, where Taverna Ores was serving syglino, the local cured pork, and an okra stew. I practised my flimsy Greek with the waitress and her mother, who kept one eye on a television gameshow while stirring the stew pots.
After lunch I stopped at Sparta – site of the ancient city state and modern metropolis. Beneath the Taygetus, in the spectral hush of the olive groves, there is an acropolis, an agora and little else. Yet the air carries something over the ruins, and it’s a short but necessary stop. A statue of Leonidas, hero of Thermopylae, stands facing the new city with the ruins at his back.
This is still the Greece of the Spartans: locals remain fiercely attached to their ancient ancestry. Monemvasia has a thrilling connection: in AD600, a bishop is said to have led the Spartan population to the rock to fortify themselves against invading tribes. Set on to a slope inside the castle walls is a town of tight passages and medieval Orthodox churches. It is a vivid encounter with Byzantine Greek architecture, as well as traces of Venetian trade: the sweet, fortified wine malvasia was once a prized export. Even my guesthouse, Kelia (rooms from €70), began as a monks’ residence on the sea-facing Chryssafitissa Square.
Leaving Monemvasia, I took a detour south for the golden sand dune beaches in Elafonisos. Reaching this island requires taking a 10-minute ferry ride from Pounta. The turquoise waters of Simos beach are deserted in the off-season – a necessary respite before my hour drive north-west to spend a night in Gythio. This working harbour town has neoclassical pastel mansions and waterfront restaurants provisioned by local fishers. Here the Mani begins.
“Victory or death” reads the Maniot banner, above the Spartan motto “With the shield, or on the shield”. The region has a reputation for a conservative way of life that might seem unfashionable in modern Greece, but I find it seductive. The Mani’s beauty comes partly from its insularity. Driving an hour to Vathia, rugged mountains are crowned by labyrinthine stone tower villages that Maniot clans built to protect themselves during periods of vendetta or skirmishes with the Ottomans. Some are now ghost towns. Others have been converted into guesthouses.
But it was in Gerolimenas that a Greek friend suggested I stay for a few nights. The seaside village is an easy base for touring both western and eastern coasts. Along the latter, I hiked to mainland Greece’s southernmost point, Cape Tainaron lighthouse and went for an impromptu dip. The Mani’s water is so gin-clear the boats appear to hover above the surface.
The Akroyiali hotel (doubles from €80 B&B) opened in the 1970s, before most of the region’s roads. It is built on Gerolimenas’s shore, so I dozed to the pulse of waves and chatter from the hotel’s taverna below, where owner Mr Theodorakakis and his family entertained guests.
“The Mani is changing at its own rhythm,” Theodorakakis told me. “This is a special place. We can’t keep hiding from the world.” Most Greeks prefer to visit off-season, he said. “You can actually explore the region without burning. But be careful of the north-eastern wind. It cuts through!”
Leaving Gerolimenas, I drove 30 minutes up the western coastal route, entering the busy town of Areopoli, where I shopped for hand-harvested sea salt and wild oregano. Pretty Limeni and Kardamyli – the home of British writer Patrick Leigh Fermor (who popularised the region) – get the Mani day-trip overspill from Kalamata. Regardless, it’s quieter in autumn. Every hairpin bend opens on to sea views, flowers and limestone.
I was lunching over one such view of a grassy cape when the taverna owner mentioned a woman in the village who knew miralogia. These are wailing Maniot lamentations sung at funerals, which are heard rarely these days. After two days of asking around, I found Kaiti Braimi in a small chapel where she agreed to sing. “In a way, they’re less necessary,” the octogenarian told me. “No more vendettas.”
The haunting rhythms of the miralogia were in mind as I left the Mani to enter Messinia – cutting through Kalamata again, but this time heading west. Here, the villagers were celebrating. Clarinets hummed in taverna gardens at Sunday family parties and relatives joined hands in circles to dance the kalamatianos. Passersby stood and clapped before being dragged in.
On the hour drive from Kalamata to Pylos – which would be my base – the Maniot mountains flattened into lush forests. Wildflowers bloomed on the roadside. Yet in Messinia’s expansive green are traces of ancient civilisations, including the bronze age palace of Nestor, north of Pylos.
My route sidetracked to the Polylimnio waterfalls. You can sidetrack easily in Messinia; there are unspoiled beaches (like Tsapi on the south coast, where mountains tumble into the sea), as well as areas for canyoning, cycling and kayaking. After a small hike, I bathed in clear pools surrounded by pines, alone mostly, apart from an Athenian couple. “We’re here for my birthday,” the man said. “Messinia is the best place in Greece for outdoor activities.” They pointed me to a canyoning trail north of the Bay of Navarino – a tip for my next visit.
That evening in Pylos’s port, only an hour from where I began my voyage in Kalamata, I paused for an ouzo at a kafenion. A group of lads were watching Greece play Germany at football on the television. They wailed their own miralogia with every missed shot, but when the game ended in a win the cafes along the harbour roared.
I thought back on my drive through the Peloponnese’s deep south, a journey that revealed a rural Greece I’d grown up romanticising from family, and believed was slowly disappearing. But not here. In the mountains and shores of Messinia, the Mani and Laconia, I found a Greece for all seasons.

UK sees growing demand for help bridging gap between end of work and start of pension
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:00:22 UTC
15:00:22 KST

Financial firms are reporting growing demand for a product that helps bridge the gap between stopping work and getting your pension.
Sales of retirement annuities have risen sharply during the last couple of years, and now advisers are seeing a fresh surge of interest in what they say is one of the market’s “lesser-known” options.
An annuity is a product that turns an individual’s pension pot into a regular, guaranteed income. The vast majority of people opt for one that provides an income for the rest of their life, called a lifetime annuity.
But more individuals are now buying a version that gives them an income for a set period – such as five or 10 years – and an agreed lump sum at the end. They can then decide what to do with that cash based on their circumstances at the time.
This type of product is called a fixed-term annuity, and the retirement specialist Standard Life says it can be a way to secure a guaranteed income for a set period while giving you the flexibility to review your options later.
After falling out of fashion, annuities have become more popular partly because of higher annuity rates and tax changes, but also because they offer some financial certainty during turbulent times.
On top of that, a fixed-term annuity can give some breathing space if, say, you don’t feel quite ready to sign up to a lifetime annuity or go into drawdown (where you withdraw a portion of your pension savings every year and leave the rest invested).
Standard Life says its data reveals there has been growing customer interest in fixed-term annuities this year, while its rival Canada Life said recently it had experienced a “significant rise in demand” for its version of this product.
So how much income might you get from a fixed-term annuity?
This week Standard Life said a 62-year-old with a £100,000 pension pot could currently get a guaranteed income of about £13,800 a year for five years, and would get a £50,000 lump sum at the end of the term.
This level of income is higher than the full new state pension of £12,548 a year. You get that when you reach state pension age, which has started to rise from 66 and will hit 67 in April 2028.
According to the latest Standard Life research, 62 is, on average, the age when people would like to retire. So someone could use a fixed-term annuity to fund the period between stopping work and getting their state pension, providing some financial certainty.
Nick Flynn at Canada Life says these types of products are resonating with retirees “because they solve real challenges, helping retirees buy time before committing to drawdown or purchasing a lifetime annuity”.
He adds: “Customers are choosing the product to bridge the gap to state pension or defined benefit pension start dates, help fund specific commitments such as mortgage payments or school fees, or stabilise income in the earlier years of retirement.”
Changes to the inheritance tax (IHT) treatment of pensions, announced by Rachel Reeves in the 2024 autumn budget, have helped give annuities a new lease of life.
The then chancellor announced that from April 2027, money left in a defined contribution (AKA money purchase) pension after someone’s death will no longer be exempt from IHT. All private pensions and most workplace schemes are defined contribution.
The changes mean “unused” pension savings could be taxed as part of someone’s estate if they exceed the IHT threshold. Unused funds are money in a pension pot that has not been used to claim an income, such as buying an annuity.
However, the insurer Legal & General says it surveyed 2,000 UK adults aged 50-plus earlier this year, and found misconceptions and confusion about annuities remained “widespread”.
For example, only 35% of respondents correctly identified a lifetime annuity as the retirement option that guaranteed an income for life. Meanwhile, 30% felt that annuities were too difficult to understand.
But L&G says: “Annuities are actually quite simple. They let you exchange some or all of your pension savings for a guaranteed income.”
However, it adds: “They are not right for everyone. Annuities generally cannot be changed once set up or cancelled after the cooling-off period.”
L&G has a myth-busting guide on its website.

The world’s biggest fine jewellery factory: How Pandora aims to make more and pollute less in Vietnam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:58:45 UTC
14:58:45 KST

Pandora invested $150 million (€132mn) in a Vietnam factory, which it says will operate entirely on renewable electricity. The company also switched to using 100% recycled gold and silver in its jewellery production in 2024.
Pandora has opened what it calls the world’s largest fine jewellery crafting facility in Vietnam, expanding production while seeking to reduce its environmental footprint.
The factory in Ho Chi Minh City is expected to employ 7,000 people when fully operational.
It will produce up to 60 million pieces of jewellery a year, increasing the Danish company’s manufacturing capacity by 50%, according to its opening announcement.
The site is Pandora’s fourth factory globally and its first outside Thailand.
"This gives us flexibility to craft all our collections, our assortments in all our materials and crafting techniques," said Pandora CEO Berta de Pablos-Barbier.
The Danish jewellery maker sold 112 million pieces in 2025, equivalent to more than three every second. It describes itself as the world’s largest jewellery brand.
Expanding production, reducing emissions
Pandora invested $150 million (€132mn) in the Vietnam factory, which it says will operate entirely on renewable electricity. The company also switched to using 100% recycled gold and silver in its jewellery production in 2024.
As it increases manufacturing capacity, de Pablos-Barbier said Pandora would continue growing "in a sustainable manner".
Gold is particularly suited to repeated reuse, according to experts.
"In many ways, it is designed for a circular economy. It doesn't oxidise. That's why it's so valuable," said Saleem H. Ali, lead researcher for critical minerals and the inclusive energy transition at the United Nations University.
"We still have the gold from the ancient Egyptians in pretty good shape."
Using recycled metals still requires energy. Refining involves heating and separating metals from other materials to remove impurities.
Pandora’s ambition is to extend renewable electricity use beyond its own operations to suppliers involved in producing its jewellery.
Challenges in a growing jewellery market
Jewellery unit sales are forecast to grow by 4.1% annually between 2025 and 2028 — around four times the rate of clothing, according to The State of Fashion 2026, a report from McKinsey and The Business of Fashion.
Pandora’s rise from a small Copenhagen jewellery shop, founded in 1982, was built around manufacturing in Thailand, which began in 1989. Its charm bracelet, launched in 2000, helped drive international expansion before its Copenhagen stock exchange listing in 2010.
But the growing jewellery market does not guarantee an easy path for Pandora.
Pandora warned in its August 2026 results that US import tariffs would continue to weigh on profitability.
The tariffs affect sales to the United States, Pandora’s largest market, where inflation and economic uncertainty are also weighing on demand for its jewellery.
Past labour disputes have also drawn scrutiny to conditions behind its production. Danish investigative outlet Danwatch reported in 2020 that a Thai labour court had ruled in May 2019 that union activity had contributed to workers’ dismissals at Pandora’s Bangkok factory.
Pandora said the cuts reflected restructuring and employee performance.
As Pandora expands in Vietnam, it remains to be seen whether it can increase production while reducing emissions and protecting workers’ rights.

The chatbot murder guide: AI’s struggle between privacy, reporting violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:50:37 UTC
14:50:37 KST

The chatbot murder guide: AI’s struggle between privacy, reporting violence
The deadly Tumbler Ridge shooting in Canada raises questions about when AI companies should report threats of violence to police, and the potential risks to an individual’s privacy.
For months before carrying out Canada’s deadliest school shooting in almost four decades, Jesse Van Rootselaar was consulting an unlikely adviser on how to perpetrate mass murder.
“In a hallway, indoors, or a crowded classroom, the 870 [Remington shotgun] is brutal … Close quarters is its playground,” OpenAI’s ChatGPT guided the 18-year-old, according to reports.
On February 10, 2026, Van Rootselaar shot his mother and half-brother at home before going to a school in the small British Columbia town of Tumbler Ridge, where he killed another six people – including five students – before taking his own life.
Earlier this week, on October 14, US authorities charged a Washington State man with allegedly conspiring with Van Rootselaar to plan the attack. But the mass shooting incident has raised questions that go beyond the traditional legal understanding of culpability.
The British Columbia government in September filed a civil lawsuit against OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman, accusing them of failing to prevent the incident and claiming they were aware of the conversations that turned deadly. Families of the victims also filed separate lawsuits. OpenAI’s leadership issued a public apology for their failure to notify authorities.
The company has not responded to requests from Al Jazeera for its comments on the lawsuits.
But as the case against OpenAI progresses, it has spurred a familiar debate: Where should a line be drawn between reporting potentially dangerous behaviour and protecting an individual’s privacy?
“The question of whether companies should be required to turn such information over to law enforcement is extraordinarily difficult, particularly if they don’t already screen chats for indications of such types of threats,” United States-based civil liberties lawyer Jenin Younes told Al Jazeera.
“Forcing companies to implement a surveillance system implicates very serious civil liberties concerns, and that’s probably a bridge too far for me,” Younes added.
“On the other hand, AI gives individuals access to types and quantities of information they didn’t have previously that may facilitate the commission of mass casualty events, a concern it’s not easy to dismiss.”
AI’s ability to distinguish thoughts from threats
One of the biggest challenges facing AI companies is determining whether a user expressing violent thoughts actually intends to act on them.
In August, Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, flagged a user to San Francisco police after discovering conversations allegedly threatening its CEO, Dario Amodei.
According to the San Francisco Standard, citing a police report, the user had claimed to possess an AR-15 gun and suggested he had Amodei “in his sights”.
However, when contacted by the newspaper, the man said he was joking and had no intention of carrying out any form of violence. The person was neither charged nor detained, the Standard said.
Fazl Barez, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford specialising in AI safety and governance, said current AI models cannot “reliably” determine whether an interaction with an AI chatbot “is purely hypothetical or is likely to lead to harmful behaviour”.
“Suppose you are a creative writer working on a fictional story and want to explore how a murder plot might unfold. From the context, it may be clear that this is simply a fictional narrative. If the threshold for flagging potentially harmful content is too low, such a writer could be wrongly flagged,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Similarly, consider a graduate student in biology or chemistry studying pathogens that, if misused, could have serious consequences. They might be trying to understand the risks associated with these pathogens and how to mitigate them. Such discussions may be necessary for legitimate research and education. Even when the subject matter is sensitive, they should not automatically be flagged without considering the broader context.”
The researcher said identifying a credible threat may require examining a user’s interactions across multiple conversations, rather than relying on isolated statements.
Barez said someone experiencing intrusive violent thoughts might turn to a chatbot for support, while another person planning an attack may reveal their intentions gradually across several conversations.
“Distinguishing between the two requires careful consideration of context, intent and patterns of behaviour, rather than relying on individual statements alone,” he added.
Chinmayi Sharma, a law professor at Fordham University, said the debate has parallels with the duty imposed on mental health professionals to warn identifiable third parties about credible threats.
However, she said there was a key difference – therapists have professional training, knowledge of their patients and enforceable standards governing their conduct. AI companies do not necessarily have comparable safeguards.
“My concern with AI companies is that right now there’s not a concerted effort to hire mental health professionals, sociologists, individuals that would have the unique expertise on what the indicators of threat are here,” Sharma told Al Jazeera.
“Secondly, licensed professionals are accountable to concrete, legally enforceable standards in their discipline. We don’t have something like that for AI companies.”
The privacy dilemma
The privacy implications extend beyond whether AI companies can accurately identify threats. Millions of people use chatbots to discuss relationships, emotional distress, mental health concerns and deeply personal experiences.
Civil liberties lawyer Younes said many users may not realise how vulnerable those conversations could be to disclosure.
“They often reflect a person’s innermost thoughts, questions, and desires. The majority of people assume that these dialogues will never be viewed by another person,” Younes, president and legal director of the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee, said.
Younes warned that the consequences of greater monitoring could extend well beyond those planning violence.
“If people fear their chats can be turned over to law enforcement simply because they express disturbing thoughts/violent fantasies etc, many will be dissuaded from using them,” she told Al Jazeera.
Younes argued that forcing companies to establish systems for monitoring users and reporting conversations could raise serious constitutional concerns in the US, including protections against unreasonable searches.
Meanwhile, Fordham’s Sharma also raised an issue about who could be disproportionately affected by heavy monitoring by AI chatbots.
“The concern is always there about either intentional or unintentional targeting, because if you have models trained on what we consider dangerous speech, they’re almost always going to reflect biases,” she said. “Certain minorities’ speech is over‑flagged as a threat, while other comparable speech is not.
“Even in a world in which everyone is benevolent, we should still be concerned about disparate outcomes,” she said, warning that machines could reproduce such disparities at scale.
‘Not a licensed therapist’ – When do AI companies become liable to report?
While AI companies may face moral pressure to prevent violence, their legal obligations are less clear, legal experts say.
Bryan Choi, a professor of law at the University of Colorado Boulder, said US law recognises a duty to warn in certain circumstances, including when mental health professionals become aware of imminent threats or when a special relationship exists between parties.
But those principles do not necessarily apply to AI companies.
“Under present case law, it seems unlikely that a company such as OpenAI would be held to have such duties to warn,” Choi told Al Jazeera. “The chatbot is not a licensed therapist. There is no special relationship between the company and the victims.”
Choi said existing negligence and product liability laws could potentially be applied to AI companies, but proving responsibility would present significant challenges.
Finding a balance
Fordham’s Sharma suggested that independent institutions could help establish reporting standards rather than leaving decisions entirely to private companies or requiring immediate disclosure to police.
Such bodies she said could develop procedures for assessing threats and explore ways of sharing only relevant information while protecting users’ identities and other personal details.
Meanwhile, Younes argued that users should, at a minimum, be clearly informed about whether their conversations are monitored and what circumstances could lead to information being shared with law enforcement.
“This is almost certainly an issue that will be wrestled with over the coming years, and I’m not sure anyone knows the solution at this particular point in time,” she said.
“Events that have not yet occurred will likely influence how these policies are shaped.”

Bulgaria offers a true culinary journey in mid-October, bringing together traditional recipes, local producers, folklore and cooking demonstrations. Bulgarians celebrate autumn with Elena dry-cured ham, Smilyan beans, roasted chestnuts and a variety of pumpkin delicacies.
PHOTO facebook.com/elenski.byt
The popular Elena Ham Festival takes place in the town of Elena in northern Bulgaria from October 16 to 18. Visitors can sample a traditional Bulgarian dry-cured pork delicacy made from a hind leg of pork and characteristic of the Elena region.
Locals say the recipe is simple: meat, salt, spices and a little patience. Yet the ham’s distinctive flavour is closely tied to the local climate, traditional curing methods and generations of experience among local producers.
PHOTO BTA
Vegetarian food lovers may be tempted to visit the Rhodope village of Smilyan, home to the traditional Smilyan Bean Festival, held from October 16 to 18.
PHOTO Facebook/ People and traditions - Brezhani
Meanwhile, the village square in Brezhani in southwestern Bulgaria hosts the Brezhani Chestnut Festival. The famous local chestnuts are smaller and have lighter-coloured shells than other varieties, but boast a much sweeter taste. Roasted on the spot, they are served with young wine made from the latest grape harvest.
PHOTO kazanlak.com
The 11th National Walnut Festival will take place this weekend in the centre of Golyamo Dryanovo, a village in the Kazanlak region. The event was first held in 2014 in honour of what was once the oldest walnut tree on the Balkan Peninsula, estimated to be 500 years old and which survived until 1993. A special postage stamp was issued in Bulgaria in 1965 in three print runs in honour of the tree. Today, Golyamo Dryanovo is still home to one of Bulgaria’s largest walnut plantations featuring local varieties, covering an area of more than 2,500 decares (250 hectares).
PHOTO nesebar.bg
The flavours of the sea will take centre stage at the 13th Autumn Fish Festival, “Autumn Shoals”, in Nessebar from October 16 to 18.
PHOTO facebook.com/festivalnazhitenatapitka
To mark World Bread Day and World Food Day on October 16, the town of Strazhitsa is hosting the Wheat Loaf Festival. The event is inspired by The Wheaten Loaf, a popular fairy tale by Angel Karaliychev, a writer born in Strazhitsa.
PHOTO BTA
The Pumpkin Festival is being held for the seventh time in the village of Dalboki, near Stara Zagora in southern Bulgaria. The programme includes a cooking competition, a variety of pumpkin dishes and a tasting of traditional rachel, a sweet pumpkin preserve.
PHOTO BTA
No visit to the town of Radomir, known as the boza capital of Bulgaria, would be complete without sampling this distinctive sweet, fermented drink popular across the Balkans. Located near Sofia, the town will host its 11th Boza Day on October 17, featuring a farmers’ market and a craft fair.
PHOTO visit.varna.bg
Varna is the destination of choice this weekend for lovers of Bulgarian wine. The coastal city is hosting the Urban Wine Fest 2026 on October 16–17, one of a series of events dedicated to Bulgarian wines in the run-up to International Mavrud Day on October 26.

The ‘Maid of Ghent’ has been the city’s symbol for 700 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:48:00 UTC
14:48:00 KST

The ‘Maid of Ghent’ can be seen in various places around the city, but fewer and fewer people are familiar with the figure that has adorned the city’s coat of arms since 1991. “She first appeared as early as the 14th century. She is not a single person, but a symbol. She embodied both the rebellious city and nationalism,” says Nina Uelpenich of Ghent University, who has now delved into her history.
In the city centre, there are several references to the Maid of Ghent. There is the café ‘De Maecht van Ghent’ on the Korenmarkt, the Corn Market. Her image adorns the tower door of the post office building and the base of the statue of Jacob of Artevelde on the Vrijdagmarkt, the Friday Market.
Historian Nina Uelpenich researched the origins of the figure and the meanings it has taken on over the past centuries. “The very first mention dates back as far as the 14th century, in a poem by Boudewijn van der Lore. At that time, the Maid was a symbol of Ghent during a conflict with the Count of Flanders.”
From a figure of the Virgin Mary to a nationalist symbol
The female figure is based on the Virgin Mary. She does not refer to any real person. “Several cities were depicted as a virginal figure. They appear everywhere: in books, during ceremonies – in Ghent and elsewhere.” She is also a popular figure in works of art from that period.
‘Even during the Calvinist period – when idols were destroyed – she endured. She is no longer merely a Catholic symbol.’ When Napoleon came to power, most city maidens lost their significance. ‘In Ghent, however, there was a revival during the 19th century.’
“At the time of Belgium’s formation, the Maid was a symbol of the region’s medieval history. Images began to appear in which she is depicted waving the tricolour. She was the face of the illustrious past that was to shape Belgian identity. She became a nationalist figure.”
The female figure was used on posters advertising the 1913 World Exhibition in Ghent. In this way she also became an international symbol of Belgium during the period between the wars.
“Chosen to tell a particular story”
The Maid lost that significance in the decades that followed. “All sorts of maidens emerged, co-existing side by side: there is a liberal Maid of Ghent, a socialist Maid of Ghent… It really became a popular symbol that could serve any form of identity formation.”
“The Maid of Ghent shows how symbols are used to shape identity. This is not a fixed reality, but a construct. They are chosen and magnified to tell a story.” A story that still resonates today, for since 1991 the Maid has adorned Ghent’s official coat of arms.

Vickrum Digwa's mother Kiran Kaur was jailed for three years in July for assisting an offender
An Indian woman jailed for helping her son after he fatally stabbed an 18-year-old student in Southampton could face deportation to India following her early release from prison, British authorities have indicated.According to new agency PTI, the UK Home Office said it would seek to deport foreign criminals at the earliest opportunity, although it did not refer specifically to Kiran Kaur, 53. Foreign nationals sentenced to at least 12 months in prison are generally considered for deportation, subject to exceptions and legal challenges.Kaur was sentenced to three years in prison in July for assisting an offender by removing the weapon used by her son, Vickrum Digwa, to kill Henry Nowak on December 3, 2025. She is expected to be released early under a government scheme aimed at reducing overcrowding in British prisons.Digwa, 23, was sentenced to life imprisonment in June, with a minimum term of 21 years before he becomes eligible for parole.Both Kaur and her son have been granted permission to challenge their sentences, with their appeals scheduled to be heard by the UK Court of Appeal on November 5.Kirpan argument sparks controversyThe case drew widespread attention after Digwa sought to invoke a religious self-defence argument involving the kirpan, a ceremonial knife that Sikhs are legally permitted to carry in the UK.
During Kaur’s sentencing, Justice William Mousley stressed that the kirpan was a symbol of religious faith and was not intended to be carried for offensive purposes. He said any use of the weapon in self-defence would have to be justified by circumstances involving great seriousness and urgency.The judge also criticised Kaur for removing the weapon rather than challenging her son’s actions and encouraging him to do the right thing.He acknowledged that she had experienced a difficult life in India before marrying and moving to the UK nearly 30 years ago. He said she had acted to protect her son rather than for personal gain and was unlikely to reoffend, while making clear that her actions warranted punishment.British Sikh organisations and parliamentarians subsequently condemned what they described as the misrepresentation of the kirpan, stressing that religious protection did not justify the violence in this case.Police conduct under investigationThe killing also triggered scrutiny of police conduct after body-worn camera footage showed officers handcuffing Nowak following Digwa’s allegations that he had been subjected to racism. Those allegations were subsequently rejected in court.
The Independent Office for Police Conduct is investigating the officers’ handling of the incident amid allegations of “two-tier” policing, referring to claims that different communities were treated unequally.The case has heightened tensions in Southampton and the wider Hampshire and Isle of Wight area.Kaur’s potential deportation remains subject to the applicable immigration process, while the outcome of the appeals against her sentence and Digwa’s life term is awaited.

Iranian, Algerian central banks governors discuss enhancing economic cooperation
TEHRAN- The Governor of the Central Bank of Iran met and held talks with Mohand Bouri, Governor of the Central Bank of Algeria, on the sidelines of the Annual Meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
At the meeting, the two sides discussed and exchanged views on the latest status of monetary, banking, and trade relations between the two countries. Enhancing the level of joint economic cooperation and utilizing mutual capacities to strengthen bilateral trade interactions were among the most important themes of the meeting.
The Governor of the Central Bank of Iran, referring to the historical and political commonalities between Iran and Algeria, emphasized the serious determination of the Islamic Republic of Iran to develop and consolidate economic relations with friendly and brotherly countries.
The Governor of the Central Bank of Algeria, while expressing satisfaction with the meeting, emphasized his country’s readiness to expand economic and banking cooperation with Iran and the need to follow up on mutual agreements in line with the interests of the two nations.
In late December, Saeed Zare’ Haghighi, the head of Iran Trade Center in Algeria, said that Algeria’s infrastructure needs offer significant opportunities for exporting technical and engineering services, making the North African country a largely untapped economic market.
He said Africa — and Algeria in particular — should be seen as a strategic destination for the private sector, noting that limited numbers of commercial counsellors made targeted entry into new markets essential.
He described Algeria as a geopolitically secure country with a strategic location close to Europe, adding that after the decline in Russian energy exports, about 20 percent of Europe’s oil and gas is now supplied by Algeria.
Zare’ Haghighi said Algeria’s foreign currency revenues had risen from around $50 billion to more than $300 billion in recent years, generating a trade surplus of $20 billion to $30 billion and creating broad scope for economic cooperation.
He pointed to strong demand in Algeria for technical and engineering services, infrastructure projects, and the construction of silos and storage facilities linked to food security, saying Iranian companies had the technical know-how and experience to meet these needs.
He also highlighted Algeria’s industrial and mining potential, including steel and phosphate, and said the trade center was ready to identify opportunities, guide exporters and promote participation in specialized exhibitions, drawing on models used by countries such as Turkey that combine trade with on-the-ground investment.

====================================================================================================

She brought Israeli agriculture to the world; October 7 changed everything
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:33:54 UTC
14:33:54 KST

For years, Danielle Abraham worked to bring Israel's agricultural expertise and innovation to countries struggling with water shortages, food insecurity and harsh climate conditions. After October 7, that mission took a new direction. Instead of taking Israeli expertise abroad, she sought to bring it home and put it to work for farmers whose livelihoods had been devastated.
Just days after the Hamas attack, Abraham launched ReGrow Israel, an initiative aimed at rebuilding farms and agricultural infrastructure in communities near the Gaza border. Initially, she envisioned it as a consulting service for farmers, with a team of experts assessing their needs and developing long-term recovery plans. But the reality on the ground was far more urgent. Farmers had been left without tractors, equipment or the infrastructure needed to resume operations. Before planning for the years ahead, they needed help getting their farms running again.
What began as an emergency response in southern Israel has since expanded to farms and communities affected by the war in the north. The initiative supports farmers by providing equipment, restoring infrastructure and bringing in professional expertise and technology, while also working to strengthen Israeli agriculture over the long term.
For this work, Abraham will receive the Nefesh B'Nefesh Sylvan Adams Bonei Zion Prize at a ceremony this coming Sunday, marking Aliyah Day. The event will be broadcast live on ynet. Now in its 12th year, the award recognizes immigrants from English-speaking countries who have made exceptional contributions to Israeli society across a range of fields. Abraham was selected in the Global Impact category.
Abraham's journey began more than 15 years ago in a lecture hall in London. An Oxford University music graduate working at Britain's Home Office, she was 23 when she attended a lecture by Israeli agronomist Yitzhak Abt. Abt, who had helped establish Israel's international agricultural assistance program through MASHAV, the Foreign Ministry's Agency for International Development Cooperation, spoke about immigrating to Israel from South Africa and his work advancing agriculture in Israel and developing countries.
When Abraham returned home from the lecture, she told her family: "When I grow up, I want to be him." The encounter changed the course of her life. Abraham left her job, sold her car and immigrated to Israel in 2010.
Israel was not entirely unfamiliar to her. She had visited during summer vacations as a child and had relatives living in the country. She grew up in a Zionist household, was active in a Zionist youth movement and had visited Israel at 16. At Oxford, she led a Jewish student society and defended Israel in public debates. Still, leaving a sought-after job in London to begin life as a new immigrant in Israel was a leap into the unknown.
'Just for a year'
When Abraham accepted a position at Israel's Foreign Ministry, she had not yet fully committed to building her life in the country. She told everyone back home that she was coming for just one year. "Only after six months did I start saying I was thinking about making aliyah," she recalled. "My family and friends said, 'We knew from the moment you got on the plane.'"
Her parents, she said, never told her what to do and supported whatever decision she made. But there was one moment when they realized she was not coming back. "When I bought a piano for my home, they said, 'Now that you have that, you're not coming back.'"
One of her first challenges in Israel was the language. She would write down unfamiliar words she heard and send text messages to a friend asking what they meant. On weekends, she went to the beach with vocabulary lists from her Hebrew classes and memorized them. She also taped the lists to cabinets in her office. "My vocabulary was mostly agriculture and developing countries," she recalled. "I couldn't order food in a restaurant, but I could talk about irrigation."
At the Foreign Ministry, Abraham joined MASHAV and later served as a senior policy adviser, representing Israel at the United Nations, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) and the German Development Bank. In many ways, she had fulfilled the ambition sparked by Abt's lecture: using Israeli expertise to solve real-world problems around the globe.
In 2017, she began leading Volcani International Partnerships, an organization that draws on Israeli agricultural knowledge and innovation to address challenges such as food security, water scarcity and farming in difficult climate conditions. Agriculture, she explained, is one of the fields in which Israel is a world leader, combining the Zionist vision with practical benefits.
Bringing the expertise home
After October 7, Abraham decided to use the experience, experts and international connections she had accumulated to help Israeli farmers. "When the extent of the destruction in the Gaza border communities became clear, I saw that some countries facing similar situations turn to outside assistance," she said. "I told everyone, 'We have everything right here: researchers, agronomists, innovation and high-tech. We just need to bring it all together.'"
ReGrow Israel began by providing emergency assistance to farmers in communities near Gaza, including replacing agricultural equipment and repairing damaged infrastructure. The initiative later expanded to farms and communities affected by the war in northern Israel.
Since its establishment, it has raised tens of millions of dollars to help rebuild Israeli agriculture. But Abraham said the goal was not simply to repair what was destroyed. She wanted to use the recovery process to build a stronger, more advanced and more resilient agricultural sector.
For Abraham, agriculture is more than an economic industry. It is closely tied to Israel's food security, the livelihoods of residents in outlying regions and the ability to sustain communities along the country's borders. "If agriculture isn't strong there, we won't have communities on the border," she said. Yet she believes Israel still does not sufficiently recognize agriculture as a strategic asset. "I still don't see enough effort being made to use it to strengthen Israel, both at home and abroad."
Despite everything October 7 changed in her life and work, Abraham has no doubts about her decision to immigrate. "Of course," she replied when asked whether she would choose Israel again. "You have to be a little crazy to live here, but you have to believe."
Looking back at the young woman who arrived alone in 2010, barely speaking Hebrew, Abraham sees a quality she is still trying to preserve. "I see a brave young woman with a kind of naivety that's important today. Everything was possible. I wasn't willing to take no for an answer," she said. "That's the spirit I try to hold on to, even as reality changes. We need people with big visions and hope, who make decisions that aren't crazy but are a little courageous, and who start with small things."
Alongside Abraham, several other immigrants will receive the Nefesh B'Nefesh Sylvan Adams Bonei Zion Prize. Naomi Stuchiner, founder of Beit Issie Shapiro, will receive the award in the Community and Non-Profit category; Dr. Philip Klipstein, a senior researcher in science and technology, will be honored in the Science and Medicine category; Rabbanit Chana Henkin, founder and dean of Nishmat, the Jeanie Schottenstein Center for Advanced Torah Study for Women, will receive the Education award; and Ami Baran, president of the Israel Athletics Association and CEO of the Israel Softball Association, will be recognized in the Culture, Arts and Sports category.
Professor Marta Weinstock-Rosin, a neuropharmacologist who developed Exelon, a drug used to treat Alzheimer's disease, will receive the Lifetime Achievement Award. Barak Swarttz, a content creator and founder of GRIT for Good, will receive the Young Leadership Award, while former ambassador Ron Dermer, who served as Israel's ambassador to the United States and strategic affairs minister, will receive a special recognition award.
For Abraham, the honor provides a platform not only for her work but also for Israeli agriculture and for immigrants seeking to find their place in the country. She said she still feels like "a little girl from London who made a small effort." To her, the message behind the award is simple: "You can come here and make a contribution, whether big or small."
In partnership with Nefesh B’Nefesh

Trade unions push for EU law to address menopause at work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:32:41 UTC
14:32:41 KST

The European Trade Union Confederation wants menopause enshrined in EU workplace legislation, as the European Parliament examines the issue and the Commission stops short of proposing a dedicated strategy.
The European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC), which represents 45 million members across 41 European countries, is pushing for menopause to be recognised in EU workplace law, arguing that a lack of support is costing women earnings, career opportunities and pension income.
“Women’s work-related health risks remain largely ignored by the law, which remains orientated around male-dominated jobs,” said ETUC Deputy General Secretary Isabelle Schömann. “It’s high time that the law caught up with the reality of the whole workforce today and the risks facing them.”
The push comes as the European Parliament examines a report calling for menopause to be treated as an economic, employment and social issue, while the European Commission has stopped short of proposing a dedicated EU menopause strategy.
Menopause, which typically occurs between the ages of 45 and 55, affects a significant proportion of the workforce. Around 30% of women experience symptoms that affect their capacity to work, including fatigue, sleep disruption, hot flushes, joint pain, anxiety and difficulties concentrating. Around 85 % of women experience at least one of those symptoms.
Research cited by the confederation found that women's earnings in Norway fell by 7.4% by the fourth year after a menopause diagnosis, with reduced working hours, sick leave and missed promotions contributing to the decline.
“Loss of pay, lost promotions, and lower pensions is the price being paid by millions of women for the failure to adapt work to the menopause,” Schömann said.
Pressure builds for EU action
The campaign comes amid growing recognition of menopause in the EU's gender equality agenda, although concrete workplace protections remain largely a matter for national legislation and employers.
In November 2025, Equality Commissioner Hadja Lahbib said the Commission was not planning a dedicated EU strategy on menopause, while pointing to research projects funded through Horizon 2020 and Horizon Europe addressing its medical and social impacts.
The Commission has since included menopause in its Gender Equality Strategy 2026-2030, published in March. The strategy commits to exchanging national best practices on tackling menstrual and menopause poverty and to a study, planned for 2028, on the economic and societal benefits of closing the women's health gap, including menopause.
The commitments mark a shift towards recognising menopause in the EU's wider equality agenda, but stop short of proposing dedicated legislation setting out workplace rights for menopausal employees.
The European Parliament is seeking to push the issue further. Spanish Socialist MEP Lina Gálvez is leading a draft report titled Menopause beyond a health issue: turning menopause into an economic, working and social priority.
The draft, which will be further discussed at the plenary session only next year, calls for a dedicated EU strategy, broader research, public campaigns to challenge stigma, better workplace support and improved access to healthcare.
“It is therefore essential to have an EU strategy that includes broader and more inclusive EU research, evidence-based public campaigns to change the social perceptions, improved workplace support and improved access to healthcare,” Gálvez wrote in the draft report. “It is time for the EU to tackle menopause.”
The report remains a parliamentary initiative, rather than adopted EU policy.
Unions want changes at work
For the ETUC, the priority is to ensure that menopause is reflected in the way workplaces are organised and regulated.
Its demands include risk assessments covering workplace temperature, ventilation and facilities; flexible hours and remote working; training for managers and human resources staff; and physical adjustments such as temperature controls and ergonomic equipment.
The confederation also wants menopause policies negotiated with trade unions, then implemented and monitored, alongside free menstrual and menopause products at work.
“The way work is organised can make a crucial difference in deciding the impact of the menopause,” Schömann said, adding that unions are already negotiating collective agreements covering workplace adjustments and flexible arrangements.

Lapland airports expect 5–10% passenger growth this winter
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:31:59 EEST
14:31:59 KST

Airports in Finnish Lapland expect passenger numbers to increase by 5–10% during the coming winter season, prompting airport operator Finavia to recruit 20% more seasonal workers and expand facilities to accommodate growing international tourism.
Finavia announced on Wednesday that airline operations at Lapland's airports are forecast to increase by 4–8%, driven by direct international flights and passengers connecting through Helsinki Airport.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The company has spent the year preparing its airports in Rovaniemi, Kittilä, Ivalo and Kuusamo for the winter tourism season, investing in infrastructure, passenger services and staffing.
Finavia opened 120 seasonal positions across the four airports in June, representing a 20% increase from 2025. The recruitment campaign attracted 460 applications, nearly 60% more than the previous year.
The additional employees will more than double Finavia's workforce at the airports during winter. The recruits include returning seasonal workers and people beginning their careers in aviation.
"We believe that tourism in Lapland will continue to grow, which is why we are developing our airports proactively," said Henri Hansson, Finavia's Senior Vice President for the Airport Network.
The company has also introduced measures to manage increasing flight volumes, particularly at Rovaniemi and Kittilä airports.
Both airports adopted international slot coordination during the 2025–2026 winter season. Under the system, an independent coordinator allocates arrival and departure times to airlines according to available airport capacity.
Finavia said the arrangement distributes flights more evenly throughout the day, reducing congestion and allowing airport operators to allocate staff and equipment according to demand.
"Slot coordination has worked well. It spreads air traffic more evenly over different hours of the day, which prevents air traffic congestion," Hansson said.
Infrastructure improvements have also been completed at several airports.
At Rovaniemi Airport, Finavia finished a ground transport development project in September, adding approximately 4,000 square metres of parking space for 130 cars.
The project also reorganised areas used by taxis, buses and private vehicles to improve traffic flow outside the terminal.
Rovaniemi and Kittilä airports have received replacement self-service check-in machines, allowing passengers to complete check-in procedures and print baggage labels.
At Ivalo Airport, Finavia installed self-service baggage drop machines to reduce reliance on staffed counters during peak periods.
The airport operator said maintaining punctuality remains a priority as passenger numbers increase.
According to Finavia's operational data from 2023 to 2026, punctuality at Lapland's airports has generally remained between 98% and 100%, including during periods of heavy snowfall and runway maintenance.
Finavia said Rovaniemi Airport achieved higher operational punctuality during the record-breaking 2025–2026 winter season than in the previous year, despite handling more passengers.
The company also reported maintaining customer satisfaction levels during the period.
Hansson said Finavia intends to continue developing airport infrastructure and operational processes as demand for travel to Lapland increases.
