02:26:33 KST

On an overcast London morning in February 1964, Satmar hassid David Eliahu Brand passed by the Westminster Reform synagogue. Looking for work as a sofer (scribe), Brand took a chance and knocked on the front door. Ruth Shaffer, a native of Warsaw, Poland, and the coordinator for the Westminster synagogue Torah restoration project, answered the door.
Speaking in his native Yiddish, Mr. Brand asked her: “Es gibt Torahs?” Do you have any Torah scrolls that have to be repaired? Ruth replied in the affirmative, but added that the synagogue possessed not just one scroll, but 1,564 Torah scrolls that had been rescued from Czechoslovakia after the war.
After that astounding revelation, Ruth introduced Brand to the synagogue’s spiritual leader, Rabbi Dr. Harold Reinhart. Thus began the most unlikely arrangement between a Satmar hassid and a Reform synagogue that would last for 27 years!
The story begins: Demise of Jewish communities of Czechoslovakia, Moravia and Bohemia: March 15, 1939
On March 15, 1939, Nazi German troops violated the Munich Agreement and marched into the capital city of Prague. This began the official annexation of Czechoslovakia. Wherever German troops entered, the Jewish communities were in danger as well.
Until 1939, the Jewish communities of Czechoslovakia, Moravia and Bohemia numbered over 120,000 Jews and boasted over 350 synagogues, including the famous Maharal synagogue in Prague.
Prague was also the home of the Old-New Synagogue, which was built in the year 1270, and the Pinkas synagogue, built in 1479.
Almost overnight, Jews were stripped of their civic rights, banned from most jobs (including the medical field), and children were expelled from all public schools.
Then, in July 1939, the Nazis established the Central Office of Jewish Emigration in Prague (directed by Adolf Eichmann), thus forcing many to abandon their communities, leaving behind their beautiful synagogues (containing hundreds of Torah scrolls) and houses of study.
The first miracle: Gathering all Torah scrolls and artifacts to the Prague Jewish Museum
The Prague Jewish Museum was built in 1906 and in 1939 was under the directorship of Dr. Karel Stein and curator Alfred Engel. Fearing that the holy and beautiful Torah scrolls in the hundreds of Czech Jewish communities would be totally lost, Stein and Engel asked permission from Nazi authorities to centralize all Jewish ritual objects in Prague in order to protect them from widespread plundering.
Over 1,800 Torah scrolls and 212,000 artifacts were transferred to the museum.
Whether the Nazi intent was merely to amass valuable silver and gold for its treasury or to build a museum to recall an extinct race (once all Jews would be murdered) is a matter of question, but nonetheless all of the Czech Torah scrolls and artifacts were brought to Prague.
There, many Jews were employed to sort, catalogue, and store all the items that arrived from over 100 synagogues in Czechoslovakia, Moravia and Bohemia. Tragically, almost all of the employees were later deported to Terezin and other death camps and perished during the Shoah.
The second miracle: Procurement of the Torah scrolls
Following the end of World War II, the Torah scrolls lay abandoned and unattended for almost 20 years in a damp, moldy warehouse in Prague.
That all changed with a tap on the shoulder in 1963. A British art dealer, Eric Estorick, was approached by a representative of the Czech State Agency to purchase some ritual objects that had been kept in storage. The Czech government, then under Communist rule, was badly in need of money and felt that this was a golden opportunity.
Estorick contacted Ralph Yablon, a British philanthropist and member of the Westminster synagogue in London. Yablon consented to provide the £30,000 necessary for the purchase and shipping of all the Torah scrolls and other religious objects that had been stored away for so long.
Yablon, aware that many of the scrolls were badly in need of repair, contacted his rabbi, Harold F. Reinhart, in order to determine which scrolls were totally unusable and which could be designated for restoration.
Finally, on February 7, 1964, two enormous trucks carrying the 1,800 stained and tightly packed scrolls arrived in London. The original idea was that these Torah scrolls would be repaired and then returned to the communities from which they came.
But soon after their arrival, it was determined that almost all of the former Czech shuls were either destroyed or the communities no longer existed.
The third miracle: Restoration of the 1,800 scrolls
By the early part of 1964, all of the Torah scrolls and hundreds of other religious objects (including 400 wimples or binders) arrived in the Westminster synagogue. That is when the divine hand of God directed David Brand to knock on the door of the synagogue.
As in the book of Shir Hashirim, which says: “the voice of my beloved knocks,” it was a most unlikely but divinely ordained moment. That is when the major work began in order to determine how many of the scrolls could actually be repaired.
Of the total of 1,800 scrolls, Brand, along with other professional scribes, slowly and meticulously determined that hundreds could simply not be repaired-the decades of storage in horrible conditions had made many unusable.
It should be noted that even if one letter of a Torah scroll is written incorrectly or if the ink dries up, the scroll cannot be used at all until repaired. Imagine what happened to the Czech scrolls when they were not used or opened for so long.
The fourth miracle: Founding of the Memorial Scrolls Trust
Of the entire collection of the 1,800 Torah scrolls, 1,564 were deemed to be usable, but then the decision had to be made as to how they would be used and to whom they would be given. In 1964, after several months of meticulous work by the scribal team, Ruth (1910-2006) took over the directorship of the Memorial Scrolls Trust (MST).
Ruth would spend almost 40 years managing, documenting, and distributing the scrolls to communities worldwide. Amazingly, the initial filing and tracking were done on index cards only, and only many years later was the entire system transferred to a digital database.
One of her early decisions was that each scroll would be given to a community or synagogue on permanent loan in order to memorialize the communities from which they came originally. In addition, since the Torah is described as a “tree of life,” the scrolls would be read and would become a living memory for all the communities that were destroyed during the Holocaust.
About six months ago, I contacted the MST to find out more information about the scrolls and where they are today. I was fortunate that Jeffrey Ohrenstein, MST trustee and chairman, wrote back, and so began a series of discussions and amazing stories.
Jeff said the oldest known scroll in the collection is one from the 13th century, and that today about 150 scrolls still remain in the museum in London. Over 1,400 Torah scrolls have been loaned out to communities around the globe, including 1,000 to the US, as well as Israel, Italy, Argentina, Chile, and the UAE (Dubai).
Over the last 62 years, these communities have become part of the ongoing memorial to the former Jewish centers, but they have also transformed the Torah scrolls into living and eternal messengers of all who perished at the hands of the Nazis.
The scrolls are not stored in the holy ark, but are read and celebrated everywhere where they have been adopted.
Like the famous and tragic death of Haninah ben Tradyon (tractate Avodah Zarah 18A), when he is asked by his students what he saw as he was being tortured by the Romans, he replied: “The parchment is burnt, but the letters are flying heavenward.” Those letters, he was saying, are eternal; they can never be destroyed by our enemies.
In the case of the Czech collection, both the scrolls and its holy letters have survived, been lovingly cared for, and preserved for eternity.

Ukraine Has Thousands of Damba Systems Countering Russian Drones. Now Lithuania Will Help Build More
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:07:17 UTC
02:07:17 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Ukraine Has Thousands of Damba Systems Countering Russian Drones. Now Lithuania Will Help Build More
Ukrainian counter-drone technology manufacturer December1 and Lithuanian defense company Pekkla signed a memorandum of understanding in Kyiv on October 14 to establish a joint venture in Lithuania. Production is scheduled to begin in 2027.
The companies have agreed to manufacture the Damba electronic warfare (EW) system, currently produced in Ukraine by December1. The partnership is being developed under the Build with Ukraine program, with support from the Lithuanian government. The finished systems will be supplied to the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
Damba is one of Ukraine’s most widely deployed electronic warfare systems—thousands of units are installed and operational along the front line and across the country, including at critical infrastructure facilities, said December1. The system is capable of countering various types of drones, including FPV drones, reconnaissance UAVs, and Shahed drones, at distances of up to 50 kilometers.
The system features precision jamming tailored to specific types of Russian UAVs and operates as a network rather than a standalone device. It also offers automated response capabilities, a critical capability amid a shortage of qualified electronic warfare specialists.
Other features include directional jamming, a remotely controlled rotating platform, and software updates that allow the system to adapt quickly to emerging threats.
Pekkla will serve as the local partner in Lithuania, overseeing infrastructure, regulatory compliance, and the recruitment of local engineering talent, while December1 will retain responsibility for technical expertise.
“For December1, this is our first experience with a partnership of this kind, and we are pleased that our partner is Lithuania—a major and unwaveringly reliable partner of Ukraine,” said Illia Kabachynskyi, Director of International Development at December1. “Establishing this joint venture will allow us to scale up production and provide Ukraine’s Defense Forces with even more of the equipment they need.”
“This is an important partnership for both Pekkla and our two countries,” said Martinas Andriejavas, CEO of Pekkla. “It will enable Ukraine to obtain the defense equipment it needs, while Lithuania will gain valuable experience, create jobs, and open up new opportunities for development. At the same time, taxpayers’ money will remain within the country. I am confident that this is only the first stage of a long-term partnership.”

Avoiding sanctions, Lebanon revokes Bank Saderat Iran's license
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:07:13 UTC
02:07:13 KST

Breadcrumb
Lebanon's central bank revokes Bank Saderat Iran's licence amid US pressure
Lebanon’s Central Bank has revoked the licence of one of Iran’s largest banks that operated in the country, amid intensifying US pressure on countries to sever financial and commercial ties with Tehran.
Central Bank Governor Karim Souaid told Bloomberg that the decision to revoke Bank Saderat Iran’s licence, taken earlier this week, demonstrates Lebanon’s determination to protect its banking sector from possible US sanctions.
One of Iran’s oldest and largest commercial banks, Bank Saderat operates several branches overseas. In Lebanon, however, it did not operate as a full-scale commercial bank or offer the extensive retail services typically provided by major Lebanese lenders. Its operations were largely confined to facilitating certain financial services linked to specific networks or entities.
Speaking on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund’s annual meetings in Bangkok, Souaid stressed that Lebanon could not afford not to take such measures. He said that while some decisions may be politically sensitive, in an apparent reference to Hezbollah, protecting Lebanon’s banking sector from foreign sanctions must remain a priority.
Limited impact on Lebanon
Financial analyst Mounir Younes said the revocation was unlikely to have a significant impact on Lebanon’s economy or banking sector, as Lebanese banks had historically avoided dealing with Bank Saderat because of the sanctions imposed on Iran.
"The impact on the local market and the Lebanese banking sector is close to zero," Younes told The New Arab. "Historically, including during the tenure of former central bank governor Riad Salameh and throughout successive rounds of sanctions, the Lebanese banking sector avoided any dealings with Bank Saderat Iran. The same was true of Lebanese customers, speaking of the wider public."
He said the bank’s customers in Lebanon were likely limited to a small number of people or entities with links to Hezbollah, the Iranian embassy in Beirut or the Iranian community in Lebanon, including both security personnel and civilians.
"The impact is therefore extremely limited on this small segment, which is the one targeted by US sanctions. The effect on the Lebanese economy and banking sector is consequently close to zero," he added.
Younes said any impact would be confined to the relatively few individuals or entities that dealt with the bank, whether through trade credits between Lebanon and Iran or transfers designed to circumvent US sanctions. He added that Bank Saderat did not have correspondent banking relationships outside Iran, with its only correspondent bank based inside the country.
Slow pace of reforms
Souaid also stressed the need for Lebanon to secure its removal from the Financial Action Task Force's (FATF) grey list, saying illicit funds and money-laundering operations must be rooted out of the Lebanese economy.
He added that the central bank had hired a specialised US firm to map Lebanon’s cash economy and identify suspicious financial activity, according to the governor.
A cash economy has flourished in Lebanon since the 2019 financial collapse, and the country remains on the FATF grey list and an EU list of jurisdictions with strategic deficiencies in anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing measures.
The seven-year financial crisis has seen the banking sector collapse and the local currency lose more than 95 percent of its value, locking millions of depositors out of their accounts.
Legislation to restructure the banking sector and unlock deposits has slowly been passed. Talks with the International Monetary Fund to secure a support package have been conditional on the country cracking down on illicit financial activity and passing sweeping reforms, which the government has promised to deliver.
But major hurdles remain, with the country’s ruling political and banking elite widely seen as resisting reforms that could undermine their influence or leave them liable for the cost of restructuring.
Revoking the licence of Bank Saderat Iran in Lebanon came following similar steps taken by other countries in the region. Last month, Turkey’s banking regulator revoked the operating licence of Bank Mellat’s Istanbul branch, while the UAE Central Bank barred all branches of Bank Melli Iran from conducting financial transactions to or from Iran, including transfers and trade finance.
Questions over legal status of Al-Qard al-Hassan
Beirut has also been under pressure from Washington to take action against institutions linked to Iran-backed Hezbollah, including the group’s financial arm, Al-Qard al-Hassan. In July last year, the Lebanese central bank issued a directive banning financial institutions from dealing with the association.
Washington has continued to pressure Beirut to shut down the institution.
Operating outside Lebanon’s formal banking sector, Al-Qard al-Hassan provides interest-free Islamic loans, often secured against gold. Critics have accused it of functioning as a shadow bank for Hezbollah, with some calling for its closure or integration into the regulated financial system. Human Rights Watch noted in October 2024 that the association provided collateralised loans despite lacking a central-bank licence to operate as a financial institution.
Younes said that, although Lebanon’s Justice Minister Adel Nassar had asked the public prosecutor at the Court of Cassation to open an investigation into Al-Qard al-Hassan, the judiciary was still waiting for information from the central bank.
"The Public Prosecution at the Court of Cassation says it is waiting for information from the central bank," he said. "For an investigation to be opened, the central bank would need to file a complaint or provide information indicating that Al-Qard al-Hassan is violating Lebanon’s banking regulations or the rules governing the sector’s operations."
Younes said that because Al-Qard al-Hassan accepts deposits and provides loans, its activities could be considered banking operations. The judiciary therefore needs information from the central bank indicating that the association is breaching banking regulations or compliance standards on combating money laundering and terrorist financing.
He added that the central bank considers the question of Al-Qard al-Hassan’s licensing to fall under the responsibility of the Interior Ministry, which granted the association its licence as a charitable organisation.
He also pointed to the role of the Special Investigation Commission at Lebanon’s central bank, which is responsible for investigating suspected money laundering and terrorist financing. However, he said, the commission had not taken action in the matter so far, to his knowledge.
Hezbollah has been significantly weakened by three years of conflict with Israel, with its weapons stockpile degraded and many of its financial and military supply routes disrupted. The US Treasury has imposed extensive sanctions on the group, and individuals it says are linked to it.
Despite this, Hezbollah has refused to disarm while Israel continues to occupy parts of southern Lebanon and carry out strikes and demolitions, despite a June framework agreement between Beirut and Tel Aviv.

The survey shows Bolsonaro holding 46.8% of overall voter preferences compared to 45.9% for Lula. When calculating valid votes, -excluding blank, spoiled, and undecided ballots-, Bolsonaro leads Lula by 50.5% to 49.5%.

As the race enters its final stretch, Bolsonaro is working to consolidate his father’s conservative base while broadening his appeal. Lula, seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, is heavily targeting the more than 33 million registered voters who abstained in the first round.
To rally support, the ruling Workers' Party achieved a major legislative victory on Wednesday as Congress approved a constitutional amendment abolishing Brazil's six-day workweek, a flagship Lula campaign pledge. The reform replaces the traditional "6x1" schedule (six workdays followed by one day off) with a five-day workweek, gradually lowering maximum weekly hours from 44 to 40 without salary reductions.
The proposal passed the Senate overwhelmingly by a 75-1 vote. Recognizing the measure's widespread popular appeal, Bolsonaro reversed his initial opposition and ultimately voted in favor of the amendment.
The labor reform anchors a series of late-campaign economic initiatives by the Lula administration, including a debt forgiveness program for micro-entrepreneurs, a college scholarship fund, fuel tax eliminations, and a proposal for a free public transit pass.

“The Whisperer” comes to Iranian bookstores
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

“The Whisperer” comes to Iranian bookstores
TEHRAN- A Persian translation of Italian writer Donato Carrisi’s debut novel “The Whisperer” has recently been published by Vazn-e Donya Publications in Tehran.
The book has been translated into Persian by Azam Rasouli.
“The Whisperer” is a psychological crime thriller that combines a disturbing series of disappearances with an increasingly complex investigation into the nature of evil. Originally published in Italian as “Il suggeritore” in 2009, the book became an international bestseller and was translated into numerous languages.
The book begins with the discovery of six severed arms buried in a forest clearing, setting off a chilling investigation. Arranged in a mysterious circle, five of the arms are believed to belong to young girls who have disappeared. The sixth victim remains unidentified, and investigators have no bodies to establish whether the missing children are alive or dead.
The case brings together Mila Vasquez, a police investigator with a particular talent for locating missing children, and Dr. Goran Gavila, a distinguished criminologist who leads the investigative team. Although their personalities and approaches differ, they must work together to uncover the truth behind the gruesome discovery.
The investigators initially believe they have identified the perpetrator, whom they associate with the name “Albert.” However, the apparent solution quickly begins to unravel. Evidence connects the suspect to the first disappearance but fails to establish his involvement in the subsequent cases. Clues surrounding another missing girl point in a different direction, raising the possibility that the team has misunderstood the crimes or that someone is deliberately manipulating the investigation.
As the case develops, the detectives confront a succession of disturbing discoveries and apparent contradictions. The possibility of a copycat killer further complicates their efforts, while the investigation exposes weaknesses within the team and places increasing pressure on its members. Vasquez and Gavila must reconsider their assumptions repeatedly as they attempt to understand the logic behind the crimes.
The search becomes more than a conventional hunt for a serial killer. It turns into a psychological contest in which the investigators must determine who is controlling the flow of evidence and why the truth remains so difficult to grasp. Their professional partnership is tested as the danger intensifies, and their personal vulnerabilities become increasingly relevant to the case.
The novel builds toward a series of revelations that challenge the investigators’ understanding of the crimes. Carrisi uses misdirection and shifting perspectives to keep readers uncertain about the identity, motives and methods of the person behind the disappearances.
The book received significant recognition in Italy, winning the 2009 Premio Bancarella. It also earned international recognition and was translated into multiple languages, establishing Carrisi as a prominent writer of crime fiction.
“The Whisperer” is the first novel featuring Mila Vasquez, a character who returns in later books, including “The Lost Girls of Rome” and “The Game of the Whisperer”. Its success helped establish a series that explores disappearances, criminal psychology and the darker aspects of human behavior.
Critics have praised the novel’s intricate plotting, unsettling atmosphere and repeated reversals of expectation, although some have found its elaborate twists excessive. Rather than relying solely on the mystery of identifying a killer, Carrisi builds suspense around the possibility that the investigation itself is being manipulated. The result is a dark, layered thriller that examines the difficulty of distinguishing evidence from deception and understanding the motives behind apparently incomprehensible crimes.
Born in Martina Franca, southern Italy, in 1973, Donato Carrisi studied law before specializing in criminology and behavioral sciences. He worked as a television screenwriter before making his literary debut with “The Whisperer”. His academic background informs the novel’s detailed treatment of criminal investigation and psychological behavior.

Beijing’s mediating power in international crises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:04:41 UTC
02:04:41 KST

Beijing’s mediating power in international crises
TEHRAN – In the new international order, the concept of “power” is no longer defined solely by the number of nuclear warheads, overseas military bases, or classical security alliances; rather, the new geometry of global power is shaped by the capacity of supply chains, currency exchanges, infrastructure investments, and economic interdependence.
Within this novel framework, China has managed to elevate its position from a mere trading power in the late twentieth century to a “structural actor in international crisis management”—an actor whose primary tools for intervening in crises are not missiles and sanctions, but economic integration and financial leverage.
The defining distinction of China’s approach to international crises is rooted in the theory of “developmental peace” as opposed to Western “liberal peace.” Beijing believes that the primary root of many geopolitical conflicts and security instabilities in the Middle East, Africa, and Central Asia lies not in a vacuum of Western democracy, but in poverty, a deficit of infrastructural development, and a lack of connection to global markets. Therefore, Beijing utilizes initiatives such as the Belt and Road and strategic energy partnerships as efficient tools to contain security shocks. When countries share tangible, mutual economic interests in the continuity of joint projects, the cost of escalating tensions and war increases dramatically for them.
A concrete and successful example of this strategy can be seen in Beijing’s historic mediation between Tehran and Riyadh. Leveraging its immense weight as the largest buyer of Persian Gulf energy and the primary trading partner of both countries, China provided an economic-strategic platform for a political agreement without the need for ideological alignments. This model demonstrated that Beijing’s crisis management levers are built on a commitment to mutual interests and non-interference in internal affairs—a factor that has made Beijing’s model attractive and acceptable among the countries of the Global South.
Furthermore, in complex crises such as the war in Ukraine or tensions surrounding maritime security, China has managed—by relying on its position as a core commodity buyer—to prevent devastating fractures in the global energy and food markets. China’s policy is to maintain a balance between trade with Russia while simultaneously safeguarding Western markets; a strategy that prevents the deepening of acute international deadlocks and the uncontrolled spread of crises into the global economy.
Ultimately, Beijing has demonstrated that economic power is not merely a source of wealth, but a decisive lever for containing shocks and moderating geopolitical behavior. Although China’s cautious policy and avoidance of direct security guarantees may appear to limit its role in certain acute crises, an undeniable reality remains: in the current post-hegemonic world, no major international crisis can be managed, sustainably resolved, or contained without considering Beijing’s capacities, considerations, and economic levers.
Mahdi Zolfaghari is an Associate Professor at the Department of Asian Studies in Allameh Tabataba’i University

In a statement on Thursday evening carried by Syria’s state-run news agency, a government source said the Druze community in Suweida "has been and will remain an integral part of the national fabric of the Syrian Arab Republic," rejecting what it described as attempts to draw the community into Israeli political campaigning.
The statement came after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Thursday that he had spoken by phone with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa during the violence in Suweida in July 2025.
Addressing an election campaign gathering of Druze citizens in the northern Israeli town of Yarka, Netanyahu described the call as "short and very sharp" and claimed he had helped stop a massacre.
"We took down the Ministry of Defense [headquarters] in Damascus, just like that, it’s gone. We struck inside the [Presidential] Palace compound, and I made a phone call to Sharaa. It was a very brief, very sharp conversation, and the massacre stopped," Netanyahu said.
Damascus has neither confirmed nor denied that the call took place.
The Syrian government source said Israel had played a "major and deliberate role" in undermining civil peace in Suweida in July 2025, accusing it of arming an outlawed militia to foment unrest and create a pretext for drawing Syria into a wider war. The source also said the government had thwarted those efforts and was monitoring what it described as continued Israeli attempts to destabilise the province.
The source said US mediation had led to a halt in Israeli airstrikes in July 2025, which it claimed had prevented the Syrian government from intervening to end the clashes between Druze and Bedouin groups.
It also said Damascus was continuing to work with the United States and Jordan to implement a joint roadmap for Suweida, aimed at reintegrating the province under a national framework that safeguards residents’ rights and promotes security and stability.
In September 2025, Syria, Jordan and the United States announced the roadmap, which included commitments to rebuild trust, promote community reconciliation, investigate violations and hold those responsible to account, as well as facilitate humanitarian aid and restore essential services. It remains unclear how far these commitments have been implemented.
A ceasefire has been in place in Suweida since July 2025, following deadly clashes that began between Bedouin tribes and Druze groups before escalating with the intervention of government forces and tribal fighters who arrived in the province to support the Bedouin side.
The fighting involved grave human rights abuses against Druze civilians, including summary executions, according to reports documenting the violence.
A Syrian investigative committee said in March that 1,760 people from all sides had been killed and 2,188 injured. Other monitoring groups have reported higher death tolls.
Suweida remains largely outside central government control. Some factions aligned with Druze spiritual leader Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri have called for Israeli protection or closer ties with Israel, while other Druze religious figures, activists and armed groups have rejected Israeli intervention and called for the province to remain part of a unified Syria.
Israel currently occupies parts of southwestern Syria, which Israeli forces stormed in December 2024 following the collapse of Bashar al-Assad’s regime. Damascus has repeatedly called on Israel to withdraw from these territories and return to the 1974 disengagement agreement.
The Israeli-occupied Syrian Golan Heights are also home to a Druze community. Israel has occupied the territory since 1967 and later annexed it, a move recognised by the United States and Colombia but rejected by most of the international community.
Syria is emerging from a brutal 14-year civil war, and the new government has struggled to reassert central authority across the country amid continuing security, social and economic challenges.

Caught in an imbroglio, Trump resorts to more blatant lies and misleading claims
TEHRAN – Donald Trump appears to be losing his grip on reality as the November 3 congressional midterm elections approach.
Aware that high fuel prices resulting from his war on Iran have put his Republican Party’s control of Congress in jeopardy, Trump seems increasingly desperate to shift the blame. One day, he blames Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for high diesel prices; the next, he seeks to mislead Americans by claiming that “Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin in our new and beautiful Greenland.”
Meanwhile, his administration has reportedly leaked information that the United States is considering using the “mother of all bombs” against Iran’s energy infrastructure and other facilities, apparently under the illusion that such threats could force Tehran to surrender to Washington’s maximalist demands.
The relatively easy abduction of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro appeared to had emboldened Trump to launch a war against Iran, with Israel taking part. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had long urged Washington to attack Iran, including during Trump’s first presidential term, which began in January 2017. This was despite Trump’s populist rhetoric and his repeated criticism of America’s involvement in “endless wars.”
Trump apparently labored under the illusion that projecting military power through aircraft carriers and advanced fighter jets would force Iran to capitulate to his unlawful demands. Now, 232 days into the war, Trump and his inner circle appear to have fully realized that Iran is a formidable adversary that cannot be brought to its knees.
“The war in Iran has significantly tarnished the global aura of U.S. airpower. It is unlikely that the Trump administration would have launched Operation Epic Fury if it had known that seven months later it would still be facing an inconclusive slugging match—one that has wasted a huge part of Washington’s complex munitions stockpile and come at exorbitant economic and geopolitical cost,” Justin Bronk, a senior research fellow for airpower and technology at the Royal United Services Institute, wrote in Foreign Affairs on October 13.
Iran’s resilience and retaliation against the unprovoked and illegal war have damaged the United States’ international standing. Iran’s performance has also forced Washington’s European and Asian allies to reassess their perceptions of American military power.
Bronk also wrote: “For months, Iran’s resilience in its war with two of the world’s most capable militaries has perplexed many politicians and confounded public expectations… Yet the Islamic Republic has not only survived but continued to maintain significant offensive capabilities.”
Against this backdrop, Trump’s attempt to blame Ukraine, which has targeted Russian oil refineries, for rising gasoline prices amounts to a distortion of the broader facts. The disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, following the U.S.-Israeli aggression and Iran’s response, has become a major factor driving uncertainty in global energy markets. The strategic waterway normally carries roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil supply, making any disruption to maritime traffic there a serious threat to global energy security.
Although fuel prices are influenced by several factors, including supply and demand, sanctions, and geopolitical tensions, the impact of the war on Iran cannot simply be ignored. Russia’s oil and gas sector has also faced extensive Western sanctions since Moscow launched war on Ukraine in February 2022. Blaming Kyiv for rising fuel prices while overlooking the consequences of the war on Iran is therefore a misleading way to explain the pressures facing American consumers.
Greenland has also contradicted Trump’s claim that massive oil and gas exploration is about to begin there.
“There are many smaller explorations underway but these could take years to become operational,” Greenland’s deputy mining minister, Jørgen Hammeken-Holm, told CNN.
His remarks highlight the gap between Trump’s ambitious claims and the practical realities of resource exploration. Even when oil, gas, and mineral deposits are present, turning them into commercially viable projects can take years and requires substantial investment and infrastructure. Presenting such developments as imminent achievements risks creating expectations that the available evidence does not support.
Trump’s misleading statements are unlikely to convince all American voters that his war on Iran has nothing to do with their economic difficulties. As households struggle with rising fuel costs, many will want concrete answers about the causes of these increases and the administration’s plans to address them. Blaming foreign leaders and promoting unfulfilled promises will not necessarily shield the president from public criticism.
With every passing day leading up to November 3, Americans and people around the world may hear increasingly dramatic statements and claims from Trump. As the election approaches, the president has a strong political incentive to divert attention from the war’s costs and portray his administration as being in control. Yet repeated assertions that conflict with the available evidence could further undermine his credibility.
As the war’s objectives become increasingly difficult to achieve, some media outlets and analysts have also raised concerns about the possibility of further escalation, including the specter of nuclear war. In an interview with Newsmax broadcast on Thursday evening, Trump sought to dismiss the need for nuclear weapons, saying, “I wouldn’t use nuclear. We don’t have to.”
All these developments suggest that Trump is caught in an increasingly difficult situation. The war has imposed economic and geopolitical costs on the United States, challenged its military reputation, and created serious political risks for his administration. If these problems persist through the November midterm elections, Republicans could lose control of Congress, weakening Trump’s ability to advance his domestic agenda.
The consequences could extend well beyond the current election cycle. A prolonged war without a clear political settlement could damage the Republican Party’s credibility for years, particularly if voters conclude that Trump led the country into a costly conflict without a realistic plan for achieving its objectives or bringing it to an end.

Israeli firm weaponized online ads to hack targets, spy on hundreds of millions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:03:50 UTC
02:03:50 KST

Israeli firm weaponized online ads to hack targets, spy on hundreds of millions
TEHRAN — An Israeli advertising company turned the banner ad into a hacking tool, and for at least two years the companies running the world’s ad platforms failed to stop it.
Two investigations published October 15, by Citizen Lab at the University of Toronto and the New York security firm Confiant, describe how Discover-Tech, founded in 2020, let surveillance vendors identify internet users and infect chosen ones without a single click.
The company’s platform, Controlium, profiled users in bulk and stripped away their anonymity. Citizen Lab calls the technique AdFection. A person opens a website or app, and dozens of firms bid in milliseconds for the ad slot. If Discover-Tech wins, it learns who is looking. If that person is on a client’s list, spyware can follow within seconds.
The ads sold phones, earbuds, games and telecom plans. Nothing about them looked wrong. They only had to load.
Citizen Lab examined roughly four billion ad records and found Discover-Tech material on more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps.
Confiant counted at least 10 million ads a day. Through cookie matching, its cofounder Jerome Dangu said, the firm could track people beyond its own ads. “Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech,” he said.
Al Jazeera in the crosshairs
The best-documented victims worked for Al Jazeera. Between 2024 and 2025, 45 Windows computers at the Qatari broadcaster were infected with spyware from Candiru, the Israeli vendor the U.S. Commerce Department blacklisted in 2021 over its use against officials, journalists, activists and academics.
Al Jazeera’s own technicians had spotted strange activity and brought in Citizen Lab, which confirmed the attack from the network’s logs.
The implant can read files, emails and messages, log keystrokes, take screenshots and switch on microphones and cameras. It is understood to have cost several million dollars.
Al Jazeera called it an assault on press freedom and demanded accountability. It has been here before. In 2020, Citizen Lab found that 36 phones belonging to the network’s journalists and executives had been hacked with Pegasus, made by another Israeli firm, NSO Group.
A whole population under watch
Dangu said the Palestinian territories were especially saturated. Almost any site there carried a Discover-Tech ad, he said, giving the firm “a very complete visibility on the digital activities of an entire country.”
Israel already controls movement, borders and much of daily life in the occupied territories. This added a layer inside the browser.
The same ads appeared in networks tied to the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, the United Nations, NATO, the European Commission and more than a dozen national governments, along with chipmakers such as Nvidia, Broadcom and Micron.
They also reached the International Criminal Court, which issued arrest warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant in 2024.
Platforms act late
Google says it removed Discover-Tech “for systematically violating our policies.” Europe’s Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB) suspended the firm last week after an audit, and Comcast’s Beeswax dropped it.
Yandex did not comment. Discover-Tech and Candiru’s owners did not answer Reuters. Confiant noted that ads it tied to Candiru were a tiny fraction of the volume.
Citizen Lab’s Wolfie Christl called it disastrous that major vendors missed the operation for years, and urged U.S. and European regulators to investigate.
Candiru has been on a U.S. blacklist for five years. The pipeline that carried its code ran through American-owned platforms until outside researchers forced the issue.

Two years after Sinwar’s martyrdom, Palestinian factions vow to continue his path

Israel assassinated Sheikh Ahmed Yassin in 2004 and his successor Abdel Aziz al-Rantisi weeks later, and Hamas went on to win the 2006 elections.
Two years after Sinwar’s death, Hamas reiterated that the sacrifices borne by the Palestinian people are part of a historical struggle against foreign occupation, maintaining that true liberation requires facing the full weight of Israeli aggression with unyielding resistance.

Gaza Health Ministry counts over 74,300 killed and over 175,000 wounded since October 2023, including at least 1,481 killed since the October 2025 truce.

The end of Saudi Arabia’s Yemen 'containment strategy'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:02:45 UTC
02:02:45 KST

The end of Saudi Arabia’s Yemen 'containment strategy'
Saudi Arabia’s bid to “contain” the Ansarallah in Yemen while doubling down on economic growth at home is collapsing, posing one of the most serious tests for Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman since he rose to power, according to analysts and diplomats.
A decade ago, the crown prince led the kingdom into a war aimed at ousting the Ansarallah from power. The conflict turned into a quagmire for Saudi Arabia, sapping its resources and sparking widespread backlash due to its devastating bombing campaign. In the end, Saudi Arabia cut its losses and maintained an uneasy truce with the Ansarallah since 2022.
“This is the collapse of Saudi Arabia’s containment strategy,” Rob Geist Pinfold, an international security expert at King's College London, told Middle East Eye.
“The way Saudi Arabia approached the Houthis (Ansarallah) in the last few years was not dissimilar to how Israel treated Hamas in Gaza before 7 October [2023]. The Saudis felt they had the Houthis where they needed them. They weren’t at the stage to reach a political solution, but they felt they had disincentivized them from escalating again.”
The conflict erupted again after Saudi Arabia bombed Sanaa airport in July to prevent a plane carrying Ansarallah officials from landing.
The Ansarallah declared a blockade against Saudi shipping as a result, and launched a lightning offensive down the Red Sea coast last month, which the kingdom and its Yemeni allies have struggled to counter.
Unlike the last time a full-scale war raged in Yemen, Saudi Arabia now has more to lose from a widening of the conflict, and the Ansarallah have become more sophisticated adversaries, experts say.
Saudi Arabia faced Ansarallah missile and drone attacks during the last round of fighting, but they were nowhere near as precise as this time.
In the last week alone, the Ansarallah struck Riyadh’s international airport three days in a row. A strike on Oct. 10 killed at least 13 people and injured 300. The group’s targeting capabilities were underscored again on Oct. 13 when they hit the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s state oil giant, Aramco, in the eastern city of Dhahran.
The strikes have caused some to question the capabilities of Saudi Arabia’s military.
The kingdom is a major buyer of American weaponry, including Patriot and THAAD air defense systems. According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, the kingdom spends 6.5 percent of its GDP on military gear, one of the highest ratios in the world.
“It’s quite striking, literally, that the Houthis can hit, at will, these incredibly important facilities in Saudi Arabia and the Saudis can’t defend them,” Gregory Gause, an expert on the Persian Gulf at the Middle East Institute, told MEE.
“They clearly have much better missiles and targeting technology than they did before,” he said.
A Western defense official in Riyadh told MEE that Saudi Arabia is absorbing the vast majority of missiles and drones fired at it, saying the number is likely in the low 90 percent range. But the Ansarallah are more skilled at penetrating the kingdom’s air defenses.
“The Houthis are a lot more effective than Iran was back in February. They learned from earlier this year,” the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity. “It is a combination of innovation, rapid speed and the latest intelligence,” the official said.

The illusion of victory over Iran
In an article, Donya-e-Eqtesad discussed what it described as Washington’s illusion of victory over Iran. Citing international affairs analyst Farid Zakaria, the newspaper argued that military success does not necessarily produce political or strategic success.

Sobh-e-No: Hormuz is completely locked

Iran, 19 countries condemn Colombia’s embassy opening in occupied Al-Quds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:58:36 UTC
01:58:36 KST

Iran, 19 countries condemn Colombia’s embassy opening in occupied Al-Quds
TEHRAN — Iran and 19 other countries have condemned Colombia’s decision to open an embassy in occupied al-Quds, warning that the move violates international law, undermines the internationally recognized status of the Palestinian city and runs counter to efforts to establish an independent Palestinian state.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry issued a strong condemnation on Thursday evening, describing the decision as contrary to the Charter of the United Nations and fundamental principles of international law. A joint statement by the foreign ministers of Turkey and 18 other countries followed on Friday, calling on Bogotá to reverse the move and uphold its international obligations.
The dispute has renewed attention to the international legal status of al-Quds, the consequences of relocating diplomatic missions to the occupied city, and the long-standing international consensus against unilateral measures intended to alter its status.
In its statement, Iran’s Foreign Ministry stressed that al-Quds is an inseparable part of Palestinian territory and that states are obligated under international law to refrain from actions that could be interpreted as recognizing Israel’s occupation.
The ministry said Colombia’s decision contradicted the country’s international obligations concerning the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination and risked legitimizing the occupation of Palestinian land. It also argued that the move conflicted with the historical struggles for independence and justice in Colombia and across Latin America.
Iran called on the Colombian government to accept responsibility for the consequences of its 'unlawful and unjustifiable' decision.
Joint condemnation by 19 countries
The joint statement, issued by Turkey’s Foreign Ministry on Friday, was endorsed by the foreign ministers of Turkey, Algeria, Djibouti, Egypt, Indonesia, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Libya, Malaysia, Oman, Pakistan, Palestine, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen.
The ministers expressed their unequivocal rejection of Colombia’s embassy opening, saying the decision violated relevant UN Security Council resolutions and weakened international efforts to achieve a just and lasting peace based on a two-state solution.
They reaffirmed that measures intended to change the legal or historical status of occupied al-Quds, or to recognize the city as Israel’s capital, are null and void and have no legal effect.
The statement cited UN Security Council Resolutions 476 and 478, both adopted in 1980. These resolutions rejected Israel’s attempts to alter the character and status of the city and called on states with diplomatic missions there to withdraw them.
The ministers emphasized that al-Quds is part of the Palestinian territory occupied in 1967 and urged Colombia to reconsider and reverse its decision, respect international law and avoid actions that prejudice the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people.
Iran’s condemnation came alongside separate objections from Jordan, Saudi Arabia and Algeria. The Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) had also previously denounced the planned embassy opening, describing it as an unlawful step and a departure from Colombia’s longstanding support for Palestinian rights.
From the 1980s diplomatic withdrawals to the US embassy move
The controversy over diplomatic missions in al-Quds has deep roots in international diplomacy. Israel declared the city its capital after occupying East al-Quds in 1967 and later took steps to consolidate its control over the city. These measures have not gained broad international recognition.
In 1980, Israel adopted a law declaring a 'united Jerusalem' its capital. The UN Security Council rejected this move through Resolution 478, determining that measures seeking to alter the city’s character and status had no legal validity and calling on states that had established diplomatic missions in Jerusalem to withdraw them.
Following the resolution, countries that had maintained embassies in Al-Quds moved their missions to Tel Aviv. For decades, the overwhelming international practice was to keep embassies outside the city, reflecting the position that its final status should be determined through negotiations rather than unilateral action.
A major departure from that practice came under US President Donald Trump. On December 6, 2017, Trump announced that the United States recognized Jerusalem as Israel’s capital. The US Embassy was subsequently relocated from Tel Aviv to Quds on May 14, 2018, during his first presidential term.
The decision marked a significant shift in longstanding US policy and drew widespread criticism from Palestinians and many governments, which warned that recognizing Jerusalem as Israel’s capital without a negotiated settlement prejudged one of the most sensitive issues in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
The United States became the first country to move its embassy to Quds in the modern wave of diplomatic relocations following the 2017 announcement. Guatemala followed in May 2018, while Paraguay briefly moved its embassy to the city that year before reversing the decision later in 2018. Honduras moved its embassy in 2021. A small number of other countries have also taken steps to recognize Quds as Israel’s capital or relocate their diplomatic missions there, although most governments have continued to keep their embassies elsewhere.

Referring to the 12-day war, Taeb said the simultaneous targeting of military commanders and scientists was part of a strategy to weaken Iran’s security infrastructure and damage the scientific capabilities underpinning its technological progress.
He said the campaign against Iranian scientists had failed to eliminate the country’s nuclear expertise. According to Taeb, the scope of attacks expanded during the 40-day war, extending to other scientific fields and claiming the lives of researchers.
Taeb argued that the objective of such attacks went beyond military damage, encompassing efforts to undermine public security and weaken the country’s capacity for scientific and technological advancement.
"Targeting one scientist would not halt the country’s progress, as more specialists would emerge to continue the work," he said.
AI and the changing landscape of military operations
Taeb described investment in artificial intelligence and cybersecurity as a strategic decision for Iran’s future, calling for these priorities to be translated into practical action by government institutions, policymakers and leading experts.
He said AI had already produced tangible results in the defense sector by improving intelligence assessment and the accuracy of target identification.
He further said AI-assisted systems had improved the detection of military vessels operating near the Strait of Hormuz and helped increase missile accuracy. Taeb argued that these capabilities had affected US military calculations and contributed to the relocation of American naval vessels farther from the area.
His remarks underscore the growing importance of AI-enabled intelligence, surveillance and targeting systems in contemporary military operations. Such technologies can help process large volumes of information, identify patterns and support faster operational decisions, although their effectiveness depends on data quality, system reliability and human oversight.
Taeb highlights disparity in military spending
Taeb also contrasted Iran’s defense resources with the much larger military budgets of the United States and Israel. He cited figures for US military spending and additional wartime funding requests, and said Israel had received $22 billion in additional US assistance for the conflict.
Despite Iran’s limited defense resources in foreign-currency terms, Taeb said the country had been able to withstand the military campaign. He argued that a comparable emphasis on scientific capability, technological innovation and strategic planning was necessary to sustain progress in the fields of AI and cybersecurity.
He called for artificial intelligence and cybersecurity to move beyond isolated technological initiatives and become part of a coordinated national strategy involving public institutions and the country’s scientific community.
The conference’s focus on young technology specialists, Taeb said, reflected Iran’s intention to expand its pool of skilled researchers and developers. In his view, strengthening domestic expertise in emerging technologies is essential not only to defense preparedness but also to the country’s broader scientific and technological development.

‘Mother of all bombs’ will not rescue Trump from Iran war quagmire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:49:46 UTC
01:49:46 KST

‘Mother of all bombs’ will not rescue Trump from Iran war quagmire
TEHRAN — The possible use of America’s largest non-nuclear bomb against Iran may offer President Donald Trump a dramatic display of military power, but it is unlikely to resolve the strategic predicament facing Washington, analysts have warned, arguing that a spectacular explosion cannot substitute for a viable path out of a protracted war.
CNN reported on October 14 that the US military had developed strike plans that could include the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, commonly known as the “mother of all bombs,” against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if Trump orders a resumption of combat operations. The report cited multiple US officials familiar with the planning.
The prospect of deploying the weapon has raised questions about whether Washington is seeking a decisive military outcome or a dramatic action that could allow the president to declare victory without achieving his stated strategic objectives.
 
Even within US military planning circles, doubts have emerged over the weapon’s effectiveness in changing the course of the war, CNN reported. Reuters subsequently reported the story, noting that it had not independently verified CNN’s account.
A dramatic explosion, but what strategic result?
Dani Citrinowicz, a former Israeli military intelligence official, told the BBC that even using the “mother of all bombs” would not force Iran to surrender.
“Even the use of the [mother of all bombs] will not force Iran to surrender; although such an attack could have psychological effects and give Trump an opportunity to claim an imaginary victory,” he said, according to the quotation provided in the BBC-attributed report.
The assessment points to a fundamental distinction between the destructive power of a weapon and its ability to achieve political objectives. A strike can cause extensive damage without compelling an adversary to accept the attacker’s demands or bringing a conflict to a favourable conclusion.
Sina Azodi, director of the Middle East Studies Program at George Washington University, similarly questioned the strategic logic behind the reported option.
“Trump has a strange fascination with the symbolic use of American military power and wants to advertise it on his personal social media account through a grand spectacle and a massive explosion,” Azodi said, according to the quotation provided.
He also highlighted the weapon’s limitations against deeply buried targets, noting that it detonates in the air and has limited capacity to penetrate far underground.
The distinction matters because the MOAB was designed primarily to produce devastating blast effects over a broad surface area. It is not the same as a specialised penetrator designed to attack deeply buried, hardened facilities.
In an October 15 Al Jazeera explainer, military analyst Elijah Magnier said that using the MOAB would not guarantee the destruction of Iran’s deeply buried nuclear installations and could amount to little more than “political theatre.”
A weapon cannot resolve a strategic deadlock
The reported plans have emerged as the Trump administration faces pressure to demonstrate progress in a war that has failed to produce a clear political resolution.
In a CNN broadcast on October 15, senior national security reporter Zachary Cohen said Trump and his advisers had spent months discussing options that could be presented to the American public as a “definitive end” to the war.
Cohen said the military had been tasked with developing fresh strike options amid the absence of a diplomatic resolution and growing unpopularity of the conflict.
He also reported that the administration’s stated strategic goals remained unfulfilled.
That assessment raises a central question: what would a MOAB strike actually accomplish that previous attacks and existing military pressure have not?
The bomb’s destructive capacity is not in dispute. The uncertainty concerns whether its use would change Iran’s calculations, compel Tehran to capitulate or create conditions for a durable settlement.
A dramatic strike might generate powerful images and headlines. But if it does not achieve its declared objectives, it could instead expose the gap between the administration’s military capabilities and its ability to translate them into a political outcome.
The limits of spectacle
The MOAB is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal. Its deployment would represent a major escalation, but its size alone does not make it an appropriate weapon for every target.
CNN military analyst and retired Air Force Colonel Cedric Leighton explained in a broadcast on October 15 that the MOAB is designed to inflict damage over a large surface area, whereas Iran’s hardened and deeply buried nuclear facilities present a different targeting challenge.
He contrasted the MOAB with the Massive Ordnance Penetrator, a different weapon specifically designed to attack hardened underground targets.
Leighton also questioned the suitability of the aircraft required to deliver the MOAB for the Iranian operational environment.
The technical limitations reinforce the broader strategic problem. A weapon capable of producing an enormous explosion is not necessarily capable of destroying every intended target, still less of compelling a country to surrender.
A face-saving exit is not the same as victory
The most consequential possibility raised by the reporting is that the proposed strike could be intended partly to shape the political narrative of the war.
CNN’s reporting suggested that the administration was examining military options that could enable Trump to present the conflict as decisively concluded. Such a scenario would make the distinction between a battlefield achievement and a politically useful declaration of victory particularly important.
Citrinowicz’s assessment, as quoted by the BBC, captures that concern: the attack might provide an opportunity to claim victory without necessarily producing the underlying result.
This is the danger of treating military spectacle as a substitute for strategy. An attack can be visually overwhelming and still leave the fundamental dispute unresolved.
For Washington, the question is not simply whether the United States can deploy a powerful bomb. It is whether doing so would bring the war closer to an outcome that can be sustained politically and strategically.
 
The quagmire remains
The possibility of using the MOAB does not, by itself, demonstrate that Trump has authorised such an attack. The reports describe contingency planning, not a confirmed decision to deploy the weapon.
Reuters said it could not independently verify CNN’s initial report. CBS News separately reported on October 15 that the White House and Pentagon had prepared plans for possible use of the weapon if ordered by the president.
If the bomb fails to achieve its intended military objectives, the administration could find itself confronting the same fundamental problem after an even more dramatic attack. If it is used primarily to create the appearance of a decisive outcome, the gap between the declaration of victory and the realities on the ground could become harder to conceal.
The “mother of all bombs” may offer Trump a spectacle of overwhelming force. But an explosion, however large, cannot by itself deliver a political settlement, compel an adversary’s surrender or guarantee a way out of war.
The real test is not the size of the blast. It is whether the strategy behind it can produce an outcome that military power alone has so far failed to secure.

Egypt discovers parts of giant pharaoh statues (PHOTOS)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:45:52 UTC
01:45:52 KST

Egypt discovers parts of giant pharaoh statues (PHOTOS)
Egyptian archaeologists have uncovered the remains of two royal statues, at least one depicting Pharaoh Ramses II, during excavations in the Nile Delta, the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities announced on Wednesday.
The discovery was made in the village of Behbeit el-Hagar in Gharbia Governorate after a local resident, Khaled el-Shahat Khalil, found an inscribed stone block on his property and alerted the authorities. Tourism and Antiquities Minister Sherif Fathy later visited the site and rewarded the man and his wife with a pilgrimage to Mecca for reporting the find.
According to Hisham el-Leithy, secretary-general of Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities, the first find is a 1.6-meter-high head of Ramses II wearing the double crown symbolizing the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt. Part of the statue’s back pillar was also recovered, bearing an inscription of one of the pharaoh’s royal titles. Archaeologists estimate that the complete monument, including its base, may have stood around 8.5 meters tall.
The second discovery includes a 2.4-meter section of another royal statue, also believed to depict Ramses II. The figure is missing its legs and base, but its head remains well preserved, with facial features resembling those of the first statue. Excavators also uncovered a 1.3-meter block of pink granite bearing hieroglyphic inscriptions with two of the pharaoh’s titles, including “King of Upper and Lower Egypt” and “Son of Ra.”
The ministry said archaeologists are continuing to study the artifacts, and their exact age has yet to be determined. However, the discovery sets clear links to Ramses II, who ruled Egypt from 1279 to 1213 BC. It’s not the first finding of the kind. In February 2024, archaeologists uncovered the upper section of a statue of the pharaoh in Minya Governorate, nearly a century after its lower half was discovered in 1930. The restored statue, standing about 6.7 meters tall, was re-erected in 2026.
Other recent finds in Egypt include three New Kingdom tombs uncovered at Saqqara in July and a Roman-era tomb discovered in the Dakhla Oasis in September, containing pottery, funerary inscriptions and a coin depicting Emperor Constantine.

FIFA fines Spain over anti-Muslim chants at Egypt game
FIFA has fined world champions Spain $20,000 over Islamophobic chants by supporters during a friendly against Egypt earlier this year.
The chants were heard during Spain's 0-0 draw with Egypt at Espanyol's RCDE Stadium in Barcelona on 31 March.
Sections of the crowd chanted "Whoever doesn't jump is Muslim", while Egypt's national anthem was also jeered before kick-off.
Spain winger Lamine Yamal, who is Muslim, condemned the chants after the match as disrespectful and intolerable.
"Using a religion as a taunt on the field makes you look ignorant and racist," he said.
FIFA said its appeals committee had upheld the sanction following an earlier ruling by its disciplinary committee.
The Spanish Football Federation has been ordered to pay a $20,000 fine and must also close at least 15% of the seating at Spain's next home friendly.
FIFA said the affected seats could instead be allocated to groups including families, students and anti-discrimination organisations.
The governing body's disciplinary judges said "harsh sanctions were necessary", while acknowledging that it was the Spanish federation's first offence and that officials had acted quickly after the chants began.
Stadium announcements were made during the match calling on supporters to stop discriminatory behaviour.
The Spanish federation also condemned the chants and co-operated with authorities seeking to identify those responsible.
Spanish police opened an investigation the following day into what they described as "Islamophobic and xenophobic" chanting.
The incident came amid wider debate over racism and discrimination in football. FIFA's current anti-racism framework includes a crossed-arm gesture allowing players and officials to report racist abuse during matches.
FIFA rejected the Spanish federation's argument that the word "Muslim" was not inherently insulting, ruling that otherwise neutral language can become discriminatory when used as a taunt or marker of inferiority.
The federation said on Friday that it considered the punishment disproportionately severe and would appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport.
FIFA has also imposed sanctions elsewhere this year for breaches of anti-discrimination rules, including a fine against the Israeli Football Association over its handling of racist behaviour by Beitar Jerusalem supporters.
The March incident came before Spain went on to win the 2026 World Cup, defeating Argentina in the final in July.
The Egypt match had already drawn wider attention to anti-Muslim sentiment in European football, an issue TNA has examined in the context of the growing far-right backlash against Muslim players and supporters.

Ghada Karmi: Zionism is racism motion is a ‘beacon of light’

The motion was passed on 4 October with 1,022 votes in favour and 813 against.
Born in 1939, Karmi, who came to London in 1949 after her family was forcibly expelled from Palestine in the Nakba (Arabic for catastrophe), said the motion is “the best thing that’s happened to me, personally, since 1948.”
The motion has been met with backlash both from political opponents and from within the party.
Green MP Adrian Ramsay said he was "deeply upset" after the motion passed.
Lawyer Adam Wagner, who has previously represented the Campaign Against Antisemitism, said the motion may violate the Equality Act of 2010 because it "will discriminate against and harass people who hold Zionist beliefs and Jewish people more generally."
Green Party leader Zack Polanski, who is Jewish, said in a statement, “antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct.”
"No-one will be made unwelcome because of their background, their faith, or where they worship."
Karmi, who thanked both Polanski and Lubna Speitan, who proposed the motion, responded to the criticism, saying, “I don’t know what the fuss is about; of course it’s racist.”
"The essence of this is really nothing to do with being Palestinian. It's to do with being non-Jewish," she said.
"We're the wrong ethnicity, and that's why we're being prosecuted. If that's not racist, I don't know what is," she continued.
The motion states that Israel is an "apartheid," "ethnonationalist" state, and calls for the establishment of a single Palestinian state "with equal rights for all."
An amendment which would have removed the call for a single Palestinian state was voted down, as was one which would have prevented people from being disciplined by the party for membership of Jewish institutions with a Zionist stance, including synagogues.
Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham responded by ruling out a future coalition with the Green Party as long as the motion stands.
In September, Labour’s Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced limited sanctions against Israeli settlements in the West Bank, but the Labour government has continued to arrest protesters supporting the proscribed group Palestine Action.
Speitan, who proposed the motion, said at the press conference that she hopes other organisations, including trade unions and political parties, will adopt the stance that Zionism is racism.

Iran ships some LPG, jet fuel despite US blockade, data shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:39:31 UTC
01:39:31 KST

Breadcrumb
Iran ships some LPG, jet fuel despite US blockade, data shows
Iran has managed to export some liquefied petroleum gas and jet fuel since July, despite a US naval blockade, shipping intelligence showed and people involved in security said.
Tehran has in recent weeks been concealing such cargoes among a growing volume of ship-to-ship transfers by other Gulf producers off Oman, news agency Reuters reported- citing four people in maritime security who track Gulf oil movements.
The Iranian exports and methodology are reported for the first time here. While a fraction of its former energy exports, the cargoes are rare evidence of petroleum products getting through a blockade that has halted Iran's crude exports.
Analysis by US advocacy group United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), which monitors Iran-related tanker traffic using ship and satellite tracking, shows at least eight gas tankers carrying Iranian LPG have left the Gulf of Oman since mid-July.
Another tanker carrying Iranian jet fuel reached Myanmar in September, additional satellite imagery and analysis by maritime intelligence group SynMax show.
The US imposed targeted sanctions in 2023 on Myanmar's jet-fuel industry, citing military airstrikes on civilians that the United Nations says have killed thousands of people. Myanmar's military government has repeatedly denied targeting civilians, saying its operations are directed against armed groups.
Six of the eight gas tankers and the jet fuel tanker are under US sanctions for transporting Iranian petroleum and petrochemical products, a Reuters analysis of the vessels and sanctions imposed on ships by the US Treasury showed.
"What we have seen passing is a handful of tankers carrying Iranian LPG, but the overwhelming majority of tankers laden with Iranian products have been redirected by US forces," said Jemima Shelley, senior research analyst with UANI.
Shelley said some Iranian LPG tankers transferred cargoes near the Omani coastal towns of Shinas and Sohar, while others waited in the Gulf of Oman before heading past the US blockade, which US Central Command has said sits across the Gulf of Oman near the Iran-Pakistan border.
The total amount of these LPG cargoes was estimated at 4.1 million barrels, Shelley said.
Shelley said the shipments were driven "more by opportunism" than showing a new trend of Iran trying to export its oil and petrochemicals by using smaller ships.
Most of the cargoes sailed to Malaysia's Eastern Outer Port Limits to conduct further STS transfers for likely destinations in China, Shelley said, based on UANI's analysis.
The Iranian government did not respond to a request for comment. Myanmar's military-backed government did not respond to a request for comment on whether the country had received Iranian jet fuel.
US MILITARY SAYS BLOCKADE 'IRONCLAD'
The US military's Centcom said its naval blockade, which was first imposed on Iran-related oil exports on April 13, is "ironclad". The blockade was lifted in June after the US reached a draft understanding with Iran, but it was reimposed on July 14 following the collapse of the agreement.
Reuters reports, citing a US military official, that the passage of a vessel does not necessarily mean it had evaded the blockade.
Every ship was assessed individually, including through a review of its papers, and some vessels could be allowed through for humanitarian reasons, the official added.
The official said the appearance of a vessel on US sanctions lists is not the only factor to make it subject to the blockade, adding that US forces are also closely monitoring some ships without taking action against them for operational reasons.
Centcom said in an update on October 13 that during the three months of the latest blockade, four commercial vessels had been disabled and 135 ships had been turned around by US forces.
The US military has turned around ships from Asia and also seized some tankers, previous Centcom statements said.
Washington has coupled its blockade with a sanctions campaign aimed at severing Iran's remaining financial links and depriving it of revenue. Last week, it imposed fresh sanctions on 17 vessels involved in transporting Iranian crude, petrochemicals and petroleum products.
A US Treasury spokesperson questioned shipping data suggesting vessels had evaded the blockade, saying ships could spoof their locations or use false identities when loading.
Such data "should be taken with a grain of salt", the spokesperson said.
The Treasury spokesperson said Operation Economic Outcast, together with the blockade, was "suffocating the Iranian regime".
Torbjorn Soltvedt, principal Middle East analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, said although there was no sign of Washington easing its blockade, worsening economic conditions in Iran could push Tehran to take greater risks.
"If Iran can move product tankers through, even in small numbers, jet fuel may be a good option. Iran's aviation industry is under increasing pressure from US sanctions, with a growing number of planes grounded, and a potential surplus of jet fuel at Iranian refineries," Soltvedt added.
Iranian crude exports fell to zero in September, according to Kpler, the first month without a shipment since the analytics firm began tracking the producer in 2013.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said the blockade prevented most Chinese purchases of Iranian oil and left Iran unable to deliver crude to customers.

Iran reaffirms Strait of Hormuz closure, says passage must be coordinated

Rear Admiral Habibollah Sayyari, deputy coordinator of the Iranian Army, said on Thursday that any vessel seeking to transit the strategic waterway must coordinate its passage with the Iranian authorities who are in charge.
