Ukraine Develops Full-Body Protective Armor That NATO Armies Do Not Currently Field
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:31:40 UTC
00:31:40 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Ukraine Develops Full-Body Protective Armor That NATO Armies Do Not Currently Field
Ukraine is introducing a new layer of body protection for frontline troops, centrally procuring 4,700 fragmentation-resistant suits for the first time, according to Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense on October 15.
The roughly two-kilogram protective system consists of a specialized jacket, trousers, and pteruges designed to shield the pelvis and upper thighs.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The pteruges include an adjustable belt and seven sections containing soft ballistic inserts: two frontal, four lateral, and one rear.
Unlike rigid armor plates, the soft ballistic packages are designed to conform to the soldier’s body while providing protection against fragments and bullets. The sections can be repositioned for fit, while the rear section includes additional padding for troops operating while seated. The suit can also be worn with a standard body armor vest, extending protection to areas that are normally left exposed.
“Our task at the Ministry of Defense is to listen to the needs of the troops and supply exactly what our warriors really need,” Deputy Defense Minister Mstyslav Banik stated. The design underwent military testing among personnel whose combat duties require high mobility before the final model was approved.
The armor is intended primarily for assault troops, medics, and other personnel operating near the line of contact, where artillery shells and drones create persistent fragmentation threats. The Ministry noted that comparable protective suits are not currently fielded by NATO countries and that a prototype of the Ukrainian design was provided to Western partners for evaluation.
Ukraine's pace of battlefield adaptation has drawn growing attention from its Western partners. Earlier in October, former US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll called it “humiliating” to watch Ukraine field better weapons despite a far smaller budget.
He argued that the US procurement system was too slow to keep pace. In May 2025, Driscoll created the 600-soldier Unmanned Assault Battalion, an experimental drones-first unit in Italy that worked alongside Ukrainian advisers.

Uzbekistan's 2 ancient canals added to World Heritage Irrigation Structures List
Uzbekistan’s Dargom and Shohrud canals were recognized as World Heritage Irrigation Structures in 2026 and added to the International Commission on Irrigation and Drainage (ICID) register, UzA reports.
The award ceremony took place on October 14 during an international congress in Marseille, France. Officials received certificates and commemorative plaques recognizing the canals.
The Dargom Canal, which supplies water to the Samarkand oasis, is believed to have been built between the 5th and 4th centuries BC. Nearly 102 kilometers long, the canal still irrigates almost 178,000 hectares of land today.
The Shohrud Canal is believed to have been dug in the 3rd-4th centuries AD. For centuries, it has played a key role in the development of Bukhara and the surrounding oasis.
Uzbekistan’s Dustlik and Eski Tuyatortar canals were also added to the World Heritage Irrigation Structures list in 2025.

Italian intelligence suggest link between Palestinian terrorists, Sicilian mafia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:19:27 UTC
00:19:27 KST

Previously classified Italian intelligence documents reveal suspected connections between Palestinian terrorist organizations and the Sicilian Mafia during the 1980s, including possible cooperation in weapons trafficking, narcotics smuggling, and explosives expertise, according to an investigation published Thursday by the Italian newspaper Il Giornale.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The investigation, by journalist Giulia Sorrentino, draws on intelligence reports, judicial records, and historical documents describing networks extending from Lebanon and Syria to Sicily and Rome. The material also includes an intelligence warning about a possible terrorist attack against the US Embassy in Rome.
Drug trafficking and Palestinian terrorism
One of the central documents, dated November 9, 1983, contains information gathered by Italy’s Carabinieri, the country's military police force, concerning international drug trafficking and Palestinian terrorist operations.
According to the intelligence report, members of Sicilian Mafia networks associated with the Greco and Gambino families were operating in Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley, then under strong Syrian influence. The area reportedly contained narcotics-processing facilities near Baalbek.
The source alleged that six AK-47 assault rifles had reached Mafia associates and been used in attacks in Sicily. It also described a shipment of approximately 900 kilograms of morphine base reportedly sent from Lebanon toward the Sicilian city of Catania in October 1983.
The same intelligence material warned that Palestinian terrorist organizations might attack Western targets if the multinational military force stationed in Lebanon intervened against Palestinian positions. The source specifically reported knowledge of a planned attack against the American Embassy in Rome.
Sorrentino's investigation also revisits the July 29, 1983, assassination of Rocco Chinnici, an Italian magistrate who played a leading role in the campaign against organized crime.
Chinnici and three other people were killed when a car bomb containing approximately 75 kilograms of explosives detonated in Palermo. The attack's use of a remotely detonated explosive device resembled techniques employed by terrorist organizations during Lebanon's civil war.
Judicial records describe how Bou Chebel Ghassan, a Lebanese police informant, had provided information about contacts with Mafia figures and efforts to obtain weapons and morphine. Days before Chinnici's assassination, Ghassan reportedly described methods of killing investigators remotely, comparing them to those used by Palestinian terrorists in Lebanon.
No record that Palestinian operatives participated in assassinating Chinnici
Although the testimony raised questions about possible foreign connections, Italian judicial proceedings established Cosa Nostra's responsibility for Chinnici's murder. The records do not demonstrate that Palestinian operatives planned or participated in the assassination.
The investigation also revisits allegations published by Corriere della Sera on June 22, 1993. In a report from Beirut, correspondent Antonio Ferrari quoted Zeid Wehbe, a Palestine Liberation Organization representative, alleging that operatives associated with Abu Nidal had infiltrated Mafia networks.
According to those allegations, Abu Nidal's organization supplied expertise in explosives and sophisticated killing devices in exchange for assistance with criminal operations.
Abu Nidal, whose real name was Sabri al-Banna, led a Palestinian terrorist faction that broke with Yasser Arafat's PLO. His organization was responsible for attacks against Israeli, Jewish, Western, and Palestinian targets.
An Italian military intelligence report dated January 13, 1986, also described connections between Abu Nidal and circles associated with the family of Syrian President Hafez Assad. The document, identified through research by Italian historian Giordana Terracina, referred to the international terrorist known as Carlos the Jackal.
The assessment followed the December 27, 1985, coordinated attacks against airports in Rome and Vienna by Abu Nidal's Palestinian terrorist organization. The assaults killed 16 civilians and injured approximately 120 others.
Sorrentino also cites an October 1990 memorandum attributed to Italian General Demetrio Cogliandro. The document raised allegations concerning Arab banks operating in Italy, financial transactions involving Middle Eastern governments, and funds allegedly reaching Italian organized crime groups for narcotics purchases.
The intelligence records became accessible through a broader Italian government initiative launched in 2014 to declassify historical documentation relating to terrorism and political violence.
The newly published investigation does not establish that Abu Nidal's organization maintained a formal operational alliance with Cosa Nostra or participated in Mafia assassinations. The allegations in the intelligence reports have not all been independently corroborated.
However, the documents demonstrate that Italian intelligence agencies were examining possible connections between Palestinian terrorism, organized crime, and Middle Eastern trafficking networks years before allegations of an Abu Nidal–Mafia partnership became public in 1993.

The Bedouin shepherd who claimed he was a kidnapped Jewish child
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:17:01 UTC
00:17:01 KST

Had this been a TV drama, someone would probably have asked the writers to tone it down. In 1956, a little boy disappeared from Tirosh, a farming community between Beit Shemesh and Kiryat Malachi. His mother had left him playing in the yard with a neighbor while she went to the clinic. When she returned, he was gone.
The boy was Yitzhak Gabay, 2. His brother David was 7 and his sister Aliza was 4. “We were going for tetanus shots,” David, now 78, recalled this week. “Mom told the neighbor, ‘I’m taking David and Aliza to get vaccinated. Keep an eye on Yitzhak.’ We were gone seven minutes. When we came back, Yitzhak wasn’t there. We asked the neighbor where he was. She said, ‘I gave him a tomato, and he headed back toward the house.’”
Relatives, neighbors and police searched for the child, but found no trace of him. “There were dozens of police officers and even a tracking dog, which died after a snake bit it,” David said. His parents spent years looking. “There wasn’t a rabbi, a sorcerer or a medium we didn’t go to.”
Of all those visits, David remembers one in particular, to the rabbi known as the Baba Sali. “We went to him right after the kidnapping,” he said. “He told us exactly when we would find Yitzhak. How many years, how many months, how many days. Even how many hours.” David remains convinced that the prediction came true.
Their mother, Zohara, had been pregnant 16 times; only David, Aliza and Yitzhak had survived. Nine years after her youngest son vanished, she died at 32. The family says she died of a broken heart. Her husband, Yisrael, stayed in Tirosh while David and Aliza married and moved to Tel Aviv. As the years passed, the family kept hoping someone would come forward with information, or recognize the boy and bring him home.
About two decades after the disappearance, an argument broke out in a Bedouin family. A young shepherd named Abdullah was quarreling with a relative when the relative snapped: “Who asked you? You’re not even Bedouin. Your mother is Jewish.” Abdullah could not forget it. He began to wonder whether the people who had raised him were his parents, and whether they had kept something from him.
He later said he began dreaming of an elderly Jewish man who told him he was Jewish. Eventually, Abdullah left his family and went to the home of Rabbi Yitzhak David Grossman in Migdal HaEmek, in northern Israel. He told Grossman he believed he was Jewish and had grown up with a family that was not his own. He wanted the rabbi’s help finding out who he was.
Word spread, and the story appeared in Yedioth Ahronoth. Families with missing children began arriving at Grossman’s door. Among those who heard about the shepherd was Yisrael Gabay. Twenty-one years had passed since his son’s disappearance.
David was then serving as an army personnel officer in Sharm el-Sheikh. “One day I got a call from the police: ‘Where are you? Get on the first flight. We need you back in Israel,’” he recalled. “As soon as I landed, Dad said, ‘We need to go to Migdal HaEmek.’” His father told him about the newspaper report and the shepherd who claimed his mother was Jewish.
“Thousands came to the rabbi, all saying he was their son,” David said. “The line stretched from Tel Aviv to Petah Tikva. Everyone had identifying marks. We arrived on Thursday, almost at the end, and we had the clearest signs. My brother had had treatments on his back as a child, and they’d left scars.” Abdullah had scars on his back, too.
Grossman had invited Yisrael to come with two friends from Tirosh. The family stayed through the Sabbath, and on Saturday night the rabbi arranged an informal identification lineup. David remembers a larger group taking part. “They brought in six or 10 men who looked more or less like Dad, but this young man went straight to him. He didn’t even look at the others. And I said, ‘That’s my brother.’ He was huge, like Dad.”
For Yisrael and Abdullah, that settled it. Abdullah began calling himself Yitzhak and moved into Yisrael’s home in Tirosh. He was also known as Abdullah-Yitzhak or Ovadia Ben Yisrael. “I remember we had a party, and Bedouin families came carrying weapons,” David said. “Then he stayed with us in Tirosh, where my father lived.”
Newspaper reports from 1977, however, said a police investigation had found no family connection. They cited a new blood test that had ruled out a biological relationship between Abdullah and the Gabays. Nearly half a century later, relatives interviewed this week dispute those reports. The story is still vividly remembered by the family and by Grossman’s assistant, who first brought it to public attention.
Abdullah tried to adjust to Jewish life with the Gabays, and they tried to help him settle in. But living together was difficult. “Abdullah was bored at Yisrael’s,” said Bracha, David’s wife. “He spoke only Arabic, and the father spoke only Hebrew. There was nothing for them to do at home in Tirosh. Back in his village, there were horses and sheep.”
David said Abdullah’s Bedouin family never explained how he had come to live with them, and the Gabays never asked. “My father died knowing he had found his son, and that this was the right child,” he said. Abdullah began spending time with the people he now regarded as his brother and sister. After a serious argument with David, he moved in with Aliza, who was raising five children.
Aliza has since died, but her son, Shimon Ben Khalifa, remembers Abdullah-Yitzhak well. To him, he was simply his uncle. “I was a baby when they found him, so I grew up with the whole story,” he said. “My mother was sure he was her brother. Nobody ever thought otherwise.”
Asked about the blood-test reports, Ben Khalifa said: “I never heard of a test like that. On the contrary, I think they did another test that showed he was my mother’s brother. There was also an older aunt, his mother’s sister, who always said that was the child. That was Yitzhak.”
Life in Tel Aviv did not suit Abdullah. By then, he had married a woman from the village where he had grown up. Relatives say she was a teacher and had even considered converting to Judaism for him. The couple tried living in Tirosh, but they were far from the families who had raised them. They eventually returned to Zarzir, where Abdullah did well raising calves and tending olive groves.
He stayed in touch with Aliza’s family. “We visited his home several times,” Ben Khalifa said. “His son was at my house two months ago. My younger brother got married two years ago, and he was at the wedding.”
“To this day, I’m sure he’s my brother,” David said. “He named his eldest daughter after our mother. Once he told me he lived between two worlds, Jewish and Bedouin.” Yisrael died 12 years ago, still carrying a childhood photograph of Yitzhak in his wallet. “Until the day he died,” David said, “he believed he had found his child.”

Ousted US general warned before Iran war of missile defense shortages lasting until 2030: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:15:38 UTC
00:15:38 KST

Ousted US Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George warned months before the US-Israeli war against Iran that American missile defense stockpiles were critically low and could take until 2030 to recover, CBS News reported Thursday.
George raised the warning in late December, two months before the conflict began, according to US officials familiar with his assessment. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed him from his post in April as the war was underway.
The general’s assessment, included in the Pentagon’s fiscal 2027 force allocation planning, identified shortages of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors and Patriot missiles, with supplies expected to remain at strategically low levels until 2030.
The officials reportedly attributed the shortfall to weapons transfers to Ukraine, US military support for Israel, and limited defense industry production capacity.
The war with Iran has further strained supplies, according to the report. A Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimate found that US forces entered 2026 with approximately 2,300 Patriot interceptors and used between 1,050 and 1,430 during the conflict.
READ: US considering using ‘mother of all bombs’ against Iran: Report
The country’s prewar THAAD inventory stood at around 355 interceptors, of which an estimated 190 to 290 were expended.
Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel and senior adviser at CSIS, told CBS News that these systems would be crucial in a potential conflict with China.
“Air defense — missile defense — that will be huge,” he said, explaining that a major confrontation with Beijing would demand substantial interceptor supplies.
Replenishing the stockpiles remains a lengthy process, the report said. The CSIS estimates that new THAAD interceptor contracts take over four years to fulfill, while Patriot PAC-3 orders take an average of 3 1/2 years.
The Pentagon rejected claims of a shortage. Chief spokesman Sean Parnell told CBS News: “Claims of U.S. munitions shortages are false.”
He added that Washington retains “everything required to strike at the time and place of the President’s choosing.”

Is Israel fighting the wrong war? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:02:18 UTC
00:02:18 KST

What if Israel is winning the military battles but losing the war that ultimately determines its survival?
Since October 7, 2023, Israel has demonstrated extraordinary military capabilities. Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran have suffered significant blows.
Yet the fundamental question remains: Has military superiority brought Israel closer to enduring security? This may be one of the most important questions for Israelis in the upcoming elections.
Or, perhaps the question should be: Are we fighting the wrong war? It is fascinating that this question is not a significant part of the political debates leading up to the decision regarding who will lead the country.
The early Zionist movement understood something that modern Israel may have forgotten.
Nation-building was a generational undertaking. Theodor Herzl, Chaim Weizmann, and David Ben-Gurion invested decades in diplomacy, institution-building, immigration, and international legitimacy.
They understood that establishing a Jewish state required more than winning individual confrontations.
Today, Israel often approaches existential threats through military operations measured in days, weeks, or months.
Our ideological adversaries are operating on an entirely different clock.
Consider the historical memory of the Crusades. European armies conquered Jerusalem, but ultimately lost their foothold in the region.
The lesson for movements committed to a generational struggle is straightforward: survive today, regroup tomorrow, and eventually your enemy will lose his will to fight and leave.
Iran’s revolutionary leadership has demonstrated comparable strategic patience, investing decades in regional proxies, ideological networks, and the pursuit of influence.
Israel cannot assume that its adversaries define victory, defeat, or acceptable sacrifice as we do.
That brings us to the first strategic trap: deterrence.
Traditional deterrence assumes that sufficiently painful consequences will discourage aggression.
But what happens when an adversary embraces martyrdom, accepts devastating casualties, or considers organizational survival itself a victory?
Yahya Sinwar understood that October 7 would provoke an overwhelming Israeli response. Yet the resulting devastation did not necessarily negate the broader political and ideological objectives of his attack.
Israel must then employ increasingly substantial military force to defeat an adversary willing to absorb extraordinary losses.
Now introduce the second trap.
When terrorist organizations embed military operations within civilian environments, Israel faces difficult operational choices. Protecting civilians, as international law requires, by definition extends military campaigns.
Civilian casualties and destruction, whatever the military circumstances, produce images that travel around the world within seconds.
A Hamas command center may be the military objective. A destroyed building becomes the television image.
CNN, Al Jazeera, TikTok, Telegram, and countless smartphones transmit those images into millions of homes.
Military time and political time are no longer synchronized.
The longer Israel fights, the more international pressure can accumulate. The more force required, the greater the potential reputational consequences. And the more international legitimacy erodes, the less strategic freedom Israel retains.
Israel can win the battlefield while losing the conditions necessary to achieve and sustain victory.
But there is another battlefield, one extending thousands of miles beyond Israel’s borders.
The Jewish Diaspora
Jewish communities in New York, London, Paris, and elsewhere are increasingly drawn into conflicts they neither initiated nor controlled.
As the war continues, images of Palestinian suffering circulate globally, accompanied by accusations against Israel that can spill over into hostility toward Jews generally.
And what is their response?
Too often, they follow Israel’s traditional hasbara (public diplomacy) playbook.
More facts. More explanations. More historical context. More attempts to correct the latest accusation.
Necessary? Absolutely.
Sufficient? Clearly not.
Because while we are explaining yesterday’s military operation, our opponents are organizing tomorrow’s political campaign.
An October 10 Fox News investigation by Asra Nomani exposed the organizational machinery behind a coordinated international anti-Israel mobilization starting this past October 8 to the 15.
The investigation identified 179 participating organizations and 322 scheduled events across three days. Organizers had prepared graphics in seven languages, common slogans, media guidance, and political demands.
The campaign extended beyond street demonstrations into universities, workplaces, corporations, and government institutions, calling for sanctions and arms embargoes.
This was not simply spontaneous outrage. It was evidence of a prepared, interoperable international network capable of transforming individual demonstrations into coordinated political pressure, just as it did on October 8, before Israel even responded to the attacks of October 7.
Our enemies have spent years building what we now know is an extremely effective ecosystem.
Not every participant shares the same ideology. But organizations with different political identities can cooperate around common objectives without surrendering their independence.
That is the power of an ecosystem. And it exposes another weakness in our approach.
We are fighting not merely an information war, but a competition for meaning.
Psychiatrist and Holocaust survivor Dr. Viktor Frankl described the existential vacuum: the emptiness people feel when they struggle to find meaning and purpose.
He suggested that our modern society, with all its technological advances, was driving this feeling of emptiness among millions.
Ideological movements can fill that vacuum by offering something more compelling than information: identity, belonging, community, moral purpose, and agency.
Their message effectively becomes: Here is who you are. Here is what is wrong. Here is who is responsible. Here are your people. And here is what you can do.
This is why a “Free Palestine” chant at a huge Ed Sheeran concert so quickly engaged tens of thousands both at the concert and via their social media platforms.
Traditional hasbara too often responds: Here are the facts you should know.
You cannot defeat a meaning system merely by correcting its facts. This is where Israel’s strategic doctrine requires fundamental reconsideration.
Military superiority remains indispensable. But Israel and global Jewry also need a permanent, decentralized, interoperable global ecosystem supporting Jewish safety, Israel’s legitimacy, and long-term societal resilience.
Further strengthened by those who realize that the anti-Israel ecosystem is focusing on Israel first, with the West next in line.
Not another government-controlled public relations campaign.
Not another emergency fundraising appeal following an antisemitic incident.
And certainly not an organization demanding that everyone agree with their view of the world.
Instead, an international network of independent Jewish and non-Jewish institutions, educators, influencers, researchers, philanthropists, cultural leaders, public-private initiatives, and civil society organizations connected by a shared agreement on fundamental principles.
The Jewish people’s historical continuity matters. Jewish safety matters. Israel’s legitimate existence matters. Human dignity and coexistence matter.
Participants can disagree on politics while sharing those foundations.
Such an ecosystem must operate continuously, building relationships, credibility, community, and meaningful participation before the next crisis erupts.
It must strengthen the Diaspora rather than leave Jewish communities perpetually defending military decisions made thousands of miles away.
And it must become an additional dimension of deterrence.
An adversary contemplating aggression should encounter not merely a formidable Israeli military, but a society and international network capable of enduring political pressure, resisting isolation, and sustaining legitimate security interests.
The Zionist movement understood the importance of building the future before the decisive moment arrived.
We must rediscover that strategic patience.
Israel cannot fight a generational ideological conflict exclusively through military campaigns measured in months.
Our military protects our ability to survive in the short term. Our ecosystem must help protect our ability to endure for the long term.
The writer is a global strategist and a strategic adviser at the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs. Follow him on X: @jeffkahn2020

Poll: right-wing People’s Party, and polarisation, growing ahead of 2027 elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Poll: right-wing People’s Party, and polarisation, growing ahead of 2027 elections
A year ahead of Swiss federal elections, pole parties from the right and left are gaining ground while centre-right parties lose out, a new poll finds.
The Sotomo institute’s election barometer, carried out on behalf of the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation (Swissinfo’s parent company), took the pulse of voters’ opinions and priorities just over a year ahead of parliamentary elections set for October 24, 2027.
The big takeaway: polarisation is growing as centre-right parties lose ground. If elections were held today, the right-wing Swiss People’s Party would be the big winner with 29.9% of the vote – a score that would surpass its own record of 29.4% set in 2015.
And in terms of progression since the last elections in October 2023, the People’s Party has also recorded the biggest jump, strengthening its electoral share by two percentage points.
The left-wing Social Democrats and Greens also currently look to be making slight gains which would boost the left’s combined strength by 1.5 percentage points in total. The increase is mainly down to the Social Democrats, currently backed by 19.3% of voters (up one percentage point since 2023); this would be the party’s best result since 2007, Sotomo notes.
Struggles for centre-right
The Centre Party, which stands at 12.6% of voting intentions, and the Radical-Liberal Party, at 13.3%, continue to shed electoral support. The two parties currently look set to lose 1.5 and one percentage point respectively compared to 2023.
Compared to a similar poll in 2025, the Radical-Liberal Party has in fact managed to gain a place and move slightly ahead of the Centre. However, its 13.3% score would still be its worst result in its entire history of House of Representatives elections, Sotomo notes.
And taken together, the Radical-Liberals and the Centre – the two traditionally dominant conservative parties – currently come to a total of 26%, an electoral share which is four percentage points lower than that of the Swiss People’s Party alone.
Climate change back on the agenda
The survey also indicates that the shake-up of support for political parties only partially reflects the population’s major concerns.
Migration, a traditional policy priority of the Swiss People’s Party, is notably moving down the list of the population’s concerns. The two political challenges currently considered most urgent by voters surveyed are the cost of health insurance premiums (39%) and climate change (36%).
The latter, “which seemed to have gone out of fashion in recent years”, has risen sharply following the heatwave-hit summer of 2026, according to Sotomo director Michael Hermann. The proportion who see it as a major challenge has jumped nine percentage points in a year.
At the same time, climate concerns have not yet translated into electoral support; while the Green Party has progressed only marginally, the centrist Liberal Greens have even dropped.
While not predicting another “green wave” like in 2019, Sotomo nevertheless notes that the current trend for the two ecological parties is “more positive than it seems at first glance” – mainly because both have “at least managed, thanks to environmental ‘branding’, to pull themselves out of the dip they were in”, the research institute writes.
Almost two-thirds (65%) of respondents in the poll think measures taken by politicians to mitigate the consequences of climate change are not sufficient. However, support for additional measures, as well as the perception of the urgency of the situation, varies greatly depending on affiliation – nearly 90% of Green voters consider climate action a priority, compared to just 5% of People’s Party voters. Concern about rising health insurance premiums, on the other hand, cuts across party lines.
Immigration and crime still big issues for the right
Behind the two prominent themes of climate and health insurance, four other issues are all cited by around a quarter of respondents: asylum policy, relations with the European Union (EU), immigration, and housing.
Concern about housing has notably progressed in recent years – from 13% in 2023 to 23% today – as has concern about crime, which has jumped from 10% to 19%. This latter is particularly mentioned by right-wing voters.
On the other hand, immigration has largely declined as a priority, after having been cited as a major challenge by 35% of respondents in 2023. But it is still the top issue for People’s Party voters.
‘Too friendly’ towards the US and Israel?
Given the importance of foreign policy issues during the current legislative term, the poll also asked about citizens’ perceptions of how the Swiss government is faring on the international stage.
Here, the population is most critical of Bern’s attitude to the US, with over 80% believing the Federal Council is too friendly with Washington – a perception which is quite uniform across party affiliations.
Similarly, nearly three-quarters of survey respondents consider the official Swiss attitude towards Israel to be too cordial. This opinion is also seen across most party bases, although less clearly for People’s Party and Radical-Liberal Party supporters.
Russia and the EU are the source of much bigger differences and ideological splits. Overall, just over half of all respondents consider Bern’s attitude towards Moscow to be too friendly: but for People’s Party voters it is less than 30%, for left-leaning voters over 70%. Meanwhile nearly 90% of People’s Party supporters consider the government to be too friendly towards the EU, compared to just 10% of Social Democrat and Green voters.
Survey respondents were also asked about their perception of the degree of influence and popularity of each member of the seven-headed federal government. Finance Minister Karin Keller-Sutter (Radical-Liberal Party) is still clearly on top for influence (63%), ahead of Environment Minister Albert Rösti (People’s Party), at 53%, and his party colleague, Economics Minister Guy Parmelin, at 42% – up from just 17% a year ago.
Parmelin, who currently holds the rotating Swiss presidency, and who is stepping down from the government at the end of this year, also now tops the popularity rankings (more than 60% of respondents like him) ahead of Defence Minister Martin Pfister (50%) and Keller-Sutter (46%).
The barometer – methodology
Data collection for the SBC election barometer was carried out online from September 10-23, 2026. Poll respondents were recruited partly via SBC web portals and partly via Sotomo’s online panel. Responses from 25,092 voters were used, and statistical weighting was used to make the sample conform to sociodemographic characteristics like place of residence, age, gender, education and political characteristics.
The poll’s margin of error is +/- 1.2 percentage points for an observed percentage of 50% with a 95% confidence interval.

Qatar announces project to develop Lebanon's electricity sector
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:59:16 UTC
23:59:16 KST

Breadcrumb
Qatar to finance, implement and operate electricity project in Lebanon
Qatar on Friday announced plans to invest in Lebanon’s electricity sector and help address the country’s chronic power crisis, including through the development of a solar power plant.
During his visit to Lebanon, where he met with President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said the two sides held "lengthy discussions" on an energy project that Doha had been discussing with Beirut for years.
"Now, thank God, we see this project getting closer to becoming a reality," he said.
Speaking at a joint press conference with Salam at the Grand Serail, Al Thani said the two countries had agreed to establish a comprehensive framework for cooperation in the energy sector and provide integrated solutions through a major investment project that would benefit Lebanon’s economy.
Salam said Lebanon and Qatar were close to reaching an agreement on a joint project to rehabilitate, develop and modernise the country’s electricity generation infrastructure.
He said the comprehensive project would cover various sources of energy production and the infrastructure required to support them, with the aim of providing a more reliable electricity supply at a lower cost.
Salam said the project would follow a build-operate-transfer (BOT) model, under which Qatari entities would finance, build and operate the infrastructure before transferring it to the Lebanese state. He stressed that Lebanon’s treasury would bear no upfront investment costs.
He said he hoped to present the project to the Lebanese cabinet soon, adding that it should be prepared with support from the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and adhere to the highest standards of transparency, governance and financial viability.
Salam said the aim was not to add another promise to the many previously made about the electricity sector, but to establish a sustainable solution by increasing generation, lowering costs, diversifying energy sources and improving management.
Al Thani also said QatarEnergy had agreed with TotalEnergies to jointly develop a solar power plant in Lebanon. He described this as an initial project, saying the two countries were now working towards a broader framework for energy cooperation.
He said Qatar hoped to see an agreement take shape soon, allowing Qatari institutions to work alongside their Lebanese counterparts.
Salam said his government did not want to add "another promise to the many that the Lebanese have heard" about the electricity sector, but instead hoped to establish the foundations for a practical and sustainable solution based on increasing generation, lowering costs, diversifying energy sources and improving management.
"Reliable electricity at an affordable cost is essential to reviving the economy, encouraging investment, restarting productive businesses and easing the burden on citizens," he said.
Lebanon’s Energy Minister Joe Saddi recently announced that he would no longer take part in cabinet sessions, citing what he called a lack of seriousness in dealing with the crisis and saying he refused to be held responsible for the lack of progress in the sector.
Saddi and fellow ministers from the Lebanese Forces party walked out of a cabinet session on Thursday over the issue.
Years of blackouts
Lebanon has suffered a decades-long electricity crisis which saw the emergence of an unofficial and largely unregulated network of private generators across the country. These generators typically run on fuel oil, contributing significantly to poor air quality in cities, while charging consumers high prices.
The energy sector virtually collapsed following Lebanon’s 2019 financial collapse, with the national grid barely keeping the lights on for two hours a day. Before this, Beirut, where many of Lebanon’s government institutions are located, had up to 20 hours of electricity a day, with rotating blackouts in the rest of the country.
Much of Lebanon has gradually moved to renewable energy alternatives, relying on solar panels to manage their electricity needs, although this option remains somewhat limited in larger cities like Beirut due to restricted rooftop space in residential buildings.
There has been an outcry among generator subscribers this year, with bills reaching hundreds of US dollars a month in some areas. Operators, many of whom control supply in particular neighbourhoods and are linked to sectarian political parties, have attributed rising costs to higher global fuel prices as a result of the Middle East war.
Lebanon’s electricity sector is estimated to have cost the country more than $40 billion since the end of its 1975-1990 civil war, largely because of heavy subsidies and the cost of importing fuel for ageing power stations. These costs account for a substantial share of the treasury’s losses.

The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) has received a dossier concerning alleged corruption at the European Economic and Social Committee (EESC), following an administrative investigation by the EU’s anti-fraud agency OLAF.
OLAF transmitted its findings to the EPPO after investigating allegations that a senior EESC official manipulated public procurement contracts, news portal Rapporteur reported Friday.
The EESC confirmed that OLAF had referred the case to the EPPO.
“The EESC was informed by OLAF today that this case has been referred to the EPPO. Under these circumstances, the EESC cannot comment further,” an EESC spokesperson told the outlet.
The allegations, which emerged in March, concern Isabel Le Galo Flores, the EESC’s secretary-general, who has been accused of running the EU advisory body as her own private business and steering contracts toward personal associates.
She has declined to comment on the allegations.
The EPPO told Anadolu that it does not generally comment on ongoing investigations or publicly confirm the cases it is handling.
“As a general rule, the EPPO does not comment on ongoing investigations, nor do we publicly confirm which cases we are working on, in order not to endanger the possible ongoing procedures and their outcome,” the prosecutor’s office said.
Earlier this month, members of the European Parliament’s Budgetary Control Committee questioned the EESC over the allegations during an annual scrutiny process.
The committee has also faced criticism over its role and continued existence.
On Wednesday, French politician Marine Le Pen described the EESC and its sister body, the Committee of the Regions, as “completely pointless.”
The EESC is an EU advisory body established under the Treaty of Rome, representing employers, workers and other civil society groups in the bloc’s policymaking process.

Ethiopia appoints new Tigray administration, plans elections within 6 months
Unknown

2026-10-16

Andrew Wasike 
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government announced on Friday the appointment of a new interim administration for the northern Tigray region, giving it six months to restore stability, rebuild public institutions and organize elections following renewed fighting.  
"The people of Tigray must emerge from the agony of conflict to reclaim their distant peace, reaffirm their right to self-administration, and be able to heal the developmental setbacks they have suffered over the many past years," the prime minister's office said in a statement.  
The government said the House of Federation approved the suspension of Tigray's previous interim administration, paving the way for a new federally supervised leadership structure.
The new administration will be headed by Asefa Abrahaga Hagos as chief administrator, with Tewodros Aregeay W/Selassie overseeing economic recovery and reconstruction.
Brig. Gen. Gebretensae Whatna Haylu was appointed to oversee security and peace, while Redai Halefom W/Selassie will handle political affairs and mass mobilization. Shishay Amare was named mayor of Mekelle, Tigray's regional capital.
According to the statement, the administration's responsibilities include restoring essential public services, repairing war-damaged infrastructure, facilitating the return of displaced residents and preparing the region for elections.
The government said the interim authorities must establish conditions for a "free and fair election" within six months, with the aim of returning Tigray to an elected regional government.
The administration will also coordinate with federal security institutions and regional forces to restore security, encourage armed fighters to return to civilian life and support reconstruction.
Addis Ababa said the new leadership would operate under federal guidance and oversight until an elected government takes office.
The decision follows renewed fighting between Ethiopian federal troops and forces linked to the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which has threatened the fragile peace established under the November 2022 Pretoria agreement.
Government troops and allied Tigray Peace Force (TPF) fighters have recently expanded their control across the region, including Mekelle and several strategic towns near the Eritrean border.
The conflict has also heightened tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea, with Addis Ababa accusing Asmara of supporting armed opposition groups, allegations Eritrea denies.
On Wednesday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged de-escalation in a telephone conversation with Abiy, warning against cross-border incursions and calling for respect for neighboring countries' sovereignty.
Tigray remains deeply affected by the 2020-2022 war, which caused widespread destruction, mass displacement and a humanitarian crisis.

Any Houthi victory in Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, would mark one of the biggest turning points in the country's long civil war, which resumed this summer after a four-year truce.
Taiz has been on the frontline between the Houthis and the government since the first days of the conflict that started in early 2015 and has long been seen as a bastion of opposition to the Iran-allied group.

Italian prosecutors announced Friday that an investigation into allegations of torture, kidnapping and mistreatment of Italian activists aboard Gaza-bound flotillas includes Defense Minister Israel Katz, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir. The investigation, which also involves senior Israeli military, police and prison officials, follows complaints filed by 50 Italian citizens detained during Global Sumud Flotilla missions in October 2025 and May 2026. Ben-Gvir's inclusion in the investigation was first reported in June.
According to Italian news agency ANSA, the allegations include torture, kidnapping, boarding vessels in violation of international law, robbery, poor detention conditions, degrading treatment and violations of fundamental rights, including access to legal representation. Rome prosecutors said activists detained during the October 2025 flotilla reported beatings, injuries, death threats, insults and accusations of terrorism. Participants in the second mission, intercepted in May, described even harsher treatment, including beatings in the dark and the use of stun guns and rubber bullets.
Investigators said they had identified senior officials within the Israeli military and police chains of command involved in the operations. In addition to Katz, Ben-Gvir and Zamir, those named include former Navy commander Vice Adm. David Saar Salama and his successor, Vice Adm. Eyal Harel; senior naval officer Tal Politis; Shayetet 13 naval commando commander Col. Eldad Borochovich; and Ashdod naval base commander Col. Eitan Paz. The investigation also names Israel Police Commissioner Daniel Levy, Israel Prison Service Commissioner Kobi Yaakobi, Ketziot Prison commander Menachem Bibas, Assaf Zagori, commander of the prison service's Nahshon escort and intervention unit, and Border Police commander Yitzhak Brik.
Ben-Gvir's conduct toward detained flotilla activists had previously sparked outrage in Italy, prompting Rome to summon Israel's ambassador in protest. In footage the minister himself released from the port of Ashdod, he was seen confronting and mocking detained activists, including Italian nationals, as they knelt handcuffed and blindfolded with their faces toward the ground. Italian President Sergio Mattarella condemned the incident, saying Ben-Gvir had reached a "new low."
Katz has not publicly commented on the Italian investigation, and Reuters reported that he did not respond to a request for comment. Zamir has also yet to respond. Ben-Gvir previously rejected reports in June that he was under investigation in Rome, saying he would "continue to stand proudly alongside our fighters."
According to Reuters, prosecutors in Rome sent Israel a request for legal assistance in June, a month after the controversy over the treatment of detained activists. The request sought information needed to reconstruct the events and establish the individual responsibility of those involved. Prosecutors did not say whether Israeli authorities had responded.
Italian prosecutors also held discussions with Eurojust, the European Union agency responsible for judicial cooperation in criminal matters, because similar investigations into the two flotilla incidents are underway in other European countries. The prosecutors did not identify those countries.
Under Italian law, prosecutors in Rome can pursue criminal charges for offenses committed outside Italy against Italian citizens. However, being named in an investigation does not establish guilt or automatically lead to prosecution. If investigators determine that sufficient grounds exist to bring charges, prosecutors can submit a formal request to put the Israeli officials on trial.

Gas injection into Europe’s UGS facilities decreasing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:45:40 UTC
23:45:40 KST

MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. The rate of gas injection into underground gas storage (UGS) facilities in Europe continues to fall rapidly as temperatures in the region drop and prices rise, according to TASS calculations based on Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE) data.
To date, Europe has managed to fill its UGS facilities to 74% of the volumes required for the upcoming winter.
As of October 14, Europe’s UGS facilities were 74.1% full (14.85 percentage points below the five-year average for this date), compared to 83% in the previous year, which is still the lowest level recorded for this date since tracking began in 2011. EU storage facilities hold around 81 bln cubic meters of gas, which is 10.6 bln cubic meters lower than last year’s levels and the lowest volume since 2013.
The European Commission requests EU members to make sure their UGS facilities are 90% full between October 1 and December 1 of each year. Moreover, 10% flexibility is allowed in the event of difficult UGS filling conditions. Thus, net injection into European storage facilities by the start of the 2026-2027 autumn-winter period must reach at least 68 bcm to meet the filling standard.

Russia Eyes AI-Powered VPN Crackdown With 95% Blocking Accuracy
Russian authorities considered using AI to identify and block VPN services with up to 95% effectiveness, according to Kommersant on October 16.
The proposal appeared in a draft national plan for introducing artificial intelligence technologies through 2030. It envisioned AI analyzing the characteristics of 70% of VPN services targeted for blocking.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russia’s Digital Development Ministry stated that the measure is absent from the plan’s current version.
Russia currently uses what Kommersant described as “intelligent algorithms” to analyze internet traffic, but these systems are not considered AI. The ministry also plans to increase the capacity of its traffic-filtering infrastructure 2.5-fold to 954 terabits per second by 2030.
“AI automates and accelerates the analysis of connection patterns,” a source in the Russian networking industry told Kommersant. The technology could analyze packet size and timing, session duration, traffic ratios, hosting providers, and neighboring IP addresses to indirectly identify VPN infrastructure.
Industry sources cautioned that introducing AI could also increase false positives, resulting in legitimate traffic being blocked. One source estimated that the current error rate is already 5% to 6%, while another warned that early-stage AI systems could produce significant numbers of incorrect blocks.
The proposed AI layer would operate alongside Russia’s existing technical systems for countering threats, or TSPU, which are installed on telecom operators’ networks. A source noted that AI-based VPN detection would also require large-scale telemetry storage, computing clusters for model training, and infrastructure to distribute updated models to filtering nodes.
The push to detect VPN traffic is part of a broader effort by Moscow to tighten state control over mobile communications.
A day earlier, a draft Digital Development Ministry order surfaced requiring smartphones on Russia's future 5G networks to support Kuznyechik, an FSB-developed encryption algorithm, starting March 1, 2032.
Because the algorithm falls outside international 3GPP standards and must be built into modem chipsets, compliance could force Apple, Samsung, and Chinese manufacturers to produce Russia-specific hardware.

Russian Attacks Leave 2,433 Ukrainian Civilians Dead or Injured in September—85% More Than a Year Ago, UN Says

Russian Attacks Leave 2,433 Ukrainian Civilians Dead or Injured in September—85% More Than a Year Ago, UN Says
At least 328 civilians were killed and another 2,105 injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine in September 2026, bringing the total number of civilian casualties to 85% above the level recorded during the same month last year, according to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine.
In its latest report, published on October 16, the UN mission documented civilian deaths and injuries across 22 Ukrainian regions and the capital, Kyiv, with particularly high casualty figures recorded in Kyiv, Kherson, Kharkiv, Sumy, and Zaporizhzhia.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Ukrainian capital experienced an unprecedented frequency of civilian casualties, with deaths or injuries recorded on 22 of the 30 days in September. According to the mission, this was more frequent than in any previous month since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
The UN emphasized that the intensified attacks in September continued a broader trend observed throughout 2026, with civilian casualty figures significantly exceeding those documented in previous years.
The situation remained critical into October, with UN monitors reporting that the first two weeks of the month were among the deadliest periods for civilians in recent years.
“The first two weeks of October were among the deadliest for civilians in recent years,” said Danielle Bell, head of the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine. “In just a few days, attacks by Russian armed forces resulted in mass-casualty incidents in Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, Kramatorsk, and Kyiv.”
The mission also documented civilian casualties in Ukrainian territories temporarily occupied by Russia. Its verified September figures included 18 civilians killed and 44 injured in those areas.
However, UN officials cautioned that the actual number of casualties in Russian-occupied territories was likely considerably higher, as limited access and a lack of independent information sources continued to complicate the verification of incidents.
The increase in civilian casualties during September and October coincided with renewed systematic Russian attacks against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
According to UN experts, Russian forces resumed widespread strikes on energy facilities across the country, triggering emergency electricity outages and further disrupting civilian life.
The intensified strikes also come amid reports of critical shortages in Ukraine’s air defense capabilities, potentially leaving the country increasingly vulnerable to further Russian ballistic missile attacks.
A source familiar with the situation told CNN on October 15 that Ukraine had exhausted its supply of interceptor missiles for US-manufactured Patriot air defense systems.
The reported shortage has reportedly undermined Ukraine’s ability to intercept incoming ballistic missiles, with the source telling CNN that “almost all the ballistic missiles from the last strike were not intercepted due to lack of the (interceptor) missiles.”

Why Ethiopia and Eritrea&#8217;s march to war demands global attention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:39:18 UTC
23:39:18 KST

The distant thunder of drones over Adigrat is not merely another African conflict. It is the sound of a continent’s most fragile peace shattering—and with it, the already slender prospects for stability across the Red Sea corridor that carries twelve per cent of global trade. Barely eight years after Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and President Isaias Afwerki embraced in Asmara, a Nobel Peace Prize laureate’s handshake now lies in ruins.
Eritrean troops have crossed into northern Tigray, advancing up to sixty kilometres into Ethiopian territory. Ethiopia has responded with multiple drone strikes targeting those forces, destroying lorries and ammunition, witnesses say, amid reports of civilian deaths. Both nations have severed diplomatic ties.
Ethiopia calls it an “all-out invasion.” Eritrea calls it an “unprovoked war of aggression.” The truth matters less than the trajectory: two of Africa’s most battle-hardened armies are edging toward a conflagration neither can afford, yet both seem convinced they cannot avoid.
The roots of this rupture are not mysterious. They are anchored in geography so cruel it functions as destiny. Ethiopia, home to 130 million people, is the world’s most populous landlocked nation. It depends on Djibouti for over 95 per cent of its maritime trade, paying between $1.5 and $2 billion annually in port fees—a haemorrhage equivalent to the cost of building a Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam every three years.
A nation that once commanded the Red Sea through the ancient port of Adulis now watches its commerce squeezed through a single corridor. This is not merely an economic inconvenience. It is a structural wound that successive Ethiopian leaders have described in existential terms.
Abiy’s response has been to demand sovereign maritime access—specifically, to the Eritrean port of Assab, barely sixty kilometres from the Ethiopian border. Eritrea, which won independence in 1993 after a thirty-year liberation struggle, views this as nothing less than a threat to its territorial integrity and the very meaning of its statehood. Asmara’s information minister has accused Ethiopia of openly working to bring about regime change by sheltering and supporting armed opposition groups. The result is a security dilemma of terrifying symmetry: each side’s defensive measures confirm the other’s worst fears.
Into this vacuum have stepped external powers with interests that have little to do with Ethiopian or Eritrean welfare. Israel has publicly endorsed Ethiopia’s Red Sea ambitions, with its ambassador describing support for the effort as “clear Israeli policy.”
The strategic logic is cold: a strong, allied Ethiopia provides a non-Arab anchor in a region where Israel seeks to counter Iranian and Houthi influence, and where its recognition of Somaliland has already signalled a willingness to redraw regional alignments. The United Arab Emirates, Ethiopia’s largest investor and a quiet supplier of military technology, forms the other pillar of this de facto axis.
The United States, by contrast, has intervened with uncharacteristic directness. On 14 October, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Abiy that “the region cannot tolerate more conflict,” demanding respect for sovereignty and an immediate halt to cross-border incursions. Washington has even lifted certain sanctions on Eritrea—a pragmatic pivot driven not by any moral reassessment but by the urgent need to secure Red Sea shipping lanes against Houthi attacks. This is containment dressed as diplomacy, and it carries an uncomfortable implication: accountability for Eritrea’s role in the Tigray war has been quietly subordinated to maritime security.
The regional picture is equally troubling. Egypt and Sudan have aligned themselves with Eritrea, driven by their own existential anxieties over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Cairo views the dam as a threat to its 97 per cent dependence on the Nile. Addis Ababa views it as a sovereign right.
The result is a “river-versus-sea” confrontation in which the Nile and the Red Sea have become inseparable theatres of competition. Ethiopia’s army chief has openly accused Egypt and Sudan of backing the very rebels now fighting federal forces.
The human cost of this geopolitical chess game is already being paid. The 2020–2022 Tigray war killed an estimated 600,000 people. A renewed interstate conflict—this time involving heavy drone strikes, conventional armies, and the potential spillover onto Eritrea’s Red Sea coast—would create a humanitarian catastrophe of a different magnitude entirely. Millions of Ethiopians already face severe food insecurity.
The fragile Pretoria Agreement that ended the Tigray war has dissolved into renewed fighting across Amhara and Afar, with former allies now united in an armed alliance against the federal government. Ethiopia cannot fight a civil war and an interstate war simultaneously without fracturing.
Yet the most disturbing truth is that neither Washington’s pressure nor the African Union’s exhortations have altered the trajectory. The AU, headquartered in Addis Ababa, is structurally compromised—it cannot credibly mediate a conflict involving its host nation.
The Gulf states possess the financial leverage to broker a settlement, but the UAE’s deep ties to Ethiopia and Saudi Arabia’s alignment with Egypt make a unified mediation unlikely. The window for diplomacy is closing, and it is closing fast.
What is required is not another communiqué. It is a recognition that Ethiopia’s landlocked status is not a moral failing to be corrected by force, but a structural reality that demands a structural solution. The path forward lies in negotiated maritime access frameworks, joint port management arrangements, and regional economic integration that makes war materially irrational.
Ethiopia’s accession to the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System in October 2026 offered a glimpse of what patient, institutional cooperation could achieve. That glimpse is now being extinguished by the roar of drones.
The international community must act with a clarity that matches the urgency. The United States, the Gulf states, and the African Union must coordinate a single, unambiguous message: there is no military solution. But pressure alone is insufficient. The world’s strategic powers must offer Ethiopia a credible economic alternative—guaranteed, legally binding access to Red Sea ports under international law, backed by investment and infrastructure. Eritrea, for its part, must be assured that its sovereignty is not a bargaining chip.
The Horn of Africa has burned before. The world watched then, and the world did too little. It must not watch again. The drones over Adigrat are not a warning. They are a countdown.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

CineCrossroads: What to watch this weekend - “Heart of the Beast,” “City of God” and “Fantastic Mr. Fox”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:32:15 UTC
23:32:15 KST

CineCrossroads: What to watch this weekend - “Heart of the Beast,” “City of God” and “Fantastic Mr. Fox”
The weekend is approaching, bringing three stories about survival in worlds where danger can emerge from nature, violence or one’s own choices. In this edition of CineCrossroads, a soldier and his dog fight their way through the Alaskan wilderness, a young photographer searches for an escape from the violence surrounding him, and a clever fox risks everything by returning to his criminal ways. Qazinform News Agency correspondent wishes you an enjoyable viewing.
Movie of the Week: Heart of the Beast (2026)
In the wilderness, survival depends on trust between a man and his most loyal companion.
Directed by David Ayer, Heart of the Beast stars Brad Pitt as James Belmont, a Special Forces officer who survives a devastating plane crash alongside his combat dog, Odin. Stranded deep in the Alaskan wilderness, the pair must confront extreme weather, dangerous terrain and the physical limits of their endurance.
Belmont’s military experience gives him the skills needed to stay alive, but the isolation forces him to rely equally on Odin. Their relationship forms the emotional center of the film, transforming a traditional survival thriller into a story about loyalty, trauma and the bond between humans and animals.
Released in cinemas on September 25, Heart of the Beast reunites Pitt with Ayer after their collaboration on the 2014 war drama Fury. It is a fitting choice for viewers seeking action, striking natural landscapes and an emotional story about companionship under the most difficult circumstances.
Classic Pick: City of God (2002)
In a neighborhood ruled by violence, a camera offers one young man a different path.
Directed by Fernando Meirelles and Kátia Lund, City of God follows several interconnected lives in a housing project outside Rio de Janeiro. At the center of the story is Rocket, a quiet boy who dreams of becoming a photographer rather than joining the criminal world surrounding him.
As rival gangs compete for control, Rocket documents a community shaped by poverty, ambition and fear. His photographs gradually become both a record of the violence and a possible route out of it.
Driven by energetic editing, vivid performances and an unforgettable visual style, City of God presents violence without turning it into simple entertainment. More than two decades after its release, it remains a powerful examination of how opportunity, environment and personal choices can determine the course of a life.
Family Pick: Fantastic Mr. Fox (2009)
Some animals are simply not made for an ordinary life.
Directed by Wes Anderson and based on Roald Dahl’s beloved book, Fantastic Mr. Fox follows a former thief who has promised his wife that he will leave his dangerous habits behind. Years later, frustrated by domestic routine, Mr. Fox secretly begins stealing from three wealthy and ruthless farmers.
His actions place his family and the entire local animal community in danger. To protect them, he must use the same intelligence and daring that created the crisis in the first place.
Featuring stop-motion animation and the voices of George Clooney, Meryl Streep and Jason Schwartzman, Fantastic Mr. Fox combines dry humor, family adventure and carefully crafted visuals. Beneath its playful surface is a thoughtful story about identity, responsibility and learning to protect the people who depend on us.

South African coalition government faces fresh rift
South Africa’s African National Congress (ANC) has called for the Democratic Alliance’s place in the coalition government to be reviewed after its governing partner opposed its court bid to reinstate barred election candidates.
Mbalula has urged ANC leaders and other Government of National Unity (GNU) partners to reconsider the DA’s place in government, opening a new front in a partnership repeatedly tested by political and policy disagreements. The GNU is made up of 10 political parties.
The latest dispute centres on the ANC’s legal challenge over the exclusion of its candidates from six municipalities ahead of the November 4, 2026, local government election. The party approached the Constitutional Court after its failure to finalise candidate submissions before the deadline left candidates off the ballot.
The DA opposed the ANC’s challenge, putting the coalition partners on opposing sides of a legal battle with potentially significant electoral consequences. The apex heard the case on October 12 and reserved judgment. The outcome could determine whether the affected ANC candidates will be allowed to contest the elections.
Mbalula’s call for a review comes amid mounting disagreements between the ANC and DA over policy, budgets and decision-making since the GNU was formed in 2024. The parties have clashed over the National Health Insurance Act, the Basic Education Laws Amendment Act, land expropriation and proposed value-added tax increases. They have also traded accusations over consultation and the handling of major government decisions.
The DA has repeatedly criticised what it sees as unilateral action by the ANC, while the governing party has continued to advance policies that the DA opposes.
These disputes have tested a coalition formed after the ANC lost its parliamentary majority in the 2024 national elections. Mbalula’s demand puts the DA’s role in the coalition under renewed political scrutiny.

In space, no one hears Zelensky scream: No euros can buy Kiev options in orbit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:28:53 UTC
23:28:53 KST

In space, no one hears Zelensky scream: No euros can buy Kiev options in orbit
No matter how European leaders pledge to support Ukraine come hell or high water and let the taxpayers foot the bill, the cold hard fact is that there are things no euros can buy, such as US intelligence and satellite communications.
Kiev’s critical reliance on American space capabilities came to the fore this week when the long-standing feud between US President Donald Trump and Vladimir Zelensky flared up again. Trump, who had struck a diesel supply deal with Russia, called Zelensky a hindrance to peace who should be replaced. Zelensky called Trump a weakling who had betrayed Ukraine, if not in those exact terms.
According to lamentations from Kiev corroborated by media reporting, the White House put a chokehold on the Zelensky government by suspending early warning about incoming Russian ballistic missiles and temporarily suspending access to Starlink satellite internet for fast-moving objects – such as drones used in Kiev’s “middle strike” operations inside what Washington recognizes as part of Ukraine.
It’s not like Kiev was not warned. During a meeting in Miami last week, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reportedly told the Ukrainians the diesel deal announcement was coming and that Kiev should not have ignored Trump’s multiple requests to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Accounts shared with Axios and Reuters suggest the Americans were polite enough not to say “what a nice deal to get intelligence and internet you have; it would be a shame if something happened to it.” But they mentioned “all that the US has done for Ukraine.” The Ukrainians did take it as a threat.
Here are the alternatives Kiev would have, should Trump push the issue further.
No match for US intelligence
Intelligence that European NATO members can provide is a far cry from what the US has been delivering for years. Already, early warning about Russian ballistic missile launches has stopped coming, just as Zelensky is complaining.
The US operates the Space-Based Infrared System (SBIRS), whose backbone is six geosynchronous orbit satellites equipped with thermal sensors that detect launch signatures, complemented by two active and two reserve payloads in a highly elliptical orbit.
SBIRS helps identify and estimate the trajectory of a weapon, but has limited ability to track missiles after the intensive boost phase. But knowing one is incoming helps ground and airborne radar systems that guide interceptor missiles.
Other NATO members rely on SBIRS intelligence and never thought they would need their own alternative.
Satellites operated by the US National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) and the Air Force’s electronic reconnaissance aircraft, such as the RC-135U Combat Sent, also collect intelligence about Russian air defense systems. It’s unclear how much data it shares with Kiev, but the media has said the US helps plan Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russia to minimize Moscow’s ability to intercept.
European NATO members do have some similar capabilities, including France’s three CERES electronic-intelligence satellites, the UK’s three RC-135W Rivet Joint aircraft, and Germany’s SARah radar-reconnaissance space program, but there is only so much they can do to measure up to the world’s largest military spender.
OneWeb not to rule them all
On the connectivity side, Starlink and its military twin Starshield remain the most capable today. It has over 11,000 satellites in low Earth (LEO) orbit that can use lasers to route traffic between each other, boosting their bandwidth.
The Starlink Mini terminal weighs just 1.1 kg and has an integrated antenna, making it usable even on even smaller military drones. Even larger variants are compact, which makes them harder to spot, and they typically consume under 100 watts of power – both valuable features in frontline applications.
The most direct non-US alternative is Eutelsat OneWeb, which already complements Starlink access in Ukraine. It only has 600+ satellites in its constellation, but nevertheless offers a high-speed connection.
However, OneWeb’s orbital component “remains rooted in an outdated architecture and technology conceived a decade ago, without any evolution of its underlying design,” Christian Freiherr von der Ropp, an independent satellite consultant, told Reuters.
OneWeb ground hardware is likewise no match for Starlink in price, size, or appetite for energy. The relatively small Hughes HL1100W terminal weighs over 10 kg and consumes around 130 watts, though there are efforts to produce smaller and less power-hungry equipment.
Kymeta Corporation announced a OneWeb terminal in March whose 100-watt consumption it said was optimized for mobile platforms. Its “compact and lightweight design” means it weighs less than 11 kg, and the producer itself is Redmond, Washington.
Dark horses in orbit
In September, EU co-founder Luxembourg announced the successful launch of the final three of a planned 13 satellites of its O3b mPOWER communication system. The low number is misleading, since the constellation is being positioned in medium Earth orbit and requires fewer satellites for coverage.
The trade off is latency, which is higher by an order of magnitude compared to LEO-based systems, but Luxembourg’s system is still good enough for some military applications and is used by NATO.
O3b mPOWER’s potential for Ukraine’s war effort is limited due to its coverage, which is between 50° north latitude and 50° south latitude. Luxembourg is right on the northern border of the band, but a large part of Ukraine, including Kiev, is outside of it. As they say, geography is destiny.
GOVSATCOM, the EU’s program to band together communication satellites owned by several member states, is somewhat of a dark horse, but public data suggests its capabilities are too limited to replace Starlink.
Amazon Leo is currently in limited preview, but it’s hard to expect an American company and a major Pentagon contractor to publicly defy Trump at Brussels’ call. Russia’s in-development Rassvet system is obviously not an option.
The EU’s proposed IRIS² system is years away from being operational, as is Canada’s Telesat Lightspeed.
In short, should Ukraine lose Starlink, in the short term Europe cannot replace it, as EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas acknowledged on Friday.

KAZAN, October 16. /TASS/. India intends to recognize the Russian language proficiency as a professional skill in the near future, Deputy Secretary of the Indian Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship Amit Kumar said at the 2nd Russian-Indian Business Forum titled "TIME: Tatarstan Initiative Mutual Efficiency" in Kazan, the capital of Russia’s Volga area region of Tatarstan.
"Another focus of our work is recognizing language proficiency as a qualification, treating language knowledge as a skill. According to Kumar, India is also developing early adaptation programs for students, identifying the qualifications they need to work in Russia. "India believes that the future of the labor field is built on partnership, where skills move, opportunities expand and economies grow together. We see huge potential here, including for the development of joint curricula, mutual recognition of skills, training of instructors, partnerships between Indian and Russian educational centers and cooperation on teaching the Russian language," he added.

The ruling was issued by Rabbi Dov Lior, one of the most prominent religious authorities among Israeli occupiers in the West Bank, and was published by Israeli Channel 13.
It comes amid escalating occupier violence against Palestinians and their property, particularly farmers during the olive harvest season.
Lior claimed that Palestinians do not own their land, arguing that they had not purchased it from the “people of Israel” or from any Jewish person and describing the land as “stolen property.”
Citing Jewish religious law, he claimed that ownership of land cannot be transferred through theft and that Palestinian land therefore remains the property of the “people of Israel.”
He also argued that Palestinians planting olive trees on their land does not give them ownership rights over either the land or its produce.
Lior claimed Palestinians had already received sufficient compensation for planting the trees by consuming their fruit over previous years, and said both the land and harvest should return to what he called their “rightful owners.”
His ruling was not limited to land near illegal settlements, however, and also permitted occupiers to take olive crops from Palestinian areas farther away.
The ruling comes as attacks on Palestinian farmers during the West Bank olive harvest season have intensified, including assaults, preventing farmers from reaching their land, damaging trees and stealing crops.
Such attacks recur during the olive harvest, which peaks in October each year, while this month has seen an increase in attacks by occupiers against Palestinians and their property.
Palestinian, Israeli and international rights organizations have accused Israeli authorities of failing to stop occupier violence or hold perpetrators accountable despite attacks targeting Palestinians, their homes, farmland, vehicles and other property.
Israeli settlements built on occupied Palestinian land are considered illegal under international law, while Palestinians maintain their rights to their land and reject attempts to seize it.

“We have agreed to establish a comprehensive framework for cooperation in the energy sector and to present viable solutions,” Sheikh Mohammed said.

The aim is to develop a major investment project “that would benefit the Lebanese economy, as well as the Qatari companies and entities participating in it”, he added.
Prime Minister Salam said he would put the plans for Lebanon’s electricity sector to the Lebanese Cabinet soon.
“The Qatari side will fund, implement and activate the project without any cost on the Lebanese state,” Lebanon’s leader said, adding that such a move is important because of the country’s financial crisis.
Lebanon’s state electricity company is one of the biggest sources of debt, haemorrhaging about $40bn over past decades with a bloated workforce and outdated infrastructure. The company provides only a few hours of electricity a day and the state, until a year ago, took advances from the Central Bank when diesel fuel ran out.
Sheikh Mohammed said Doha stands in “solidarity with the Lebanese people” and the entire region “in this dire hour”. Lebanon has been struggling with multiple energy crises in recent years and the situation has been compounded by the country’s financial collapse and Israel’s ongoing assault.

Israeli attacks on southern Lebanon have continued despite a ceasefire agreed in June. Under the agreement brokered by the US, the Lebanese government is to disarm Iran-backed Hezbollah. In return, Israeli forces will gradually withdraw from southern areas that they occupy. However, Hezbollah is not part of the agreement and has refused to disarm until Israel withdraws from the country.

Lebanon’s PM Salam thanked Qatar for its “continuous” support during some of Lebanon’s “darkest hours”.

Russian wrestler strikes gold at world championships in US
