Ukraine exports gas for first time since start of full-scale war
Companies sold about 12.75 million cubic metres of natural gas at the first export auction held by the Ukrainian Energy Exchange (UEEX) on 15 October.
Source: the auction results published by the UEEX
Details: The sale prices ranged from €69 to €69.03 per MWh.
The largest volume was sold by Naftogazvydobuvannia PrJSC, at about 7.78 million cubic metres. The remaining gas was sold by Naftohazdiia LLC, Naftohazheorozvidka LLC and Kosul LLC. All four companies belong to the DTEK Group, Ukraine's largest private energy company.
In total, they sold about 12.31 million cubic metres of gas.
All four companies initially offered the gas at €87 per MWh. The final prices were about 21% lower. They were also 19% below the last recorded price at the Dutch TTF hub, which stood at €85.5 per MWh.
The export price was 89% higher than the domestic price.
Deliveries are scheduled to take place at the Polish border between 26 October and 31 December. Full prepayment is required for all lots. Deliveries will proceed subject to the sellers obtaining the relevant export licences from the Ministry of Economy.
For reference: Following the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, the government banned gas exports. A government decision on 7 October 2026 reintroduced permission to export gas.
Background:
- In late August, Ukraine accumulated enough gas to meet the basic scenario for getting through the winter.
- The export sales limit stands at 15% of the volume of gas delivered by a producer to the gas transmission system in the previous month. Gas exports are prohibited during winter.

Laboratory worker Darya Shipilova, 28, died on October 2 after reportedly breaking a test tube containing live bacteria at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute, and hundreds of her contacts were placed in quarantine.
Russian authorities attributed her death to unidentified pneumonia and denied that an outbreak was occurring. Unconfirmed reports of a second death emerged on October 6, while Mongolia, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan tightened health controls.

TikTok’s Career Ladder Creator Max Klymenko and Etnodim Turn Ukraine’s Fading Traditional Crafts Into Charity Shirt
Ukrainian embroidered clothing brand Etnodim has partnered with British content creator of Ukrainian origin Max Klymenko to launch a charity shirt inspired by his popular TikTok series Career Ladder, with profits from sales going toward supporting Ukrainian children affected by Russia’s war.
The collaboration brings together Klymenko’s internationally recognized social media project, which has helped him attract nearly 10 million TikTok followers, and traditional Ukrainian craftsmanship.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In his Career Ladder series, Klymenko interviews people from a wide range of professions, including public figures such as Will Smith, Gordon Ramsay, French President Emmanuel Macron, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
The concept of exploring different careers inspired Klymenko and the Etnodim team to highlight traditional Ukrainian occupations, some of which are gradually disappearing.
The resulting shirt features embroidered representations of historic crafts and professions, including blacksmithing, pottery, harvesting, and milling, reflecting the importance of preserving Ukraine’s cultural heritage.
“We wanted to convey the idea of equal opportunities without stereotypes and remind people that every profession has its own value. The embroidery features traditional Ukrainian crafts that are gradually disappearing, including blacksmithing, pottery, harvesting and milling. The composition on the shirt’s side panel is inspired by Apple Picker, a work by Ukrainian artist Oleksandr Saienko,” the Etnodim team explains.
Beyond its connection to the TikTok series, the design also draws on Klymenko’s personal memories of growing up in Ukraine, particularly his childhood experiences with his grandmother.
According to the press release, conversations about his upbringing, family memories, and current work helped shape the creative direction of the collaboration.
“When I think about my childhood, I immediately think of my grandmother: the time I spent with her, the little forts made of yarn I used to build when visiting her, and all the wonderful things in her house that have stayed in my memory. Decorative plates, a large wooden spoon with classic red and colourful Ukrainian patterns, and a knitted picture of Mykolaiv landscapes hanging on the wall—that picture is probably the most vivid work of art I remember from childhood,” Klymenko said.
The partnership also reflects Klymenko’s continued involvement in charitable initiatives supporting Ukraine and his efforts to introduce Ukrainian culture and experiences to international audiences.
As part of the initiative, profits from sales of the Career Ladder shirt will be donated to Kids of Ukraine to support its SviTY programme, which assists teenagers affected by the war.
The programme focuses on emotional recovery, education, and personal development, helping young people acquire new skills, identify their strengths, and explore future career opportunities.
Through the collaboration, Etnodim and Klymenko aim to combine the promotion of traditional Ukrainian crafts with practical support for children and teenagers navigating their futures amid the ongoing war.
In another recent collaboration, German sportswear brand PUMA joined forces with Ukrainian fashion label CHER’17, marking its first partnership with a local fashion brand in Ukraine.
According to a press release, the CHER’17 x PUMA collection explores the unpredictability of everyday life under the campaign slogan “No plan is a plan.” The collection reinterprets PUMA’s signature designs through details inspired by unexpected mishaps and everyday imperfections.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Ukraine Could Get Starlink Deep Inside Russia in Exchange for 100-Day Oil Strike Pause, WSJ Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

21:10:35 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Could Get Starlink Deep Inside Russia in Exchange for 100-Day Oil Strike Pause, WSJ Says
Two Republican US senators have proposed expanding Starlink coverage roughly 300 kilometers, or 186 miles, inside Russia in exchange for Ukraine suspending strikes on Russian oil refineries for 100 days, The Wall Street Journal reported on October 15, citing people familiar with the discussions.
Senators Roger Wicker and Kevin Cramer presented the proposal to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during an October 9 visit to Kyiv as part of a bipartisan congressional delegation, according to the report.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Zelenskyy indicated that he was prepared to accept such an arrangement, the sources said.
The expanded coverage could give Ukrainian forces reliable satellite connectivity during operations against Russian ballistic missile launchers located deeper behind the border.
That would potentially allow Ukraine to target the systems before they launch missiles rather than relying solely on air defenses to intercept incoming weapons after they are fired.
Zelenskyy has publicly said Ukraine could also consider halting strikes on Russian refineries in return for additional US-made Patriot interceptors. The Starlink proposal would offer a different form of protection by helping Ukrainian forces target the launch platforms themselves.
According to the WSJ, the senators viewed the proposed arrangement as a possible first step toward reviving a stalled diplomatic process.
The discussions come amid growing pressure from Washington for Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian oil infrastructure. US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on October 11, after which Ukraine temporarily suspended strikes on Russian energy facilities.
Despite Kyiv observing the pause, Ukrainian forces subsequently stopped receiving US early warnings about Russian ballistic missile launches, according to Ukrainian officials. The military version of Starlink, Starshield, was also restricted, complicating frontline operations and middle-strike missions against Russian military targets.
Reuters separately reported that the instruction to restrict Starshield came from the White House, although its sources did not identify who specifically ordered the measure. A senior US official said Trump personally had not issued the order.
Previously, Ukraine lifted restrictions on strikes against Russian oil refineries and other energy infrastructure after observing a three-day pause requested by Washington, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated.
“The ban has been lifted. We’ve had enough,” Zelenskyy said.

Head of State Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has addressed the COP17 Leaders’ Summit on Biodiversity in Yerevan, Armenia, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the press service of Akorda.
Welcoming the Summit participants, the Head of State thanked the Prime Minister of Armenia, Nikol Pashinyan, for a warm welcome and a high level of organization of the event.
In his remarks, the President emphasized the need to coordinate international efforts and uphold a shared responsibility to future generations for preserving the environment
"We have gathered here to expand international cooperation aimed at preserving our shared natural heritage. This is a collective responsibility to future generations, who may face serious challenges and threats. It is also a matter of survival for our civilization, as biodiversity is vital to human well-being, economic resilience, and long-term security. Healthy ecosystems play a crucial role in food production, the protection of water resources, and the livelihoods of millions of people.
At the same time, desertification, water scarcity, and other environmental challenges pose a serious threat to the fragile balance between people and nature. For millions, water shortages and land degradation have already become an everyday reality. Most concerning is that these processes transcend national borders, undermining sustainable development and threatening global stability.
Environmental agenda, based on a balanced approach and concrete action, must take precedence over political differences. Our shared priority should be international cooperation based on true partnership, impartiality, and, above all, a commitment to achieve practical results," the President said.

Tokayev highlights Kazakhstan's success in restoring rare animal populations

Tokayev highlights Kazakhstan's success in restoring rare animal populations
President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said Kazakhstan has achieved significant progress in biodiversity conservation, citing the recovery of populations of the saiga antelope, snow leopard, Turan tiger, Przewalski's horse and Caspian seal, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the press service of Akorda.
The President described the revival of the saiga population as one of the country's greatest conservation achievements.
“This ancient animal survived the last Ice Age and remains very essential to the natural balance of our steppes. Today Kazakhstan is home to around 98 percent of the world’s saiga population. In 2003, just 21,000 species remained in our country. By the spring of this year, their numbers had reached an estimated 4.7 million,” Tokayev said.
He also noted encouraging signs in the recovery of the snow leopard, “a proud symbol of our mountain heritage.”
“Around 70 percent of its range in our country are within protected areas. Reliable and sustained protection and systematic scientific monitoring have helped its population grow from critically low levels of 90s last century to nearly 190 animals today. Behind all these recoveries are years of hard and dedicated, determined work by the authorities, scientists and international partners,” he noted.
Kassym-Jomart Tokayev expressed his gratitude to the Russian Federation and its President, as well as the United Nations Development Programme, the World Wildlife Fund, and other international partners, including NGOs, for their assistance in restoring the population of the Turan tiger.
He emphasized that in July this year, a tiger was released into the wild for the first time in 70 years, marking a milestone for Kazakhstan.
The Head of State also noted that efforts are underway, in cooperation with Czech, German and Hungarian partners, to reintroduce the Przewalski’s horse to Kazakhstan.
The President also highlighted the need to protect the Caspian Sea and its unique biodiversity.
“At the recent first Caspian Environmental Summit in Turkmenistan, I called for urgent, coordinated action to prevent fatal damage to this fragile ecosystem. The future of Caspian seals causes a particular concern. Its population has fallen from one million to 270,000 over the past century. In Kazakhstan, the Caspian seal has been officially listed as a rare and endangered animal. We urge all five littoral states and international community to increase efforts to protect these species. The tragedy of the Aral Sea is a stark reminder of the devastating cost of reckless exploitation of nature and we must not allow the Caspian Sea to suffer the same fate,” Kassym-Jomart Tokayev emphasized
Earlier, it was reported that Kassym-Jomart Tokayev arrived at the Meridian Expo and Event Center in Yerevan, Armenia, to attend the COP17 Leaders' Summit on Biodiversity.
Addressing the summit, the President called for greater international cooperation to preserve biodiversity and presented the Taza Qazaqstan initiative.

Starvation killed 466 Palestinians since 2024, says Gaza Health Ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:05:11 UTC
21:05:11 KST

- More than 1.4M people are expected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through end of 2026.
- More than 158,000 cases of acute malnutrition recorded among children under 5
At least 466 Palestinians, including 157 children, have died from malnutrition and starvation since 2024, Gaza's Health Ministry said Friday.
The figures were released on World Food Day, observed annually on Oct. 16.
At least 189 elderly people died of starvation, representing 40.5% of the deaths, it said.
In August 2025, the UN declared famine in Gaza.
More than 1.4 million people are expected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026, the ministry added.
 
Starvation as a weapon
Israeli authorities have used starvation as a weapon during the genocide in Gaza since October 2023, according to Palestinian government bodies and rights organizations.
Israel tightened restrictions on crossings in March 2025, preventing thousands of aid trucks waiting at border crossings from entering the enclave.
The restrictions followed widespread hunger in northern Gaza caused by the blockade and limits on food and relief supplies, forcing some residents to eat animal feed and wild plants.
In late May 2025, Israel allowed 87 aid trucks to enter Gaza for the first time after 81 days, according to Gaza’s government media office.
Aid later continued to enter on a limited and intermittent basis under strict restrictions until February 2026, when Israel allowed a limited increase in the number of trucks entering the enclave under a ceasefire agreement.
Palestinian officials said the shipments still lacked sufficient quantities of essential food items.
According to Gaza’s government media office, Israel has allowed in only about 34% of the humanitarian aid trucks agreed upon.
 
Malnutrition reaches 'catastrophic levels'
“Malnutrition and starvation rates in Gaza have reached catastrophic levels that are killing children, the elderly and vulnerable groups,” the Health Ministry said.
More than 1.4 million Palestinians, around 67% of Gaza’s population, are expected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026.
More than 158,000 cases of acute malnutrition were recorded among children under 5 from 2024 through August 2026, the ministry added.
Of them, 18% of children were suffering from severe acute malnutrition that threatened their lives, while 12.2% of children were affected by stunting, indicating the impact of food shortages on their development.
The mortality rate among children under 5 rose from 13.6 to 33.4 deaths per 1,000 live births between 2022 and 2025, the ministry said.
It estimated that 74,200 children will need treatment for acute malnutrition through April 2027.
 
Pregnant women
Among pregnant women, the ministry said the prevalence of anemia rose to 61% in 2026, compared with 41% before the war.
“Around 4,000 pregnancy losses were recorded during the first half of 2026, more than three times the number recorded during the previous six months,” it added.
“One in three pregnancies in Gaza is now classified as high-risk,” the ministry continued.
“The figures show that the health consequences of the food crisis are increasingly affecting mothers and unborn children, in addition to children,” it said.
 
Calls for urgent international action
“The right to food is a fundamental human right that does not cease to exist during war,” the ministry said.
It called on the international community and the UN to take immediate action to ensure the safe, sustained and unrestricted entry of food, therapeutic nutritional supplements and medicines into Gaza.
The ministry urged that children, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and the elderly be given priority as the groups most vulnerable to malnutrition.
It also called for support to revive local food production to help curb the worsening humanitarian crisis.
The figures come amid the humanitarian consequences of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, which has caused widespread destruction to infrastructure, health facilities and food production sources.
The war has also damaged farmland, food production facilities and water networks, undermining residents’ ability to meet their basic needs locally.
Repeated displacement, loss of income and soaring prices have further increased families’ dependence on humanitarian aid, while access remains irregular.

Somalia sets date for delayed presidential election

Somalia sets date for delayed presidential election
Somalia has scheduled its presidential election for May 15, 2027, following constitutional changes that extended President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s term by one year, the country’s electoral commission announced on Thursday. The decision comes amid opposition criticism of the amendments adopted earlier this year.
The announcement was made by Abdikarim Ahmed Hassan, chairman of the National Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission, during an appearance on state television. Elections for both chambers of parliament will take place on April 15, one month before the presidential vote, he said.
The commission also released a timetable for preparations, with voter and political party registration set to begin on November 1, 2026, according to the Somali National News Agency (SONNA).
Mohamud’s presidential term was originally due to expire in May 2026. However, constitutional amendments approved by parliament in March extended the presidential and parliamentary terms from four to five years, pushing elections back to 2027. Opposition leaders, including former presidents and prime ministers, rejected the changes and called for elections to be held as originally scheduled.
Former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed has challenged the constitutional amendments in the Supreme Court, arguing that they were adopted without proper legal procedures or broad political agreement. He also rejected the new election timetable, warning that it could lead to “parallel elections, political divisions, internal conflict and a threat to Somalia’s statehood,” Somalia Today reported on Thursday.
Somalia last held a presidential election in 2022, when lawmakers elected Hassan Sheikh Mohamud for a second term, defeating Mohamed Abdullahi Mohamed. The vote followed months of delays and was conducted through an indirect system in which members of parliament chose the president.
The country also faces continuing security challenges from Al-Shabaab, an armed group affiliated with Al-Qaeda that has fought Somalia’s federal government since 2007. The terrorist group conducts raids, bombings, and targeted assassinations in an effort to destabilize the Somali government and regional security structures, and also establish its own rule based on a hardline interpretation of Sharia law.

Heavy cost for US to return to confrontation with Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

The experience of recent conflicts has demonstrated that possessing advanced weaponry and massive firepower does not necessarily equate to achieving strategic objectives. Factors such as depletion of military stockpiles, damage to military equipment, need to procure replacement ammunition, and Iran’s capacity to restore its defensive capabilities all serve to complicate the White House’s calculations regarding a potential re-engagement in military confrontation with powerful Iran.
In a report citing the financial and military costs of past US strikes against Iran, the British newspaper “The Times” highlights the significant strain this conflict has placed on Washington’s military resources. According to the report, US expenditures have exceeded $43 billion in this war, dozens of American aircraft have sustained damage, and the US stockpiles of interceptor missiles have come under pressure. Regardless of the final assessment of the conflict's military outcomes, these figures indicate that sustaining large-scale operations against Iran requires substantial financial and material resources, the resources that cannot be replaced or replenishment in the short term is impossible.
The significance of this issue becomes even greater when the direct costs of military operations are weighed alongside their strategic consequences. In military calculations, the number of attacks carried out or the volume of ammunition expended is not, in itself, the definitive measure of victory. What truly matters is the ratio between the costs incurred and the objectives intended to be achieved through those expenditures. If a military operation entails the extensive use of ammunition and damage to equipment, yet fails to eliminate the adversary’s capacity to continue their resistance, persisting with the same approach may simply lead to mounting costs with no guarantee that the desired outcome will ever be attained.
Erosion of Military Stockpiles: Washington’s Hidden Challenge
One of the most significant consequences of a military conflict is the strain placed on stockpiles of weapons and ammunition. The extensive use of interceptor missiles to counter threats from missiles and drones, particularly when attacks are sustained, can deplete ready-to-use stockpiles, thereby increasing the need for production and resupply. This issue is of particular importance to the United States. In addition to its military commitments in West Asia, Washington must also ensure its forces remain prepared to address potential crises in other parts of the world.
Replenishing arms stockpiles is not merely a matter of securing funding. The production of certain advanced systems and the ammunition they utilize requires complex supply chains, specialized raw materials, and specialized industrial capacity. However, even if new budget allocations are made, rapidly replacing expended stocks is not necessarily feasible. The higher the rate of ammunition consumption in a conflict, the greater pressure placed on production schedules, the prioritization of arms deliveries, and the allocation of resources toward other military missions.
Under such circumstances, Washington’s decision to launch a new round of strikes is not limited merely to an assessment of operational capability; rather, it must also account for the opportunity cost of expending munitions and the subsequent impact on US military readiness. In other words, every missile used in an operation must be evaluated within the context of the United States’ broader defense requirements.
Iran’s Capacity for Recovery and Difficulty of Achieving a Definitive Outcome
On the other side of this equation lies Iran’s capacity to maintain and restore its defensive capabilities. In a report, “The Times” notes that, despite military attacks and pressures, Iran has managed to recover a portion of its missile and drone capabilities. This is significant from the perspective of military calculations, as the effectiveness of an offensive operation depends, to a large extent, on the degree of its lasting impact on the adversary’s capabilities.
If military strikes fail to permanently dismantle a nation’s defensive capacity, inflicting damage at a specific point in time does not necessarily equate to eliminating that nation’s ability to continue its resistance. The potential to repair equipment, restore certain operational capabilities, and maintain the capacity to produce or deploy weaponry can alter the conflict’s equation over time. In such a scenario, the aggressor may be compelled to repeatedly expend further munitions and equipment to sustain military pressure—all while the ultimate outcome of this process remains uncertain. The strategic implication is clear: as long as the adversary retains the ability to continue resisting, one cannot conclude that their defensive capacity has been exhausted based solely on the volume of attacks carried out.
Why could a renewed attack be more costly?
The United States re-engaging in a confrontation with Iran could trigger a repeat of that same costly cycle. New operations would require ammunition, logistics equipment, fuel supplies, the movement of troops, and the protection of military bases and facilities. Should equipment sustain damage or the scope of the conflict expand, costs would rise accordingly. Furthermore, a prolonged crisis could impact energy markets and economic expectations, extending the repercussions well beyond the military battlefield.
On the other hand, the United States must also consider the possibility of a prolonged conflict and the need to remain prepared for unforeseen scenarios. Military operations might begin with limited objectives, but reciprocal responses and shifting conditions could expand their scope. Under such circumstances, the final cost will not necessarily align with initial estimates.
The fundamental question for the White House is whether the costs of a new confrontation would yield commensurate gains. If the objective is to durably weaken Iran’s defensive capabilities, the persistence of its missile and drone capacities could make achieving this goal more difficult. Furthermore, if the aim is to compel Tehran to accede to Washington’s demands, it remains to be seen whether military pressure would truly lead to such an outcome, or if it would merely generate additional costs.
The White House’s Strategic Calculus Test
A report by “The Times” once again draws attention to the gap between military superiority and the achievement of strategic outcomes. Possessing extensive military capabilities enables the infliction of damage, but it does not, in itself, guarantee that the adversary will cease resistance or that the aggressor’s political objectives will be realized. When assessing a conflict, one must simultaneously consider the costs incurred, the resilience of the parties involved, and the extent to which objectives have been achieved.
For Washington, returning to a confrontation with Iran—without regard for the lessons of past costs—means re-entering a path with a predetermined outcome. The strain on U.S. military stockpiles, combined with Iran’s ability to restore parts of its defensive capabilities, suggests that repeating such attacks will not necessarily shift the equation in favor of the aggressor.
Ultimately, the primary challenge for the United States is not merely the capacity to launch a new operation, but the ability to achieve a sustainable outcome at a manageable cost. If previous strikes failed to realize Washington’s intended objectives, any decision to follow the same path requires a clear answer to the question: what will be different this time? Absent such an answer, a renewed attack risks becoming less of a solution to the crisis and more the beginning of another phase of resource depletion and escalating strategic costs for the United States.

He added that some agricultural land could remain unsown because of the risks created by Russia, which would also affect prices next year.
“Therefore, the consequences are already being felt, and they will only intensify. The Black Sea could become a second Strait of Hormuz, this time in terms of food security,” Sybiha stressed.
He noted that all mediators actively involved in the process were now awaiting a response from Russia, while Ukraine was working with all its European partners to maximize the transit of Ukrainian grain through their countries to designated destinations.
“This will be difficult because Ukraine is one of the world’s largest agricultural producers and can feed up to 400 million people. Collective pressure is therefore needed to force Russia to unblock the Black Sea,” the head of Ukrainian diplomacy concluded.
As Ukrinform reported, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said that European partners are becoming increasingly aware of the threat posed by Russian escalation and the need to counter the “shadow war” Moscow is waging against the West. They also recognize Ukraine’s important role in strengthening European security.

‘Trying to dominate’: How Israel is embedding itself in the Cypriot state
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

20:54:10 KST

‘Trying to dominate’: In Cyprus, some fear Israel’s growing influence
Israel now reaches into Cyprus’s water, gas, health and defence and a number of Cypriots fear their island is losing control.
Nicosia and Limassol, Cyprus – Heavily bearded and wearing a loose shirt, Christos Achniotis speaks about the history and demographics of Cyprus and runs off dates from memory.
He was 16 when Turkish troops landed in Cyprus in mid-1974. At one point, Limassol has long had a large Russian community, he said, but that revolved around property investments.
Now, he believes there is pressure from Israel, which he says is “trying to dominate as much as possible, land-wise, company-wise”, as well as politically and militarily.
Israel’s reach in Cyprus now runs through the state’s most vital systems.
Mekorot, Israel’s state water company, helps supply the island’s water. Israel Aerospace Industries, a state-owned arms maker, is supplying its new air defences. And Israeli firms run a growing hospital network and hold a stake in the country’s largest gasfield.
Israel’s economy is about 15 times Cyprus’s, according to the World Bank, and Israel’s military spending is about 73 times that of Cyprus.
Cyprus’s government presents the ties as a security alliance against Turkiye, but several Cypriots interviewed by Al Jazeera said they feared their country is handing another state control of systems it cannot live without.
Israel is “a small area with big money and a big military”. Cyprus is strategically placed in the Mediterranean and, just a 35-minute flight away, is an attractive piece of land, said Achniotis.
‘Our resources’
Cyprus gets about 80 percent of its drinking water from the sea.
With its dams just 21 percent full in March, desalination plants supply most of what comes out of its taps, according to the Water Development Department.
Agriculture Minister Maria Panayiotou said in June that desalination would cover almost all domestic demand by next year.
Mekorot has joint ventures with Cypriot firm Netcom that run two of the island’s five permanent plants, at Larnaca and Episkopi, according to the Water Development Department. In August, Mekorot expanded its cooperation with Cyprus, signing a memorandum with the Nicosia District Water Board to help manage water and sewerage in the capital.
For Danae Laou, who works in hospitality in Limassol, the water deals crossed a line.
“It’s terrifying to see, but at the same time, we have no power,” she said.
Today’s occupation of Palestine is in part facilitated by control of vital resources. “I can see the same thing happening here”, she said.
Palestinians know Mekorot well.
In the occupied West Bank, the company is on the United Nations list of businesses linked to illegal Israeli settlements.
Najla Abdellatif Vallander, a Swedish-Palestinian environmental advocate who founded Zero Waste Palestine, has tracked Mekorot’s work in Palestine and abroad and told Al Jazeera that its operations in the West Bank are akin to “water theft”, diverting Palestinian sources to illegal Israeli settlements.
“Israeli settlers are able to enjoy almost unlimited amounts of water while Palestinians are not allowed to use their own water sources,” she said.
Palestinians “have to buy back their own water sources from Mekorot”, and are mostly barred from digging their own wells. “This is water apartheid,” she said.
At the time of publishing, Mekorot had not responded to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
‘Leverage’
Israel’s economic footprint has grown fast.
Investors in Israel held 5.1 billion euros ($5.7bn) of investment in Cyprus at the end of 2024, more than six times what they held in 2017, according to the Central Bank of Cyprus.
The true figure may be higher as the data excludes Israelis living in Cyprus or elsewhere, and may miss money routed through companies whose owners are hard to trace.
The Tel Aviv Stock Exchange is also weighing a bid for the Cyprus Stock Exchange, which the government is privatising, Cyprus Mail and the Israeli business daily Globes reported this month.
The Cypriot exchange’s European Union licence would give Israel “greater access to the Eurozone market”, a source close to Cyprus’s Ministry of Finance told the Cyprus Mail.
Health is the newest.
Hadassah Medical Centre Limassol, the Israeli hospital group’s first centre in Europe, began seeing patients in July and was formally opened on Thursday.
Its opening was ratified in Israel by Hadassah’s governing bodies, including the Hadassah Women’s Zionist Organization of America.
Offshore, Israel’s NewMed Energy owns 30 percent of the Aphrodite gasfield, according to its filings to the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange.
The two governments are also negotiating over the field, which Israel says extends into its waters.
‘Create a problem’
Israel has also been flexing its military muscle.
Israeli special forces have trained in Cyprus’s Troodos mountains, whose terrain resembles southern Lebanon, according to Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies.
In 2022, the two armies held their largest joint exercise yet, simulating a war with Hezbollah, The Jerusalem Post reported.
Cyprus is replacing its Russian-made air defences with the Barak MX, built by Israel Aerospace Industries, with deliveries beginning in late 2024.
Israel presents itself as a guardian against Turkiye.
Following a coup in Cyprus backed by Greece’s military government in July 1974, Turkiye invaded the island and has occupied its northern part ever since. Only Turkiye and its Turkish Cypriot leadership recognise Northern Cyprus.
In late December 2025, Israeli and Cypriot military officials signed a 2026 cooperation plan covering joint exercises, training, and “strategic military dialogue”, the Israeli military said.
On Tuesday, a pro-Israel advocacy group, the Israel Allies Foundation (IAF), launched a caucus of six Cypriot lawmakers from three parties in Nicosia. Its president, Josh Reinstein, told reporters after the group’s meeting with the Cypriot president at the presidential palace on Wednesday that Turkiye is a “common adversary”, according to the Cyprus Mail.
The opposition party AKEL called it “extremely provocative”, asking what credibility Cyprus has in demanding pressure on Turkiye while backing “another occupying and settler state”, the Cyprus Mail reported.
Last month, Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told the United Nations General Assembly that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan “illegally occupies northern Cyprus, an EU member”.
Netanyahu “knows what he’s doing”, said Ioanna Lamprou, a writer in Limassol.
Cypriots who feel the world has forgotten the occupation, she said, will “become more sympathetic to Israel and to Netanyahu’s government because of this”, but they “don’t understand that what’s happening in the West Bank is illegal occupation as well”.
Laou understands the government’s reasoning; from its perspective, she said, “Cyprus can’t protect itself from anything.”
Ceylan Hassan, a Turkish Cypriot researcher and environmental social scientist, said the British had won over Cypriots the same way, by promising to keep them safe from a bigger threat.
Israel is doing “the whole colonial thing of let’s create a problem and then be the solution to it and never let it go”.
‘Athens or Crete’
In 1902, Theodore Herzl, the founder of political Zionism, presented a pamphlet to a British Parliamentary Committee with the idea of establishing a Jewish homeland in Cyprus. He offered a pamphlet with the title: The problem of Jewish immigration to England and the United States solved by furthering the Jewish Colonisation of Cyprus.
Britain’s colonial secretary refused, saying Greeks and Muslims lived there, according to Herzl’s diary.
Herzl mused, “The Greeks will gladly sell their lands at a good price and migrate to Athens or Crete.”
Achniotis has thought about that history more since the genocidal war on Gaza began.
Watching what is happening to Palestinians, he said, “I think it can happen to anyone.”
As the onslaught happened so easily, with the acceptance of the US and European governments, “you feel a kind of insecurity,” he said. “Why are they going to respect you?”

Natland was hired by a 17-year-old known as "Generalen." A court in Norway last year convicted the teenager of attempting to “contribute to murder” and sentenced him to 14 years in custody. A 16-year-old is awaiting trial in Norway for his role in the conspiracy.

Tehran hosts 8th national conference on soil conservation and watershed management
TEHRAN – Tehran played host to the 8th national conference on soil conservation and watershed management on October 13 and 14, under the theme ‘successful experiences, national and international lessons learned’.
The conference was hosted by the International Center for Integrated Management of Watershed and Bio-Resources in Arid and Semi-Arid Regions (ICIMWB), as one of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) category 2 centers in the field of water and natural sciences, the Agricultural Research, Education, and Extension Organization, and Iran’s National Commission for UNESCO.
Bringing together researchers, experts, executive managers, and representatives from national and international institutions, the 8th conference served as a platform for the exchange of knowledge and experience, and the enhancement of collaborations for the conservation of fundamental resources and the sustainable management of watersheds.
Addressing the event, Secretary-General of Iran’s National Commission for UNESCO Hassan Fartousi, highlighted the protection of water and soil as the fundamental requirement for food security and sustainable development.
Referring to challenges such as water scarcity, soil erosion, drought, and land degradation, the official emphasized the importance of integrated watershed management and the use of scientific and interdisciplinary approaches.
The conservation of natural resources needs to be integrated into the country’s development plan. The realization of the goal requires connecting research, policymaking, and practical implementation, as well as promoting the participation of responsible agencies and local communities, he noted.
For his part, Levan Bouadze, the newly appointed Resident Representative of the United Nations Development Program (UNDP) in Iran, said soil erosion and land degradation are among the major environmental challenges whose consequences extend beyond the natural environment, affecting the economic and social well-being of human societies.
Highlighting that soil health and food security are interconnected, the official said that the loss of soil resources not only threatens food security, but also impacts the livelihood of local communities and the sustainability of ecosystems.
The official called for enhancing management capacities and utilizing scientific knowledge to identify natural hazards and mitigate the vulnerability of ecosystems.
Referring to the UNDP’s cooperation with Iranian institutions, the official said the implementation of joint projects aimed at protecting natural resources and combating land degradation provides a great opportunity for the exchange of expertise and the development of practical solutions.
The official went on to say that researchers and scientists can facilitate precise decision-making by generating knowledge and providing scientific solutions, while the government can translate these findings into actionable plans and measures.

Energy shock pushes major central banks toward higher rates as growth risks mount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:48:13 UTC
20:48:13 KST

- Fed, ECB and Bank of Japan tighten policy as UK policymakers weigh further rate increases amid higher inflation forecasts
- Economist Huw Dixon warns growth could stall heading into 2027, with recessions probable in several G7 economies
Rising energy costs are renewing inflation pressures across major economies, prompting interest-rate increases and complicating central banks’ efforts to contain prices without undermining growth.
The US Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan raised borrowing costs in September, while the Bank of England held its benchmark rate steady despite growing concerns about the inflation outlook.
Huw Dixon, emeritus professor of economics at Cardiff University, told Anadolu that the energy crisis triggered by the Iran war had substantially changed expectations for inflation and monetary policy since the beginning of the year.
He warned that growth could stall heading into 2027, with recessions probable in several Group of Seven economies.
“Interest rates will have to rise to control inflation, but perhaps we will see policy rates high but below inflation again so as to limit damage to the real economy,” he said.
Dixon argued that central banks would not repeat the shift toward zero interest rates seen during the 2008 financial crisis unless a conflict with Russia broke out.
His assessment highlights the competing pressures facing policymakers as higher energy bills squeeze spending while also raising businesses’ costs.
 
US and eurozone inflation accelerate
US annual consumer inflation rose to 3.7% in September from 3.4% in August, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Prices increased 0.6% month-on-month, with a 9.1% jump in gasoline prices accounting for more than half the overall rise. 
Annual core inflation, excluding food and energy, accelerated to 2.6% from 2.4%.
Energy prices were 20.4% higher than a year earlier. Gasoline prices rose 34.2% annually, while fuel oil prices climbed 74.2%.
Price pressures also extended beyond energy. Shelter costs increased 0.4% over the month, while recreation, used vehicles, education and airline fares also became more expensive.
The Fed raised its benchmark federal funds target range by 25 basis points to 3.75%-4% on Sept. 16 in a unanimous decision.
It said inflation remained elevated and the increase would support a timelier return to its 2% goal. However, its assessment of activity remained relatively firm, pointing to resilient domestic spending, strong productivity growth and robust capital investment.
In the euro area, annual inflation accelerated to an estimated 3.8% in September from 3.2% in August, according to Eurostat’s flash release.
Energy inflation climbed to 18.8% from 14.3%, while services inflation increased to 3.2% from 3%. Inflation excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco edged up to 2.5% from 2.4%.
The ECB raised its three key rates by 25 basis points on Sept. 10, taking its deposit facility rate to 2.5%.
It warned that the Middle East conflict was generating inflation pressures likely to keep price growth well above target for an extended period.
Its September projections put average inflation at 3% in 2026, 2.5% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028, with the latter two forecasts revised upward from June.
The ECB nevertheless projected continued growth of 0.9% this year and 1.4% next year, distinguishing its baseline outlook from Dixon’s warning of possible recessions. It identified upside risks to inflation and downside risks to growth, while avoiding a commitment to a particular rate path.
 
UK expectations shift toward tighter policy
The Bank of England maintained its benchmark rate at 3.75% on Sept. 17 by a 6-3 vote, with three policymakers favoring an increase to 4%.
UK inflation reached 3.1% in August. The bank’s updated assessment indicated inflation could reach around 3.75% in the fourth quarter, compared with the 3.2% projected in July, and slightly above 4% in early 2027.
Policymakers reported little evidence of substantial spillovers into wage and price-setting so far, but judged that the risk would grow the longer energy costs remained elevated.
Dixon said that before the US-Israeli attack on Iran, UK inflation had been expected to fall to 2% by April and interest rates to decline to a range of 3%-3.5%.
He now expects inflation to reach 4% by year-end and potentially rise further in 2027 if the war resumes.
“Bank of England rates will rise,” he said, describing a similar shift in the outlook for Western Europe and the US.
The bank’s September minutes showed that survey respondents anticipated a prolonged period of unchanged rates, while market pricing pointed upward.
Policymakers cautioned that risk premiums partly explained the market curve, meaning it did not simply represent expectations of future rate decisions.
Higher market borrowing costs were already reaching households: quoted two-year fixed mortgage rates were around 95 basis points above their pre-conflict level.
 
Japan tightens despite lower headline inflation
Japan’s annual headline inflation stood at 1.9% in August, while inflation excluding fresh food was 1.7%, according to the Statistics Bureau.
The Bank of Japan nevertheless raised its overnight policy-rate target to around 1.25% on Sept. 18 by a 7-2 vote.
It cited rising medium- to long-term inflation expectations and the risk that underlying inflation could exceed its 2% target as companies increasingly passed higher wages and input costs into selling prices.
The bank also identified high crude oil prices, yen depreciation and demand for artificial intelligence-related products as sources of price pressure.
It expected inflation excluding fresh food to accelerate clearly above 2% in the second half of fiscal 2026, while signaling further rate increases depending on economic and price developments.
Dixon warned that prolonged uncertainty could undermine confidence in central banks’ ability to maintain price stability.
“Expectations have been anchored in recent years, but there is so much uncertainty I suspect this may break down if central banks let inflation get out of control again,” he said.

Why is China buying up gold?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:38:11 UTC
20:38:11 KST

Why is China buying up gold?
Beijing’s gold purchases reflect a shift away from reliance on US dollar assets, experts say.
China is increasing its gold reserves in a bid to reduce its dependence on US dollar assets and protect against financial and geopolitical risks, analysts say, while households are turning to the precious metal amid uncertainty over the domestic economy.
The People’s Bank of China reported buying gold for a 23rd consecutive month in September, when the country’s central bank also made its largest monthly purchase in nearly three years. The sustained buying points to a longer-term effort to spread risk associated with its vast reserves, experts say.
Among concerns is high US debt and Western governments’ freezing of assets, which has highlighted the inherent risk in holding money overseas, particularly for emerging market and Global South economies. Gold bought and stored domestically offers protection against that risk because access does not depend on the will of another government.
But central bank buying and household demand for gold in China have different drivers. While Beijing is managing its financial exposure, private investors are seeking somewhere to preserve their savings. Here is what we know.
How much gold has China bought?
China’s central bank added approximately 23 tonnes of gold in September, bringing its reported holdings to about 2,410 tonnes, according to the World Gold Council. That was its largest monthly purchase since October 2023. Gold accounted for 8.5 percent of China’s total official reserves at the end of September, compared with 5.5 percent at the end of 2024.
Reserves are assets central banks hold to ensure they can meet international payments and respond to financial disruption. They usually include foreign currencies, foreign government debt and gold.
Private demand for gold within China has also risen, with purchases of gold bars and coins 28.4 percent higher in the first half of 2026 than during the same period last year, according to the China Gold Association. The buying of gold has continued amid falling prices, with gold down around 8.5 percent over the month.
The World Gold Council attributed the decline in gold prices partly to a stronger dollar and higher returns on US government debt. With interest rates going up in an attempt to curb inflation, these investments are attractive for buyers as they pay interest, making them more attractive to private investors than gold, which does not.
Why is China buying more gold?
A key objective is to reduce dependence on US government debt, known as Treasuries, according to Thu Lan Nguyen, head of commodity research at Commerzbank in Frankfurt.
China holds substantial reserves in dollar-based assets and, therefore, buying gold reduces its exposure to decisions taken in Washington. “China’s gold purchases are part of a broader effort to make its reserves more resilient,” Nguyen told Al Jazeera.
The freezing by Western countries of roughly $300bn in Russian Central Bank overseas assets following Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 demonstrated how reserves held abroad can quickly become inaccessible.
The concern for China may be that a future confrontation with Washington could expose some of its overseas assets to similar restrictions. “Gold held domestically has a crucial advantage in this respect: it does not represent a claim on another country and is therefore much less exposed to sanctions or asset freezes,” Nguyen said.
“I would interpret it primarily as risk management,” she added, pointing to increased geopolitical tensions and economic and fiscal risks.
America’s rising debt, which hit $40 trillion for the first time in history earlier this year, adds another source of uncertainty. In February, the US Congressional Budget Office projected that federal debt held by the public would rise from 101 percent of the size of the US economy in 2026 to 120 percent in 2036. That provides context for concerns about Washington’s ability to repay that debt going forward should an economic crash occur. Much of this debt is held by China. Gold, therefore, offers a less volatile and risky asset to hold.
Chinese households have different motivations for buying gold. When confidence in other investments weakens, gold can become more attractive as a way to hold savings. “Strong demand for gold can partly reflect a search for alternative stores of value,” Nguyen said.
The World Gold Council has identified weak Chinese share markets as one factor supporting domestic demand for gold, while its property market is burdened by heavy borrowing and overbuilding, contributing to a fall in housing prices, making it a poorer investment.
What this means for the US dollar
Analysts warned that China’s increased buying of gold does not signal an imminent end to the dollar’s global dominance. “I would be cautious about describing this as a major shift away from the dollar,” Nguyen said. “The dollar remains by far the dominant global reserve currency.”
But a gradual shift could still matter if China and other central banks put more of their new reserves into gold, buying fewer US assets than they normally would. That could weaken one source of demand for US government debt. But the effect would depend on how widely and quickly the shift developed.
“The key point is, therefore, that this is likely to be a slow diversification process rather than a sudden abandonment of the dollar,” Nguyen said. She added that the consequences for the US economy would remain limited unless the trend broadened and accelerated substantially.
Central banks also need readily available foreign currency to support international payments and the dollar remains central to those transactions. So gold can provide financial protection, but it cannot directly replace all the functions of dollar reserves.
Who else is buying gold?
China is part of a wider trend, particularly among central banks in emerging economies, Nguyen said.
“The trend is particularly visible among emerging market central banks,” Nguyen said. “But sanctions are only part of the story.”
Poland has also become a more prominent buyer. Its central bank purchased 31 tonnes in the first quarter of 2026 and another eight tonnes in July, according to the World Gold Council.
Large holdings do not necessarily indicate recent purchases. India, for example, confirmed in June that its physical gold stock remained unchanged at about 880.5 tonnes. India’s gold reserves have changed little since mid-2025, according to the World Gold Council. It bought about four tonnes in 2025, down from 73 tonnes in 2024.
Despite China’s sustained buying, its reserves remain far smaller than those of the United States. Its holdings of about 2,300 tonnes at the end of 2025 amounted to less than one-third of the US stockpile of approximately 8,133 tonnes.

Two Israeli women accused of smuggling 100 kg of khat released on bail in Poland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:37:04 UTC
20:37:04 KST

After three and a half months in detention, a court in Krakow has released on bail two young ultra-Orthodox Israeli women arrested on suspicion of smuggling 100 kilograms of khat, a plant classified as an illegal drug in Poland and the European Union.
The court accepted an argument from their Polish lawyer, Wit Steidler, in favor of their release. The women must report to police weekly and are prohibited from leaving Poland until the legal proceedings are concluded.
Steidler said that under Polish law, the amount of khat found in their suitcases was enormous. "This is a very serious crime in Poland," he explained. "Khat is included on the list of prohibited substances and is classified as a drug. If they are convicted, they could face between three and 23 years in prison. We managed to convince the court that it was inappropriate to continue holding them in detention.
"Even I, as their lawyer, was surprised by the court's decision to release them. But they are young women, this is the first time they have done something so foolish, and there is no point in keeping them isolated. We proposed bail and weekly police supervision. I was lucky the judge listened to me."
The two women, ages 23 and 24, were arrested on June 19 after arriving in Krakow on a flight from Israel. Each was carrying 50 kilograms of khat in her luggage.
There is considerable demand for khat in Europe among immigrants from Ethiopia and Eritrea. According to the report, individuals in Israel recruit young people, usually from the ultra-Orthodox community, to transport the plant in exchange for airfare and a payment of 5,000 shekels. They tell the recruits that if they are caught, the worst they can expect is a small fine or confiscation of their luggage.
However, Poland is considered one of the strictest countries when it comes to khat smuggling. In practice, the immediate consequence is often harsh pretrial detention. As soon as suitcases containing khat are discovered, typically weighing between 40 and 80 kilograms, the couriers are arrested and sent to detention facilities in Poland for periods ranging from several weeks to several months while their cases are examined.
For young people with no previous involvement in crime, the experience can be extremely traumatic: harsh detention conditions in a foreign country, separation from family, a lack of kosher food for those who observe Jewish dietary laws, and language barriers. Polish law enforcement authorities use detention as a form of shock treatment and as a punitive measure in itself, even before a trial begins.
Attorney Mordechai Tzivin, who represents Israelis facing legal difficulties abroad and assisted one of the women voluntarily alongside the Polish lawyer, said the Polish law enforcement authorities deserved thanks for the humane treatment they had shown his client, recognizing that numerous mitigating circumstances should be taken into account.

Turkey's Istanbul hit by worst floods in 80 years, with at least 4 dead
Catastrophic flooding in Istanbul was the worst in more than 80 years, Turkey’s interior minister said Friday as the death toll rose to four.
Istanbul, Turkey’s largest city with 16 million residents, was hit by more rain in the 48 hours up to Thursday morning than the combined historical average for September and October, the state-run Anadolu Agency reported.
“We are trying our best to help our citizens, but we are also experiencing the biggest flood disaster since 1942,” Mustafa Ciftci said during a visit to one of the areas hit hardest by Wednesday night’s downpour.
The body of a 66-year-old man was found Friday under a bridge in Istanbul's Sariyer district. Three other deaths were previously reported, including a teenager who was electrocuted in the storm.
Homes and businesses were flooded as water covered streets and parks across the city. Vehicles were washed away and many ended up piled up at the bottom of hills.
Before the discovery of the body on Friday, Ciftci told reporters in Sariyer’s Ayazaga neighborhood that four people remained missing.
He said there were 9,850 reports of damage and other issues related to the floods and that 46,000 personnel were working to clean up debris and help residents in Istanbul.
Murat Kurum, the minister for the environment, urbanization and climate change, accompanied Ciftci to the flood-hit neighborhood.
Addressing concerns that the floods were exacerbated by urban development close to waterways, he said that dealing with the problem was “essential.”
Kurum, who will chair the UN climate change conference, COP31, next month in the Turkish city of Antalya, also linked the floods to the effects of climate change. “Combating climate change is not a choice, but a necessity,” he said.

Malaysia’s welcome for Min Aung Hlaing undermines its stand on justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:32:50 UTC
20:32:50 KST

Malaysia’s welcome for Min Aung Hlaing undermines its stand on justice
As the US attacks the ICC, Kuala Lumpur welcomes a leader the court’s prosecutor wants arrested. Middle powers must defend international justice.
On October 8, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim received Myanmar’s President Min Aung Hlaing in Putrajaya with a guard of honour and an official luncheon, in the military chief’s first visit since the 2021 coup. Nine days earlier, Malaysia sent 1,476 Myanmar nationals back by sea in the first phase of a plan to return 5,000 people.
Kuala Lumpur calls this pragmatic diplomacy. In reality, it lends a middle power’s credibility to the Trump administration’s retreat from international accountability, weakening the laws and institutions smaller states rely on most.
Domestic pressures
Since May, a surge of online hate speech and misinformation has targeted the Rohingya, Malaysia’s largest refugee community. By late July, at least nine Rohingya community schools had closed or faced closure orders, and more than 100 Rohingya told UNHCR that residents of their Penang village had driven them out.
The hostility ignores the facts: Malaysia’s police chief says Rohingya account for 0.02 percent of crime. Yet research by INITIATE.MY and the Center for the Study of Organized Hate found AI-generated content amplifying anti-Rohingya disinformation across Malaysia, Indonesia, India and Bangladesh, casting refugees as a threat and legitimising vigilante violence.
Electoral politics plays a part. After heavy losses in three state elections, and with a general election due by February 2028, Anwar’s coalition may see a hard line on Rohingya returns as a show of control, though voter disillusionment and right-wing rivals make any electoral gains uncertain.
Impunity goes mainstream
Malaysia is not acting alone. Mongolia hosted Vladimir Putin in 2024 despite an ICC arrest warrant, and Hungary welcomed Benjamin Netanyahu in 2025 despite another. Kuala Lumpur denies this is recognition, yet Anwar says Malaysia will work towards Myanmar’s full reintegration into ASEAN, and Min Aung Hlaing wants a seat at the bloc’s November summit in Manila. Each welcome makes the next easier and tells leaders accused of atrocities, from Netanyahu to Min Aung Hlaing, that diplomatic rehabilitation is possible without accountability.
ASEAN has tried this before. In April 2021, Min Aung Hlaing agreed to the Five-Point Consensus, then ignored it: The violence continued, the ASEAN special envoy never met Aung San Suu Kyi, and inclusive dialogue never began. The bloc’s one real lever was excluding military leaders from its summits. Myanmar Specialist, Arkar Hein, said “Welcoming him back with nothing asked in return rewards that defiance and tells Naypyidaw that time and a staged election can achieve what
compromise would otherwise require. Each handshake abroad also makes the regime less willing to offer its opponents real concessions, and convinces them that only the battlefield will decide Myanmar’s future.”
A question of consistency
Malaysia has spent decades building its credibility as a regional peacemaker, a hard-won reputation it now puts at risk. It has facilitated the Bangsamoro peace process since 2001, helping negotiate a landmark peace agreement in the southern Philippines, and has facilitated talks in southern Thailand since 2013. In November 2024, Anwar welcomed the ICC’s arrest warrants for Netanyahu and his former defence minister, saying they “should be arrested even if they are visiting other countries”. That same month, the ICC prosecutor sought an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing for alleged crimes against humanity targeting the Rohingya, and an Argentinian court has since issued its own.
The Gambia’s genocide case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice centres on the 2016-17 operations Min Aung Hlaing commanded, which killed thousands of Rohingya, included mass rapes and burned hundreds of villages, driving more than 700,000 people into Bangladesh. UN investigators called for him to face genocide charges. Malaysia is not a party to the Rome Statute and has no legal duty to arrest him. But its credibility as a peacemaker and on Palestine rests on applying one standard to everyone.
Returns without safeguards
The returns rest on assurances no independent body can verify. UNHCR says it was not involved in the returns and had no access to verify that they were voluntary, and that safe conditions do not exist. Those returned reportedly included 27 children. Though not a party to the Refugee Convention, Malaysia is bound by the customary principle of non-refoulement, and the UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar has warned of substantial risks.
Naypyidaw says no Rohingya are involved because it does not recognise them as citizens, but other returnees also risk arbitrary detention, prosecution and forced recruitment. The military does not even control Rakhine State, where the Arakan Army holds more than 90 percent of the territory. On September 28, a day before returns began, a military air attack reportedly killed at least 50 civilians there, following more than a dozen other mass killings by the military earlier this year.
Nor can the military-backed government deliver the peace that safe return requires. Its election saw no voting in 67 of 330 townships, and when Min Aung Hlaing offered peace talks in April, the National Unity Government (NUG) and major ethnic armed groups refused. Without a ceasefire and an inclusive political process, assurances of safe return ring hollow.
Malaysia’s frustration is nonetheless legitimate. It has hosted refugees for decades with little international support, and resettlement has shrunk since the Trump administration suspended United States refugee admissions in January 2025. But failed burden-sharing cannot justify returns without safeguards.
Pressure on the court
The ICC exists so that victims of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity can find justice when their own states fail them. That mission now faces unprecedented pressure. On October 9, hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize, the Trump administration sanctioned the court itself. Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger, Chad and Venezuela have announced their withdrawal.
Yet middle powers can push back. Seventy-nine ICC members, including Canada, Brazil, Mexico and South Africa, backed the court after the first US sanctions in February 2025, and in May Hungary’s new government reversed its predecessor’s withdrawal. In Southeast Asia, the Philippines surrendered former President Rodrigo Duterte to The Hague, and on October 8 judges found him fit to stand trial for crimes against humanity, with proceedings due to begin on November 30.
Middle powers should say no
Middle powers like Malaysia, and blocs such as ASEAN and the European Union, cannot stop US sanctions, but they need not follow the Trump administration’s lead. As Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told the World Economic Forum in January, middle powers “must act together, because if we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu”.
Malaysia and its neighbours should lead by saying no: No to efforts to weaken the court, no to treating Min Aung Hlaing’s presidency as a clean slate, and no to Rohingya returns into an active conflict. Malaysia should back efforts to hold him accountable if ICC judges issue a warrant, and reconsider acceding to the Rome Statute, a move it abandoned in 2019.
Saying no does not mean disengaging. Kuala Lumpur should tie Myanmar’s reintegration into ASEAN to real progress on the Five-Point Consensus, starting with an end to violence and inclusive dialogue involving the NUG and ethnic armed organisations. At home, it should pause returns until an independent body confirms they are safe and voluntary, and hold accountable those who evict, threaten or attack refugees.
Malaysia should not carry this burden alone. ASEAN partners, members of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation and donors should fund refugee registration, education and integration, and resettlement countries should restore their commitments. Governments should also hold tech platforms accountable for amplifying anti-refugee disinformation and require swift action against incitement.
For years, Malaysia has offered refuge to the Rohingya and others fleeing Myanmar when few countries would. That record gives it the standing, and the responsibility, to defend the system of international justice it has long championed.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

UN Geneva meeting to coordinate Sudan peace efforts
The United Nations and Switzerland will host a major coordination meeting in Geneva on peace initiatives for Sudan. The parties to the conflict will not be attending.
A total of 27 delegations are expected at the Palais des Nations for this sixth meeting, said Naila Hajjar, a member of the team working with the UN Special Envoy for Sudan, Pekka Haavisto. Previous meetings had taken place in other countries.
On the agenda are efforts to reduce clashes and advance the political process. In particular, it is necessary to assess how the various initiatives can reinforce one another, Hajjar explained.
Among the countries expected to attend are the members of the Quad (the United States, the United Arab Emirates, Egypt and Saudi Arabia), as well as Qatar, Turkey, Germany and Norway, which are also involved.
The permanent members of the UN Security Council and international organisations active in Sudan will also take part.
More
Impunity is stalling all peace efforts in Sudan. Can it end?
On this occasion, Sudan’s neighbouring states will be involved to discuss the regional dimension of the conflict. However, neither the Sudanese government nor the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary group will be represented, as Wednesday’s meeting is reserved for the ‘mediators’ in the conflict.
Nevertheless, information will be relayed to these parties, particularly following the meeting. The aim is to produce a joint statement. The delegations will be led by ministers, deputy ministers or senior officials.
Sudan has been embroiled in a civil war for the past three years. An International Fact-Finding Mission condemned a genocidal campaign by the RSF to seize control of El-Fasher, in Darfur, a year ago.
Tens of thousands of people have been killed in the conflict. Nearly 13 million people have been displaced, including four million refugees. Tens of millions of people are in need of assistance.
The situation in El-Obeid in Kordofan has also been a cause for concern for the international community. The Mission will conduct an urgent investigation at the request of the UN Human Rights Council.

Europe increasingly recognizing threat of Russia’s ‘shadow war’ – FM Sybiha
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
“I see that our partners have a deeper understanding of the situation in Ukraine. I see greater recognition of the need to define a new role for Europe in international discussions. Our European colleagues are aware of the risks of further Russian escalation. I see that they understand that Russia’s actions in Europe have gone far beyond hybrid warfare. I have even heard them use the term ‘shadow war’ to describe the war Russia is waging against Europe, and they understand that it must be countered,” the Foreign Minister said.

“Military officials are the most aware of Ukraine’s role and importance from a security perspective. They understand that Ukraine’s armed forces, economy and experience give Europe strategic advantages, and that our cooperation is a two-way street,” the minister said.

At the same time, Ukraine’s top diplomat warned of the growing influence of populist and radical forces in Europe that exploit anti-Ukrainian and anti-immigrant rhetoric.
“We are now facing a very challenging period: more than 50% of Europe’s population will vote in elections next year. We are witnessing an era of populism and the growing influence of radical forces seeking to exploit anti-Ukrainian and anti-immigrant rhetoric. Each country has its own particular circumstances, but this rhetoric is based on manipulation,” Ukraine’s top diplomat stressed.
