Disaster Risk Reduction Week: building resilience starts at home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:08:04 UTC
20:08:04 KST

Disaster Risk Reduction Week: building resilience starts at home
TEHRAN – Iran is marking Disaster Risk Reduction Week from October 13 to 19, focusing on the importance of improving the health of individuals, families, and the safety of homes, raising public awareness, and strengthening family economic resilience before the disaster strikes.
The beginning of the week coincided with the International Disaster Risk Reduction Day, IRNA reported.
 
The days of the week highlight the following topics:
 
Tuesday, October 13, ‘healthy individual, the cornerstone of societal resilience’
 
Wednesday, October 14, ‘family mental health, the first step towards resilience’
 
Thursday, October 15, ‘a safe and resilient home for everyone’
 
Friday, October 16, ‘raising social children, a resilient generation’
 
Saturday, October 17, ‘a resilient home, simple steps to take from now on’
 
Sunday, October 18, ‘resilience culture, training everyone’
 
Monday, October 19, ‘family economy, a resilient family’
The International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction was started in 1989, after a call by the United Nations General Assembly for a day to promote a global culture of risk-awareness and disaster reduction. Held every 13 October, the day celebrates how people and communities around the world are reducing their exposure to disasters and raising awareness about the importance of reining in the risks that they face.
Themed ‘Resilience Starts at Home’, this year the day highlights that everyone deserves a home that is safe, affordable and able to withstand the hazards around it. There’s no place like home. It is where we seek comfort, safety and shelter. But when floods rise, extreme heat takes hold or other hazards strike, the place meant to protect us can become the frontline of disaster.
Making that possible takes more than individual preparedness. Governments need safer planning and building standards; businesses must put long-term safety before short-term gains; and communities need information, resources, and a voice in decisions about where and how they live.
Around the world, solutions are already taking shape — from families moving to safer homes in the Philippines to centuries-old earthen building techniques keeping homes cooler across West Africa.
 
Because resilience is not only about rebuilding after disaster. It starts before disaster strikes, and it starts at home.
UNESCO chair inaugurated
In September, Minister of Science, Research, and Technology Hossein Simaei-Sarraf, and the Secretary-General of Iran’s National Commission for UNESCO, Hassan Fartousi, inaugurated the UNESCO Chair in Disaster Risk Reduction and Resilience Engineering at Kharazmi University.
The chair is established on a synergistic approach aligned with the Sendai Global Framework for Risk Reduction, the Sustainable Development Goals, and UNESCO’s approaches to expanding education, science, technology, knowledge exchange, climate considerations, and the development of sustainable communities, msrt.ir reported.
According to Kharazmi University, the establishment of the chair represents a scientific and strategic imperative, given the current national and regional conditions in the country, such as climate change, the growing complexity of hazards, the expansion of human settlements, technological and human-induced risks, and the cascading effects of disasters.
This UNESCO Chair develops effective methods to assess and mitigate risks from natural hazards to existing and new school infrastructure, contributing to improved equitable access to safe learning environments for children in vulnerable communities, ensuring continuity of education services, and reducing life losses. The Chair has created a community for resilience engineering exceeding 3,000 members from more than 100 countries, instrumental in sharing knowledge to support disaster risk reduction initiatives.

Sudan: Over 6,500 detainees held by RSF in West Darfur face major food shortages
Over 6,500 detainees held by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary group in West Darfur are facing major food shortages and dire conditions, The Sudanese Doctor’s Network warned on Thursday.
The detainees are being held in El Geneina, an area that has witnessed horrors amid the war between the Sudanese army and the RSF which started in April 2023. Clashes in the area have killed over 10,000 people, mostly from the Masalit population, while mass graves have also been found in the region.

It specified that there are 709 women and approximately 500 children under the age of 18 in the detention facilities.
The network has previously raised the alarm over the welfare of civilian detainees across Sudan, and reiterated its concerns over the food shortages and worsening health conditions in detention centres on Thursday.
It noted that there was a rising death toll in detention centres, as well as many cases of serious health and humanitarian issues threatening the lives of thousands.
The Sudanese Doctor’s Network issued an urgent call for an investigation to be carried out into the causes of the poor conditions and for international groups to ensure they receive adequate medical care and food.
It further pushed for humanitarian organisations to be granted access to the detention centres and for transparency regarding the safety and whereabouts of the detainees, which comes amid reports of torture and ill-treatment of thousands of them.
Sudanese authorities and human rights organisations estimate that the RSF are holding around 19,800 people in their prisons, including military personnel, civilians, women and children under the age of 18.
Last month, the RSF stepped up its deadly drone attacks in government-held towns in the frontline state of North Kordofan.
Reports state that drone attacks have become the weapon of choice increasingly when it comes to the conflict in Sudan. The UN also said last month that drone attacks by both sides killed more than 1,000 civilians in the first half of this year.

Pezeshkian urges ‘peace diplomacy’ to protect biodiversity, condemns ecocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

20:05:55 KST

Pezeshkian urges ‘peace diplomacy’ to protect biodiversity, condemns ecocide
TEHRAN – President Masoud Pezeshkian has called for “peace diplomacy” to protect biodiversity, condemning the devastating environmental impact of wars of aggression as ecocide and urging the international community to establish effective, transparent and enforceable mechanisms to safeguard natural heritage during wartime.
Speaking on Friday, October 16, at the summit of heads of state and government held as part of the 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in Yerevan, Pezeshkian said war is not only a threat to people and infrastructure but also a direct driver of environmental destruction. “War burns forests, destroys wetlands, contaminates soil and water, and displaces wildlife,” he said.
Pezeshkian described environmental cooperation as a bridge between nations, stressing that biodiversity conservation could serve as an important pillar of “peace diplomacy.”
“In a region facing security crises stemming from the illegal and expansionist presence of powers, as well as climate change, water scarcity and ecosystem degradation, environmental cooperation can build bridges between nations,” he said.
Such cooperation, he added, can pave the way for peace and security for all, peace with nature, and a future in which human life is aligned and in harmony with the natural world.
“Today, we stand at a pivotal moment in history when biodiversity is no longer merely a scientific or environmental concern. It is also an issue of peace and security, human health, food and water security, and intergenerational justice for all the inhabitants of our planet,” Pezeshkian stressed.
“The Islamic Republic of Iran was among the first countries to recognize the legal and international significance of this issue and become a party to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD). However, Iran’s relationship with biodiversity goes far beyond its membership in an international convention.
With an ancient tradition of living in harmony with nature and an extraordinary diversity of ecosystems, species and genetic resources, Iran is the custodian of an invaluable and irreplaceable natural wealth. This heritage is the result of millions of years of evolution, natural dynamism and adaptation, and is reflected in the culture, customs, livelihoods, indigenous knowledge and historical identity of the people of this land.
Owing to its exceptional geographical location, Iran lies at the intersection of several biogeographical regions. From the Hyrcanian and Arasbaran forests to the Zagros Mountains, and from arid and desert landscapes to the coasts of the Persian Gulf, the Sea of Oman and the Caspian Sea, Iran is home to thousands of plant and animal species, as well as valuable genetic resources. These natural assets underpin the country’s ecological stability and sustainability, provide a vital foundation for water and food security and human health, strengthen resilience to natural hazards, and serve as a cornerstone of sustainable development.
In Iran, biodiversity, together with climatic and geographical diversity, is deeply intertwined with human history and civilization. Friendship with, respect for and protection of nature are integral to the cultural, religious and ritual identity of Iranians. Nature has long been regarded as an inseparable part of human life and a trust to be preserved for future generations. Many traditional ways of life, agricultural and livestock-raising practices, the use of medicinal plants, and the indigenous knowledge of Iranian communities have evolved over time through an understanding of and adaptation to nature, reflecting thousands of years of interaction between humans and the natural world.
For Iran, therefore, biodiversity conservation means far more than protecting species and their habitats. It means safeguarding a natural, cultural and civilizational heritage.
In my country, drawing on a long-standing culture of respect for nature and in line with national and international goals and commitments, the National Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plan has been developed and approved. The Department of Environment has been designated as the national coordinating authority, while a mechanism for non-governmental participation, with priority given to local communities, has also received government approval.”
He highlighted that protecting threatened species and restoring vulnerable populations are among the key priorities. These efforts include expanding protected areas and monitoring flagship wildlife species.
“War does not target only human lives and economic infrastructure. It also damages nature: burning forests, destroying wetlands, contaminating soil, threatening water resources, destroying habitats, displacing wildlife, and introducing chemicals and heavy metals into natural cycles. The environmental consequences of war can persist for years after hostilities have ended.
The international community now recognizes that environmental destruction during armed conflicts is not a minor or incidental consequence of war. Such damage is directly linked to the security and well-being of future generations.
In our region, including Iran, the environmental consequences of military conflicts must receive greater attention from the international community. The war of aggression launched by the United States and the Israeli regime in our region has threatened natural ecosystems and damaged environmental protection infrastructure built over years of efforts to conserve biodiversity. Attacks on industrial and energy facilities, fires, pollutant emissions, and soil and water contamination have all contributed to these threats.
This is not merely a domestic issue or one confined within a country's political borders. Nature recognizes no political boundaries, and the spread of water, soil, and air pollution does not stop at national frontiers. The environmental damage caused by war is therefore global in nature and requires international solutions.”
The effects of war on ecosystems can persist for years or even generations, affecting areas hundreds or thousands of kilometers away. One stark example is the scale of destruction in Gaza, where, according to experts, parts of the territory's soil may remain incapable of supporting natural life, vegetation, and ecological cycles for hundreds of years. The destruction caused by wars of aggression in our region amounts to what is known as “ecocide,” or environmental genocide, and must be condemned, Pezeshkian underlined.
“The international community is expected to establish effective, transparent, and enforceable mechanisms to protect natural heritage and biodiversity. No country should be allowed to treat nature as a silent and defenseless victim of war.
The Islamic Republic of Iran is committed to implementing the Convention on Biological Diversity and advancing global goals for nature conservation. In Iran, we pursue the protection of natural areas, wetlands, forests, rangelands, wildlife habitats, and genetic resources alongside sustainable development.
However, we must be realistic and fair. A country facing the mounting pressures of climate change, drought, water scarcity, desertification, and dwindling natural resources, while also grappling with the effects of economic sanctions and restricted access to technology and financial resources, needs genuine international cooperation to implement its environmental programs and repair the damage it has sustained. This is particularly true when the country has been targeted in two consecutive years by what it describes as criminal wars involving the extensive use of destructive and prohibited weapons, with attacks in many cases allegedly intended to cause environmental damage, including strikes on fuel storage facilities in the capital.”
He emphasized that biodiversity conservation will remain confined to negotiations, resolutions, and the setting of targets unless it is backed by adequate financial resources, equitable access to knowledge and technology, and capacity-building.
“If developing countries are expected to protect their forests, wetlands, species, and genetic resources, they must also be provided with the means to fulfill that responsibility. This is the true meaning of environmental justice.
We therefore call on United Nations agencies, international financial institutions, and relevant organizations and bodies working in environmental protection and sustainable development to strengthen mechanisms for mobilizing financial resources, assessing environmental damage, restoring damaged ecosystems, and supporting affected countries in addressing the environmental consequences of armed conflicts.”
In conclusion, Pezeshkian said that the Islamic Republic of Iran stands ready to cooperate constructively with the international community in this joint effort by sharing its scientific and academic capacities and experience with other countries. “We believe that biodiversity conservation can serve as an important pillar of “peace diplomacy.”
In a region grappling with security crises stemming from the unlawful and expansionist presence of powers, climate change, water scarcity, and ecosystem degradation, environmental cooperation can build bridges between nations. These bridges can pave the way toward peace and security for all, peace with nature, and a future in which human life is aligned with and harmonious with the natural world.
 
It is a future free from war, bloodshed, and destruction, in which biodiversity serves as a shared foundation for the well-being and prosperity of present and future generations.”

‘It was fake’: Indian villagers allege forgery behind Adani mine project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:05:45 UTC
20:05:45 KST

‘It was fake’: Indian villagers allege forgery behind Adani mine project
Forged signatures and thumbprints – even of dead and fictitious people – allegedly used to get land for bauxite mine.
Koraput, India – Raghunath Khara was shocked to look at his thumb impression on a piece of paper that declared he had consented to a government proposal to mine his village’s pristine forest land for bauxite.
He says he never gave that thumb impression.
“I always sign in English. It was someone else’s thumb,” alleged Khara, a shopkeeper in Balda village in the tribal-dominated Koraput district of Odisha state in eastern India.
Khara is among hundreds of people from Indigenous tribes in Balda and neighbouring Bannur village who have lost their lands to the new bauxite mine. It is being developed by Kalinga Alumina Limited, a subsidiary of Adani Enterprises Limited, a conglomerate owned by Gautam Adani, India’s second richest businessman and close to Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
The $24m project will consume a large chunk of the tabletop Balda Hill – home to forests, grasslands and caves that are considered sacred by at least 10 tribal villages surrounding it.
To push the project, the purported signatures and thumb impressions of nearly 600 tribals were allegedly collected during village council meetings in Balda and Bannur held on October 9 last year. Bannur is 5km from Balda.
Khara says he never attended the meeting at Balda and was instead protesting against the proposed mine with his wife, sister and other villagers about 100 metres from the village council office.
“It [thumb impression] was fake. We didn’t attend the village meeting at all. We were all busy protesting outside,” he told Al Jazeera.
India’s constitution recognises the rights of Indigenous communities over their traditional lands. Forest laws and laws granting autonomy to tribal areas dictate that village council resolutions are mandatory for any diversion of such lands for other purposes.
A resolution passed in a village council meeting is valid only if 50 percent of all the adults in the village consent to it in writing. Government documents claim all the 580 adults – 360 in Balda and 227 in Bannur – agreed to give up their land for the Adani mine. But the elected village heads in both villages denied any signatures were collected and called the two meetings “invalid”.
Even photographs taken by villagers at both council meetings show a combined attendance of about 100 people – nearly 40 in Balda and 68 in Bannur – far below the minimum 50 percent quorum required to pass a valid resolution.
Moreover, the villagers allege that most signatures on the resolution documents are fake, forged or impersonated.
They also claim the documents contain signatures of fictitious persons and even the names of people who died years ago. Some even said their signatures from a previous, unrelated village council meeting were fraudulently pasted onto the bauxite mine document.
Al Jazeera emailed the Adani group and its communications chief on August 18 seeking responses to the accusations of forgery and fraud. Then we followed up with a second request for comments on September 25, but did not receive any response. Al Jazeera also sought responses from Manoj Satyawan Mahajan, the district magistrate — the most senior bureaucrat in Koraput – to the concerns raised by villagers but did not receive a response. Rohit Varma, the superintendent of police for Koraput district, also did not respond to Al Jazeera’s queries.
‘They took the paper away from me’
Many of those who attended the meetings said they were opposed to the mining project.
“We were told that if mining was allowed, the village would get roads, jobs, drainage and water connections and a school built,” said Madhav Kuntili, a farmer in Bannur.
Koraput is one of India’s least developed districts and similar promises often have a significant sway. Kuntili said a document was passed around, seeking signatures.
“I said if the forest was being diverted, then I would not sign it. They took the paper away from me,” he told Al Jazeera.
Across Balda and Bannur, Al Jazeera met many villagers who said they were shocked to find their signatures or thumb impressions on the resolution.
Rama Hantal sat motionless by the doorway of his rusted tin-and-wood hut. The 60-year-old has been paralysed for several years and is unable to talk.
“There is no chance he could have attended the meeting or even signed,” said Chandrama Hantal, his daughter-in-law.
While Hantal had apparently signed the consent form in Odia, Odisha’s official language, Chandrama saw a thumb impression against her name. She also denied attending the meeting.
Among the signatories are three Gurubari Kharas – their purported thumb impressions in support of the mining project.
In Balda, villagers could only track two “Gurubaris” – one living 3km away who denied attending the meeting – and another from the village itself, who had died well before the village council meeting was held.
“My mother died in February 2025. How can they forge her presence and signature eight months later?” asked her son, Sahdev. She was nearly 75 when she died of natural causes.
Two other persons from the first Gurubari’s family are also listed as signatories – her bedridden husband, who has been paralysed since falling from a tree three months before the council meeting and her nephew. Both deny attending the October 9 meeting.
The third Gurubari remains untraced.
Al Jazeera interviewed more than 20 people and accessed records from both Balda and Bannur villages, but could not trace at least 67 persons named as signatories in the resolution.
In Bannur, at least three deceased persons were represented through thumbprints. The families of all three – who are also listed in the documents as consenters – confirmed the deaths of their kin.
“My mother died four years ago,” said Nakul Alang, the 35-year-old son of Sanai Alang who is listed at serial number 108 in the Bannur resolution.
Nakul’s signature appears in Odia, but he says he was working at a construction site in Visakhapatnam, a coastal city in Odisha’s neighbouring Andhra Pradesh state 170km (105 miles) from Koraput.
“I don’t know who put our names and signatures,” he told Al Jazeera.
Hurried, ‘fraudulent’ meeting
On page 10 of the 16-page Bannur resolution document, 13 names are written by the same hand, followed by a neat array of thumb impressions next to them.
When Sunadhar Muduli, a 50-year-old farmer, saw the sheet, he immediately recognised that it was his own handwriting.
“But none of us ever attended the Gram Sabha meeting,” he said.
Muduli said Ramnath Pungi, who works for the local revenue office on contract, visited the village in December and handed him a registry. He was asked to fill the names of those residents who wanted to get their traditional lands recognised by the government.
Many tribal communities, who have been historically kept out of land documentation, have been cultivating on “government-owned” lands for generations. There have been frequent promises to transfer such lands to their names, and it is not uncommon practice in the region to send contracted officials to collect information about farmers.
“He said he needed everyone’s signatures. I told him I would gather the residents, but he said that was not necessary. That I could sign on their behalf,” said Muduli, who then called some residents to get their permission.
“I wrote down the names on one side of the page and then he and I placed our thumbs alternatively against the name. It was his idea and I just followed the instructions,” he said.
It was only in June when Al Jazeera visited Bannur that Muduli saw the inclusion of the same sheet as part of the mining resolution draft.
Pungi also confirmed to Al Jazeera that the signatures were taken on another pretext.
“I was paid 3,000 rupees to collect documents and sign land settlement documents from each village. That’s what I did. I only submitted the signed sheet to the [revenue] office,” he said.
“I did not know they would use it for this [Adani project]. I am also against mining in our region.”
Official guidelines state that the announcement of a Gram Sabha meeting should be made two weeks before the scheduled date in order to ensure a quorum.
However, several residents told Al Jazeera that the notices announcing the meeting were pasted outside the village council offices on October 8, only a day before the meeting. The notices, accessed by Al Jazeera, were dated September 22 and September 23, 2025.
‘Abnormally rushed’ mining approval
Meanwhile, the government pushed the Adani mining project in Odisha – hastily, according to the residents and activists.
In February 2023, the Odisha government declared Adani Enterprises as the preferred bidder for the mine at Koraput, triggering immediate protests by the tribal people in Balda and Bannur. They marched to the local government office to protest against the mining of 157 hectares of forest land by destroying the trees around them and displacing residents.
Two years later, on March 6, 2025, the state government held a public hearing – a mandatory process to obtain approvals where villagers are given details of the project and their objections formally recorded. An overwhelming number of villagers expressed their opposition to the mining project.
Despite the objections, an environmental clearance – a key approval given by the government after assessing possible ecological damage of a project – was granted a few months later.
Under Indian laws, forest-dwelling communities who have been historically left out of land -ownership can seek individual or community rights over traditional forest lands. Balda and neighbouring communities applied for rights over 2,500 hectares of forest land in 2025. A majority of those claims overlapped with the mining lease area.
Usually, the settlement of claims involves the collation of claims and documents, approval from local bodies, verification by officials and ample time for appeals if the claims are modified or rejected. The process is usually notoriously slow.
In January, authorities “settled” these community rights claims without informing the village councils in the area. Less than one-fifth of the claimed area was recognised while the entirety of the mining area was excluded from the claims. Villagers are usually given time to appeal.
However, in this case, two appeals committees affirmed the decision in just three days, without even allowing the villagers time to submit their appeals, allege the villagers.
Ajaya Muduli is part of a three-member team authorised by the affected villages to approach any court in India, sign documents, take necessary legal steps and liaise with government committees in their fight to prevent the takeover of their lands.
Muduli told Al Jazeera that the land acquisition process was “abnormally rushed”.
“We have safeguarded this sacred land for centuries and yet were not even consulted,” Muduli told Al Jazeera. “This is a clear tactic forcing the mines on us without our consent while snatching our rights.”
Immediately after the October 9 Gram Sabha meetings, the villagers wrote to the local authorities asking for the deliberations to be held again. They flagged the hurried nature of the meetings and pointed to the fact that the village heads had declared them “invalid”.
Yet, on October 15, the allegedly forged resolutions were added to the official file. It was only on February 11 this year that those documents were made public on the environment ministry’s website.
So far, more than 50 people from several villages in Koraput have issued sworn affidavits declaring that they did not attend the village council meetings and that their signatures or thumb impressions were forged. They have also filed petitions in court and with district authorities, as well as complaints with the police, alleging forgery and demanding an investigation into the land given for the Adani mine.
In March, the 10 affected villages around Balda Hill held meetings where they rejected the previous resolutions passed by their village councils and reiterated their opposition to the proposed bauxite mine.
In May, Muduli approached the court on behalf of the villagers. But it was too late.
On May 7, all required approvals were granted to Kalinga Alumina Limited and the forest land was handed over for the $24m bauxite mining project, with an associated alumina refinery on a lease of 50 years. No compensation has been promised to the villagers.
“What they have done is illegal, but we will not back off,” Balda resident Rajendra Khara told Al Jazeera.
While the approvals have been granted, actual work has not started on the ground. Villagers have vowed to stop construction. “Whatever happens, we are never going to give it to Adani. This is our ancestral land,” Rajendra said.
‘Deeply troubling trend’
Arpitha Kodiveri, assistant professor of political science at Vassar College in the United States who has worked on environmental law and justice related to mining in India, told Al Jazeera that bypassing the consent of landowners sets a trend for illegal practice.
“What you are starting to see across multiple jurisdictions is an administrative approach to bypassing the consent provision. What I fear is that it has become an illegal administrative practice of implementing the consent provision without adhering to procedure and law, and that is something we should be worried about,” she said.
Kodiveri said alleged irregularities in the consent process could also provide grounds for the affected parties to challenge the government clearance granted to such mining projects. She also argued that the rules should make consequences for irregular consent practices clearer and must seek accountability when mandatory provisions are bypassed.
“Guidelines must be established so this process is implemented in spirit and not just in letter, and to signal to administrative actors that there are consequences for practising fraudulent signatures or taking signatures of the deceased. This has happened so many times in Odisha and elsewhere that it is a deeply troubling trend.”
Land Conflict Watch, a New Delhi-based research organisation, has tracked at least 28 instances of consent-related “conflicts” from projects such as mining, plantation, energy and other infrastructure across India since 2003. The organisation also found allegations of forgery, evasion of mandatory public consultations and forceful mining of ancestral land while studying such conflicts.
Even the studies conducted by the government show a similar trend.
A 2024 report by India’s Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG), an independent constitutional authority, on land management in tribal-dominated areas revealed 136 consent violations in mining and other projects. In 73 of these violations, no Gram Sabha meetings were held, while in another 29, land acquisition was done while disregarding the views of the village council.
Over the past few years, however, allegations of outright forgeries of Gram Sabha resolutions have emerged.
In 2023 in Sijimali, about 180km from Balda, villagers discovered similar forged consents and meetings for a bauxite mine by Vedanta Resources, India’s largest mining company backed by a London-based conglomerate. At least eight villages denied consent to hand over 708 hectares of forest land, despite official documents claiming otherwise.
Sijimali has seen near-continuous protests since, escalating to violence in April when clashes between the police and protesters injured 70.
“If the Gram Sabha has not given consent, then the forest clearance given is illegal. It has to be quashed. They are making a mockery of the law,” Shomona Khanna, a Supreme Court lawyer specialising in environmental and tribal law, told Al Jazeera.
“These are criminal offences … Any person who dispossesses a forest dweller of their forest right or interferes in the enjoyment of the forest right is committing a crime, which is called an atrocity under Indian law,” she said.
Back in Balda, the villagers fear that if mining starts, the rainwater-fed streams that sustain paddy cultivation will dry up. Forests that provided gourds, fruits, flowers, bark, firewood and medicinal plants will be affected.
Like many Indigenous tribal communities, their animist faith is linked to the surrounding forests – home to small shrines, idols and caves considered to be sacred.
“The forest is everything for us,” said Raghunath Hanthal, a 70-year-old priest in Balda. “Our maa [goddess] is here.”
On the official document, the priest’s name is listed as serial number 171, with his purported signature in Odia.
“I did not even go to the meeting. We were here, protesting that day,” he said. “Taking away our forests will not just destroy our livelihood, but it will incur the wrath of our goddess.”

India-Russia trade jumps in first half of 2026 – envoy
Trade between India and Russia reached $38 billion in the first half of this year and is on track to reach the $100 billion annual target set for 2030, Indian Ambassador to Russia Vinay Kumar has said. 
“We think we are on the right path to achieve the target,” Kumar told The Tribune newspaper on the sidelines of the second Russia-India TIME Business Forum in Kazan on Thursday. He said India was sourcing energy and fertilizers from Russia while exporting pharmaceuticals and expanding opportunities for skilled workers. 
The two countries are making a concerted effort to diversify trade and deepen economic ties, with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin giving personal attention to the relationship. The Kazan forum, in the Russian Republic of Tatarstan, follows the INNOPROM.India trade fair held in New Delhi last month. 
The $100 billion trade target was set during Modi’s visit to Moscow in July 2024.
15 октября 2026 года в Казани состоялось торжественное открытие II Российско-индийского бизнес-форума «TIME: Индия – Россия. Взаимная эффективность», организованного Генеральным консульством Индии в Казани совместно с Агентством инвестиционного развития Республики Татарстан. Форум объединяет представителей органов государственной власти, деловых объединений и ведущих компаний Индии и России, преследующих общую цель — укрепление практического сотрудничества и разработку новых совместных проектов. В церемонии открытия приняли участие Председатель Государственного Совета Республики Татарстан г-н Ф.Х. Абдулганиев, Чрезвычайный и Полномочный Посол Индии в Российской Федерации Его Превосходительство г-н Винай Кумар, член Законодательного собрания Дели Шри Хариш Кхурана, а также другие высокопоставленные представители органов власти и деловых кругов. В программе двухдневного форума – выставка «Индия и Россия: межрегиональное партнёрство», серия экспертных сессий по вопросам образования, культуры, промышленности, информационных технологий, туризма и другим направлениям, встречи в формате B2B, промышленные экскурсии, культурная программа, Фестиваль индийского кино и другие мероприятия. @PMOIndia @MEAIndia @PIB_India @DDNewslive @airnewsalerts @ANI @PTI_News @IndianDiplomacy

The strong growth in trade has continued beyond the six-month period cited by the Indian envoy. Bilateral commerce reached $47.7 billion in January-July, up 24.3% year-on-year, according to Indian Commerce Ministry figures cited by Russian lender Sberbank.
India’s imports from Russia totaled $44.9 billion during the seven months, including $36 billion in crude oil purchases. Indian exports reached $2.8 billion as Russia bought more chemicals, electrical goods, medical equipment, seafood, tea, and spices.
Bilateral goods trade grew from around $13 billion in 2021-22 to nearly $60 billion in 2025-26, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar said in August. However, the trade imbalance also widened as India bought Russian oil in huge quantities amid disruptions in the Middle East caused by the US-Israeli attacks on Iran.
New Delhi is seeking to expand shipments of pharmaceuticals, engineering goods, chemicals, food products, and auto components to Russia to lower the deficit.
Both sides are working on a bilateral investment treaty and strengthening local currency payment mechanisms to facilitate trade. India has also launched free trade negotiations with the Eurasian Economic Union, which includes Russia, to expand market access.

INTERVIEW – Armenian church official sees Türkiye-Armenia normalization as path to ‘stronger friendships’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

INTERVIEW – Armenian church official sees Türkiye-Armenia normalization as path to ‘stronger friendships’
Vice president of Surp Giragos Armenian Church Foundation welcomes efforts to improve bilateral ties, expresses hope that land border will soon reopen
Beril Canakci
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
DIYARBAKIR, Türkiye
A senior official of the Armenian church foundation in southeastern Türkiye’s Diyarbakir province has voiced support for the ongoing normalization process between Ankara and Yerevan, saying growing contact between the two sides will deepen friendship.
“We view the ongoing rapprochement between Armenia and Türkiye very positively,” Ohannes Gafur Ohanyan, vice president of the Surp Giragos Armenian Church Foundation, told Anadolu.
Ohanyan spoke during a visit by 7 Turkish and 7 Armenian journalists to Surp Giragos Armenian Church in Diyarbakir’s historic Sur district as part of an EU-funded media tour aimed at supporting normalization between Türkiye and Armenia.
“We believe that as these kinds of visits and events increase, the friendship between the two countries will grow even stronger,” he said. “Hopefully, the borders will open soon too.”
Türkiye and Armenia do not have diplomatic relations, and their land border has been closed since 1993. The two countries launched a normalization initiative in late 2021, appointing retired Turkish Ambassador Serdar Kilic and Armenian parliament Deputy Speaker Ruben Rubinyan as special envoys.
Türkiye’s Foreign Ministry said in May that technical and bureaucratic work to reopen the shared border with Armenia was still ongoing, although preparations for direct trade had been completed.
In early May, Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz visited Armenia, where officials signed a memorandum on the joint restoration of the historic Ani Bridge, a medieval structure spanning the border between the two countries.
During a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York last month, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan also discussed advancing normalization, strengthening trade and economic ties, and improving regional transport links.
Center of attraction for Armenians worldwide
The local Armenian community in Diyarbakir comprises roughly 60 to 65 people, according to Ohanyan. Despite its compact size, social and community life surrounding the church remains active, with regular religious services organized around major holidays.
"Because we do not have a permanent resident clergyman here, we hold around 8 to 10 services a year during important religious holidays," Ohanyan said.
Describing Surp Giragos as an 800-year-old church and the largest Armenian church in the Middle East, he said it draws Armenians from Armenia as well as from the diaspora in Europe and the US.
Following decades of disuse, comprehensive restoration initiatives spearheaded by the local foundation and supported in subsequent years by Turkish state institutions including the Culture and Tourism Ministry, allowed the site to formally reopen for worship.
The church was later damaged during 2015 clashes in Sur involving the terrorist group PKK. It was restored with funding from Türkiye’s Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Ministry, under the coordination of the General Directorate of Foundations, and reopened for worship after seven years.
The foundation’s second church, the roughly 500-year-old Surp Sarkis in the Alipasa neighborhood, fell into disrepair over time because it had no congregation and was further damaged in the February 2023 earthquakes centered in Kahramanmaras. Restoration work began in 2024 with a grant from the Culture and Tourism Ministry.
"Surp Sarkis has been in ruins for nearly a century," Ohanyan noted. "We have made considerable progress and have largely completed the structural work on the main building."
Ohanyan also called on businesspeople, philanthropists and the wider public for further support.

Student protests sweep Europe amid anger over costs of living
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:53:00 UTC
19:53:00 KST

Student protests that began with high school blockades in France have spread across Europe, drawing young people into the streets over deteriorating school conditions, teacher shortages, rising education costs and a housing crisis that is making it harder to study.
From France and Belgium to Albania, Greece, Spain and Italy, demonstrations have included school occupations, mass marches and protest camps, with some escalating into clashes with police.
Though national grievances differ, the unrest reflects growing frustration among young people who say governments are failing to provide the resources and opportunities they need to build their futures.
The protests began in mid-to-late September, when students in the Paris region, particularly around Creteil, blockaded school entrances with trash bins and makeshift barriers.
They cited missing teachers, overcrowded classrooms and deteriorating facilities, including mold, broken toilets and classrooms reaching 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) during heat waves.
Students have also criticized demanding schedules and Parcoursup, France's university admissions platform, which they say adds stress and uncertainty to the transition to higher education.
The demonstrations quickly spread nationwide, disrupting hundreds of schools. At the peak, more than 200 high schools were reportedly fully closed, while others faced partial closures or interruptions to classes. University students have also joined the movement.
Turnout estimates have varied widely. On Oct. 13, the Interior Ministry counted at least 161,500 demonstrators, while unions estimated participation at nearly 480,000. Other major protest days earlier in October also drew large crowds.
Climate activist Greta Thunberg joined demonstrators at a blockaded school in Saint-Denis, north of Paris, on Oct. 13, arguing that young people were being denied a meaningful role in decisions affecting their futures.
Police conduct has become another flashpoint. A teenager lost a hand in Lens, prompting authorities to suspend the use of stun grenades. Other reported injuries included eye damage and dental trauma, while complaints alleging police brutality were under investigation.
Justice Ministry figures cited in reports put the number of people taken into custody at roughly 6,800 to 8,000, with about 85% to 86% of those detained being minors.
Students, school staff and officers were among those reported injured. Although most marches remained largely peaceful, some ended in clashes involving tear gas, police charges and property damage.
Student unions are demanding an emergency school renovation program, large-scale teacher recruitment, improved schedules and greater student representation. They also want major changes to Parcoursup or its repeal, alongside more nurses, psychologists and career advisers.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced plans to deploy about 3,000 substitute teachers to the hardest-hit schools. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu promised a broader plan by the end of October, including consultations and adjustments to the 2027 budget, while citing financial constraints.
President Emmanuel Macron has called for patience and dialogue, but student leaders have dismissed the initial measures as insufficient and vowed to continue demonstrating.
In Belgium, students began demonstrating in early October against tuition reforms, overcrowded classrooms and funding cuts. Some categories of students face fees of up to 1,194 euros for the 2026-27 academic year. Protests spread from Liège to Brussels and other cities, with arrests reported during disorderly demonstrations.
Students also joined a nationwide union-led strike on Oct. 9 against austerity measures. The action drew tens of thousands of participants, while isolated clashes near Brussels Central Station involved water cannon, tear gas and fires.
In Albania, student grievances over university conditions, education costs and limited job prospects have merged with wider protests against corruption and inequality.
Demonstrations have overlapped with the months-long Flamingo Revolution, which opposes a luxury coastal resort project linked to Jared Kushner.
Protests in Tirana escalated into violence, with demonstrators attacking government buildings, banks and infrastructure. Police responded with tear gas, water cannon and batons. Reports described more than 100 arrests at peak points, injuries and significant property damage.
Prime Minister Edi Rama has refused to resign, pledging to address legitimate education concerns while condemning violence and defending his government's push for European Union membership.
In Greece, students set up tents in Athens' Syntagma Square opposite Parliament around Oct. 13 to protest soaring rents and inadequate public housing. Small apartments can cost 500 to 600 euros a month or more, putting accommodation beyond many students' budgets.
Demonstrators are demanding rent controls, more student housing, increased subsidies and better education funding. School sit-ins have also increased over teacher shortages and poor conditions.
In Spain, an indefinite teachers' strike began in the Madrid region on Oct. 14, bringing together educators, students and families under the Marea Verde, or Green Tide, movement. Protesters want increased public funding, smaller classes, higher salaries, reduced teaching hours and more specialized staff. Critics also accuse the regional government of encouraging privatization at the expense of public schools.
In Italy, students have occupied high schools in Turin and Rome, adopting slogans inspired by France as they protest underfunding, deteriorating buildings and rising living costs. Smaller demonstrations elsewhere reflect similar concerns.
Across Europe, the protests expose mounting pressure on public education systems after years of financial constraints, teacher recruitment difficulties and aging infrastructure. Rising rents, energy bills and everyday expenses have compounded those problems, making education increasingly difficult to afford.
Young people also express frustration over their future prospects, arguing that governments are failing to address barriers to education, employment and housing.
France's demonstrations have drawn comparisons with the student unrest of May 1968, although today's movement focuses largely on practical demands involving school conditions, staffing and access to education.
Governments have offered targeted concessions and promised dialogue while emphasizing budget limitations. Yet allegations of police excess, mass arrests and injuries have intensified scrutiny of how authorities respond to youth-led dissent.

The European Central Bank (ECB) has authorized Italy’s UniCredit to raise its stake in Germany’s Commerzbank above 30%, clearing a key hurdle in its bid to take control of the German lender.
UniCredit said Thursday that the approval allows it to cross the 30% ownership threshold and "increase its stake further without upper limits."
The bank expects to secure the remaining regulatory approvals and meet the offer conditions around year-end, giving it approximately 50% of Commerzbank’s voting rights and enabling it to take control of the bank.
UniCredit described the decision as a significant milestone in the acquisition, saying it reflected the ECB's positive assessment of the transaction and confidence in UniCredit's financial foundations and position within Europe's banking sector.
The transaction comes as the ECB advocates cross-border banking mergers as a way to strengthen the European Union's single market.
 
Berlin seeks guarantees
The takeover has faced resistance from the German government and Commerzbank’s management, but Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil on Friday described talks with UniCredit as constructive.
Speaking on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund’s annual meeting in Bangkok, Klingbeil said discussions between the two sides’ teams were continuing after a “very constructive start” to his talks with UniCredit Chief Executive Andrea Orcel, German news agency dpa reported.
Berlin wants to protect jobs, preserve Commerzbank’s Frankfurt headquarters and stock market listing and maintain its lending to small and midsize businesses.
“I have not seen any hardened positions, but rather believe that all these issues can be addressed constructively together,” Klingbeil said.
The German government, which rescued Commerzbank with billions of euros in taxpayer money during the financial crisis, still holds a 13.3% stake in the bank.
Commerzbank's management, led by Chief Executive Bettina Orlopp, has long resisted the takeover effort while seeking a negotiated solution with UniCredit.

Indonesia tests dry ice technology to disperse toxic haze from forest fires
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:45:03 UTC
19:45:03 KST

Faisal Mahmud
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Indonesia has begun testing dry ice technology to disperse toxic haze from forest and peatland fires, with officials reporting improved visibility near an airport in South Sumatra.
The National Disaster Management Agency said Thursday that the trials use atmospheric modification techniques to disperse smoke without requiring rain clouds, according to state news agency Antara.
Berton S.P. Panjaitan, acting head of the agency's data, information and communication center, said the method targets dense smoke directly, unlike conventional cloud seeding, which uses salt particles to stimulate rainfall.
He explained that forest fires create atmospheric inversion layers that trap hazardous smoke close to the ground.
Response teams release 3-millimeter dry ice granules at minus 75C (minus 103F) to disrupt these layers and help smoke disperse.
A Cessna Caravan aircraft flew two flights Thursday at an altitude of 4,500 feet, releasing 1,600 kilograms (3,527 pounds) of dry ice over Palembang's Sultan Mahmud Badaruddin II International Airport.
The disaster agency said that following the operation, visibility jumped from 650 meters (2,133 feet) to 2,800 meters (9,186 feet).
The trials are set to continue through Sunday before authorities assess possible expansion to other affected provinces.

Ukrainian military tests new SkyFall drone for aerial evacuation of wounded soldiers – AP

Ukrainian military tests new SkyFall drone for aerial evacuation of wounded soldiers – AP
Ukrainian company SkyFall has developed the StarGate drone for aerial evacuation of wounded soldiers and handed it over to the military this week for frontline testing.
Source: Associated Press
Details: A SkyFall spokesperson said the idea emerged after a request from the military.
Quote from AP: "Last year, Flint, commander of the 475th Separate Assault Regiment, known as Code 9.2, approached SkyFall's founder about developing a safer way to evacuate wounded soldiers from hard-to-reach positions."
Details: In some parts of the front line, the so-called kill zone – an area constantly exposed to drone and artillery fire – extends 10-15 km (6-9 miles) or more. StarGate can fly up to 15 km one way, potentially reaching critically wounded troops stranded deep within this dangerous zone.
According to a unit commander with the alias "KVN", ground robots usually take two to three hours to reach a position.
"Covering 10 km in minutes would be a drastic change on the front line," he said.
StarGate has a maximum payload capacity of 150 kg (330 pounds), the manufacturer says, enough to transport a wounded soldier in body armour with their combat gear.
The drone has a cruising speed of 65 km/h (40 mph) and a maximum speed of 105 km/h (65 mph). Preparing it for flight takes about 10 minutes.
The StarGate has two communication channels: Starlink and its own L-Link system. The drone is operated remotely, while AI features help it function without GPS and in conditions of electronic warfare interference. According to the developers, if communication is completely lost, the drone can independently plot a route to a safe area.
During a field demonstration, a StarGate took off carrying a stretcher loaded with equipment simulating a wounded soldier wearing body armour. The test range also simulated an FPV drone attack and activated electronic warfare systems. When one of the drones approached, StarGate fired a net that entangled it and knocked it off course.
SkyFall estimates that one system will cost at least US$50,000, depending on its configuration. The company plans to ramp up production to as many as 1,000 units per month by the end of 2026.
The military is currently testing the StarGate in frontline conditions. KVN said at least a month of use will be needed to assess the drone's effectiveness.
SkyFall is a Ukrainian manufacturer of heavy Vampire drones, known as Baba Yaga, and Shrike FPV drones. The company has also developed the P1-SUN interceptor drone.
Background: In March, Ukrainian company Gurzuf Defence unveiled the Ayudag-6 heavy drone, capable of carrying up to 90 kg of cargo. The multicopter is also being considered for evacuating wounded soldiers from the battlefield.

Israel’s Arab-led parties could play key rol in election
Unknown

2026-10-16

19:37:47 KST

Israeli lawmaker Mansour Abbas, right, leader of the Ra'am party, speaks to supporters during a campaign event ahead of Israel's general election in the northern Israeli town of Baqa al-Gharbiyye, Oct. 8, 2026. (AP Photo/Mahmoud Illean)
Arab-led parties could emerge as kingmakers in Israel’s Oct. 27 election, despite Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rivals ruling out coalition agreements with them, as the country’s Palestinian minority faces growing discrimination, rising crime and restrictions on freedom of expression.
Mansour Abbas, leader of the Islamist Ra’am party, broke a longstanding taboo in 2021 by bringing an Arab party into an Israeli coalition government.
He condemned Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack and has focused on local issues, including crime, rather than the war in Gaza and Israel’s occupation of the West Bank. Critics accuse him of sidelining the broader Israeli-Palestinian conflict to gain political influence.
Palestinian citizens and their descendants make up about 20 percent of Israel’s population. Although they hold citizenship and voting rights, activists say they face discrimination and inadequate protection from violent crime.
The homicide rate among Palestinian citizens is more than 22 times higher than among Jewish Israelis. The Abraham Initiatives, an Israeli organization advocating equal rights, has recorded 184 crime-related killings in Arab communities so far this year, with only 12% of cases reported in the first half of 2026 solved.
Authorities have also restricted anti-war protests, displays of Palestinian flags and online expression, according to the rights group Adalah.
The Israeli government maintains that minorities have equal rights and says restrictions are rooted in security concerns.
Tensions have worsened since the 2023 attack and Israel’s subsequent offensive in Gaza, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to local health authorities. Mohammad
Darawshe, a director at the Givat Haviva Center for a Shared Society, said an initial period of solidarity between Jewish and Palestinian citizens faded as Israel’s military response alienated many Palestinians.
Arab parties could hold significant leverage in the election because no single party is expected to secure the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
However, Netanyahu, centrist opposition figure Gadi Eisenkot and former coalition leader Yair Lapid have all ruled out forming a government with Arab-led parties. A deadlock could force another election, leaving Netanyahu’s government in a caretaker role.
Despite their political marginalization, some Palestinian citizens say voting remains essential to securing better representation and addressing local problems. Ahmed Kadan, a 50-year-old guidance counselor in Baqa al-Gharbiyye, plans to vote for Ra’am, saying the government has neglected Arab communities despite their contributions to Israeli society.
“We live in this state and not in any other place,” Kadan said. “We’re doing our duty but not getting what we need.”

Türkiye targets stronger laws against capital market crimes by early 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:31:31 UTC
19:31:31 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Türkiye plans to complete legal changes to strengthen its fight against capital market crimes by the beginning of 2027, Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek said Friday.
The planned measures will also address coordinated transactions by funds, Simsek said in a statement on Turkish social media platform NSosyal, outlining steps to improve market transparency and bolster investor confidence.
Relevant institutions are implementing significant regulations, taking into account assessments by international index providers, he said.
Regulations introduced by the Capital Markets Board have strengthened the flow of information and made ultimate share ownership more transparent, Simsek added.
A fund guide announced at the end of August enabled weekly disclosure of hedge fund portfolios, alongside announcements when funds traded on the Turkish Electronic Fund Trading Platform, known as TEFAS, cross specified shareholding thresholds.
The measures also introduced concentration limits for funds and required borrowing transactions to take place on organized markets on a collateralized basis.
Simsek said authorities would closely monitor the results and take any additional steps without delay in consultation with stakeholders.
“Our priority is to complete the liquidation of problematic funds and protect investors' rights,” he said.
Sanctions will be applied resolutely against those who disrupt the fair and competitive functioning of markets, he added.
“Our goal is to establish a transparent, reliable, and efficient capital market where investor rights are protected,” Simsek said.

Ukraine Gets Two-Thirds of Its Allied Intelligence From Europe, France Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:31:30 UTC
19:31:30 KST

- Category
- World
Ukraine Gets Two-Thirds of Its Allied Intelligence From Europe, France Says
European countries now provide roughly two-thirds of the intelligence Ukraine receives from its international partners, with France among the major contributors, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on France Inter on October 15.
“Two-thirds of the intelligence provided to Ukraine today comes from Europeans, including France,” Barrot said.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
His comments come as Kyiv faces uncertainty over US intelligence support following tensions surrounding Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries. The figures suggest that Europe has already assumed a much larger role in supplying the battlefield and strategic intelligence Ukraine needs than it had earlier in Russia’s full-scale war.
According to Militarnyi, European assistance covers a broad range of intelligence capabilities, including optical and radar satellite imagery, signals intelligence, information on Russian force movements, and warnings about ballistic missile threats. The latter have become especially important because ballistic weapons leave Ukrainian civilians and air defense units very little time to react after launch.
European countries can detect some ballistic threats using ground-based electronic intelligence systems and long-range radars capable of tracking missiles once they rise beyond the radar horizon. France is also investing heavily in expanding those capabilities.
Paris recently announced a major modernization of its Nostradamus strategic radar in the Eure-et-Loir department. The over-the-horizon system is capable of detecting activity thousands of kilometers away, covering an area stretching from the North Sea toward the Ural Mountains without mechanically rotating its antennas.
Developed by France’s ONERA aerospace research agency in the 1990s, Nostradamus spent years largely mothballed. France is now bringing the system back into a more active role amid growing threats from Russia and Iran, investing more than €50 million in its modernization.
Unlike conventional radar, Nostradamus uses high-frequency radio waves reflected by the ionosphere, allowing it to detect objects far beyond the normal line of sight. Its antennas are arranged across roughly 12 hectares in a star-shaped configuration and can monitor an enormous volume of airspace extending from ground level to an altitude of around 250 kilometers.
Earlier, Russian leader Vladimir Putin stated that Moscow will consider using all available weapons, including its nuclear arsenal, if Kaliningrad or any other Russian territory faces a direct attack or blockade.

Türkiye targets 4.2% growth in 2027 as government unveils budget proposal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:27:45 UTC
19:27:45 KST

Türkiye expects economic growth to accelerate to 4.2% in 2027 from a projected 3.3% this year, supported by an improving global outlook and a recovery in external demand, Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz said Friday with next year's proposed budget in hand.
Presenting the government's 2027 budget proposal at the presidential complex in Ankara, Yilmaz said stronger growth among Türkiye's trading partners would create opportunities for exports and support balanced economic expansion.
The Turkish economy grew 3.7% in 2025, he said, adding that investment outpacing private consumption had strengthened production capacity and improved the composition of growth.
“In 2027, we expect our growth to rise to 4.2%, supported by the anticipated improvement in the global outlook and the recovery in external demand,” Yilmaz said.
The government aims to gradually accelerate growth to 5% by the end of its medium-term program through policies focused on productivity, technological transformation, and innovation, he said.
Employment is expected to increase by 657,000 people next year, with labor force participation reaching 53.4% and unemployment declining to 8%, from a projected 8.1% in 2026.
 
Inflation forecast to decline to 21%
Yilmaz said annual inflation, which fell below 30% in September, was expected to reach 28.4% by the end of this year before declining to 21% by the end of 2027.
“Price stability is the fundamental priority of our program,” he said.
Fiscal discipline and incomes policies will continue to support monetary policy, while supply-side measures, particularly in social housing and food, will reinforce disinflation.
Despite fluctuations stemming from energy and commodity prices, the underlying inflation trend continues to improve, Yilmaz said, reiterating the government's medium-term goal of achieving lasting single-digit inflation.
He said the current account deficit was expected to fall below 2% of gross domestic product next year from a projected 2.6% in 2026.
Türkiye will continue policies to boost exports, strengthen energy supply security, and reduce dependence on energy imports, he added.
Goods exports this January-September rose 5.2% year-on-year to $211 billion, bringing the rolling annual total to a record $283.7 billion, Yilmaz said.
The share of medium-high- and high-technology products in exports reached 44%, compared with around 28% in the early 2000s, he added.
 
Budget spending projected at $551.2B
The 2027 budget proposal projects expenditures of 27.276 trillion Turkish liras and revenues of 23.408 trillion liras ($551.2 billion), with national income expected to reach $2.24 trillion.
The figures imply a budget shortfall of $78.1 billion, equivalent to a projected 3.5% of GDP. Excluding earthquake-related expenditure, the deficit is forecast at 2.8% of GDP.
Yilmaz said the proposal would be submitted to parliament with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's signature, calling it a budget of “resilience, prosperity and transformation.”
Interest expenditures are projected at $80.2 billion, personnel spending at $143.7 billion, and current transfers at $206.7 billion. The budget is expected to maintain a primary surplus next year.
For 2026, the government forecasts a deficit of 3.1% of GDP, below the initial 3.5% projection, despite spending pressures from higher energy and commodity prices.
Urban transformation funding will rise 176% to $5.57 billion in 2027, Yilmaz said, with disaster resilience remaining a priority alongside expanded social and rental housing provision.
Earthquake reconstruction spending over 2023-2026 totaled $109 billion at current prices, equivalent to $104 billion, he said, with 455,357 independent units completed and delivered.
Türkiye's EU-defined general government debt declined to 22.3% of GDP in the second quarter from 23.1% in the first, Yilmaz added, describing low public indebtedness as an important advantage amid global uncertainty.

Turkish foreign minister to attend Muslim bloc OIC meeting in Baghdad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:22:43 UTC
19:22:43 KST

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan will attend a meeting of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), scheduled to take place in Baghdad on Saturday and Sunday.
According to Turkish Foreign Ministry sources, Türkiye will hand over the OIC chairmanship to Iraq at the meeting, which will be held under the theme, Dialogue and Solidarity: Two Essential Pillars for Promoting Peace and Sustainable Development.
Türkiye has held the rotating chairmanship since June 2025.
The meeting is expected to address Israel's ongoing genocidal policies in Gaza, its occupation and annexation activities across Palestine, developments in other conflict zones across the Islamic world, counterterrorism, UN reform, Islamophobia and the situation of Muslim communities in non-OIC member states.
The meeting is expected to conclude with the adoption of the "Baghdad Declaration."
Fidan is scheduled to address the meeting and hold bilateral talks with his counterparts on the sidelines of the visit.
 
Unity on Palestine
In his address, Fidan is expected to stress that Israel's aggression and expansionist policies remain the greatest security threat in the Middle East.
He is also expected to emphasize the need for OIC member states to demonstrate a united stance in response to Israel's actions and coordinate their efforts with responsible international actors.
Fidan is expected to call for decisive measures against countries that relocate their embassies to Jerusalem and efforts to prevent further initiatives of this kind, stressing the importance of preserving the city's status.
He is also expected to reiterate that implementing a Palestinian state based on a two-state solution is the only path to a just and lasting peace, and underline the vital importance of ensuring that humanitarian aid reaches those in need in Gaza fully and without interruption.
 
Regional security and minority rights
He is further expected to highlight the importance of demonstrating strong solidarity with Turkish Cypriots and supporting efforts to end the unjust isolation they face.
Fidan is also expected to stress the importance of OIC-led efforts to protect the fundamental rights and freedoms of the Muslim Turkish minority in Western Thrace and the Muslim Turkish population living in the Dodecanese Islands.
On Syria, he is expected to call for continued joint efforts to preserve the country's territorial integrity and unity, revive its economy and help it achieve a prosperous future.
Regarding Lebanon, he is expected to underline the importance of safeguarding the country's sovereignty and territorial integrity for regional stability and stress that Israel must withdraw completely from southern Lebanon.
Addressing tensions in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, Fidan is expected to highlight their adverse consequences, particularly for Gulf countries, and describe attacks against these states as unacceptable.
He is also expected to emphasize that ensuring freedom and security of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is essential for regional stability and global trade.
Fidan is further expected to strongly condemn Houthi attacks targeting civilians and critical infrastructure and reaffirm Türkiye's solidarity with Saudi Arabia.
 
Organization of Islamic Cooperation
The OIC, formerly known as the Organization of the Islamic Conference, was established on Sept. 25, 1969, at a summit in Rabat, Morocco, in response to the arson attack on Al-Aqsa Mosque in occupied East Jerusalem.
With 57 member states, the OIC is the world's second-largest intergovernmental political organization after the United Nations and the only official body representing Muslims worldwide.
The Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), Russia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Thailand and the Central African Republic hold observer status at the OIC.
Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed of Mauritania was elected the organization's new secretary-general at the 23rd Extraordinary Session of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers, held in August this year.
 
Türkiye and the OIC
Türkiye is one of the OIC's 25 founding members. Its Permanent Mission to the organization began operations in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, on July 24, 2015.
Türkiye assumed the OIC chairmanship for its 51st session at the Council of Foreign Ministers meeting held in Istanbul on June 21-22, 2025. It has previously hosted Council of Foreign Ministers meetings three times, in 1976, 1991, and 2004.
Türkiye hosts the second-largest number of OIC-affiliated institutions after Saudi Arabia.
Several OIC-affiliated bodies are based in Türkiye, including the Statistical, Economic and Social Research and Training Centre for Islamic Countries (SESRIC), the Research Centre for Islamic History, Art and Culture (IRCICA), and the Standing Committee for Economic and Commercial Cooperation of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (COMCEC), one of the OIC's four standing committees.
Other affiliated institutions, including the Islamic Cooperation Youth Forum (ICYF), also operate from Türkiye.

Trump rules out using a nuclear bomb on Iran: Why that matters
It is the first time the president has definitively addressed nuclear weapons, but he did not deny US could use ‘mother of all bombs’.
United States President Donald Trump has for the first time explicitly ruled out the use of a nuclear weapon against Iran, but has not denied US media reports that his administration is considering deploying the US’s most lethal non-nuclear munition, nicknamed the “mother of all bombs” in the near future.
In an interview published on Thursday by right-wing American news site Newsmax, Trump suggested he does not plan to use nuclear weapons, but also clarified that the devastating aerial weapon, the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb (MOAB – ‘mother of all bombs ) “is not nuclear”.
“I wouldn’t use nuclear. We don’t have to. We’re the greatest nuclear power in the world,” he told Newsmax.
The comments marked Trump’s first definitive statement on the nuclear topic following speculation about a possible atomic conflict earlier in the US and Israel’s war on Iran. They also appeared to confirm speculation that another phase of the war is imminent, likely after the US midterm elections on November 3.
Here’s what we know:
What did Trump say?
Trump told Newsmax that the US might indeed launch another strike on Iran’s nuclear sites, particularly on Pickaxe Mountain, where Tehran is believed to be hiding a nuclear facility deep under layers of granite.
He ruled out using a nuclear weapon or a tactical nuclear weapon.
“I wouldn’t use nuclear. We don’t have to. We’re the greatest nuclear power in the world,” he said.
He also clarified that the MOAB, which CNN reported the US government is considering using, “is not nuclear”.
Responding to a question about whether the MOAB is “tactical nuclear” – meaning smaller nuclear munitions – Trump reiterated that it is not.
“Well, the mother of all bombs is not nuclear,” Trump said. “It’s not nuclear at all. This is just an extremely large bomb.”
Trump declined to say whether he had authorised its use in Iran.
Trump also suggested renewed attacks are likely in the near future. The US cannot end the war now because it has to ensure Iran cannot produce a nuclear weapon, he argued, saying he believes that “if they had it, they would use it, in my opinion, instantaneously”.
Trump also reiterated that the war would end “very soon” whether by force or diplomacy and that oil prices would then drop.
When asked if he would put “troops on the ground”, Trump said: “No, I don’t see that, I don’t see it.” Earlier in the war, Trump had made comments regarding sending in troops, a move analysts said would be devastating for US soldiers because of Iran’s mountainous territory.
What is the ‘mother of all bombs’?
The MOAB carries a massive payload of about 8,500kg (18,000 pounds or 8.5 tonnes) of high explosives. It weighs 9,800kg (21,605 pounds or nearly 10 tonnes) – about the same as four cars – and is just over nine metres (about 30 feet) long. Stealth bombers are too small to carry it, so it has to be deployed by larger, Lockheed C-130 Hercules transporters.
It is designed to explode a few metres above the ground, sending out intense fireballs that can blast buildings and other hard-surface structures within a 1km radius, experts have told Al Jazeera. It is so powerful that a mushroom cloud from its blast has been seen 32km (20 miles) away in tests, the US Air Force has said.
“Its large explosive charge can produce devastating blast effects against exposed personnel, equipment and vulnerable structures,” Brussels-based military and weapons analyst Elijah Magnier said. “Its purpose is to generate an exceptionally powerful blast across a surface area.”
However, Magnier said there is doubt about whether using the massive surface explosive would be effective against deeply buried nuclear installations in Iran. He added that the terrain in Iran could be difficult for larger cargo aircraft to access.
What has Trump previously said about nuclear weapons?
Trump has never explicitly mentioned using a nuclear weapon, but he has also never ruled it out.
Speculation regarding whether Washington might use nuclear weapons was rife in the early days of the conflict, largely because of the extreme nature of Trump’s numerous threats against Tehran.
In April, for example, as Iran enforced a blockade on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, Trump posted on his Truth Social site that “…a whole civilisation will die tonight, never to be brought back again”, if Iran did not agree to a peace deal and reopen the strait.
He also threatened to destroy Iran’s infrastructure, saying a bombing campaign “will be Power Plant Day and Bridge Day, all wrapped up in one”, in Iran.
Experts widely interpreted his statements as a threat of nuclear destruction, but one that still failed to force Iran to the table.
Although Trump largely moved away from his sabre-rattling rhetoric in the following weeks, he reiterated at the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month that he could “annihilate” Iran. He also told the assembly that he believed a deal would emerge after the midterms.
What is a ‘tactical’ nuclear weapon?
“Tactical” nuclear weapons (TNW) are smaller nuclear munitions designed for the battlefield as opposed to strategic nuclear munitions designed for mass destruction.
Some perceive TNWs as having a lesser impact than an atomic bomb, but experts warn that their names are misleading and they can nevertheless be devastating. Their explosive yield, between 0.3 and 50 kilotons, can impact areas within a 500-600km radius.
The US dropped a 15-kiloton nuclear bomb on Hiroshima, meaning that weapon would today be considered a TNW. The US, North Korea and Russia have TNWs in their arsenals, although no country has ever used them. TNWs are not subject to any international treaties and are largely unregulated.
What might another US attack on Iran look like?
With Trump failing to rule out dropping the MOAB, analysts speculate that the US might launch another – perhaps final – intensive bombing campaign targeting Iran’s nuclear and defence sites, particularly Pickaxe Mountain.
The US could also continue its naval blockade on Iranian ports, while providing escorts for commercial ships through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran has vowed to respond to escalatory strikes by targeting oil and digital infrastructure in neighbouring Gulf states.
Senior defence officials have also warned that Iran will invade its neighbours if the US launches a ground operation, although Trump appears to have ruled that out.
Earlier in the war, he hinted at the possibility of sending ground forces to retrieve some 400kg of highly enriched uranium that Washington and Israel claim Tehran has hidden underground.
Trump’s phone calls in March to Kurdish militia groups fighting Iran provoked speculation that Washington could coordinate with them for an invasion, although that did not happen.

Italy keeps border controls with Spain in place for another week

Italy will extend its suspension of the Schengen Agreement for travellers arriving from Spain for another week, government sources told Italy’s ANSA news agency on Friday.
The extension aims to align Italy’s suspension with the latest border controls introduced by Spain.
The two countries’ interior ministers are also set to hold talks on ending the border checks in the coming days, sources said.
Spain recently extended temporary border controls on travelers arriving from Italy by air and sea for another 15 days, until October 22.
The controls were initially introduced after Italy imposed border checks on travellers from Spain following the mass arrival in late July of around 72,000 migrants in Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta from Morocco.
Spain responded by introducing controls on travellers arriving from Italy on August 8, formally citing migration pressure on the Central Mediterranean route and unauthorised onward movements from Italy to other Schengen countries, including Spain.
