The international community cannot remain silent in the face of persistent Israeli violations of international law, Turkish Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus said on Friday.
Addressing a meeting of the European Conference of Presidents of Parliament in Rome, Kurtulmus said: “We cannot let impunity go unpunished."
Kurtulmus called upon the international community to take concrete steps to uphold international law.
The erosion of the rules-based international order is starkly reflected in the years-long humanitarian catastrophe and genocide in Gaza, he said.
“We can no longer turn a blind eye to the humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza and the wider region and the blatant human rights violations and crimes against humanity perpetrated by the Israeli government against the people of Palestine,” he urged.
“This is not merely a political question but also a test for the humanity's common conscience,” he said.
Underlining that the Israeli aggression is not confined to Gaza, Kurtulmus said: “Destruction, displacement, and settlers' violence persist in the West Bank, and Israel continues to threaten the territorial integrity and sovereignty of regional countries, including Syria and Lebanon.”
It is imperative that parliaments step up and assume an active role to help put an immediate end to the suffering of the Gazan people and the violations of international humanitarian law, he stressed.
Kurtulmus called on parliaments to take an active role in urgently ending the suffering of the people of Gaza and violations of international humanitarian law.
“We believe that coordinated action by parliaments can strengthen international efforts to uphold international law and confront persistent violations,” he added.
 
International order fails to prevent conflicts
The current international order has proven its inability to prevent conflicts and wars, even in Europe's immediate territory, according to Kurtulmus.
“The war between Russia and Ukraine, continuing for almost five years now, has turned to a war of attrition affecting all of Europe rather than a conflict between two nations,” he said.
Moreover, the international order has failed to stop the genocide perpetrated by the Israeli government in Gaza for more than three years, Kurtulmus said.
Kurtulmus warned that the rules-based international order is suffering a profound erosion in terms of legitimacy and function.
He highlighted that to build a fairer and more credible international order, parliaments must play an active role in shaping, debating, and supporting the new rules and arrangements required for this purpose.
“This is where parliamentary diplomacy becomes particularly important. It can complement traditional diplomacy, keep communication channels open, and when necessary create new ones,” he added.
“Placing the entire burden of resolving crises on the UN and relying solely on UN reform will not yield results.”

Türkiye targets 4.2 percent growth in 2027 as government unveils budget proposal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:16:26 UTC
19:16:26 KST

Türkiye expects economic growth to accelerate to 4.2 percent in 2027 from a projected 3.3 percent this year, supported by an improving global outlook and a recovery in external demand, Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz said on Oct. 16 with next year’s proposed budget in hand.
Presenting the government’s 2027 budget proposal at the presidential complex in Ankara, Yılmaz said stronger growth among Türkiye’s trading partners would create opportunities for exports and support balanced economic expansion.
The Turkish economy grew 3.7 percent in 2025, he said, adding that investment outpacing private consumption had strengthened production capacity and improved the composition of growth.
“In 2027, we expect our growth to rise to 4.2 percent, supported by the anticipated improvement in the global outlook and the recovery in external demand,” Yılmaz said.
The government aims to gradually accelerate growth to 5 percent by the end of its medium-term program through policies focused on productivity, technological transformation and innovation, he said.
Yılmaz said annual inflation, which fell below 30 percent in September, was expected to reach 28.4 percent by the end of this year before declining to 21 percent by the end of 2027.
“Price stability is the fundamental priority of our program,” he said.
Fiscal discipline and incomes policies will continue to support monetary policy, while supply-side measures, particularly in social housing and food, will reinforce disinflation.
Despite fluctuations stemming from energy and commodity prices, the underlying inflation trend continues to improve, Yılmaz said, reiterating the government’s medium-term goal of achieving lasting single-digit inflation.
He said the current account deficit was expected to fall below 2 percent of gross domestic product next year from a projected 2.6 percent in 2026.
Türkiye will continue policies to boost exports, strengthen energy supply security and reduce dependence on energy imports, he added.
The 2027 budget proposal projects expenditures of 27.28 trillion Turkish liras and revenues of 23.41 trillion liras ($551.2 billion), with national income expected to reach $2.24 trillion.
The figures imply a budget shortfall of $78.1 billion, equivalent to a projected 3.5 percent of GDP. Excluding earthquake-related expenditure, the deficit is forecast at 2.8 percent of GDP.
Yılmaz said the proposal would be submitted to parliament with President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s signature, calling it a budget of “resilience, prosperity and transformation.”
Interest expenditures are projected at $80.2 billion. The budget is expected to maintain a primary surplus next year.
For 2026, the government forecasts a deficit of 3.1 percent of GDP, below the initial 3.5 percent projection, despite spending pressures from higher energy and commodity prices.
Urban transformation funding will rise 176 percent to $5.57 billion in 2027, Yilmaz said, with disaster resilience remaining a priority alongside expanded social and rental housing provision.
Earthquake reconstruction spending over 2023-2026 totaled $109 billion at current prices, equivalent to $104 billion, he said, with 455,357 independent units completed and delivered.

Iran–Vietnam trade ties expand: bitumen MOU, Iran Med 2026 talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:16:14 UTC
19:16:14 KST

Vietnamese trade delegation seeks deeper direct trade with Iran
TEHRAN — A Vietnamese trade delegation arrived in Tehran on Tuesday, October 6, and is scheduled to remain until October 18. Led by Mr. Nguyen Dang Dinh, who is visiting Iran for the third time, the delegation has a packed agenda: visits to various regions, assessments of cooperation opportunities, and trade meetings. In an exclusive interview with the Tehran Times, Dinh said the mission aims to expand Vietnam’s commercial reach in the Middle East and engage directly with Iran’s sizable market. Vietnamese businesses seek to boost direct exports of agricultural products—coffee, cashews, pepper, rice—and consumer goods, while exploring imports of high-quality Iranian industrial inputs and raw materials.
The delegation’s working report provides the following detailed account of its program and findings:
REPORT ON THE WORKING VISIT AND TRADE PROMOTION MISSION TO IRAN
1. 9 October – Bandar Abbas, Hormozgan Province
The delegation visited and conducted an on-site assessment of Shahid Rajaee Port in Bandar Abbas, Hormozgan Province. As Iran’s largest seaport, Shahid Rajaee plays a key role in the country’s foreign trade and serves as a transit gateway for neighbouring landlocked countries.
The delegation toured five terminals and met with Mr. Yousefi Karami, the manager responsible for import and export container operations at Terminal 2. Discussions covered port operations, particularly the accumulation of empty containers as a result of the war. According to information provided during the meeting, shipping companies are eligible for storage charge relief for up to 60 days and may request an additional extension of 15–30 days, subject to approval by the port management, taking into account their operating history and cargo volumes.
The delegation also inspected bonded storage facilities and explored the possibility of leasing land for the storage of unprocessed agricultural commodities and other goods imported into Iran for subsequent re-export to neighboring markets.
2. 10 October – Bandar Abbas
The delegation visited Petro Pasargad’s privately owned refinery, which has more than 15 years of experience in bitumen production. During the visit, the delegation met with Mr. Yousefi, Technical Director, and obtained samples of 60/70 penetration-grade bitumen currently exported by the company to Viet Nam.
The visit provided an opportunity to exchange information on product specifications, production capacity and prospects for commercial cooperation with Vietnamese partners.
3. 12 October – Shiraz
The delegation attended the Expo Shiraz International Exhibition, organized by the Trade Promotion Organization under Iran’s Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade. The delegation visited six selected exhibition stands representing agriculture, petrochemicals, construction, tourism, healthcare, and handicrafts.
The exhibition was large in scale and professionally organized, providing a valuable platform for business networking and exploring international partnerships. The organizers invited the delegation to take part in an interview and facilitated introductions to relevant companies to support business-to-business (B2B) engagement.
4. 15 October – Tehran
4.1. Meeting with Petro Pasargad
At Petro Pasargad’s headquarters, the delegation met with the Chief Executive Officer to discuss potential forms of commercial cooperation and signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU).
According to the company, its plant produces approximately 300–400 tonnes of bitumen per day, supplied in jumbo bags and steel drums. Before the war, its products were exported to China, Malaysia, Singapore, African markets, Bangladesh, and Viet Nam.
The company reported that, owing to the blockade affecting seaports and difficulties in export operations, it currently offers its products primarily on a Free on Board (FOB) basis. Bitumen prices fluctuate daily, driven mainly by global oil prices and the US dollar exchange rate in Iran.
4.2. Visit to the MED 26 International Medical Equipment Exhibition
In the afternoon, the delegation visited the MED 26 International Medical Equipment Exhibition at the Shahr Aftab Exhibition Centre, organized by Iran’s Ministry of Health.
At the exhibition, the delegation met with Dr. Reza’i, a former Deputy Minister of Health who currently oversees Iranian medical equipment manufacturing and export enterprises. Through his introductions, the delegation established contact with Ohad Group, a manufacturer of oxygen generators and ventilators.
According to information presented by the company, its products are used in approximately 80% of hospitals across Iran and are exported to Iraq, Russia, Belarus, and the Philippines. The company is also implementing a technology transfer agreement for production in Indonesia.
Ohad Group expressed interest in establishing a joint-venture manufacturing facility in Viet Nam, with phased technology transfer to help strengthen domestic medical equipment production capacity.
5. Conclusions and Recommendations
The mission enabled the delegation to assess logistics infrastructure, examine industrial production capabilities, engage with Iranian exporters, and establish business contacts in the medical equipment sector.
Key outcomes included an initial assessment of bonded storage and land-leasing opportunities at Shahid Rajaee Port; the signing of an MoU with Petro Pasargad to advance cooperation in the bitumen sector; and the establishment of contact with Ohad Group to explore joint-venture manufacturing and medical equipment technology transfer in Viet Nam.
It is recommended that follow-up engagement with the Iranian partners focus on clarifying commercial terms, logistics arrangements and specific cooperation mechanisms, while assessing the legal, financial and technological feasibility of the proposed projects in Vietnam.
On Friday, October 16, in Tehran, a memorandum of understanding was signed between DHT Mining Joint Stock Company, represented by Mr. Nguyen Dang Dinh, and Petro Pasargad Hormozgan Company, represented by Mr. Mostafa Hajihosseini. The MOU covers the provision and distribution of bitumen of POH origin in Vietnam.
The same day, the Vietnamese delegation visited the specialized exhibition for medical, dental, laboratory, and pharmaceutical equipment, “Iran Med 2026,” at the Shahr-e Aftab International Exhibition Center. The delegation held intensive B2B negotiations with Iranian counterparts. During its stay, the delegation has also visited various cities, including Bandar Abbas, and Shiraz Expo.
Dinh identified banking restrictions as the main operational concern. He called for flexible settlement frameworks, such as bilateral barter trade or compliant local-currency clearing, to reduce exchange costs and transaction friction. Official Vietnam–Iran trade is around $170 million, but much of the real trade may pass through third countries. He said actual potential is significantly higher because the two economies are complementary. To make flows more direct and transparent, businesses need market intelligence, trade expos, and official business-matching platforms.
The most realistic sectors for immediate cooperation, he said, include agriculture and food processing; industrial raw materials such as specialty chemicals, construction supplies, and polymers; and healthcare and pharmaceuticals, including medical equipment, active ingredients, and biotechnology. Key supply-chain bottlenecks include long transit times, high freight costs, and differing quality-compliance frameworks such as Halal certification. He recommended direct links with regional logistics providers and mutual recognition between regulators to standardize inspections and expedite customs clearance.
Vietnam’s 17 free trade agreements and access to 60 economies offer a platform for joint ventures or Vietnam-based production. Iranian firms can add value inside Vietnam and jointly access ASEAN and wider international markets under compliant arrangements. For the business community, a successful mission means vetted leads, initial contracts, and MOUs for non-sanctioned goods. Chambers of commerce and trade promotion agencies should maintain direct communication and organize regular exchange delegations to turn these discussions into long-term trade and investment partnerships.

ICC serves Europe’s ‘colonialist interests’ – analyst (VIDEO)
The International Criminal Court (ICC) has become a tool of Western influence that selectively targets countries of the Global South while shielding European interests and ignoring crimes in Ukraine, international legal analyst and academic Alexandre Guerreiro has said. He accused the tribunal of applying double standards rather than delivering universal justice.
Criticism of the ICC has intensified in recent months amid growing accusations of political bias and selective justice. Venezuela, Chad, Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger have moved to withdraw, accusing the court of serving Western interests and engaging in “neocolonial repression.”
In an interview with RT on Thursday, Guerreiro argued that the court had abandoned its original purpose as an independent institution capable of holding perpetrators accountable regardless of nationality, and has become increasingly politicized and dominated by European powers.
“In practice, what we have is a court that serves European interests, colonialist interests,” he said, arguing that the tribunal is used to pressure Global South nations while avoiding similar scrutiny of European countries.
Guerreiro pointed to the court’s handling of cases involving Afghanistan, Iraq and Kenya, arguing that political interference had repeatedly undermined the principles of impartial justice.
He also accused the ICC of ignoring alleged crimes in Ukraine, including the deadly May 2014 Odessa clashes between Ukrainian nationalists and opponents of the Western-backed coup in Kiev, as well as the sniper shootings during the preceding Maidan unrest.
“This is not justice,” he said, arguing that the court only pursues cases that serve the interests of the current Ukrainian authorities and the Western bloc as a whole.
The remarks come days after Washington imposed sweeping new sanctions on the ICC, accusing it of overstepping its jurisdiction in cases involving American and Israeli nationals. The court issued arrest warrants in 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
Meanwhile, the ICC’s investigation into alleged war crimes by American forces in Afghanistan has produced no criminal charges against US personnel.

Turkish exports to BRICS nations top $18.2 bln in January-September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:14:21 UTC
19:14:21 KST

Türkiye’s exports to the 10 member states of the BRICS grouping totaled $18.2 billion in the first nine months of the year, according to the Turkish Exporters’ Assembly (TİM).
While Türkiye’s total global exports this January-September grew 5.2 percent to $210.9 billion, Russia was the largest destination among other BRICS member states, receiving $4.1 billion in exports despite a 2.5 percent annual decline.
BRICS includes longtime members Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa, plus recent additions Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, and the United Arab Emirates.
The UAE followed Russia as the second-largest destination for Turkish exports to BRICS, accounting for $3.3 billion even after a 4.12 percent contraction in export volume.
Egypt followed with a rise of 28.6 percent to $3.1 billion, China with a surge of 40.8 percent to $3 billion, and Iran with $1.8 billion, making the country the fifth-largest BRICS destination for Turkish goods.
Turkish exports increased in eight of the 10 BRICS member states, with shipments in Ethiopia surging the most by 79.6 percent.
The chemicals and chemical products sector accounted for most of these exports to the bloc, generating $3.5 billion in the first nine months of the year, the data showed.
Mining exports grew 33.5 percent to $2.1 billion, a net gain of roughly $539 million, followed by the jewelry sector, whose exports fell 45 percent to $1.3 billion.
The textiles and raw material exports climbed 8.7 percent to $1.2 billion at the same time.

Indian police warn 'Cockroach' movement founder against holding protest
Police warned the founder of India's 'Cockroach' movement against going ahead with a protest on Friday, local media reported, setting the stage for a possible confrontation with the group that is demanding the resignation of the election chief.
The youth-led 'Cockroach Janta Party' (CJP), opposition groups, and student organisations have held almost daily protests this month demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation over a revision of voter lists that critics say favours Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
More than 130 million voters were deleted during the revision but the Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol. The BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke called Friday's protest in support of two CJP leaders detained and sent to jail this week for five days for demonstrating at a protest site in violation of a ban.
The group and left-wing student organisations have urged supporters to gather at the Central Park in New Delhi's busy Connaught Place shopping and food district on Friday evening to wave and hoist the national flag.
Dipke said police visited him and served a notice saying the group was engaging in "unlawful activities and inciting people".
"Don't we even have the freedom to hoist our own tricolour in our own nation?" he said in a statement.
The notice said that prohibitory orders were in effect in Connaught Place and no permission had been given for a rally, news agency ANI reported, citing police sources.
The notice also said that legal action would be taken if Dipke went to the location, ANI said.
Delhi Police did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.
'Don't join', Police warn
Security was stepped up in the city and police urged people not to join "such assemblies", saying it can instead facilitate a group of select people to carry the national flag and sing the national anthem at a "suitable place".
The civic authority said the park itself would be closed for two days "due to administrative reasons".
Traders in the area petitioned the Supreme Court to prevent the protest, which they say "would cause severe loss", and demanded compensation for losses suffered during a similar rally planned over the weekend that was foiled by a security crackdown.
The cockroach movement has emerged as one of the biggest political challenges faced by Modi and his BJP in his 12 years in power.
A weeks-long sit-in by its supporters earlier this year forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation over exam paper leaks.
The latest demonstrations erupted after The Indian Express newspaper reported that Kumar's two deputies raised concerns internally about voter list changes, registration procedures and digital systems.
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said the demonstrations were main opposition Congress party's attempt to "seize power".
"Instead of channelling the energy of the youth toward nation-building, they are being used as pawns in the politics of anarchy," he said at a media briefing on Friday.

Türkiye, 18 nations condemn Colombia’s embassy move

Unknown Publisher

Türkiye and 18 other countries on Oct. 16 strongly condemned Colombia’s inauguration of its embassy in Jerusalem.
In a joint statement released by Türkiye’s Foreign Ministry, the ministers expressed their “unequivocal rejection” of the decision.
They said the move violates relevant U.N. Security Council resolutions and undermines international efforts to achieve a just and lasting peace based on a two-state solution.
The statement was issued by the foreign ministers of Türkiye, Palestine, Saudi Arabia, Syria, Egypt, Qatar, Pakistan, Indonesia, Lebanon, Yemen, Somalia, Jordan, Algeria, Oman, Sudan, Libya, Kuwait, Malaysia and Djibouti.
The ministers reaffirmed that any measure or decision intended to alter the legal or historical status of occupied Jerusalem, or to recognize the city as Israel’s capital, “is null and void and has no legal effect.”
They cited U.N. Security Council Resolutions 476 and 478, which reject attempts to change Jerusalem’s character or status and call on states to withdraw their diplomatic missions from the city.
The statement described Jerusalem as part of the Palestinian territory occupied in 1967.
The ministers called on the Colombian government to reconsider and reverse its decision, uphold its obligations under international law, and refrain from measures that prejudice the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people.
They also reiterated their support for the Palestinian people’s right to an independent and sovereign state, with east Jerusalem as its capital.

The planned measures will also address coordinated transactions by funds, Şimşek said in a statement on Turkish social media platform NSosyal, outlining steps to improve market transparency and bolster investor confidence.
Relevant institutions are implementing significant regulations, taking into account assessments by international index providers, he said.
Regulations introduced by the Capital Markets Board have strengthened the flow of information and made ultimate share ownership more transparent, Şimşek added.

Şimşek said authorities would closely monitor the results and take any additional steps without delay in consultation with stakeholders.

Sanctions will be applied resolutely against those who disrupt the fair and competitive functioning of markets, he added.
“Our goal is to establish a transparent, reliable and efficient capital market where investor rights are protected,” Şimşek said.

Israel cannot afford another election: Why Netanyahu, Eisenkot must consider unity - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:08:30 UTC
19:08:30 KST

In the summer of 2019, Yuli Edelstein, then speaker of the Knesset, came to meet with us at The Jerusalem Post.
Israel had held an election in April that failed to produce a government and was forced back to the polls in September. It was the first time in the country’s history that one election had led almost immediately to another, and Edelstein, then a senior figure in Likud, had a clear message: This would not happen again. Whatever the personal differences between the political camps, the country would find a way to form a government.
Sadly, he was wrong, as were many of us who believed that Israel’s politicians would eventually come to their senses. Instead, the country went to the polls five times in three-and-a-half years, until the current government was established following the election at the end of 2022.
When people think about October 7, they understandably focus on the intelligence failures, the IDF’s failure to defend the border, and the questions surrounding the warnings that did or did not reach Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Some go further back to the year before the attack, when the government’s judicial overhaul tore Israeli society apart. Rarely, though, do we go back further than that.
The truth is that Israel arrived at October 7 battered, divided, and polarized in ways we have yet to fully process. The judicial overhaul was devastating, but it did not come out of nowhere. It followed five elections marked by relentless political fighting, personal rivalries, and the growing belief that defeating the other side mattered more than governing the country. The overhaul deepened those divisions, eroded trust in institutions, and made the country weak and vulnerable.
Hamas saw an opening in this division and took it on October 7. The fact that we have yet to establish a commission of inquiry into the events that led to the attack is a gamble with Israel’s future.
This history matters as we approach the October 27 election, because the polls suggest that another stalemate is a real possibility. Neither bloc appears to have the 61 seats needed for a conventional majority government, and neither seems capable of persuading enough politicians from the other side to join it. Much can change before election day, particularly with undecided voters and parties hovering around the electoral threshold. But we need to ask now what outcome is actually in the country’s interest.
The opposition’s criticism of Netanyahu is legitimate. He has been in office for too long, the failures have piled up, and it is time for change. His decision to govern with the far Right has caused Israel immense damage, internally and internationally. But Netanyahu is also right that the opposition’s boycott of him has contributed to the prospect of deadlock. This is what happens when personality politics overwhelms almost everything else.
Three possibilities to avoid another election
ANOTHER ELECTION, in my mind, would be catastrophic. Israel is militarily stronger today because its enemies are weaker, but military superiority does not remove the danger of political paralysis. With so many challenges still unresolved, returning to the cycle of election after election would put us back on the same destructive path that preceded October 7.
If avoiding that outcome is the objective, there are essentially three possibilities.
The first is that one side wins 61 seats, as hard as that is to imagine based on current polling. It could be Netanyahu and it could be the opposition. This would be the clearest outcome – one side would win, and while the other would be angry and disappointed, the voters will have spoken. Even if one side does not get 61 in its current form, we cannot rule out defections – parties switching alliances – something that has happened repeatedly in the past.
The second possibility is that neither side reaches 61 seats and the opposition tries to establish a minority government. The most plausible version would bring together Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Avigdor Liberman, and Yair Golan. They would not need the Arab parties to vote in favor of the government, but they would need enough Arab MKs to not vote against it.
Such a government could remove Netanyahu from office and establish a state commission of inquiry into October 7, a lofty objective that should have been done a long time ago. Beyond that, however, it will not be able to function, and the minority government would be established simply to take the country straight back to another election.
As tempting as this might be, there is a danger in this that the opposition should not underestimate. Firstly, the path leads anyhow to another election, no different than the deadlock option. Second, there is a chance that Netanyahu would return even stronger after the next election, arguing that he had warned voters Eisenkot and Bennett would govern with the support of Arab parties and that they had proved him right.
The third possibility is what is often referred to as a unity government. I know how unrealistic this sounds today, but it deserves consideration if the alternative is yet another election. In many respects, this would not even be unity across an enormous ideological divide. The principal obstacle between Netanyahu, Eisenkot, Bennett, Liberman, and Golan is not necessarily their view of Israel’s central security challenges but their view of one another.
Set aside judicial reform for a moment and consider the major issues. Is there really such a vast difference between them on confronting Iran, rebuilding support in the United States, the future of the Palestinian conflict, or maintaining far stronger defenses along the borders with Gaza and Lebanon?
There are meaningful disagreements on the rule of law, the West Bank, and responsibility for October 7, and they cannot be wished away. But there is also more than enough common ground to at least explore whether a stable government could be formed.
THE OBVIOUS objection is that Netanyahu cannot be trusted. He has broken political promises in the past, manipulated coalition partners, and brought down governments when it served his interests. All of that is true, and anyone considering joining him would have to enter such an arrangement with eyes wide open and an incredible amount of suspicion.
But politics is not about choosing between a good option and a bad one. Often, it is about deciding which of the bad options will do the least damage. If the alternative to exploring a unity government is another election, followed perhaps by another stalemate, which course would be worse for the country?
Netanyahu has been a central figure in Israeli politics for more than 30 years, since first becoming prime minister in 1996. He is a political chameleon who knows how to move left, shift right, settle in the center, and adapt his alliances based on political survival. If staying in office requires him to govern with different partners, and to accept different constraints, he usually knows how to do so.
None of this means that Netanyahu can suddenly be trusted politically, and we have no way of knowing whether he has changed. Is survival in office the only objective for him today, or is there still something within him that will put the country first even if it means restraints and policies that for the last four years he has avoided, like a commission of inquiry?
It is true that such a government might prove impossible, and that even if formed it will quickly collapse. But surely we owe it to ourselves to test the possibility rather than dismiss it outright.
Edelstein’s warning in 2019 was that Israel could not afford to become a country incapable of forming a government. We ignored that warning and allowed years of political division to become normal. October 7 should have taught us that national security depends not only on military strength but also on social cohesion and leadership capable of putting the country ahead of personal rivalries.
Hopefully, October 27 will produce a clear winner. If it does not, Israel’s political leaders will have to decide whether their refusal to sit together matters more than the country they are supposed to serve. After everything Israel has endured, another round of elections cannot be treated as an acceptable outcome.
The writer is a co-founder of the MEAD policy forum, a senior fellow at JPPI, and a former editor-in-chief of The Jerusalem Post. His newest book is While Israel Slept.

UK expands sanction powers, enabling action against companies supporting West Bank settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:08:06 UTC
19:08:06 KST

Britain brought new regulations into force on Thursday, significantly expanding its sanctions powers in a move that could enable action against construction companies, developers, and financial institutions supporting settlement expansion in the West Bank.
The measures took effect four days before the deadline for submitting bids for construction in the E1 area between Jerusalem and Ma'aleh Adumim, amid a diplomatic dispute between Israel and Britain over the closure of the British consulate in east Jerusalem.
The new regulations expand Britain's sanctions framework concerning human rights and international humanitarian law. They allow sanctions against individuals and entities directly involved in activities classified as serious violations of international law, as well as those financing, facilitating, or promoting such activities, subject to specified legal conditions.
Possible measures include asset freezes, financial restrictions, travel bans, and disqualification from serving as company directors. The regulations could also allow sanctions against entities involved in settlement-related activities if they meet the established criteria, but do not impose blanket restrictions on all companies operating in the area.
UK sanctions expansion comes ahead of E1 settlement construction deadline
The timing is particularly significant as Israel advances construction plans in the E1 area. The deadline for submitting bids for 1,234 housing units, part of a broader plan involving approximately 3,400 units, is scheduled for October 19, while consideration of the bids by the tender committee has been postponed until after November 19.
Britain opposes the project, arguing that construction in the area would undermine the territorial continuity required for a future Palestinian state. Israeli officials view the development as part of settlement expansion and efforts to strengthen continuity between Jerusalem and Ma'aleh Adumim, rejecting the argument that international opposition should prevent the project from proceeding.
The tender is expected to close in the coming days despite the postponement of the committee's review. Companies seeking to participate must therefore submit their bids before it becomes clear whether Britain intends to exercise its new sanctions powers against entities connected to the project.
British advocates of expanded sanctions are seeking to deter companies and financial institutions from participating at the bidding stage, before contractors are selected and construction begins.
British lawmakers warn banks over financing E1 construction
Political figures and organizations in Britain opposed to settlement construction have also been working to increase pressure on businesses that could participate in the project.
Last month, members of Parliament contacted banks and financial institutions, warning of the risks associated with financing construction in E1. This week, the Britain Palestine Project, an organization supporting measures against settlements, warned that companies and contractors participating in the development could jeopardize their international business relationships.
In letters sent to financial institutions, lawmakers called on banks to assess their potential exposure to the E1 project and raise the issue at board level, including the legal, economic, and reputational risks involved.
Although the letters represent requests from lawmakers rather than binding government directives, they are intended to increase pressure on banks and other institutions providing financing and guarantees, encouraging them to avoid involvement in the project.
Concerns over possible future sanctions could influence commercial decisions even before Britain announces restrictions against specific companies.
Peace Now warns British sanctions could affect broader Israeli economy
The Israeli settlement watchdog Peace Now responded sharply to the regulations taking effect on Thursday, warning that their consequences could extend beyond companies directly involved in settlement construction.
"This is a real alarm. Today, it is already clear that settlements are not only an obstacle to peace and a danger to security, but also an economic threat to the country's future," the organization said.
Peace Now accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich of advancing construction in E1 and warned that the consequences of sanctions could eventually affect the broader Israeli public.
"The price of this messianic adventure could be paid not only by settlers, but by millions of law-abiding Israeli citizens," the organization said. "Today, these are sanctions on settlements. Tomorrow, they will reach every household in Israel."
Concerns about broader economic consequences were also raised last month. According to concerns expressed within the Israeli government, foreign importers and financial institutions could struggle to distinguish between companies operating in settlements and other Israeli businesses, potentially imposing stricter commercial conditions on companies that are not themselves subject to sanctions.
For now, these remain assessments of possible consequences, and the scale of any economic damage, if it occurs, remains unknown.
New sanctions rules could increase scrutiny of Israeli companies and banks
The regulations could also have further implications for the financial sector.
If sanctions are imposed on a particular company or entity, financial institutions subject to British law would be required to comply with the applicable restrictions, including asset freezes and prohibitions on making funds or economic resources available.
Companies not included on sanctions lists could also face additional information requests and more stringent reviews by banks and business partners, as part of compliance and risk-management procedures intended to ensure that transactions do not violate the restrictions.
However, business ties with the West Bank do not, in themselves, automatically constitute grounds for sanctions against a company or bank.
UK expands global human rights sanctions and introduces fast-track mechanism
The new regulations also cover matters unrelated to settlements. Britain will be able to impose sanctions for obstructing humanitarian assistance and for serious violations of the right to liberty and personal security, including unlawful detention.
The regulations also introduce a mechanism allowing London to temporarily adopt sanctions already imposed by partner countries for up to 112 days while considering whether to introduce independent British sanctions.
The mechanism will allow the British government to apply restrictions through an accelerated procedure based on decisions already taken by other countries.
Britain advances separate restrictions on settlement trade and imports
The British move forms part of a broader plan presented by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband on September 8, which also includes a proposed ban on imports from settlements and restrictions on related commercial activities.
Separate legislation introducing the import ban has not yet been completed. In recent months, Britain has also coordinated with other countries in taking action against individuals and entities accused of involvement in settler violence and its financing.
According to London's plan, the separate trade legislation also includes restrictions on advertising and marketing settlement real estate in Britain.
In September, 12 European and Western countries, including Britain, France, and Canada, announced support for advancing trade restrictions concerning settlements, each in accordance with its domestic procedures. In some countries, the measures remain in the drafting and legislative stages.
British opposition raises concerns over Palestinian workers
The sanctions have also generated debate within Britain.
The opposition Conservative Party has previously warned that economic restrictions could harm Palestinian workers and businesses not involved in the activities targeted by the government.
Conversely, Emily Thornberry, chair of Parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee, has supported measures against settlements while criticizing the time required to complete the legislation.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham clarified in Parliament this week that security and intelligence cooperation with Israel continues despite the political disagreements.
The potential impact on Palestinian workers was also raised in a parliamentary question submitted to the British government.
In a response issued earlier this month, the government emphasized that its measures target settlement activity it considers illegal, as well as violence and extremism, while Palestinian businesses will continue to benefit from existing preferential trade arrangements.
However, the response did not include an estimate of the number of Palestinian workers who could be affected by restrictions on economic activity in settlements.
The British government has not yet presented data that would allow an assessment of the potential impact on those workers.
UK-Israel diplomatic tensions continue over east Jerusalem consulate
The regulations took effect one week after understandings were reached between Israel and Britain concerning the British consulate in east Jerusalem.
Israel reduced Britain's diplomatic presence and halted additional activities in response to London's measures, but Britain has not reversed its sanctions policy.
Although the new regulations are now in force, no new sanctions have been announced under them against companies, developers, or financial institutions involved in E1 construction.
British Foreign Office clarifies sanctions are global, not Israel-specific
A spokesperson for the British Foreign Office clarified that the updated regulations represent a change in global sanctions policy rather than a measure specifically targeting Israel or settlements.
According to the spokesperson, the existing framework had allowed Britain to impose sanctions on individuals and entities involved in serious human rights violations or breaches of international humanitarian law worldwide.
The updated policy expands the range of serious violations that could trigger sanctions, regardless of where they occur.
The spokesperson stressed that the regulations are separate from the legislative process and sanctions measures concerning settlements considered illegal under international law, and do not introduce any trade-related restrictions.
The Foreign Office also emphasized that the updated policy does not target any specific country.
Rather, it is intended to allow Britain to respond more quickly to individuals and organizations involved in serious human rights violations or breaches of international humanitarian law anywhere in the world.

The battle for Israel: As Netanyahu rallies the Right, Eisenkot makes his move for power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:07:56 UTC
19:07:56 KST

As the election nears, Netanyahu targets right-wing alternatives, while Eisenkot seeks the commanding lead that would make him the opposition’s undisputed PM candidate
Think of Israel as one big cruise liner. Considering the country’s hyper-stressed reality, that may require some imagination, but bear with it for a moment.
On the starboard side of the ship, the right side, are all the voters in the pro-Netanyahu camp, split into different halls and ballrooms.
The Likud occupies the biggest hall, with smaller rooms for Shas, United Torah Judaism, Otzma Yehudit, and the Religious Zionist Party.
On the port side, separated from starboard by a hallway with doors leading to both sides, are the rooms of the anti-Netanyahu camp.
Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar has the biggest room there, followed by Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad, with smaller rooms for the Democrats and Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu.
In the hallway itself stand Ofer Winter’s People of Israel party and Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha’s reservist-economist party. Behind the ship, in a separate tugboat, sail the two Arab parties.
As the cruise liner steams toward its destination, Election Day, just 11 days away, representatives of the two sides shout the expected accusations across the hallway.
From one side: “You are responsible for the worst disaster in Israel’s history and are leading the country toward catastrophe.” From the other: “You will join forces with those in the tugboat and establish a Palestinian state.”
But the more consequential action is taking place on each side of the ship.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu looks down the hallway, trying to persuade Winter’s and Hendel’s voters to abandon them and come to his side of the ship. Over on the port side, Eisenkot is trying to expand his already large ballroom at the expense of the rooms occupied by those sharing his side of the liner.
Netanyahu intensifies campaign to consolidate right-wing voters
Those two maneuvers are dominating the final stretch of the voyage to Election Day. And what is a sure sign the campaign has entered that final stretch? Netanyahu’s sudden ubiquity on the airwaves.
After months when the prime minister’s interviews were largely reserved for foreign media, ABC, CBS, Fox News, and various podcasts, he showed up in Israeli studios this week, and not only on Channel 14.
Granted, on Tuesday he was, again, on Channel 14, where a “home crowd” greeted him rapturously. But the next day he was on Channel 11, and in between he appeared on Army Radio.
His message had two parts: the election is perilously close, and right-wing voters cannot afford to gamble.
The first is familiar. Netanyahu has sounded the same alarm in numerous campaigns, warning his voters that victory is slipping away. On Channel 14, he anticipated the obvious response: people would dismiss this as his traditional gevalt campaign. This time, he insisted, he really is worried. The race is tied, he said.
And where, precisely, did he see right-wing voters gambling?
Once you cut through the familiar warnings about Eisenkot joining forces with Ahmad Tibi and the election determining whether a Palestinian state will be established, a much smaller target comes into view: Winter’s party.
Netanyahu’s relentless attacks on the retired brigadier-general stand out in this final stretch. At a time when he might be expected to concentrate his fire on Eisenkot and Bennett, he is devoting considerable energy to a small party standing in the hallway.
Netanyahu said he had tried to persuade Winter to join the Likud and, when that failed, to team up with another small right-wing party. That, too, failed, so now he is going after him mercilessly.
In one of the anti-Winter messages he put out this week, Netanyahu charged that Winter would take right-wing votes and carry them over to Liberman on the port side of the ship.
“It’s no coincidence that a senior figure on Liberman’s list, Yulia Malinovsky, says that ultimately Winter will join a government with Liberman. That’s what will happen. That’s the plan,” Netanyahu said.
Then came a blistering comparison with Bennett, who formed a government in 2021 with Yair Lapid’s Yesh Atid and Mansour Abbas’s Ra’am.
“If he walks like Bennett and talks like Bennett, he’s Bennett. Vote Likud, vote Right. Winter is not right-wing. Winter is Bennett 2. We mustn’t squander the Right’s votes. Don’t vote for Winter.”
Winter's coalition conditions complicate Netanyahu's election strategy
Netanyahu’s concern is twofold.
First, Winter’s party will fail to cross the 3.25% electoral threshold, sending votes cast by people on the Right down the drain. Of the 19 major polls taken since October 1, the party crossed the threshold in 11, including four of the seven taken in the last week.
That is enough to keep Winter in the race, but hardly enough to reassure Netanyahu that the votes will count.
The second concern is that Winter will cross the threshold, then peddle his seats elsewhere.
Winter and others in his party say they will recommend Netanyahu to the president as prime minister. But they also say they will not join a government in which the haredi parties hold the balance of power unless those parties agree to a widespread haredi conscription law.
But what if Netanyahu does not accept those conditions? Asked precisely that in a Channel 12 interview on Saturday night, Winter replied, rather inelegantly, that Netanyahu could essentially “go take a hike.”
Nobody owns me, he declared
Winter did not explicitly rule out joining an Eisenkot or Liberman government. He did, however, rule out sitting with Yair Golan, because “he smears Israel abroad.”
For Netanyahu’s campaign, that left an opening wide enough to drive a campaign bus through.
A recommendation is one thing; a commitment to join a government is another. Winter is offering the former, with conditions attached to the latter. Netanyahu wants right-wing voters to hear that distinction and draw the conclusion he is supplying: Winter could be Bennett all over again.
The pressure has extended to billboards and signs in areas where candidates on Winter’s list live. Davidi Ben-Zion, eighth on the list, withdrew, reportedly telling colleagues that pressure on his family, including negative posters strategically placed near the bus stops his children use, had become too much.
Netanyahu’s concerns also extend to the other party in the hallway: Hendel and Zelekha’s.
In the Channel 14 interview, Netanyahu went after Zelekha, whom Netanyahu – as finance minister – appointed accountant-general in 2003. Despite the party’s appeal to right-wing voters, Netanyahu charged that Zelekha had voted for Meretz in the past and participated enthusiastically in anti-government protests on Balfour Street in Jerusalem and Kaplan Street in Tel Aviv.
He also attacked Zelekha on his home turf, the economy, challenging his credentials as a free-market champion.
Hendel and Zelekha’s party crossed the threshold in all seven major polls taken this week. But unlike Winter, they have not pledged to recommend Netanyahu. Hendel says the party will use its leverage to establish a broad Zionist government without the Arab and haredi parties.
Given the coalition arithmetic, how that government would come together remains an enigma. Like Winter, Hendel is clearer about his conditions than about how he would assemble a government that meets them.
But Netanyahu doesn’t need their coalition plans fully worked out to worry about them. He needs the voters attracted to those parties back in his camp.
Eisenkot seeks commanding lead to establish opposition leadership
Across the ship’s hallway, Eisenkot has a different calculation.
His campaign to make Yashar the largest party is aimed, in part, at voters already on his side of the boat. He wants them to leave the other rooms and enter his ballroom.
For Netanyahu, the immediate task is to consolidate the camp. For Eisenkot, it is also to establish who commands it.
That is why the leaders of the other parties in his bloc are less than enthusiastic about his strategy. A voter moving from Bennett, Liberman, or Golan to Eisenkot does not enlarge the bloc. It enlarges Eisenkot.
The bigger Yashar is, and the wider its lead over the Likud, the stronger his claim to form the next government – even if his bloc falls short of 61 seats.
Eisenkot repeated one phrase this week: Netanyahu must not be allowed to win by losing. By that, he means Netanyahu must not remain caretaker prime minister through another cycle of inconclusive elections simply because no one else can form a coalition.
In a Yediot Aharonot interview this week, Eisenkot said, “If you [Netanyahu] think you will do to me what you did to others in the past – meaning, remain in office at the head of a caretaker government – that will not happen.” When Israel held five elections in under four years, from April 2019 to November 2022, Netanyahu served 19 months as caretaker prime minister over two stretches.
Eisenkot considers minority government to prevent Netanyahu remaining in office
One route Eisenkot envisages to prevent a repeat of that scenario is to bring a minority government to the Knesset for approval and secure the support of a majority of those voting.
A government does not need 61 members to win such a vote; it only needs a majority of those in the plenum casting a vote. This scenario would be made possible, for instance, if the Arab parties simply don’t vote.
Once this minority government is approved, Eisenkot can then attract defectors from the other side of the ship. A substantial lead over the Likud would give that effort greater public legitimacy.
There are other considerations, too.
First, in the unlikely event that a rotation agreement with the Likud became a serious possibility, a decisive lead in seats would bolster his claim to go first as prime minister.
More immediately, the larger Yashar becomes, the harder it would be for Bennett or Liberman to argue that someone else should lead the bloc.
The four parties in the “change bloc” have yet to agree on a mechanism to determine their prime ministerial candidate after the election.
Eisenkot has said, logically enough, that the leader of the party that wins the most votes should be the bloc’s candidate. Since Yashar currently leads the bloc by a considerable margin, that formula would obviously favor him.
It remains unclear, however, whether the others are prepared to accept this. But the wider the gap, the harder it would be to explain why the leader of a much smaller party should get the top job.
Eisenkot is campaigning both against Netanyahu and for an outcome within his own bloc that would make his leadership hard to challenge.
Both Netanyahu’s and Eisenkot’s maneuvers make sense.
Netanyahu wants to prevent right-wing votes from being lost or carried into another government. Eisenkot wants to ensure that, if there is an opportunity to replace Netanyahu, he will be the one to seize it.
But both maneuvers have their limits. For Netanyahu, keeping his passengers together does not guarantee enough support to retain command. And for Eisenkot, having the biggest ballroom on one side of the ship does not guarantee enough support to become captain of the whole vessel.

Thai farmers, fishermen and workers marched through Bangkok on Friday as global finance and business leaders gathered for IMF and World Bank meetings, demanding a say in policies shaping their livelihoods.
Hundreds of protesters, many wearing straw hats and colourful scarves, had hoped to reach the main conference centre but were stopped by a line of police more than a kilometre away, the road blocked by shipping containers.
Some carried fishing nets and hoisted banners reading "World Bank, stop destroying the poor", a reference to criticisms that the global lenders extract too high a price from countries which borrow money.
Some protested specific projects, notably the World Bank-backed Pak Mun dam, a hydropower project completed in 1994 that fishing communities say damaged their livelihoods.
"There are no more fish. They can't swim upstream," said fisherman Putta Muansaen, 67, who travelled overnight from northeastern Ubon Ratchathani province.
"The water has changed, the river has changed, and the ecosystem has changed," he told AFP.
Somporn Yamyong, 62, travelled from rice-rich central Suphan Buri province to draw attention to years of debt and meagre earnings.
The rice farmer said she wanted Thai leaders and the IMF and World Bank to hear about the "hardships facing farmers" like her.
Thailand received an IMF loan three decades ago but paid this off in 2003. It has some projects with the World Bank.
Coconut farmer Sombat Chuekrod, 51, from Prachuap Khiri Khan province, south-west of Bangkok, added: "Thai people are already poor. Please don't make us any poorer."
There were some non-Thai protesters in the crowd, including Harry May, a 59-year-old South African activist and researcher, who said global lenders were "bankrupting our countries, especially developing countries".
"We shouldn't be indebted to the same people who say they're going to relieve debt and provide development and then just create more debt for those countries," he said.
On Thursday, there were brief scuffles when police blocked protesters as they tried to hang a banner from a footbridge in the Thai capital, but there was no sign of trouble on Friday morning.

Türkiye's Fidan to attend OIC foreign ministers' meeting in Baghdad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:01:07 UTC
19:01:07 KST

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan will attend the 52nd session of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation’s (OIC) Council of Foreign Ministers in Baghdad on October 17-18, Türkiye’s Foreign Ministry has said.
Held under the theme “Dialogue and Solidarity: Two Essential Pillars for Promoting Peace and Sustainable Development”, the meeting will see Türkiye transfer the organisation’s rotating presidency to Iraq, which it has held since June 2025.
Discussions are expected to cover Israel’s actions in Gaza and across the occupied Palestinian territories, other conflicts in the Muslim world, counterterrorism, United Nations reform, Islamophobia and the situation of Muslim communities in non-member countries.
The meeting is expected to conclude with the adoption of the Baghdad Declaration.
Fidan to call for coordinated action on Palestine
In his address, Fidan is expected to describe Israel’s aggressive and expansionist policies as the biggest security threat to the Middle East and urge OIC members to coordinate their response with responsible international actors.
He is also expected to call for steps to protect Jerusalem’s status, oppose further moves by countries to relocate their embassies there, and reaffirm that a two-state solution leading to an independent Palestinian state is the only path to a just and lasting peace.
Fidan is expected to stress the need to ensure uninterrupted humanitarian aid reaches people in Gaza.
Regional security and freedom of navigation
The Turkish foreign minister is also expected to address rising tensions in the Gulf and around the Strait of Hormuz.
He is expected to emphasise the importance of ensuring safe and free navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al Mandab for regional stability and global trade, while condemning Houthi militia attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure and reaffirming Türkiye’s solidarity with Saudi Arabia.
Fidan is also expected to call for the protection of Syria’s and Lebanon’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, including a complete Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon.
OIC to discuss rights of Muslim communities
The meeting is also expected to address the rights of Turkish Cypriots, who face what Ankara describes as unjust isolation, as well as the fundamental rights and freedoms of the Muslim Turkish minority in Western Thrace and Muslim Turkish communities in the Dodecanese islands.
The OIC, established in 1969, has 57 member states and is the world’s second-largest intergovernmental organisation after the United Nations.
Türkiye is one of its 25 founding members and took over the rotating presidency at the previous Council of Foreign Ministers meeting in Istanbul in June 2025.
Fidan is also expected to hold bilateral meetings with counterparts on the sidelines of the Baghdad gathering.

Copenhagen establishes support groups for parents of children missing school
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:01:06 UTC
19:01:06 KST

A new parents’ association has signed a four-year agreement with the City of Copenhagen to establish support groups for families whose children experience prolonged, involuntary school absence.
Such absence is often connected to poor well-being and is considered concerning when a pupil misses at least 20 percent of school for two consecutive quarters. That corresponds to about 10 days per quarter.
The first groups will be funded by Copenhagen and include eight to nine parents who meet approximately once a month, education news outlet Folkeskolen.dk reported.
A family therapist will lead the meetings, with a parent from Forældrekommissionen, or the Parents’ Commission, also participating.
Louise Gielov and Jens Langorn helped establish the association after their family appeared in the Danish public broadcaster DR documentary “Skolens tabte børn,” which showed daily life with children unable to attend school.
The couple received more than 1,000 messages from parents in similar situations after the documentary aired.
The association now has 2,545 members and aims to establish parent groups across Denmark. It also plans to use families’ experiences to promote earlier intervention and broader changes to prevent school absence.
The proportion of pupils with prolonged concerning absence increased from 2.4 percent in the 2019-2020 school year to 5.1 percent in 2024-2025.
The association has also secured 7 million DKK from foundations.
The 21-year-old singer has gone from posting piano videos on TikTok to becoming one of Denmark’s biggest pop stars. On Friday, she received the top prize at DR’s annual P3 Guld music awards.
Danish singer Annika has won P3 Prisen, the main award at one of Denmark’s most prominent annual music events, P3 Guld.
The 21-year-old received the award Friday evening at DR Koncerthuset in Copenhagen, a year after being nominated for the same prize but losing out to Danish band Aphaca.
P3 Guld is the annual music awards show organised by P3, the youth-oriented music and entertainment radio station run by Danish public broadcaster DR.
The event celebrates artists who have made a significant impact on Danish music over the past year, with P3 Prisen regarded as its main award.
Annika, whose full name is Annika Wedderkopp, was selected by a P3 jury ahead of fellow nominees Zar Paulo and producer Anton Westerlin, who is also her boyfriend.
“With an authentic foundation in her own life, Annika creates massive hits about breakups and infatuations, about doubt and a steely belief that everything will naturally work out,” the jury said.
From TikTok to the Danish charts
Annika’s rise has been rapid.
She began by posting videos of herself singing at the piano on TikTok before breaking through with “Knuser hjerter” in 2024.
She followed it with several successful releases, including “Så længe jeg er sexy”, and won P3 Talentet, the event’s talent award, that same year.
Last year, she released her debut album “AW”, which includes “Stolt”, a collaboration with Danish rapper Lamin. She also opened Roskilde Festival’s Orange Stage, the festival’s largest and most prestigious stage.
Previous recipients of P3 Prisen include some of Denmark’s best-known contemporary artists, including The Minds of 99, Tobias Rahim, Artigeardit, Lamin, Tina Dickow and Jada.
Other winners
Several other awards were presented at Friday’s ceremony.
Guldimund and Saveus won P3 Lytterhittet – the listeners’ choice award – for their song “Vil du noget?”.
Zar Paulo received P3 Live, an award recognising an artist who has distinguished themselves on Denmark’s live music scene. The award returned this year after previously being presented in 2001 and 2009.
Danish-Faroese artist Friða Saiya won P3’s Næste, a new award that has replaced P3 Talentet and highlights emerging artists.
Criticism over lack of women
This year’s P3 Guld also faced criticism before the ceremony over the gender balance among its performers.
Twelve men and two women were scheduled to perform during the evening.
Ditte Christiane Jensen, head of editorial at DR Ung, defended the lineup in a written response to Ritzau.
“Talent, creativity and artistic quality are not about gender,” she said.
“This year’s lineup was put together based on the artists and bands that have left a significant mark on the music year and in P3’s universe.”

Trump: Greenland deal biggest real estate deal ever
The US president says he “got it for nothing” after signing a new defence agreement with Denmark and Greenland that expands the American military presence on the island.

Speaking at a Republican campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia, Trump portrayed the agreement as a major achievement for the United States.
“What do you think of the deal I made on Greenland? Got it for nothing,” Trump told supporters.

His comments come after months of tension over Greenland, an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark. Trump has repeatedly said that the United States wants control and ownership of Greenland, arguing that the island is crucial to American national security.
Two new US military bases
The United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a new security and defence agreement on Greenland at the end of September following lengthy negotiations.
The agreement was signed at the United Nations in New York shortly after Trump addressed the UN General Assembly.
It allows the United States to establish two additional military bases in Greenland.
The US currently operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, which plays an important role in missile warning, space surveillance and Arctic security.
The new agreement also opens the possibility of deploying parts of the planned US Golden Dome missile defence system in Greenland. The system is intended to protect the United States against threats including missiles and drones.
Despite Trump’s description of the agreement as a “real estate deal”, it does not transfer ownership of Greenland to the United States.
Trump’s comments came as Republicans campaign to retain control of Congress in the November midterm elections. Democrats are currently polling more strongly in the race for the House of Representatives, while control of the Senate remains more uncertain.
Republicans currently hold majorities in both chambers.

Denmark’s shift from fossil fuels to electricity is accelerating
Electric cars, heat pumps and electric boilers are driving a sharp increase in the share of Denmark’s energy consumption covered by electricity.
Denmark is becoming increasingly electrified as electric cars, heat pumps and electric boilers replace fossil fuels.
Electricity accounted for 23.4 percent of Denmark’s total energy consumption in 2025, according to figures highlighted by industry organisation Green Power Denmark.
That was an increase of 1.5 percentage points in just one year.
The increase is significant. Between 2016 and 2024, the share of electricity in Denmark’s total energy consumption rose by only 3.8 percentage points.
The acceleration is being driven particularly by the growing number of electric cars and by district heating companies investing in electric boilers and heat pumps.
Kristian Jensen, CEO of Green Power Denmark, says the development will gradually make Denmark less dependent on imported oil and natural gas – and therefore less exposed to international energy prices and geopolitical developments.
“We are freeing ourselves from what is going on in the Middle East and American politics,” Jensen told Ritzau.
“When Danes experience that gasoline, diesel and electricity have become more expensive than they were a year ago, it is because we are still dependent on the price set in the rest of the world.”
Target: 60 percent by 2035
Green Power Denmark wants electricity to account for 60 percent of Denmark’s total energy consumption by 2035.
Reaching that level will require a much faster transition in Danish industry, according to Jensen.
He points to heat pumps as one of the technologies that can help companies replace natural gas with electricity. Iron foundries and food producers, including dairy group Arla, have already demonstrated that large heat pumps can be used in industrial production.
Jensen argues that other companies should follow their example.
“It will not only reduce the companies’ CO2 emissions, it will also reduce energy expenses and thereby improve their competitiveness,” he said.
Figures for Denmark’s electrification rate in 2026 are not yet available, but Green Power Denmark expects the shift towards electricity to continue.

Denmark’s oldest-ever person was a member of the Danish Nazi party
Records show that 112-year-old Kirsten Schwalbe joined Denmark’s Nazi party during the German occupation. She says she did so at her husband’s request and did not sympathise with Nazism.
Kirsten Schwalbe, who this week became the longest-living Dane in recorded history, was a member of Denmark’s Nazi party during the German occupation.
The 112-year-old joined the National Socialist Workers’ Party of Denmark (DNSAP) in August 1941, according to Kristeligt Dagblad.
Her name appears in the Bovrup registry, a record of people who were members of DNSAP. Two historians have independently confirmed to the newspaper that the entry matches Schwalbe’s date of birth and address, although her surname is misspelled as “Schalbe”.
Schwalbe has confirmed that both she and her former husband were members of the party, but says she only joined because her husband urged her to do so.
She rejected the suggestion that she had sided with Nazi Germany.
“Not at all. I barely knew what it was, because I have never taken an interest in politics,” she told TV Midtvest when asked whether she had sympathised with the Nazis.
Schwalbe said she found it unfair that she should have to “pay for it” more than 70 years later, adding that “back then, wives didn’t look into such things”.
Membership does not show level of involvement
DNSAP was founded in 1930 and was strongly inspired by Adolf Hitler’s German Nazi Party, the NSDAP.
But Charlie Krautwald, a historian at the University of Copenhagen, cautioned against drawing conclusions about Schwalbe’s level of involvement from the registry alone.
The record shows that a person joined the party, he told Kristeligt Dagblad, but not why they joined, how long they remained a member or whether they paid membership fees.
A person could therefore appear in the registry without having been active in the party.
TV Midtvest has followed Schwalbe for several years and manages an Instagram account about her life. Two of the broadcaster’s employees have also recently published a book about her.
Her membership of DNSAP had not previously been mentioned. TV Midtvest editor-in-chief Marc Killigren Akselsen told Kristeligt Dagblad that the broadcaster had not known about it.
Schwalbe, who lives in Struer in western Jutland, became the longest-living Dane on record on Wednesday, when she reached the age of 112 years and 218 days.

Lidl has Denmark’s cheapest basket of organic groceries, analysis finds
Lidl offers the lowest prices on a selected basket of organic groceries among seven Danish supermarket chains, according to an analysis by price-monitoring service Madprisluppen.
A basket containing 22 organic products cost 355.20 DKK at Lidl. The same basket cost 449.60 DKK at Meny, the most expensive chain in the comparison.
Madprisluppen said the Lidl basket was 26 percent cheaper than the one at Meny.
“We want to make it easier for Danes to make room for organics in everyday life, and here price plays an important role,” Lidl Denmark purchasing director Peer Sandtner said.
Rema 1000 was the second-cheapest supermarket, with its basket costing only 5 DKK more than Lidl’s.
SuperBrugsen was the second-most expensive, though its total was almost 35 DKK below Meny’s.
The analysis also included Netto, 365discount and Føtex. Prices were recorded from October 9 through October 12.
Products included milk, eggs, vegetables and dry goods. Meat was excluded because Madprisluppen found it difficult to identify comparable products across the chains.
The monitoring service also found that supermarkets carry fewer organic products than they did six years ago. Organic prices have increased, and such products appear in special offers less frequently than non-organic groceries.
Norway to lend 10-meter Viking boat to Danish museum for 10 years
A Norwegian Viking boat will be displayed at Moesgaard Museum near Aarhus under an unusual 10-year loan agreement.
The oak boat is almost 10 meters long and nearly two meters wide. It was among three smaller vessels discovered when archaeologists excavated Norway’s Gokstad ship in 1880.
The Gokstad ship is Norway’s largest preserved Viking ship.
“The boat is a very important cultural treasure from the Viking Age, and it is not an everyday occurrence that we grant permission for such a boat to be taken out of the country,” Kaare Stang of Riksantikvaren, Norway’s cultural heritage authority, said.
The three smaller boats had been chopped into pieces, possibly as part of a burial ritual, according to archaeologists.
The Museum of Cultural History in Norway owns the boat and applied for permission to lend it to Moesgaard Museum for a new exhibition.
Norwegian authorities normally approve loans for no more than three years. Moesgaard Museum must therefore submit a report on the boat’s condition every three years during the loan period.
Stang said Norwegian authorities trusted the Danish museum to protect the boat but emphasized that it must eventually return to Norway.
No arrival date has been announced.
Moesgaard Museum already displays a 6.5-meter Gokstad boat that was used to transport crews and exchange orders between warships.

Dane becomes first European participant to receive combined flu and Covid vaccine
A 65-year-old Dane will become the first person in Europe to receive a new combined influenza and Covid-19 vaccine as part of a clinical trial Friday.
The trial will examine whether one injection can protect against both diseases as effectively as, or better than, the two separate vaccines currently used, Danish public broadcaster DR reported.
The first participant will receive the vaccine at Gentofte Hospital.
“We are investigating whether one shot with this new vaccine is just as effective or potentially better than the two shots given today at preventing hospitalizations with influenza and Covid-19,” said Tor Biering-Sørensen, a professor and senior physician at Herlev and Gentofte Hospital who is leading the trial.
About 165,000 Danes have agreed to participate. More than 300,000 people are expected to join over the next two years.
Half of the participants will receive one dose of the combined vaccine. The other half will receive separate influenza and Covid-19 vaccinations.
People age 65 and older in Denmark are automatically invited to receive free vaccinations against both diseases. The Danish Health Authority said about 1.3 million residents received invitations in September.
People with chronic illnesses or other conditions placing them at increased risk are also eligible for the free program.
The vaccines are intended to reduce the risk of severe illness and hospitalization during the winter respiratory infection season.

Denmark’s weekend will begin with mild and rainy weather before turning cooler and windier, with some periods of sunshine.

Archaeologists uncover more than 1,000 graves in Copenhagen park
Archaeologists have excavated more than 1,000 graves containing human remains beneath Hans Tavsens Park in Copenhagen’s Nørrebro district.
The park, located next to Assistens Cemetery, was previously used as a burial ground for Copenhagen’s poorest residents. Victims of the city’s 1853 cholera epidemic are among those buried there.
“We can use it to gain insight into the poor population from this period and Copenhagen’s history,” Museum of Copenhagen archaeologist Olivia Persson told Danish public broadcaster DR.
The excavation is taking place before Hans Tavsens Park and the neighboring Hans Tavsens Gade are redeveloped into a connected green space.
The project will also allow the park to collect water during cloudbursts, helping prevent flooding of nearby roads and basements as Denmark experiences wetter weather.
Construction began in autumn 2025 as part of the City of Copenhagen’s plan for managing extreme rainfall. The redevelopment is expected to be completed in spring 2028.
Most of the remains will be transferred to the University of Copenhagen’s Anthropological Laboratory for storage and examination. Some will undergo additional analysis, while the remainder will be reburied in the park.
Researchers will examine the health of selected individuals. They will also study how the graves were arranged to better understand religious and cultural attitudes toward death among Copenhagen’s poorer population at the time.

Greenland’s parliament unanimously adopted a resolution Thursday directing the government to draft legislation temporarily banning deep-sea mining.

The proposed change has been submitted for public consultation.
Electric ovens are expected to reduce both environmental effects and the financial cost of cremations.
Michael Smidemann, chair of the Danish Crematoria Association, said crematoria were interested in replacing their existing ovens.
“The background is a desire to sharpen the green profile, even though it is somewhat mixed how green the electricity we receive actually is,” he told Ingeniøren.
Electric cremation ovens can reach 750 degrees. Requiring them to reach 800 degrees would demand additional heating elements, increasing electricity use and causing heavy wear on the ovens’ brickwork, according to Ingeniøren.
Denmark recorded 58,185 deaths in 2025, according to the Danish Crematoria Association.
Of those who died, 51,252 were cremated, corresponding to 88.1 percent of all deaths.
A cremation typically takes about 90 minutes, according to information from the City of Copenhagen and other sources.
