India’s mass voter purge is hollowing out democracy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

India’s mass voter purge is hollowing out democracy
The SIR is disenfranchising marginalised communities and advancing the Hindu nationalist project.
Over the weekend, thousands of protesters demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, faced mass detentions and a heavy police crackdown in New Delhi. The demonstrations, which have brought together youth activists and opposition parties, centre on the removal of more than 130 million names from India’s electoral rolls, raising profound questions about the state of Indian democracy.
The deletions are the result of the controversial Special Intensive Revision (SIR) undertaken by the Election Commission of India (ECI). The ECI periodically revises electoral rolls to add new voters and remove the names of those who have died or permanently moved away. The last intensive revision was completed in 2003-2004. What makes the current SIR unprecedented, however, is its scale, the arbitrariness and overreach of its procedures, and the mass disenfranchisement that has followed. The exercise has disproportionately affected Muslims, women, migrants and other marginalised communities while also raising questions about the legitimacy of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party’s (BJP’s) electoral victories in Bihar and West Bengal.
Both the ECI and the ruling party have defended the exercise by using the language of “purification”. In a caste society, that rhetoric is deeply troubling but also revealing. The bureaucratic procedures and technological infrastructure underpinning the exercise barely mask its intention to create two classes of citizenship in India, one endowed with political voice through the right to vote and the other reduced to what the philosopher Giorgio Agamben calls “bare life”.
The SIR’s intent, procedures and outcomes reveal a sinister design: to maximise voter exclusions rather than enhance voter participation. This subverts the promise of universal adult suffrage, a cornerstone of India’s constitutional democracy. The ECI initially excluded the government-issued Aadhaar card from the list of documents accepted for voter verification during the SIR, supposedly because it was considered “overinclusive”. If that did not expose the exercise’s exclusionary intent, the ECI’s invention of the category “logical discrepancy” during the West Bengal SIR certainly did. This pseudo-legal innovation accounted for 2.7 million of the nearly 9 million names removed from electoral rolls in Bengal. The demand for educational certificates, land records, legacy documents and family trees as evidence also places a heavy burden on poor and marginalised voters, especially in regions still reeling under mass poverty, landlessness and rampant illiteracy. With the “burden of proof” shifted to ordinary voters, the SIR aims to achieve precisely what it set out to do: mass deletions and consequent disenfranchisement.
Customised apps and online forms, digitised electoral rolls and the requirement to upload scanned documents in prescribed formats are all presented as evidence of the SIR’s efficiency and objectivity. But this approach ignores the digital divide in a deeply unequal society. Technology does not operate outside relations of power. In fact, it often serves as a mechanism of control. The category of “logical discrepancy” relies on an AI-enabled application, ERONET (Electoral Roll Officers’ Network), which compares voters’ details with older electoral rolls and flags discrepancies in names and family relationships. The use of such centralised systems has also raised questions about who controls electoral data and how these discrepancies are assessed. Women are particularly vulnerable to these procedures. Many change their names or addresses after marriage and may lack the documents needed to establish links with older electoral records. The excessive exclusion of women demonstrates how ostensibly neutral technological procedures can reinforce existing inequalities and weaken people’s political voice.
The SIR’s purported neutrality is at odds with its effects, which fall heavily on the weak and the marginalised. Among religious minorities, Muslims across the country bear a particularly heavy burden of deletions. In Bengal, Muslims reportedly accounted for about 65 percent of the 2.7 million people removed from electoral rolls on grounds of “logical discrepancy”. With only 19 specially constituted tribunals to handle more than 3.8 million appeals, the corrective process in effect has remained inaccessible to many excluded voters. In Hyderabad, 1.94 million names were marked for deletion under the “absent, shifted, dead and duplicate” (ASDD) category. An estimated 40.7 percent of those entries appeared to belong to Muslim voters, compared with Muslims’ 30 percent share of the city’s population. In some constituencies in Hyderabad’s Old City, Muslims accounted for as much as 80 percent of the names marked for deletion. The pattern is repeated in the National Capital Region, Delhi, where nearly one-third of the existing electorate was missing from the draft SIR roll. Studies flag especially high rates of exclusion in areas with large minority and migrant populations and among residents of informal and unauthorised settlements. The disproportionate exclusion of Muslims suggests an ideological alignment between the SIR’s ostensibly impersonal bureaucracy and the social and political programme of the Hindu right.
As a political and ideological instrument, the exercise has proved to be doubly potent. Through mass deletion of voters from targeted social categories, such as Muslims, it has contributed to shrinking the electoral base of the BJP’s principal rivals. The elections in Bihar and Bengal after the SIR suggest a discernible pattern. In the 2020 Bihar Assembly elections, the Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD)-led alliance lost to the BJP-led alliance by just 0.03 percentage points in vote share. In contrast, in the 2025 elections after the removal of 6.8 million names from the existing rolls and the addition of 2.1 million new voters, the BJP alliance’s lead increased to nearly 9 percentage points. Analysis of the 2026 Bengal Assembly elections also points to the decisive role SIR deletions played in the electoral outcome. The exercise disproportionately affected Muslim, migrant and poorer voters in districts where the BJP had historically struggled to gain support. In many constituencies won by the BJP, the number of deleted or disputed voters exceeded the party’s margin of victory.
Furthermore, the bureaucratic exercise reinforces the larger ideological project of a “pure Hindu” nation. It has also legitimised calls for the expulsion of “Rohingyas”, “infiltrators” and “Bangladeshis”, terms used as dog whistles for Muslims, helping to polarise elections along communal lines. Although Bengali Hindus and others also found their names removed from electoral rolls, the political messaging around the SIR in a communally charged election campaign cast Muslims as a suspect community, imperilling their civil and social rights. Predictably, the newly elected BJP governments in Bihar and Bengal moved to deny Public Distribution System benefits to those who found their names expunged from the electoral rolls.
The SIR is thus fuelled by the imagined spectre of a vile and illicit intruder who must be expelled to preserve the existing order. It follows the Supreme Court-supervised National Register of Citizens (NRC) in Assam, which left 1.9 million of the state’s residents, mostly Bengali speakers, essentially stateless. It also resembles the Citizenship Amendment Act of 2019, which introduced religiously differentiated access to citizenship, an affront to the republic’s secular structure. The recently established High-Level Committee on Demographic Change, mandated to assess demographic changes occurring across India due to “illegal infiltration” and “abnormal” population changes among “religious and social communities”, is cut from the same cloth. Ultimately, the SIR is one of several instruments at play to criminalise, disenfranchise and denationalise social groups and communities considered inimical to the Hindutva vision of an ethnic state.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Press review: Russian asset grab back on EU agenda and Starlink or no, Ukraine to fight on

Unknown Publisher

MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. This week's EU summit returns to the idea of seizing Russian assets; facing threats of being cut off from Starlink, Ukraine makes other plans; and what is the future of the US Green Card Lottery. These stories topped Friday's newspaper headlines in Russia.
Izvestia: EU revisits idea of confiscating Russian assets at summit
The EU opened a two-day summit in Brussels on October 15. For the first time since the special military operation began, the Europeans postponed discussions on Ukraine to the second day of the event as they decided to discuss the European Union’s new budget for 2028-2034 first. Earlier, the European Commission (EC) proposed a bloated budget of €1.76 trillion.
Meanwhile, European auditors are ringing alarm bells about the growing debt, which could climb to €1 trillion by 2027 and cause a "hole" in the current budget. Moreover, all EU economies are struggling amid the energy crisis around the situation in the Strait of Hormuz.
The problem is also aggravated by Kiev's growing demands. According to the draft budget, the EC proposed allocations of up to €88.8 billion for 2028-2034.
However, there is no extra money, and the EU is now coming back to the idea of using frozen Russian assets by transferring them to a special European structure to finance Ukraine further down the road. "This idea is being considered and revisited," French member of the European Parliament Thierry Mariani told Izvestia. "Belgium, which holds the bulk of these funds, dissuaded its partners from putting that idea into practice in December, and the EU eventually agreed a €90 billion loan. Today, Kiev insists that this issue be reconsidered," he noted. "As regards Belgium, it considers this idea crazy as Moscow could immobilize European assets in response," Mariani warned.
Today, the likelihood of using these assets for a loan to Ukraine is extremely low. Such a step would require absolute unanimity within the European Union, Mikhail Vedernikov, a senior researcher at the Institute of Europe of the Russian Academy of Sciences, explained to Izvestia. However, some leaders, including Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico, have openly opposed this initiative and promised to block it. Nevertheless, Slovakia will hold an early election in 2027, with Fico’s positions assessed as quite weak. If left-liberal politicians who support the policy course pursued by Brussels come to power in Bratislava, a decision on assets may well be made in a year, the expert concluded.
Apart from Russia’s assets, European bureaucrats will discuss additional restrictions on Moscow. According to Politico, the EU is planning to call for more restrictions on Russian oil exports in the summit communique. Earlier, Brussels approved a 22nd sanctions package, blacklisting hundreds of new Russian individuals, lenders and oil tankers. However, the EU’s sanctions policy cannot affect Russia’s policy on Ukraine, Mariani argued. "This shows that this sanctions policy does not work and only leads to impoverishing the population," the politician maintained.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: Ukraine ready to push ahead amid potential Starlink cutoff
Tensions between Kiev and Washington will seemingly escalate after Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky said that the Ukrainian armed forces will continue to target Russian oil refineries. Earlier, according to media reports, the Americans warned Kiev that the United States would in that case "immediately" cancel intelligence sharing, cut off the Starlink satellite internet system, and halt military aid.
Even as this has not happened yet, the possibility remains, observers say. Therefore, the Zelensky regime is apparently preparing to wage combat against Russia without support from the United States, relying on NATO’s European allies and the EU instead. This slightly increases Russia’s chances of achieving the objectives of its special military operation and defeating the enemy faster. Whether things progress that way - only time will tell.
A recent remark from SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has been making the rounds in the media and with pundits, after the billionaire called on Zelensky to resign, otherwise "the slaughter" would continue. The call came after almost identical statements from US President Donald Trump.
"It is Musk who owns the rights to Starlink, therefore he can de facto influence Ukraine’s defensive capabilities," retired Lieutenant-General Yury Netkachev, a military expert, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. According to him, with the diesel deal and ambitions to ease sanctions on Russia, Trump has provided Moscow with an opportunity not only to improve its economic situation but also buttress its position in negotiations to end the conflict.
However, Netkachev warned, one should not be lulled into a false sense of security by this "friendly" position of the current US administration, for Trump’s foreign policy options could be significantly curtailed following the Congressional election, and the US political elite may return to supporting Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Kiev's intelligence situation isn't all lost without the US. "Two-thirds of the intelligence received by Ukraine come from European countries, primarily France," French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told France Inter. According to him, among other things, European countries share satellite images that Kiev uses to detect targets. His remark came amid reports that the US has threatened to limit information sharing because of strikes on Russian oil refineries. Barrot also said the Europeans provide the bulk of support for Ukraine. The EU has recently transferred €6 billion to Kiev, he added.
Vedomosti: Odds US brings back Green Card Lottery
The US State Department was ordered to reopen the Green Card Lottery by October 18 and publicly announce the registration dates on its official platforms. The order came from a US federal judge in California, according to the court’s database updated on Wednesday night. Registration will remain open for 30 days, in line with the court order. In other words, anyone who wants to can enter the 2027 drawing.
The issue reverberated after the Trump administration formally refused to open registration citing delays, even as back in November 2025 the US Department of State shared plans to reopen registration for the 2027 fiscal year running from October 1, 2026 on its website.
It is worth noting that the Green Card Lottery is a mandatory process, as Congress authorizes the allocation of up to 55,000 such documents annually to foreign citizens. However, only a portion of all available Green Cards are distributed through the lottery, not all of them. According to the US Department of State’s website, 20.8 million people applied for the 2026 program, from which 129,516 individuals were selected. Among Africans registered for the DV-2026 Diversity Visa Program, the bulk was from Algeria (5,457 applicants), Afghanistan led all Asian countries with 4,200, the Bahamas - North America with 23, 599 Australians led the way for Oceania, and 1,596 Peruvians from South America. Russia led all European countries with 5,510 registered and selected applicants, followed by Ukraine with 5,283.
Even as the DV-2026 program was mandated by federal law enacted by Congress, the Trump administration effectively delayed the start of the registration process, Marina Chernykh, a research fellow at the Institute for US and Canadian Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences, explained to Vedomosti. According to her, the California court ruled that the US State Department provide an opportunity for applications to be submitted, whereas the federal government insisted that it is no longer possible to carry out the program as originally intended now that the established deadlines have passed. The Trump administration has the right to appeal the ruling at the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. Filing an appeal would not automatically nullify the court ruling as a separate court decision will be required for that. The case could eventually be taken to the US Supreme Court, the expert noted.
"And the US Supreme Court is highly likely to rule in Trump’s favor as the majority of judges there are conservative. At the same time, it cannot be assumed that the administration can simply ignore the ruling as it was handed down by a court of first instance," the expert concluded.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Archaic Russia-EU partnership agreement clashes with present-day antagonism
The agreement on partnership and cooperation concluded between Russia and the European Union signed more than three decades ago makes little practical sense after Brussels openly declared Russia its opponent and adversary, said participants in a round table discussion at the Federation Council on Thursday.
The EU has essentially transformed into an anti-Russian military bloc, Rossiyskaya Gazeta quoted Grigory Karasin, chairman of the upper chamber’s Committee on International Affairs, as saying. There have been statements from European politicians, including Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski or European Commissioner for Defense Andrius Kubilius, about preparations for war with Russia in 2029-2030.
The matter is not limited to rhetoric only as Sweden and Finland have joined NATO, EU countries are sharply increasing their defense expenditure, military construction has been expedited, and exercises to simulate scenarios of a blockade of the Kaliningrad Region and Russia’s Baltic seaports are held near national borders.
Karasin also pointed to the EU’s expansion plans at the expense of Moldova, Ukraine and Armenia. At that, the senator emphasized, Russia is not threatening European countries nor is it planning to do so, while the European people seem to agree, as evidenced by the rising popularity of opposition parties in Germany and France.
The EU has undergone a major evolution, Federation Council Deputy Speaker Konstantin Kosachev argued. Originally a purely economic association, the EU is increasingly mulling militarization, including its own army. "Never before has there been a single international organization built on regional economic integration that set establishing an army as its goal. This is a first," Kosachev noted. "The idea of militarization has completely consumed the minds of European politicians, who have also embraced extreme Russophobic rhetoric," he added.
Kosachev commented on the Partnership and Cooperation Agreement, which was signed in 1994 and entered into force in 1997. He singled out Article 55 as the most objectionable part of the document which envisaged the unilateral harmonization of Russian laws with European ones. "Thank God, this article--along with all the other provisions of the agreement--has been frozen," he said. The agreement’s initial ten-year term expired in 2007 and it has been automatically renewed on an annual basis ever since until one of the parties provides written notice to the contrary. "It has lost any practical meaning. The EU has openly declared us its adversary and enemy, while the agreement envisages partnership and cooperation," Kosachev maintained.
Vedomosti: Russia could step in to meet Africa's growing electricity needs
African countries are facing electricity shortages even as they have enough oil and gas and capabilities to generate power from renewables. Key obstacles include a lack of capital and grid weaknesses. Russian technology could be in demand in the fields of nuclear-and natural gas-based power generation, hydropower and energy-related engineering, but prospects here depend on project economics and the specific needs of certain countries. Russian and African experts told Vedomosti which areas of partnership can yield a long-term effect and what has prevented a transformation from individual supplies to complex projects.
Today, African countries need to supply electricity to a growing population, their industries, transport, and digital economy, Alexey Maslov, a professor and director of the Institute of Asian and African Studies at Lomonosov Moscow State University, noted. While many of these countries possess gas, oil, and coal reserves, along with potential for hydropower, solar, and wind energy generation, the mere availability of such resources does not guarantee a stable supply, he argued.
According to Nikita Panin, an expert at the analytical department at the HSE Centre for African Studies, countries with a developed industrial base need large-scale power generation. Meanwhile, the need for localized power generation is already reflected in projects currently under discussion between Russian companies and their African partners. There is no universal solution for the continent as the specifics of each country require an individual approach, he explained.
As African partners view it, technology transfer should be accompanied with the development of local competences, Anna Abaho, a senior lecturer in international relations and security research at Nkumba University in Uganda, told Vedomosti. She linked Russian-Ugandan cooperation to industrial electrification, food production, irrigation and refrigeration of agricultural products. The country needs engineers and technical specialists capable of maintaining the equipment for that, she said.
A transition to purer energy does not mean Africa will abandon traditional sources in the next few years. The continent is expanding access to electricity amid the rising demand from industries, transport, and cities. For this reason, a variety of technologies, ranging from gas and hydropower to solar generation, energy storage, and nuclear projects, will be needed in the energy mix, Maslov argued.

Pickleball Mania Hits Copenhagen: New Arena Debuts October 17
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:58:00 UTC
18:58:00 KST

On Saturday, 17 October, Danske Pickleballers will unveil a new indoor facility, transforming the industrial expanse of Nordhavn’s Tunnelfabrikken into a dedicated winter arena for the sport.
The facility, located at Tunnel Arena, is a notable architectural pivot for the building, which in the 1990s served as the site where tunnel elements for the Øresund link were cast. Now, the raw industrial hall is set to become the city’s primary hub for pickleball enthusiasts, offering six new professional-grade courts.
A transatlantic inspiration
The journey to this new facility began across the Atlantic. In April 2024, Joachim Litman, co-founder of Danske Pickleballers, visited his father in New York. While he had originally hoped to play padel, the high cost of courts in the city led him to a local schoolyard in East Harlem instead.
Pickleball is a very sociable game where both kids and seniors can have fun. Photo: Danske Pickleballers
There, he discovered the distinct culture of pickleball—a game defined by its low barrier to entry and social nature. Litman recalls being hooked from the “first dink,” struck by the ease of joining a game: you simply place your paddle in the queue and wait for four players.
It was a space where he could play alongside a five-year-old and a 95-year-old on the same day, a level of inclusivity that left a lasting impression.
Upon returning to Copenhagen, Litman founded Danske Pickleballers alongside friends Mathias and Lucas. The club, which began with chalk lines in city parks, has grown to over 100 members, with its activities conducted in both Danish and English.
The grand opening
The opening event at Tunnel Arena is designed not just for seasoned players, but as a social meetup for those looking to try the sport. The event runs from 11:00 to 20:00 on Saturday, 17 October, at Oceanvej 1, Nordhavn.
The programme for the day includes:
- 13:00: Official opening and ribbon-cutting ceremony.
- 13:45: Opportunities to play with coaches, with no prior experience necessary.
- 14:00–16:00: First sushi service.
- 16:30: Exhibition match featuring some of Denmark’s top players.
- 17:15: A social tournament with rotating partners and a DJ, aimed at helping attendees meet new people.
- 18:00–20:00: Final sushi service.
Entry is 25 DKK, which includes the use of paddles and balls. Whether arriving solo or with friends, the club encourages newcomers to join in, aiming to make the venue a social hub throughout the winter months.

US greenlights Iraqi cabinet with blacklisted factions: diplomatic sources

Khazali and his brother Qais, the leader of Asaib Ahl al-Haq, are both designated as "global terrorists" by Washington, which sees them as "violent proxies" of Iran.
But their group has emerged as a major political force, winning 27 seats in the latest parliamentary elections.
It was among the first to back Zaidi's plan to bring all arms under state control, says it has begun handing over its own weapons, and has not been publicly linked to recent attacks on US interests.
Ex-detainees
Washington accuses the Khazali brothers, both former US detainees, of attacks on its forces after the 2003 invasion of Iraq, including a 2007 attack that led to the capture and killing of five American soldiers.
A second diplomatic source confirmed that the US had given Zaidi the green light to complete his government with the participation of some factions.
One such faction, the Iran-backed Kataeb Sayyid al-Shuhada, part of the Islamic Resistance in Iraq that has recently claimed hundreds of attacks on US interests, secured the tourism ministry.
The US has previously turned a blind eye to the participation of some blacklisted factions in Iraqi governments.
But, this time the shift came after months of mounting pressure on Zaidi to disarm Iran-backed groups, which have long targeted US interests in Iraq and stepped up their attacks during the Middle East war in support of Tehran.
"Things changed," the first diplomatic source said, adding that the US had already shown in Syria its willingness to shift tactics, with its support for Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, who was previously designated a terrorist.
Zaidi, who assumed office earlier this year with US blessing, initially set 30 September, the date marking the end of the US-led coalition mission in Iraq, as the deadline for factions to hand over their weapons.
He later withdrew it as talks continued, and then set a new deadline of 30 June.
Zaidi announced part of his cabinet in May, but the remaining portfolios were held up by negotiations among political parties, including demands from some factions for government representation.

New laser factory opens in Lithuania with ambition to become one of world's largest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:52:00 UTC
18:52:00 KST

A new laser factory, Litilit, has opened in Vilnius, with its founders aiming to make it one of the largest in the world.
“The factory being established in Lithuania will be one of the world's largest in terms of femtosecond laser production capacity and will serve as a model that we plan to replicate in other regions in the future, together with international partners,” said the company's chief executive, Nikolajus Gavrilias.
The factory aims to produce up to 1,000 lasers a year in its first year of operation, with capacity set to increase to 3,000 within a few years, he said.
The factory on Plungės Street, near Gariūnai in Vilnius, covers about 4,000 sq m. It will house a metalworking workshop and automated laser assembly and testing facilities.
“Lithuania has more than 40 years of experience in developing ultrashort-pulse lasers. We undoubtedly have one of the world's strongest photonics communities. By this measure, we are as much as 100 times ahead of any other country in the world,” Gavrilias said.
Economy and Innovation Minister Edvinas Grikšas said Lithuania had all the necessary conditions to become not only a developer of advanced technologies but also a global manufacturer.
“The opening of Litilit's new factory is an excellent example of how Lithuanian science, engineering expertise and business ambition are being turned into products for the global market. The €6m investment and planned capacity of up to 3,000 lasers a year show that Lithuania's laser industry has significant growth potential,” he said.
“Our goal is to create the conditions for companies like this to expand in Lithuania, create high-value jobs and strengthen the country's position as a global technology leader,” Grikšas added.
Gintarė Verbickaitė, head of the largest startup organisation in the country, Unicorns Lithuania, who attended the factory's opening, said: “This is a truly exciting moment. We sincerely hope that Litilit will become Lithuania's first high-tech unicorn and inspire a new generation of high-tech innovators.”
In April, Lithuania's national development bank ILTE lent €8m to support the development of laser technology by the start-up Litilit. The technology uses next-generation femtosecond laser systems that generate ultrashort pulses.
Litilit's chief executive previously told the BNS news agency that the funds were intended for a research and development (R&D) project.
The laser technology sector is one of Lithuania's strongest industrial sectors. It has grown from fundamental research, which began more than 50 years ago, into a self-sustaining ecosystem.
According to the Lithuanian Laser Association, more than 60 companies currently operate in the sector, employing at least 2,250 specialists. Together, they generate annual revenue of €345m.

Documents
Details
If consultation is to be undertaken on an amendment to the regulations or the implementation of new regulation, the MAA will issue an NPA. The NPA will explain the rationale behind the amendment, the possible impact on the regulated community (developed into an impact assessment (IA)) and set the deadline for comment/feedback. Feedback is important to further develop the IA.
Comments or enquiries on any NPA are to be sent to DSA-MAA-MRPEnquiries@mod.gov.uk by the date stated in the NPA. Please use the NPA Response Form template provided below to return your consolidated comments.
After the comments closure date, the NPA will be removed from the website.
NPA comment response sheets contain the collated MAA responses to individual NPA publications.
In the final preparation for publication similar Regulated Community comments have been consolidated into one response.
Some of the MAA responses to the Regulated Community comments may have been superseded by further internal review prior to the official publication of the new issue.

Israeli ad firm under fire over harvesting data to deploy spyware
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:50:41 UTC
18:50:41 KST

Israeli digital advertising firm Discover-Tech exploited a vast commercial ad network to collect personal data and deliver mercenary spyware to targeted devices worldwide, according to an investigation published Thursday by Canadian cybersecurity watchdog Citizen Lab and New York-based ad security firm Confiant.
The operation used advertising infrastructure for covert surveillance, allowing operators to identify potential targets, track their online activity and deliver spyware while evading detection. Confiant described the campaign as highly sophisticated, citing its anti-interception measures and precise targeting capabilities.
The investigation linked the operation to Israeli spyware company Candiru, which has been blacklisted by the United States and rebranded as Integrity Labs, and surveillance vendor Intelos. The companies allegedly exploited commercial advertising inventory across major platforms, including Google, Beeswax and Russia's Yandex, to track targets and compromise consumer devices.
"The core finding is the weaponization of ad infrastructure for advanced staging, preliminary targeting, and payload delivery, characterized by exceptional technical sophistication, robust anti-interception measures, and surgical micro-targeting," Confiant said in its findings.
Citizen Lab described the campaign as the first public technical confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through online advertising, a method researchers called "AdFection."
Devices belonging to staff members at international news network Al Jazeera were among those infected through weaponized ad placements, which operated silently without visible pop-ups or suspicious links.
Discover-Tech operated a specialized system called Controlium that turned routine commercial advertising auctions into a surveillance system.
After analyzing 4 billion bidding records, researchers found that the company distributed ads across nearly 200,000 unique websites and mobile apps on Android and iOS devices in dozens of countries over a four-month period.
"Discover-Tech serves roughly 10 million ad impressions a day, and each one feeds an identity graph built from device fingerprints, IP addresses, advertising IDs, and often the publisher’s own first-party cookies," Confiant said.
Investigators found that the ads routinely collected user session cookies, authenticated login tokens and personal identifiers directly from publisher websites, exfiltrating the data even when European Union privacy regulations prohibited processing without consent.
Citizen Lab also identified an affiliated threat actor, dubbed Dark Cartographer, that used Discover-Tech's infrastructure to exploit vulnerabilities across mobile telecommunications providers. The group matched digital advertising identities with phone numbers to identify mobile subscribers on a large scale.
Geographic data revealed sharp spikes in traffic that researchers said pointed to deliberate intelligence operations rather than ordinary commercial advertising campaigns.
Palestine emerged as the most heavily targeted territory, where Discover-Tech served nearly 2% of all digital advertisements, peaking at roughly 10% on April 7. One in every 36 Android ads in the territory originated from the firm.
Surveillance traffic also reached sensitive administrative and institutional networks, including the Armenian Prime Minister's Office, international organizations, judicial agencies, universities and defense organizations.
Investigators detected targeted connections to Candiru servers in nine countries, with Belgium accounting for 56% of observed activity, followed by the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Mexico, Spain and other countries.
Following disclosure of the joint investigation, Google, the European advertising association IAB Europe, Beeswax, Vungle and Eskimi cut off Discover-Tech's access to their digital advertising systems.

NAZA premieres in UK as filmmakers condemn silence over Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:50:12 UTC
18:50:12 KST

Breadcrumb
NAZA premieres in UK as filmmakers condemn silence over Gaza and Israeli threats
Israeli documentary NAZA premiered in UK cinemas on Thursday evening, with its filmmakers denouncing the silence surrounding Israel’s genocide in Gaza as they face threats of prosecution and loss of citizenship from Israeli authorities. The nationwide screenings preceded its general release on Friday.
Speaking at a London Q&A, co-director Yuval Abraham said the soldiers and intelligence officers who testified in the film had "different motivations to speak", with some describing their disillusionment after joining the military following the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.
"There are soldiers who describe going to the army after the massacre of October 7th, feeling like that’s what they should be doing–and then after a moment or after some time having disillusionment or a sense that they are themselves involved in crimes," he told a packed London audience.
Others, he said, spoke because they felt there was no space for their accounts in Israel’s media.
"Much of the Israeli mainstream media has been either justifying or completely ignoring the crimes in Gaza, and so sometimes all it took was asking a question," Abraham said.
"These questions that you saw tonight … are still unfortunately not asked enough."
Directed by Abraham and Rachel Szor, two of the four filmmakers behind the Oscar-winning documentary "No Other Land", NAZA draws on anonymous testimony from 24 Israeli soldiers and intelligence personnel about the systems underpinning the mass killing of Palestinians. Its title is a Hebrew military acronym for "collateral damage", used to describe the anticipated killing of civilian in an airstrike.
But Abraham said the interviews were not straightforward accounts of remorse. Some participants moved between regret and justifications for their actions, revealing the human mechanisms that allow the military’s machinery to function.
"In the same human being … on the one hand there was maybe regret over what they’ve done, or even an intuitive sense that they should be speaking out," he said. "But on the other hand, it was just as easy for them to justify and to put on the hat of the intelligence operative or soldier, and to speak from that place."
The filmmakers were interested in those contradictions, he added, because alongside examining systems operating at scale, "we are also looking at the mechanisms that allow human beings to do this to other human beings".
The film’s rooftop interviews from Tel Aviv are interspersed with views into Israeli homes, including people watching television news. Szor said those images examined an everyday Israeli ritual–sitting down for the evening bulletin–and what was absent from it.
The intention was "to see the absence of what is there, or justification or the dehumanisation, the words that [are] being used in the media", she said.
Abraham also challenged the idea that intelligence officers necessarily remained detached from the Palestinians whose deaths they helped authorise and were responsible for. While military terminology stripped people of their humanity, surveillance could also simultaneously give officers intimate access to their lives.
"As one person says in the film, we don’t say 15 people will be killed–men, women, children. We say 15 naza," he said.
Yet officers could sometimes access a microphone or phone inside a home being targeted, he added.
"They can listen in and they hear the family or they hear children … that’s [a] very intimate kind of knowledge about the people you are about to kill."
Szor placed that surveillance within the wider infrastructure of Israel’s occupation, linking physical control over Palestinians to control over their telecommunications. "Palestinians have been under Israeli military occupation for a very long time," she said. "The control is not only physical control … but it’s also control over telecommunication infrastructure, and this leads to mass surveillance."
The film, she added, examines "the relationship between the surveillance of that controlled population and the killing of that population"–a relationship with roots not only in Gaza but also in the occupied West Bank.
Israeli threats against filmmakers and sources
Thursday’s premiere came days after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu demanded an investigation into the anonymous military sources featured in the documentary.
His office said on Sunday that he had asked the military chief of staff, the head of the Shin Bet domestic intelligence service and the state attorney to investigate the participants and prosecute them. Netanyahu also described the film as "false, misleading and biased".
The move followed his September pledge to advance legislation stripping citizenship from people who "defame" Israeli soldiers and increasing the statutory damages available in defamation cases twentyfold. Culture Minister Miki Zohar has accused the directors of "treason against the state", while far-right activists have demonstrated outside their families’ homes.
At the Q&A, Executive Producer Jonathan Glazer described the authorities’ reaction as "the rage of cognitive dissonance" when a society is confronted with violence that challenges its understanding of itself.
"You only have two choices, which is to kind of move into some place of truth and honesty, or to sort of explode like a volcano," he said. "I think that reaction … the film describes it."
Paul Lewis, Head of Investigations at The Guardian, said the filmmakers’ relative privilege compared with Palestinian journalists documenting Israel’s assault did not diminish the personal risks they faced.
"There is a cost to them both. The response from the Israeli government is absolutely appalling," he said. "No one who works as a filmmaker or a journalist should be punished for an exercise in telling the truth."
The panellists pointed to the tension between official efforts to discredit the testimony and threats against those who provided it.
"One of the things they say is … this film is false, misrepresentative, tells lies. Simultaneously, Bibi Netanyahu [is] saying that people in the film should be prosecuted for revealing state secrets," Lewis said. "Those two things don’t really make sense."
Despite the backlash, NAZA has secured theatrical distribution in more than 50 countries. Following its Venice premiere, where it won the Special Jury Prize, the film screened at the New York Film Festival and began its US cinema release in late September. Its international rollout includes France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Canada and Australia.
Israeli cinemas, however, had not agreed to show the documentary as of Thursday, despite an offer to screen it without charge. Abraham has said the filmmakers approached cinemas in Israel in the hope that audiences there could watch it alongside its international release.
The film will also be available worldwide for free on The Guardian’s website from late November, providing an online route for Israeli viewers to see the testimonies. Abraham has said access will have no time limit, citing the film’s "interest and public importance".
For Szor, however, reaching audiences does not guarantee that the violence documented will end.
Reflecting on "No Other Land", which she and Abraham previously made with Palestinian filmmakers Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, she questioned what international recognition had changed for the communities whose destruction it recorded. The documentary won the Oscar for best documentary in 2025.
"We won the Oscar with that film, and still … the communities there are still destroyed," she said, referring to Israel’s continued displacement and annexation of communities in the South Hebron Hills, where much of the film takes place. "A lot of the world has seen it. It’s all known, and those things are still going on."
"We still made another film, so of course we still either believe in it, or that’s what we chose to do," she added. "I don’t know if it has an impact or it doesn’t."

Population of rare Hainan gibbons gradually increasing — newspaper
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:49:52 UTC
18:49:52 KST

HAIKOU /China/, October 16. /TASS/. The small population of rare gibbons in the southern Chinese province of Hainan is gradually increasing, Hainan Ribao reported.
According to the newspaper, there are now 44 gibbons on the island, comprising seven groups, compared to 35 five years ago. The local ecosystem continues to recover and thrive. Since the establishment of the Hainan Rainforest National Park on October 12, 2021, scientists have discovered 91 new species of wild flora and fauna within its boundaries.
The article pointed out that the International Union for Conservation of Nature has recognized Hainan’s gibbon conservation model as an exemplary model for protecting rare species. Thus, the global community has adopted the experience of China’s southernmost province to restore biodiversity in other regions of the world.
Hainan Ribao noted that the abovementioned forest park effectively protects more than 95% of the territory where trees have virtually remained untouched by human activity, which comprises 55% of the island’s natural forest. The Chinese authorities provide round-the-clock monitoring and control of this area, including through the use of satellite data. According to official statistics, the Gross Ecosystem Product (GEP) of this region increased by nearly 4.4 billion yuan, or about $655 million, from 2019 to 2024.
The newspaper emphasized that a 466-kilometer tourist route encircles the forest park. It connects nine provincial administrative units and boosts revenue for local companies operating in the culture and tourism sectors.
Hainan gibbons inhabit the central and southern parts of the island. They prefer to live in the tree canopy about ten meters high, making it difficult to monitor these primates that do not reproduce well in captivity. These mammals feed on both plant matter and small animals. In China, they are under the vigilant protection of the state.

Cyber attackers hit Zurich and Swiss Post pension funds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:49:29 UTC
18:49:29 KST

Cyber attackers hit Zurich and Swiss Post pension funds
Following a cyberattack on an external software provider, personal data at the Zurich pension fund – and possibly also that of Swiss Post – was also stolen.
The Swiss city of Zurich said that the pension funds and payments are still functional. Other Swiss pension funds have already been victims of cyberattacks in recent days.
The attack took place at the end of September, Zurich said. Ahead of a switch to a new management system, the pension fund’s data had previously been transferred. The pension fund has filed a criminal complaint.
The fund is trying to determine exactly what information has been stolen and how many people are affected. In the worst-case scenario, the data breach includes personal contact details (name, address, email, telephone number), social security number, marital status, information on partners, the IBAN number and pension-related data such as insured income and assets.
The administrative system used by the funds to manage assets and pay out pensions is not believed to have been affected by the attack.
The Swiss Post pension fund also stated this evening in a press release that it had been the victim of the attack on the software provider. It is not yet clear whether policyholders’ data has been compromised.
In any case, pension assets and pension benefits are not at risk, according to the statement from Swiss Post. However, personal data such as name, address, date of birth, social security number, contact details, email address and pension details may have been affected by the cyberattack.
The cyberattack has also affected other pension funds. Last week, it emerged that data had also been stolen from the Bern Pension Fund and the Bern Teachers’ Insurance Fund.

UK government signals possible intervention in Sky’s $2.1B ITV broadcasting deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:48:04 UTC
18:48:04 KST

Rabia Ali
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
The UK government has signaled it could intervene in Sky’s proposed £1.6 billion ($2.1 billion) takeover of ITV’s broadcasting and streaming business over concerns about media ownership, the diversity of news coverage and viewers’ access to quality programming.
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said in a written statement to Parliament Thursday that she was “minded to” issue a public interest intervention notice, a formal step that would trigger reviews by media regulator Ofcom and the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA).
The deal would give Sky, owned by US media giant Comcast, control of ITV’s Media and Entertainment business, including its television channels and streaming platform ITVX. ITV Studios, its television production business, is excluded.
Nandy raised concerns about freedom of expression and the diversity of views in the news media as well as the concentration of media ownership.
She also questioned how the deal could affect the availability of varied, high-quality programming on streaming and other on-demand services used by UK audiences.
Existing legislation does not explicitly cover the impact of mergers on programming availability through on-demand services, Nandy said, adding that the government could extend the relevant public-interest rules.
Sky announced the deal on July 6, saying the combined business would account for around 20% of all in-home viewing in the UK.
The company said the takeover would strengthen British broadcasting’s ability to compete with global streaming platforms.
“We remain confident that bringing Sky and ITV's Media & Entertainment business together will create a stronger British media business, better able to compete with global streaming platforms, support great British programming and trusted news and deliver more for audiences,” a Sky spokesperson said.
Sky has also pledged to preserve ITV’s identity, free-to-air services and public-service broadcasting obligations, and maintain separate editorial voices for ITV News and Sky News.
Nandy said no final decision had been made. Sky and ITV have until next Tuesday to submit written responses.
If she issues the notice, Ofcom would examine the deal’s public-interest implications, while the CMA would assess its potential impact on competition. Nandy would then decide whether a more detailed investigation was needed.

Danish PM says Ukraine needs frozen Russian assets as it is running out of money
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen has said Ukraine needs funding to continue fighting Russia and that frozen Russian assets are the most obvious source of additional EU support.
Source: Frederiksen speaking ahead of the second day of the European Council meeting in Brussels on 16 October, as reported by European Pravda
Quote: "Waging war is expensive… And Ukraine is now running out of money. This has already happened. They cannot buy what they need. They cannot produce what they need."
Details: Frederiksen noted that Russia's attacks on Ukrainians have become even more intense than they were "until quite recently".
"So we have an urgent problem in finding funding for 2026 at the European level. We must ensure there will be enough funds at the European level for the war effort in 2027. This is what I will raise at the meeting," the Danish prime minister stressed.
She pledged that Denmark "will continue to provide whatever assistance we can".
Asked where additional funding for Ukraine could come from, Frederiksen stressed that "frozen assets are the most obvious source to turn to".
Quote: "Not only would this help finance Europe's defence, but it would also mean that Russia, which is currently causing so much damage to Ukraine and Europe, would have to pay for everything it is doing… I still believe this is one of the best solutions we have right in front of us."
Background:
- The EU's support for Ukraine is to be discussed with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in attendance at the EU leaders' summit in Brussels. EU leaders have publicly assured Zelenskyy that sanctions against Russia will under no circumstances be eased.
- Meanwhile, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever has firmly opposed discussing the idea of using frozen Russian Central Bank assets to benefit Ukraine.
- European Pravda previously reported that the EU leaders' summit on 15-16 October would not produce decisions on funding for Ukraine or Russian assets because no agreement has been reached on the issue.

Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,790 Troops, 6 Aircraft in One Day
Russia lost an estimated 1,790 troops and six aircraft over the past 24 hours, while fighting across the front surged to 304 combat engagements, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on October 16.
The latest Ukrainian estimate puts Russia’s cumulative personnel losses since the start of its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022, at approximately 1,561,020. The six additional aircraft raised Russia’s estimated aviation losses to 449, while helicopter losses remained unchanged at 356.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian forces also lost 15 armored combat vehicles, bringing the cumulative figure to 25,552, while tank losses remained at 12,414. Ukraine recorded nine additional artillery systems, one multiple-launch rocket system, and one air defense system, bringing those totals to 51,242, 2,217, and 1,708, respectively.
Another 693 operational-tactical UAVs were added to the tally, pushing estimated cumulative losses to 565,590. Ukraine also reported three unmanned ground systems lost, bringing that category to 2,958. Russia’s cruise missile losses remained unchanged at 5,130, while naval losses stayed at 35 ships and boats and two submarines.
Another 230 vehicles and fuel tankers were recorded as lost over the latest reporting period, raising the cumulative total to 163,554. Three additional pieces of special equipment brought that figure to 4,833.
The General Staff said Ukrainian and Russian forces clashed 304 times over the past day, indicating an exceptionally high level of battlefield activity. According to updated figures, Russian forces carried out 83 airstrikes and dropped 271 guided aerial bombs.
Russia also deployed 7,059 one-way drones and carried out 2,551 strikes against Ukrainian positions and populated areas, including 76 using multiple-launch rocket systems.
Earlier, the General Staff reported that Russia has lost 350,260 military personnel since the beginning of 2026 and added that September saw the highest Russian personnel losses of the year, with 46,230 recorded.

How a Ukrainian Developer Built an FPV Simulator to Hunt Russian Shaheds

- Category

How a Ukrainian Developer Built an FPV Simulator to Hunt Russian Shaheds
Ukrainian FPV combat drone simulator Remote Reaper officially launched out of Steam Early Access with version 1.0, marking the software’s largest update since development began.
The full release introduces airborne targets—specifically Shahed drones—alongside a time trial racing mode, new missions, and various technical enhancements, according to dev.ua.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Developer Vladyslav Fomenko built the project independently in direct collaboration with active military drone operators. To recreate flight mechanics with high accuracy, Fomenko personally tested uncrewed aerial vehicles at training grounds.
The software recreates real operational conditions, simulating the impact of electronic warfare systems, adverse weather, armored vehicle protection, and terrain topography.
"Shooting down Shaheds is more fun with friends," Fomenko noted, highlighting the simulator's online cooperative multiplayer feature, as reported by dev.ua.
The addition of aerial targets stands out as the core upgrade in version 1.0. Intercepting Iranian-designed attack drones requires operators to apply distinct handling techniques and approach vectors compared to ground strikes, alongside detonating the payload while airborne.
The update also incorporates a time trial mode featuring three dedicated tracks for flight skill practice, as well as new combat scenarios covering multiple rocket launcher hunting, infantry engagements in foggy conditions, and expanded tutorial courses.
Visual damage displays appear on struck targets, while opposing infantry can now deploy smoke screens to break line of sight.
Control options expanded to include gamepad support within a simplified control scheme, improved navigation on Steam Deck devices, and an updated flight compass with target tracking markers.
The program retains a detailed drone builder that factors component weight into flight duration, alongside a custom mission editor supported by Steam Workshop integration.
Previously, it was reported that Ukrainian defense company TENETA developed a new lightweight, single-use anti-drone device designed to counter enemy FPV drones and reconnaissance quadcopters.

Nearly 400 Foreign Companies Request Access to Ukraine’s Russian Weapon Intelligence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:45:20 UTC
18:45:20 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Nearly 400 Foreign Companies Request Access to Ukraine’s Russian Weapon Intelligence
The Ministry of Defense of Ukraine has received more than 650 registration applications for its unified research portal for captured adversary hardware, known as TrophyLab.
Among these requests, 389 applications have come from foreign manufacturers of military equipment and weaponry. Registration on the portal is also accessible to Ukrainian manufacturers, military units, and government institutions, according to the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
TrophyLab gathers unique information regarding captured Russian military hardware to support engineers, scientists, and defense technology producers from Ukraine and partner nations.
The database is actively populated by units of the Defense Forces of Ukraine, the Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense, the Security Service of Ukraine, and specialized scientific institutions.
Every registered researcher has the opportunity to submit a request to receive a sample or its physical fragment for independent evaluation.
According to the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, access to TrophyLab enables faster and secure information sharing regarding Russian hardware to accelerate the creation of effective countermeasures for the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
The development comes as Russia continues introducing new weapons into its arsenal. Ukrainian military technology expert and defense adviser Serhii Flash said on July 14 that Russia has begun deploying the low-cost, highly maneuverable Banderol cruise missile, although production has yet to reach the planned rate of 120 missiles per month.
According to Flash, achieving that production target would allow Russia to launch an average of four Banderol missiles per day. However, he said the manufacturing facility has not yet reached the required output. The missile is launched from airborne platforms, primarily the Orion medium-altitude, long-endurance unmanned aerial vehicle.

Sanctions working: FM Sybiha urges allies to maintain pressure on Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:38:00 UTC
18:38:00 KST

Sanctions working: FM Sybiha urges allies to maintain pressure on Russia
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
“It is also important not to pause sanctions policy: rather than waiting for new packages to be adopted, sanctions should be imposed continuously, in a targeted, focused and sector-specific manner, because this is producing results. Whatever Russia may say, sanctions are working, and we know that. They will gradually have a critical impact on the Russian economy. Even if the Russians circumvent sanctions, even if they adapt, this still hurts any economy – all the more so the economy of a country waging such aggression,” the Foreign Minister stressed.
According to Sybiha, Ukraine is proposing tougher restrictions on Russia’s “shadow fleet,” including a complete ban on maritime services and sanctions against the captains of such vessels.
“This is also a very sensitive issue. We know that many captains refuse to work on shadow fleet tankers because doing so poses a serious reputational risk. We will continue working in this area,” Ukraine’s top diplomat said.
Kyiv is also calling for a ban on the transit of Russian grain and other agricultural products through Europe, including Baltic ports, as well as further restrictions on Russian banks’ access to the SWIFT system.
“Russia still uses SWIFT, and Russian banks need to be disconnected from the system to the greatest extent possible. It is important to keep up the pressure on Russia to ensure that these sanctions have a truly shocking and devastating effect. There is still room to do more,” Sybiha said.
He stressed that sanctions pressure must raise the cost of Russia’s continued aggression. According to Ukrainian estimates, the war costs Russia about $1 billion a day.
“Putin understands only strength. To seriously force him to negotiate, pressure is needed, and the cost of continued military action must be raised,” the minister said, citing sanctions, the use of frozen Russian assets, international isolation and restrictions on access to technology as tools of such pressure.
Sybiha recalled that an EU sanctions package covering around 1,600 individuals and legal entities was adopted at a meeting of EU Foreign Ministers in Luxembourg. He said particular attention was paid to Russia’s defense industry and efforts to counter sanctions evasion.
The Ukrainian Foreign Minister also criticized the decision to remove Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the EU sanctions list. Ukraine, he said, will seek to have both men reinstated and is proposing sanctions against more than ten other Russian oligarchs linked to Russia’s military-industrial complex and Putin’s inner circle.
Sybiha added that the United Kingdom had assured Ukraine it intended to maintain sanctions against Usmanov and Fridman. He emphasized that Kyiv would continue working with its partners to strengthen and expand restrictions against Russia.
As Ukrinform reported, the Council of the EU adopted additional restrictive measures against 1,569 individuals and entities linked to Russia’s military-industrial complex.

Tesla unveils new Roadster sports car
Tesla has unveiled its redesigned Roadster electric sports car, featuring SpaceX cold-gas thrusters and a suction system designed to enable extraordinary driving maneuvers, reports a Qazinform News Agency correspondent, citing Tesla’s official website.
The company presented the vehicle yesterday, showcasing technology that combines active aerodynamics, powered fans and rocket-inspired components.
“We already put Roadster in a rocket. Now we put a rocket in Roadster,” Tesla said.
Real life, baby https://t.co/3QEqn18wig
— Tesla (@Tesla) October 16, 2026
According to the manufacturer, the car’s fan and ground-sealing system pulls air from beneath the vehicle, generating enough suction to hold it upside down even while stationary. Active wings and powered fans are designed to improve traction and cornering performance.
Tesla says the vehicle’s cold-gas thrusters use electric actuators to make rapid adjustments, helping stabilize it in flight. The company specifies that flight-related features are available only with the Rocket configuration, which will not be offered in all regions.
Tesla has outlined three configurations: Performance, Thrust and Rocket. In its announcement, the company described Performance as a two-seat version intended for road use, while the two-seat Thrust adds rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters for claimed acceleration from zero to 60 mph, approximately 97 km/h, in under one second.
The manufacturer notes that the specifications displayed on its Roadster webpage primarily reflect the optional Thrust upgrade.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Tesla had planned to unveil its long-delayed second-generation Roadster on October 1, nearly nine years after first presenting the high-performance electric sports car.

Parashat Noah: The main thing is the intention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:32:29 UTC
18:32:29 KST

One of the most dramatic events to shape the world and humanity was the Flood, which swept across the earth and destroyed everything on it, leaving only Noah and his family, the animals he had brought into the Ark, and the fish in the waters.
At the beginning of Creation, the world was created in perfection and goodness, destined to exist without death or disease.
However, following Adam’s sin and his expulsion from the Garden of Eden, evil entered the human experience.
Humanity eventually reached a state in which, in the words of the Torah, “the earth was filled with violence.”
Violence, corruption, and the absence of moral boundaries undermined the very foundations of human existence, until the world reached a breaking point.
The Flood was therefore a turning point in the history of Creation, an attempt to halt the downward spiral and open a new chapter in the history of the world.
When Noah and his family emerge from the Ark, they encounter a world entirely different from the one they had known: ruined, desolate, and silent, no longer filled with the human activity that had been inseparable from their lives.
Try to imagine that moment. A small family stands before an immense, empty world, with no cities, no communities, no other human beings, and nothing of the familiar world they once knew.
No one is there to welcome them. There is no one with whom to share their feelings, and no certainty about what life will look like from that point onward.
What would be the first thing you would choose to do in such a moment? How does one respond to destruction on a scale that is almost impossible to comprehend?
The Torah describes Noah’s first act:
“Noah went out, together with his sons, his wife, and his sons’ wives.
“Noah built an altar to the Lord, and taking from every clean animal and every clean bird, he offered burnt offerings on the altar” (Gen. 8:18-20).
Noah does not begin his new life by trying to rebuild the world, constructing a home for himself, or first attending to his family’s practical needs. The first act described in the Torah is building an altar and offering a sacrifice to God.
This act acknowledges the Creator’s sovereignty, gives thanks, and submits oneself before the One who governs the world. Noah recognizes that even when reality appears harsh and incomprehensible, the world does not operate by chance. In the very midst of devastation and destruction, he expresses his connection with the One who spoke the world into existence.
Then an unexpected turn takes place. The Torah describes how Noah’s act leads to a divine promise concerning the future of all humanity:
“The Lord smelled the pleasing aroma, and the Lord said to Himself: I will never again curse the ground because of man, for the inclination of the human heart is evil from his youth; nor will I ever again destroy every living thing as I have done” (Gen. 8:21).
World continues to exist with evil in it
God promises that He will never again bring a Flood to destroy all life on earth, and that the world will continue to exist even though evil remains within it.
Yet this very promise raises a question. For many years, Noah stood alone against an entire generation, admonishing its members, trying to influence them and change their ways. Nevertheless, the Flood was not averted. Yet now, after the destruction, a single act of his elicits such a profound response. What was it about this act that gave it such extraordinary power?
The Mishna in Tractate Makkot states:
“Rabbi Hananya ben Akashya says: The Holy One, blessed be He, wished to bring merit to Israel; therefore, He gave them an abundance of Torah and commandments, as it is stated: ‘The Lord desired, for the sake of His righteousness, to make the Torah great and glorious’” (Makkot 3:16).
The Rambam, Maimonides, explains this teaching of the Mishna, establishing an important principle for understanding the significance of the commandments:
“One of the fundamental principles of faith in the Torah is that if a person fulfills one of the 613 commandments properly and correctly, without involving any worldly objective whatsoever, but performs it purely for its own sake, out of love, that person merits the World to Come through it.
“Rabbi Hananya therefore said that because of the great number of commandments, it is impossible for a person not to perform at least one of them perfectly at some point during his lifetime, thereby meriting the eternal survival of the soul through that act” (Commentary on the Mishna, Tractate Makkot).
These words express a central principle of serving the Creator. The commandments are not merely a list of actions a person must perform; they express the relationship between the individual and God.
A person may perform a good deed to earn honor or gain status. He may also act out of habit or loyalty to the tradition in which he was raised. In the language of our Sages, all these may be considered commandments performed shelo lishma – not purely for their own sake.
Maimonides points to the central goal of fulfilling the commandments: performing them lishma, for their own sake, out of love for the Creator and a desire to fulfill His will, without any personal interest mixed in.
We can now understand that Noah’s efforts before the Flood do not diminish his righteousness. However, when a person acts before an entire community, additional motives may accompany his actions.
After the Flood, the situation is entirely different. Noah builds an altar and offers a sacrifice without seeking to prove his righteousness to anyone, compete with anyone, or gain status. After all, the world is empty of other people. He acts solely because he wishes to serve his Creator and acknowledge His goodness. This is a pure act performed lishma, for its own sake.
Such a clean and genuine act, performed entirely for the sake of Heaven, has the power to ensure the world’s continued existence forever. For this is the very purpose of Creation, and now that this purpose has been fulfilled, humanity can endure.
This idea is relevant to our everyday lives as well. The deeper test often comes precisely when no one is watching.
Imagine someone driving alone late at night who finishes drinking a cup of coffee. He could throw the empty cup out the window, thinking that no one will notice.
Yet in that moment, he discovers whether keeping the environment clean and acting responsibly toward it are values he truly believes in, or whether he observes them only because he fears the reaction of others.
In a generation in which sharing our experiences and actions has become central to social life, this aspect of serving God deserves our attention as well.
People share acts of kindness, charitable donations, volunteer initiatives, and other good deeds on social media.
This has a positive side: publicizing a good deed can inspire others, encourage them to act, and create additional circles of generosity.
However, alongside the benefits of sharing, we must not lose the ability to do good without telling anyone about it.
When every action becomes an opportunity to share, a person may grow accustomed to measuring a deed’s value by the degree of exposure and recognition it receives. Instead of asking whether he has done the right thing, he may find himself wondering whether he will receive positive responses and whether others will think more highly of him as a result.
It is therefore important to preserve an inner space where our good deeds remain between ourselves and our Creator, without needing applause or expecting recognition.
The writer is rabbi of the Western Wall and holy sites.

World Bread Day: Kazakhstan exports wheat to 29 countries up to USD 1.6B

Unknown Publisher

World Bread Day: Kazakhstan exports wheat to 29 countries up to USD 1.6B
Kazakhstan exports wheat to 29 countries, with shipments worth 1.6 billion US dollars, according to data released by the Kazakh Agriculture Ministry ahead of World Bread Day, celebrated annually on October 16, Qazinform News Agency reports.
More than half of Kazakhstan’s wheat exports go to Uzbekistan, which accounts for 51% of total exports, or 4.2 million tonnes. Other major destinations include Tajikistan with 16% (1.3 million tonnes), Azerbaijan with 8% (652,000 tonnes), Afghanistan with 6% (496,300 tonnes), and Italy with 5% (418,700 tonnes). Other importers include Algeria and Kyrgyzstan.
The country’s export capacity is supported by strong grain production. Kazakhstan harvests an average of 18 million tonnes of grain annually, while domestic consumption and processing amount to nearly 9.5 million tonnes. This allows the country to fully meet domestic demand while maintaining substantial export volumes.
Flour production is twice the level of domestic consumption, ensuring that the baking industry operates primarily on locally sourced raw materials. Between January and August 2026, Kazakhstan produced 325,500 tonnes of bread.
The annual production capacity of the country’s bakeries stands at 502,000 tonnes, with current utilization at 35.5%. Producers continue to expand their product range in response to consumer demand, manufacturing both bakery and flour-based confectionery products with short and extended shelf lives.
To support the sector, the Government has introduced several support measuers. Under the 2021-2030 Agro-Industrial Complex Development Concept, enterprises expanding production of bakery or confectionery products with annual capacities exceeding 2,000 tonnes are eligible for reimbursement of 25% of investment costs. Flour producers also benefit from a tax incentive, with value-added tax reduced by 80% under Article 490 of the Tax Code.
World Bread Day was established in 2006 at the initiative of the International Union of Bakers and Confectioners. The date coincides with the anniversary of the founding of the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) on October 16, 1945.
Earlier, it was reported that Kazakhstan’s grain harvest reached 23 million tonnes.
Reports highlighted Kazakhstan’s grain rail shipments hit record 1.45 mln tons in September.

Source: De Wever at a press conference following the first day of the EU summit, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The Belgian prime minister, who has consistently opposed the transfer of frozen Russian funds held in the EU to Ukraine, told journalists that his position remains unchanged.
He believes dialogue can begin only after the war ends, meaning the funds cannot be used now.
"In every war, even in World War II, they [immobilised assets] were never touched. But at the end of a conflict, there is always a peace deal. And part of this peace deal is the use of immobilised assets," he said.

It's the best answer I can give you," he said.
The Belgian prime minister also noted that the current rules require unanimity for any action to be taken regarding the funds.
Background: No decisions on financing for Ukraine or on frozen Russian assets are expected at the summit due to a lack of agreement on these issues.

Parashat Noah: How prayer becomes an ark that carries us through turbulent times - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:31:55 UTC
18:31:55 KST

‘And God said to Noah, ‘Come into the teiva, you and all your household’” (Gen. 7:1).
The teiva – the ark – is one of the defining images of the parasha: a vessel of refuge carrying Noah, his family, and the living creatures through the waters of the Flood toward a renewed world.
Yet the Hebrew word “teiva” has another meaning. It can also mean “a word.” The Baal Shem Tov, the 18th-century founder of the Hassidic movement, takes “Bo el hateiva” (“Come into the ark”) as an instruction to enter the words of prayer.
Fittingly, this teaching opens “Amud Hatefila” – “The Pillar of Prayer” – an extensive compilation of his teachings on prayer found in Baal Shem Tov al HaTorah, parashat Noah.
Here the ark becomes the starting point for an entire approach to prayer – one of deep concentration, attachment to the sacred letters, and awareness of the Divine within them.
In prayer, he teaches, you should immerse yourself in each word “with your whole body and all your powers.” Rather than allowing the words simply to pass through our lips, we are invited to experience them fully.
'Worlds, souls, and Divinity'
The Baal Shem Tov takes the teaching further. Within every letter, he says, are “worlds, souls, and Divinity.” As letters join together to form words, prayer becomes more than a sequence of words to be recited. The teiva itself becomes a spiritual space that can hold and carry us.
Yoram Raanan’s painting gives striking visual expression to this understanding of “teiva.” He created the work spontaneously, allowing paint to drip and flow across the canvas. From this spontaneous process, a ship emerged. Its great curved form fills the lower half of the painting, while long vertical lines rise like masts above it.
Within the form of the ship, a stringed instrument, perhaps a lute, came into being. The curved hull becomes the body of the instrument, while the vertical lines perform both functions visually – at once masts and strings. Ship and instrument inhabit the same form – one carrying us across, the other giving voice to sound.
Above them, small forms move through the expansive blue-green field. Some appear as golden birds, others as drifting clouds, while still others remain more elusive. “They intermingle,” Raanan says, “like the words of prayer.”
The transformation seems particularly fitting for the Baal Shem Tov’s understanding of “teiva.” The ship carries us; the instrument gives voice to prayer. The word becomes both vessel and sound.
Throughout the painting, forms seem to shift and flow into one another. Water becomes sky. Ship becomes lute. Birds and other forms seem to pass between different realms.
The painting gives visual form to something difficult to describe: to enter the teiva is not merely to pronounce a word of prayer, but to enter its sound, its movement, and the world it contains. Just as the ark carries its passengers through the waters of the Flood, the words of prayer can become a vessel that carries us.
But the ark does more than carry. It is also a place of protection. When the world outside becomes stormy, the teiva offers refuge.
The Baal Shem Tov’s teaching gives this ancient image an inner dimension. In difficult or turbulent times, we, too, can find a protective space within sacred words and prayer.
And Raanan’s lute adds another possibility: music, too, can become a place of refuge. Sound moves through us and changes how we feel, carrying us when words alone are not enough.
This image has particular resonance just after the cycle of the Jewish holidays. We have emerged from weeks of prayer, reflection, celebration, and sacred time, and suddenly we are back in the ordinary rhythm of the year.
The Baal Shem Tov’s teaching offers us a way to take something of that experience with us: the words of prayer can carry and sustain us as we move into the year ahead.
Noah could not remain in the ark forever. Eventually, the waters receded, the door opened, and he stepped onto dry land to begin again. The ark had carried him through the Flood; now he had to build life anew.
Raanan’s teiva, at once ark and lute, seems to hold both possibilities. The ark offers refuge; the lute gives us a song for the journey. We enter the teiva, and it carries us into the year ahead.
The writer is the author of Art of Revelation: A Visual Encounter with the Jewish Bible, a commentary on the paintings of her husband, artist Yoram Raanan. She teaches Jewish meditation and is currently writing ‘Art of Transformation,’ a book exploring the relationship between art, Jewish spirituality, and inner transformation, from which this article is adapted.

Heads of Polish and Ukrainian national remembrance institutes hold first meeting since 2018
