Senior delegations from Poland and Ukraine’s state institutes of national remembrance have held talks in the Ukrainian city of Lviv, marking the first time the heads of the two organisations have met in eight years.
The meeting, at which the two sides discussed issues including exhumations of World War Two victims and possible joint research projects, comes as Poland and Ukraine seek reconciliation over historical issues that have regularly caused tensions between two otherwise close allies.

➡️ Stronie polskiej przewodniczył kierujący… pic.twitter.com/qHpZwLeCEa

News of the meeting was announced on social media by Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), which noted that it was “the first direct, working meeting between the heads of these institutions since 2018”.
The IPN is currently headed by its deputy president, Karol Polejowski, because Poland’s parliament has been unable to agree on a permanent new president. The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINR) is led by Oleksandr Alfyorov.
“The first topic of discussion,” according to the IPN, was the planned reburial of 115 Polish soldiers recently exhumed in Lviv, where they died in 1939 defending the city (then part of Poland and known as Lwów) during the Nazi-German and Soviet invasions.
Polish and Ukrainian researchers have exhumed the remains of 115 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending Lviv – now in Ukraine but then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of WWII https://t.co/yQNeq2D54E
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026
Their exhumation resulted from a diplomatic breakthrough last year between Warsaw and Kyiv that saw Ukraine lift a moratorium on exhumations that had been in place since 2017 in protest at the dismantling in Poland of a monument to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA).
Ukraine has also allowed the exhumation on its territory of Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres, which were led by the UPA. Poland likewise recently granted permission for Ukraine to search for Ukrainian victims of a massacre led by the Polish Home Army in the village of Łasków (Laskiv in Ukrainian).
At this week’s meeting, the UINR gave an update on its work in Łasków, where it has uncovered the remains of 30 people.
The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance has found 30 human remains in a village in Poland where Polish partisans killed Ukrainian civilians in WW2
It thanked Poland for permission to search the site, calling it a step towards "true reconciliation" https://t.co/BeeEtl6gCa
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026
The IPN and UINR also discussed planned exhumation work in the now-depopulated village of Huta Pieniacka (Huta Peniatska in Ukrainian), where the local Polish population was massacred in 1944 by a Nazi SS regiment mainly made up of Ukrainians.
There was also “willingness on both sides to restore cooperation in the field of historical scientific research”, said the IPN. “The possibility of undertaking joint educational initiatives was also discussed.” The two sides also agreed to hold another meeting in Warsaw, though no date has been set.
This week’s meeting comes after a period of tension over historical issues between not only Poland and Ukraine more broadly, but also the two countries’ remembrance institutes.
In February this year, the IPN criticised Alfyorov over an interview in which he initially called the Volhynia massacres “one of Poland’s state myths”, before later appearing to correct himself and saying it was “not a myth, but one of the key elements of the Polish grand narrative”.
By contrast, “for most Ukrainians, this is just a local episode of history”, added Alfyorov. Referring to Poland’s recognition of the massacres as a genocide – a term Ukraine rejects – he asked if Polish massacres of around 28,000 Ukrainians during the war should also be called a genocide.
In response, the IPN called Alfyorov’s remarks “outrageous” and declared that the Volhynia massacres were “not an ‘episode’, but rather one of the largest genocides against civilians in 20th-century Europe”. It also condemned Ukraine for honouring figures associated with the massacres.
The UINR, for its part, criticised a law proposed by Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki (a former head of the IPN), that would criminalise the promotion of ideologies associated with World War Two Ukrainian nationalist groups.
Ukraine has criticised a law proposed by Poland's president that would criminalise promotion of historical Ukrainian nationalist ideologies, equating them with Nazism and communism
It warns of "retaliatory measures" if the bill is passed https://t.co/TaX2Vj5z8v
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2025
In another sign of reconciliation, in May the UINR and Poland’s Mieroszewski Centre held a historical congress in Warsaw, bringing together more than 100 historians “to discuss complex issues of the shared past and explore common approaches to their interpretation”, in the words of the Ukrainian foreign ministry.
However, that same month, President Volodymyr Zelensky prompted a diplomatic crisis by approving the naming of a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted Nawrocki to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle.
Since then, both sides have made efforts to reach a diplomatic solution, including a pledge by Zelensky to “grant a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”.

France and Germany have reached an agreement on a joint approach to securing the future of the European automotive industry. Our shared ambition is clear: to successfully transform our automotive industry while maintaining our climate ambition and ensuring that the cars of the future are produced in Europe.
Our course remains unchanged: to achieve substantial reductions in CO₂ emissions while strengthening Europe’s capacity to develop and manufacture the next generation of electric vehicles. This is what European preference means in practice: ensuring that the transition to clean mobility goes hand in hand with investment, innovation and production in France, Germany and across Europe.
To that end, France and Germany propose a comprehensive package that combines an ambitious European decarbonisation pathway with the regulatory flexibility needed to reflect different market realities and technological conditions. It also provides concrete incentives for investment, research and development, European production, and resilient supply chains.
This balanced approach will enable the European Union to pursue its climate objectives while strengthening the technological sovereignty, industrial base and international competitiveness of its automotive industry.
Europe must be a continent that innovates, invests and produces, while protecting the climate and safeguarding jobs. This is the purpose of our commitment and the guiding principle of our joint approach.
France and Germany are determined to build on this momentum and work swiftly with their European partners towards an agreement. We owe it to our workers, our industries and our citizens to ensure that Europe remains a leading force in the global automotive transition.
Our objective is clear: a competitive, innovative and decarbonised European automotive industry, producing in Europe and creating the jobs of tomorrow.

German MPs clash over colonial genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:22:55 UTC
18:22:55 KST

German MPs clash over colonial genocide
German lawmakers have clashed over demands for reparations for the killing of tens of thousands of Africans in colonial-era Namibia in what is widely regarded as the first genocide of the 20th century.
The Bundestag debated opposition motions on Wednesday seeking recognition, an apology and redress for the Ovaherero and Nama communities. Both proposals were referred to the German Foreign Affairs Committee for further consideration.
Germany ruled present-day Namibia from 1884 to 1915. Between 1904 and 1908, its forces waged an extermination campaign against the Ovaherero and Nama, driving families into the desert and imprisoning survivors in concentration camps. Estimates suggest that up to 80% of the Ovaherero and about half the Nama died.
Berlin recognized the atrocities as genocide in 2021 and pledged €1.1 billion ($1.23 billion) over 30 years for reconstruction and development. It, however, explicitly ruled out legal compensation claims arising from the arrangement.
Christian Democratic Union lawmaker Thomas Rachel criticized the German government’s prolonged failure to confront the atrocities.
“I am still ashamed today in the face of the indescribable suffering inflicted on people at that time… One might note that it took a long time before the German federal government recognized the horrific atrocities in Namibia as genocide,” Rachel told the legislature.
Green MP Jamila Schafer urged parliament to “explicitly recognize the genocide against the Ovaherero and Nama, as well as colonial crimes committed against the Damara and San, and ask their descendants for forgiveness.”
Alternative for Germany MP Ronald Glaser opposed the €1.1 billion commitment, arguing that Berlin had no legal obligation to pay. He called for a commission of historians to investigate the events.
The Left’s motion sought recognition of legal liability and comprehensive reparations paid directly to descendants, alongside measures to return land, looted cultural property and human remains.
Ovaherero and Nama representatives have rejected development funding as a substitute for reparations and say they were excluded from negotiations. Germany maintains that community representatives were involved on the Namibian side.
The dispute comes amid growing African and Caribbean demands for redress for slavery and colonial crimes. The African Union has designated 2026–2035 a reparations decade and established expert bodies to develop a common continental position and legal strategies. The Caribbean Community has revised its ten-point reparations plan, seeking measures including monetary compensation, debt cancellation and investment in health and education.
On March 25, the UN General Assembly adopted a Ghana-led resolution declaring the trafficking and racialized enslavement of Africans “the gravest crime against humanity” and calling for reparations. The measure secured support from 123 countries, including Russia and China, while the US, Israel, and Argentina voted against the resolution, and the UK and all the EU states abstained.

“What interests him is being bigger than Likud and entering negotiations from a position of strength to form a government with Netanyahu,” Liberman wrote. He also accused Eisenkot of seeking a coalition with Netanyahu’s ultra-Orthodox partners.
Liberman dubbed Eisenkot “Benny Gantz 2” and argued that military experience was no substitute for political experience. Gantz, another former military chief, entered a unity government with Netanyahu in 2020 after campaigning to replace him.
The attack followed Liberman’s declaration Thursday that he would not support a minority government, even temporarily, rejecting an option Eisenkot had floated should the opposition fail to secure a parliamentary majority. Liberman said Likud without Netanyahu could be a coalition partner.
Eisenkot had publicly rejected a government role for Netanyahu earlier in the week, after Naftali Bennett suggested he could serve as a minister under certain conditions. Eisenkot said those who held leadership positions during the October 7 attack were unfit to return to senior office. Bennett subsequently ruled out serving alongside Netanyahu.

China-North Korea border bridge may do little to spur trade, experts say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:21:40 UTC
18:21:40 KST

China-North Korea border bridge may do little to spur trade, experts say
Sanctions and a North Korean leadership that prioritises security dim prospects for economic cooperation, analysts say.
As China and North Korea cut the ribbon on New Yalu River Bridge this week, officials described the new border crossing in momentous terms.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang said the 3km (1.9-mile) bridge, which links China’s Dandong and North Korea’s Sinuiju, would “vigorously promote” trade and “strengthen emotional bonds”.
North Korean Premier Pak Thae-song expressed his belief that the crossing would “accelerate the advance for the prosperity of the two countries” and “add fresh vigour” to their economic cooperation.
Analysts on China-North Korea ties are much more circumspect.
While the bridge is a concrete symbol of China and North Korea’s efforts to revitalise relations that have waned from their Cold War-era peak, the prospects for trade are hindered by obstacles ranging from international sanctions to a North Korean leadership that prioritises security above all else, experts say.
“It reflects China’s renewed effort to strengthen its relationship with North Korea at a time of changing regional alignments,” Phillip Park, a professor at the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, South Korea, told Al Jazeera.
“But whether this leads to substantially deeper economic integration, greater North Korean dependence, or a significant shift in Pyongyang’s strategic orientation remains an open question.
“The bridge could facilitate trade and logistics, but it does not remove international sanctions,” Park added.
China, whose troops fought alongside Pyongyang in the 1950-53 Korean War, has long been North Korea’s most crucial economic benefactor.
China accounts for as much as 95 percent of official trade with the secretive country, which is among the world’s most diplomatically and economically isolated states.
Before the four-lane New Yalu River Bridge officially opened on Thursday, road and rail freight between Dandong and Sinuiju, the main route for China-North Korea trade, travelled exclusively via the ageing Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge.
Opened in 1943, the bridge, which has a single-lane road and a rail track, can only carry vehicles weighing a maximum of 20 tonnes.
Jae-woo Joo, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Kyung Hee University in Seoul, said the new bridge could “tremendously” boost trade between the sides, including the transfer of components banned under sanctions against Pyongyang’s nuclear and missile programmes.
“It is therefore really significant to open this bridge with China,” Joo told Al Jazeera.
After coming under strain from North Korea’s nuclear weapons tests in the mid-2000s, Beijing-Pyongyang ties have warmed under Chinese President Xi Jinping and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
At Xi and Kim’s most recent meeting in June, their seventh summit since 2018, the leaders pledged to enhance cooperation in areas spanning trade, defence, agriculture, law, science and technology.
Analysts have, in part, cast Beijing’s deepening engagement with Pyongyang as a response to the latter’s growing ties with Moscow, which have included the deployment of thousands of North Korean troops to the front lines of Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Last month, North Korean and Russian officials opened the first road bridge linking their countries across the Tumen River.
North Korea and China’s two-way trade grew 25 percent in 2025 to reach $2.74bn, according to figures from China’s General Administration of Customs.
Bilateral trade has continued to grow in 2026, jumping nearly 20 percent to reach $1.5bn in the first half of the year, putting it on track to reach its highest volumes since the COVID-19 pandemic.
But while growing, trade remains relatively minuscule in the context of global commerce.
With China’s overall trade hitting $6.36 trillion in 2025, North Korea’s contribution to the total was a little more than 0.04 percent.
Official trade between the neighbours also remains substantially below its 2010s heyday.
Trade hovered around $5-6bn throughout much of the decade, peaking at $6.45bn in 2013.
Economists have offered explanations for the slowdown that range from tightened sanctions to China’s waning reliance on imports amid its efforts to boost economic self-reliance.
Christopher Green, a senior consultant for the Korean Peninsula at International Crisis Group, said the new border crossing’s significance should not be overstated, considering that China-North Korea trade “is fundamentally driven by politics”.
“Lack of cross-border transit routes is not the main obstacle,” Green told Al Jazeera.
“If the bridge opening signifies a political desire on both sides to give political cover to rising trade volumes, then a boost to trade should follow,” Green said, describing ties up until now as “steady-as-she-goes” economic engagement.
“Time will tell. But the key is the politics of national security, not economics.”
As much as officials have hailed the New Yalu River Bridge as a reflection of Chinese-North Korean cooperation, the project had a long and torturous road to completion.
Construction began in 2011 and was finished on the Chinese side in 2014.
But North Korean authorities only completed roads and customs facilities on their side of the river this year following repeated pauses in construction amid tensions with Beijing.
“The 12-year delay certainly suggests that economic cooperation is more conditional than the language of friendship might imply,” Marco Mari, a PhD researcher at Bocconi University in Italy who studies China-North Korea economic ties, told Al Jazeera.
“The bridge can facilitate supplies and economic activity, while Russian support gives North Korea alternatives that diminish Beijing’s leverage,” Mari added.
“This does not necessarily imply broader economic reform or a comparable improvement in ordinary people’s lives.”
Weiqi Zhang, an associate professor at Suffolk University who studies relations between North Korea and China, said the history of China-North Korea economic ties is littered with abortive projects, such as the Hwanggumpyong Special Economic Zone, a North Korean-Chinese development near Dandong.
“There were cases, like the Hwanggumpyong Special Economic Zone – established by China and North Korea – where China built infrastructure on its side, but North Korea didn’t even pave the road on their side,” Zhang told Al Jazeera.
“One reason is that, unlike its neighbours, North Korean government doesn’t really pay much attention to trade for economic development,” Zhang said.
“International trade is used by North Korea more like a foreign policy tool.”
With China wishing to demonstrate its “indispensability” as a trade partner and North Korea eager to strengthen their economic ties, trade is likely to grow, said Edward Howell, a lecturer in international Relations at the University of Oxford.
Even so, economic engagement will be subject to political considerations, Howell said.
“North Korea will obviously want to avoid facing any Chinese influence to change its economic model, but Pyongyang will want to reap the economic benefits of trade with its principal economic benefactor,” Howell told Al Jazeera.

Indian police launch New Delhi clampdown for Cockroach Party rally

Founder of India’s ‘Cockroach’ movement detained amid police crackdown
Police said Abhijeet Dipke and student leaders taken into ‘preventative detention’ in New Delhi ahead of mass protest.
Indian police have detained the founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), student leaders and supporters, as hundreds of people poured into New Delhi to join a protest over the jailing of two activists.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke was detained on Friday as he was leaving a house in central Delhi. Officers dragged him into a police car and drove away after a brief argument, witnesses said.
“Abhijeet is detained by Delhi Police,” CJP posted on X. “This government is so scared of the youth waving national flag.”
Student activist Neha Bora, a prominent face of the protests, was also detained as she tried to reach Connaught Place, a gathering point for protests during the ‘cockroach’ demonstrations.
Senior police officer Sachin Sharma told the Reuters news agency that Dipke and Bora had been taken into preventive detention.
The latest arrests come amid a police crackdown after near-daily protests demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, India’s election chief.
Kumar is at the centre of a controversial revision of voter lists which critics say favours Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The BJP accuses rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
‘Not afraid’
Thousands of additional police officers were deployed in the Indian capital earlier on Friday, as the Indian government appeared to prepare for further confrontations.
CJP supporters had been called to gather in New Delhi’s Central Park at 5pm (11:30am GMT). The rally was called after two of the movement’s leaders were jailed for five days this week for allegedly trespassing at a protest site.
Earlier on Friday, police met Dipke and warned him against going ahead with the protest. Authorities also closed the park, citing “administrative reasons” and set up metal barricades at key intersections.
Despite that, nearly 500 protesters managed to reach Connaught Place in groups and protested in about half a dozen places around Central Park, waving flags and shouting slogans. A few were detained and taken away in a police vehicle.
Prior to his arrest, Dipke suggested that police may try to arrest him, but declared he and his supporters were “not afraid” and were “ready” to go to jail.
In a social media post, Dipke accused the government of hypocrisy and denounced police crackdowns against the movement.
Members of the government may never have come to power had they experienced similar protest restrictions, he asserted.
“The very party that is in power today spent decades organising protests, taking to the streets and questioning the governments of the day when it was in opposition,” Dipke said.
“Had the same restrictions, intimidation and police crackdowns been used against them, many of those who occupy positions of power today might never have reached where they are.”
Modi under pressure
The rally is just the latest to face a crackdown by the authorities.
The CJP has held almost daily demonstrations this month demanding electoral reforms and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Kumar.
He oversaw the removal of more than 130 million names from the electoral roll and is accused by the CJP of voter fraud. Election authorities said the changes were made to remove duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries.
The CJP was founded in May amid anger over the leaking of exam papers and the poor prospects facing India’s youth.
The movement swiftly became a conduit for India’s Gen Z, many of whom feel disenfranchised during an unemployment crisis under Modi’s right-wing government. The movement has since forced the resignation of the education minister.
With the political opposition quick to support the protests, Modi has come under intense pressure, with some analysts saying he is now facing the worst crisis since becoming PM in 2014.
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said the demonstrations were the main opposition Congress party’s attempt to “seize power”.
“Instead of channelling the energy of the youth toward nation-building, they are being used as pawns in the politics of anarchy,” he said at a media briefing on Friday.

UK government courted UBS over London HQ move
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

UK government courted UBS over London HQ move
Former UK Chancellor of the Exchequer Rachel Reeves pitched the City of London as an alternative home for the Swiss bank, which is weighing its options amid new capital proposals.
Britain’s Labour government sought to persuade UBS to shift its headquarters and stock market listing to London in the event of the bank relocating out of Switzerland because of strict new capital rules.
Rachel Reeves pitched London as a potential new home for UBS in discussions with the bank’s chair Colm Kelleher during her time as chancellor, according to people briefed on the talks.
The pair discussed the possibility of UBS moving its legal headquarters and listing to the UK if it were to redomicile, the people added, with the most recent meeting taking place earlier this year.
The discussions illustrate how foreign governments have attempted to court Switzerland’s biggest bank while it is mired in a protracted political battle over regulatory reforms in its home market.
UBS relocating to London would represent a major coup for the UK, with its valuation of CHF129 billion ($157 billion) making it the fourth-largest company in the FTSE 100, behind only HSBC, Shell and AstraZeneca.
UBS already has a significant presence in the UK, where it employs about 8,000 people across investment banking, wealth management and asset management.
The bank suffered a setback last month when Swiss lawmakers pressed ahead with strict new rules that the lender said would require it to hold about $16 billion of additional capital, rejecting a compromise proposal.
>> How new Swiss capital requirement rules have sparked debates about a possible UBS move:
More
‘Switzerland has spoken’. Will UBS leave?
While UBS has said that its goal is to continue operating out of Switzerland, Kelleher publicly acknowledged last month that the lender could reconsider its Swiss base if the regulatory clampdown proved too onerous.
Two major shareholders have also called on the board to consider moving its headquarters, with US asset manager Artisan Partners saying in recent weeks that Switzerland was “no longer an attractive or desirable location” for UBS.
UBS’s board has examined contingency plans in response to the capital reforms, including redomiciling, the FT previously reported. However, there is no indication that the bank is actively planning to relocate to the UK or any other jurisdiction at present.
Many industry observers view the US as the most likely alternative for the Swiss lender given its lighter regulatory regime and UBS’s ambitions to compete in wealth management with Wall Street rivals such as Morgan Stanley.
Senior executives at the bank last year held talks with Donald Trump’s administration officials about a potential relocation to the US.
However, some analysts have questioned the feasibility of a move, citing legal complexities and the possibility of Switzerland imposing a hefty exit tax on the bank. Others believe a merger with a large US or European bank could be a more likely alternative.
The discussions between Reeves and Kelleher also underline how Labour has sought to court international businesses since assuming power in 2024.
Reeves won praise from banking executives after sparing the sector from tax rises in last year’s Budget following an intense lobbying campaign.
However, there is concern among executives that her successor, John Healey, could target the industry for tax increases in his first Budget this month.
UBS and Reeves declined to comment.
The Treasury did not respond to a request for comment.

Turkish exports to BRICS group countries top $18.2B in January-September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:07:22 UTC
18:07:22 KST

Yunus Turk and Emir Yildirim
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Türkiye’s exports to the 10 member states of the BRICS grouping totaled $18.2 billion in the first nine months of the year, according to the Turkish Exporters’ Assembly (TIM).
While Türkiye’s total global exports this January-September grew 5.2% to $210.9 billion, Russia was the largest destination among other BRICS member states, receiving $4.1 billion in exports despite a 2.5% annual decline.
BRICS includes longtime members Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa, plus recent additions Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, and the United Arab Emirates.
The UAE followed Russia as the second-largest destination for Turkish exports to BRICS, accounting for $3.3 billion even after a 4.12% contraction in export volume.
Egypt followed with a rise of 28.6% to $3.1 billion, China with a surge of 40.8% to $3 billion, and Iran with $1.8 billion, making the country the fifth-largest BRICS destination for Turkish goods.
Turkish exports increased in eight of the 10 BRICS member states, with shipments in Ethiopia surging the most by 79.6%.
The chemicals and chemical products sector accounted for most of these exports to the bloc, generating $3.5 billion in the first nine months of the year, the data showed.
Mining exports grew 33.5% to $2.1 billion, a net gain of roughly $539 million, followed by the jewelry sector, whose exports fell 45% to $1.3 billion.
The textiles and raw material exports climbed 8.7% to $1.2 billion at the same time.
Türkiye’s top five exporter provinces -- Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Kocaeli, and Bursa -- accounted for a combined $12.5 billion of all Turkish exports to BRICS.
Istanbul was the largest source of these exports, making up $8.2 billion of the output, followed by Ankara with $1.9 billion, Izmir with $1 billion, Kocaeli with $703 million, and Bursa with $658 million.

Why a new US–Israeli war against Iran could carry enormous risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:00:22 UTC
18:00:22 KST

In recent days, three developments have emerged as key preliminary indicators that the US may be preparing to step up its military campaign against Iran. First, the dispatch of a third aircraft carrier strike group alongside additional American forces toward the waters surrounding Iran; second, the directive from the United States Central Command (CENTCOM) to achieve full operational readiness; and third, the continuation of economic pressure, sanctions, and blockades, alongside disputes over the Strait of Hormuz and diplomatic friction surrounding negotiations.
While these developments clearly signal an expansion of military options and an intensification of coercive pressure, they do not, on their own, constitute definitive proof of an executive decision to launch a broad war. This new force posture serves at least three strategic functions: deterrence, diplomatic leverage in negotiations, and operational preparation of a military option. Consequently, while a war posture increases the statistical probability of conflict, it does not in itself demonstrate a definitive decision to enter a major war.
Military power is not measured solely by the quantity of aircraft carriers, planes, or missile launchers. Rather, sustained combat power is a function of the equilibrium between consumption capacity, stockpiles, production, replenishment, human resources, logistics, and the ability to absorb the total costs of warfare.
Consequently, transforming a military posture into a major war requires the simultaneous presence of at least four structural capacities.
First, a sufficient reserve of munitions and weaponry must exist to execute initial operations and sustain subsequent engagements against Iran—a country that possesses the largest and most diverse missile arsenal in the region.
Second, robust equipment replenishment capacity is required, ensuring that if missiles, ammunition, aircraft, defence systems, or command assets are consumed or destroyed during hostilities, military industries can replace them at a commensurate rate—an outcome that appears practical implausible for the US regime.
These two requirements would appear to be unachievable at the moment. An April 21 report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies shows that in four out of the seven key categories of munitions analysed, expenditure during the 40-day conflict likely exceeded half of pre-war inventories, and replenishing some of these stockpiles could require between one to four years.
Alongside the depletion of ammunition stockpiles, the Ramadan War has imposed tangible costs upon the air fleet of the hostile United States administration. According to an official report by the US Congressional Research Service on 5 October, at least 81 US military aircraft, including fixed-wing planes, helicopters, and unmanned systems, have been destroyed or damaged.
Third, sufficient human resource and logistical capacity must exist to sustain long-term operations at a vast distance while simultaneously maintaining the US regime’s existing military commitments and global readiness across other regions.
Fourth, the capacity to absorb the economic and geopolitical fallout must be present, including the ability to withstand spikes in energy prices, supply chain disruptions and diminished oil transits through the Strait of Hormuz, fiscal strain, the depletion of strategic reserves, vulnerable military bases, and domestic political pressure ahead of the November elections.
Iran’s ability to disrupt confidence at the world’s primary energy chokepoint has become a strategic lever that substantially raises the cost of any military adventure for the global economy and decision-makers in Washington.
The cumulative weight of munitions constraints and the economic variables examined places enemy decision-makers before three plausible strategic trajectories:
In the first scenario, the American and Zionist regimes rely on the continuation of a heavy military posture, economic sanctions, maritime pressure, intelligence operations, and cognitive warfare without initiating a major new conflict. Operationally, this option is entirely feasible. Its primary appeal for Washington lies in avoiding further depletion of its vulnerable stockpiles of Patriot, THAAD, and Tomahawk missiles, as well as preventing additional aircraft losses. Nevertheless, evidence suggests that this path is not without cost or hazard: maintaining a state of neither war nor peace entails persistent insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz, oil flows remaining below normal capacity, recessionary pressure on global energy demand, continuous attrition of forces deployed to the region, and increasing difficulty in managing unintended maritime incidents.
In the second scenario, the US/Zionist axis considers executing limited, phased air and missile strikes against specific targets—including Iranian military, missile, nuclear, or energy infrastructure—rather than entering directly into an all-out war; an option cited by Axios sources as one of the plans under active consideration. Although the presence of three aircraft carrier strike groups and current stockpiles render such strikes operationally viable in the short term, the central dilemma of this scenario remains escalation control. When an actor initiates a limited attack under the assumption that the opponent’s response will remain bounded, it exposes itself to inadvertent escalation due to asymmetrical perceptions of thresholds and the absence of unilateral control over the defender’s decisions.
The third scenario—direct entry or a gradual slide into a full-scale regional war—represents the most costly and perilous trajectory facing the US regime and the genocidal Zionist entity. Should such a scenario materialise, the conflict is unlikely to remain unidimensional. Operationally, it could encompass, simultaneously or sequentially, high-intensity air combat, mass missile exchanges, severe disruption of the Strait of Hormuz, cyber operations, and strikes against enemy regional bases and energy infrastructure across the broader region. In such a context, a punitive operation could rapidly degrade into a multi-front war of attrition.
Alongside military variables, the autumn political and electoral calendar constitutes another factor influencing calculations regarding the timing and ceiling of escalation. The deployment of a third aircraft carrier and 10,000 additional troops toward the waters surrounding Iran coupled with the Pentagon’s directive to US Central Command to complete operational preparations explicitly demonstrates that the timing of potential operations within Washington and Tel Aviv’s decision-making circles is being weighed against the November congressional mid-terms, as well as the Zionist parliamentary elections scheduled just one week prior.
A further dimension concerns apprehension over Iran’s potential capacity to sever subsea internet cables, thereby completely severing connectivity across the Arabian Peninsula as well as the aggressor Zionist state, and disabling all exchange and financial markets dependent on this network infrastructure. Crucially, through the establishment of its National Information Network and its relative independence from western-dominated internet financial transactions, Iran has shifted the balance in this domain to its own strategic advantage.
From the standpoint of deterrence theory, inflicting costs that outweigh the scale of the initial strike often serves as a rational mechanism to fundamentally reshape the adversary’s cost-benefit calculus regarding subsequent actions. Given Iran’s documented capabilities, should such a miscalculation be committed by the US or the Zionist regime, a plausible strategic posture for Tehran would involve launching a multi-domain, asymmetrical, and extensive response designed to defy containment or mitigation. Consequently, even a limited military strike would impel Iran to formulate a response that far exceeds the initial scale of aggression. This underlying logic of an escalatory response to limited warfare significantly raises the calculative risks of any new military venture.
The principal danger in the current security environment is not necessarily a pre-planned decision to wage an all-out war, but rather the escalation—whether intended or unintended—of a small war into a major war through crisis instability.
If the deployment of military force as a pressure tactic leads to a miscalculation and a limited strike, and that limited strike is met with an asymmetric, multi-domain response, a cycle of reciprocal retaliation will take hold. This chain reaction could impose a war whose full consequences its initiators lack the capacity to absorb.

Swiss luxury group ‘interested in buying’ diamond giant De Beers
Swiss luxury goods group Richemont is reportedly part of a consortium that aims to buy South African diamond giant De Beers.
According to Bloomberg, the Richemont is in talks with the major United States jewellery retailer Signet Jewelers to join a consortium that intends to acquire the South African company.
The entity in question, the Global Diamond Consortium (GDC), is reportedly in a very strong position in the acquisition negotiations, according to Bloomberg, which cites several sources close to the sale process.
The GDC is led by former De Beers CEO Gareth Penny and is said to have been designated as the preferred bidder in July by De Beers’ owner, the British firm Anglo American, which holds an 85% stake in De Beers and has stated its intention to divest as early as 2024.
The consortium also includes the governments of Namibia and Angola, as well as major diamond producers.
The sale of De Beers comes at a time when demand for precious stones is recovering from one of the deepest crises the sector has ever seen, said Bloomberg.
When contacted by the agency, neither GDC, Signet Jewelers nor Richemont confirmed any interest in acquiring De Beers.

The foreign ministers of Türkiye and 18 other countries on Friday strongly condemned Colombia’s inauguration of its embassy in Jerusalem.
In a joint statement released by Türkiye’s Foreign Ministry, the ministers expressed their “unequivocal rejection” of the decision.
They said the move violates relevant UN Security Council resolutions and undermines international efforts to achieve a just and lasting peace based on a two-state solution.
The statement was issued by the foreign ministers of Türkiye, Algeria, Djibouti, Egypt, Indonesia, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Libya, Malaysia, Oman, Pakistan, Palestine, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen.
The ministers reaffirmed that any measure or decision intended to alter the legal or historical status of occupied Jerusalem, or to recognize the city as Israel’s capital, “is null and void and has no legal effect.”
They cited UN Security Council Resolutions 476 and 478, both adopted in 1980, which reject attempts to change Jerusalem’s character or status and call on states to withdraw their diplomatic missions from the city.
The statement described Jerusalem as part of the Palestinian territory occupied in 1967.
The ministers called on the Colombian government to reconsider and reverse its decision, uphold its obligations under international law, and refrain from measures that prejudice the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people.
They also reiterated their support for the Palestinian people’s right to an independent and sovereign state, with East Jerusalem as its capital.

Egypt's army is intensifying strikes on Sudan's 'illicit mines'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:54:52 UTC
17:54:52 KST

Breadcrumb
Egypt's army is intensifying strikes on Sudan's 'illicit mining activities'
Tensions are rising between Egypt and Sudan—at the pubic level at least for now—after the Egyptian army bombed sites mined by hundreds of Sudanese for gold on 11 October, killing dozens of miners and wounding others.
Over 70 Sudanese artisanal miners were killed in the strikes, according to eyewitnesses who were present at the site at the time of the Egyptian strikes.
Videos filmed during and after the Egyptian aerial attacks showed the bodies of the dead victims spread out in the area as smoke billowed in the background.
Having affirmed that the strikes were carried out on the Egyptian side of the border, the Egyptian army said they were part of its campaign against "illicit mining" activities in the area.
It added in a statement on 12 October that warning leaflets were dropped to people in the area to caution against illicit mining for gold.
The strikes were the second by the Egyptian army on the Egyptian side of the border with Sudan in less than five months.
In mid-June, army fighter aircraft bombed mining sites in the border area, killing around 23 Sudanese artisanal miners. Law-enforcement personnel and army troops also rounded up hundreds of miners.
Increasing mining activities, particularly gold, Egyptian military analysts said, are part of fallout from the civil war in Sudan which has caused chaos on the shared border with Egypt.
"Criminal gangs are stepping up their activities in the border area, using the Sudanese army's preoccupation with fighting inside Sudan," Gen. Nasr Salem, the former Egyptian reconnaissance commander, told The New Arab.
"This adds more pressure on the Egyptian Armed Forces which have to solely bear the responsibility of securing the border," he added.
In its 12 October statement about the strikes, the Egyptian army said law-enforcement personnel would continue to impose full sovereignty within Egypt's boundaries to protect its capabilities and national wealth.
Public outrage
The strike triggered a wave of anger inside Sudan, raising questions about its possible effects on relations between Cairo and Khartoum in the near future.
Reaction from the Sudanese in the immediate aftermath of the attacks was mainly confined to social media, but it then seeped into the streets.
On 12 October, a Sudanese gunman opened fire on Egyptian truck drivers south of Khartoum, killing two and leaving a third injured.
A day later, protests were reported in a number of Sudanese cities, especially in Nyala, the capital of the state of Southern Darfur in south-western Sudan.
Photos circulating on social media showed the demonstrators carrying the Sudanese flag and placards criticising alleged silence by Sudan's ruling Transitional Sovereignty Council (TSC).
Most of the anger on the Sudanese side was driven by belief that the strikes were carried out on the Sudanese, not the Egyptian, side of the border.
This was why some people called on the STC to issue an official condemnation of the attacks and launch an enquiry into them.
Cairo moves to contain crisis
The Egyptian Foreign Ministry said it closely followed the killing of the two Egyptian truck drivers, describing the event as "sorrowful".
The Egyptian ambassador in Khartoum, who had just submitted his credentials to TSC Head Gen. Abdel Fattah al-Burhan only a day earlier, had also checked on the condition of the wounded victim who was hospitalized at a hospital in the Sudanese capital.
The statement of the Egyptian Foreign Ministry on the shootout came only a day after the Egyptian and Sudanese foreign ministers talked on the phone.
During the call, each of the two top diplomats expressed respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the other's country, according to a statement by the Egyptian Foreign Ministry.
Concern over rising anti-Egypt sentiments in Sudan reverberated, meanwhile, quickly across Egyptian social media sites where users expressed support for actions taken by the Egyptian army to defend national borders against intrusions by Sudanese artisanal miners.
Egypt, analysts argue, has been solely bearing the brunt of securing its shared border with Sudan since the outbreak of the Sudanese civil war in April 2023.
Gen. Salem said illicit mining was only a small detail in the larger picture of a long list of other border infringements from the Sudanese side, including the smuggling of subsidized Egyptian goods into Sudan and the trafficking of Sudanese persons into Egypt.
The war has also caused around 1.5 million Sudanese to cross the border into Egypt for refuge, adding to the economically-struggling northern neighbouring country's economic strains.
RSF financial engine
The Transitional Sovereignty Council has mourned the death of the artisanal miners and ordered the formation of a panel to investigate the incident, in an apparent attempt to appease an angry Sudanese public.
However, most condemnation for the strikes came from the backers of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the paramilitary militia battling the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) for control over Sudan.
This probably highlights links between the militia and rampant illicit mining activities and gold smuggling in the border area between Egypt and Sudan, Sudanese analysts said.
Sudanese political analyst Salah Khalil described gold mining and smuggling as major "financial lifelines" for the RSF.
"The militia uses revenues from mining and smuggling operations to bankroll its military activities and war against the SAF," Kalil told TNA.
He added that the paramilitary group also uses the same revenues in the purchase of arms from other countries.
Nyala is known to be a stronghold of the RSF. On the same day of the Egyptian airstrikes against Sudanese artisanal miners, the Sudan Founding Alliance, an organization established by the RSF in February 2025, claimed that the Egyptian strikes were staged in North Al-Wadi, a mountainous gold-mining region in the far northeast of Sudan's Red Sea State.
It slammed Egypt for allegedly violating Sudanese sovereignty and accused it of wanting to wrest Sudan's resources.
According to international investigative organization Global Witness in 2019, RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo (Hemedti) has used front companies and banks based in Sudan and the United Arab Emirates to capture a large part of Sudan's gold industry.
Beyond gold
Several Egyptian and Sudanese analysts link the war in Sudan to a larger struggle redrawing the regional map and control over vital maritime chokepoints and ports.
The crackdown on gold mining and smuggling would deal a painful blow to the RSF and consequently attempts by the militia's regional backers to defeat the SAF and control Sudan, Sudanese analysts said.
Nevertheless, the same measure would be far from enough to defeat the militia once and for all, they added.
Khalil called for parallel measures to gradually weaken the militia, including cutting off support from Sudan's neighbouring countries, especially Libya, Chad and Ethiopia.
"Severing these lifelines will leave the militia high and dry and contribute to its defeat over time," he said.

Israel halts commercial shipments into Gaza as winter shortages loom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:53:56 UTC
17:53:56 KST

Israel has halted commercial shipments into Gaza for a second consecutive day, cutting off a vital source of food and other essential supplies as Palestinians face worsening hardship and prepare for winter.
Israeli authorities blamed the suspension on Palestinian merchants protesting taxes imposed by Hamas, but Gaza's private truckers union disputed that account, accusing Israel of imposing the restrictions itself.
The suspension threatens to disrupt supplies of fresh food, meat and winter clothing in the war-ravaged territory, where nearly 2 million people depend on goods entering through Israeli-controlled crossings.
With access to Gaza tightly restricted, any interruption to commercial deliveries risks driving up prices and leaving families struggling to afford basic necessities.
Humanitarian organizations warn that aid deliveries alone cannot meet the population's needs.
While aid agencies generally supply staples such as flour, private merchants play a crucial role in bringing in perishable foods, including fruit and meat, according to data released earlier this year by COGAT, the Israeli military body responsible for coordinating humanitarian affairs in Gaza.
A functioning commercial market is also essential to keeping prices within reach for families who have already endured years of war, displacement and severe shortages.
"The humanitarian sector on its own cannot meet the needs of all the people," said Shaina Low, a spokesperson for the Norwegian Refugee Council. "The markets need to be functioning."
COGAT announced the suspension Wednesday, saying it had followed a decision by Palestinian merchants a day earlier to stop coordinating shipments because of Hamas-imposed charges and alleged threats against importers.
"We were prepared to coordinate the entry of their trucks as usual, but the vendors informed us that they were cancelling the coordination due to Hamas's taxation mechanism and threats against them," said Lt. Daniel Kantorovich, COGAT's deputy spokesperson. "The merchants don't want to bring goods into Gaza."
The agency said no private-sector vendors had attempted to bring goods into the territory since merchants notified Israeli authorities Tuesday.
But Nahed Sheheiber, head of Gaza's private truckers union, rejected Israel's explanation, saying Israeli restrictions, rather than a voluntary decision by merchants, were responsible for the suspension.
"The merchants are not the ones who stopped the shipments," Sheheiber said. "The Israeli coordinator is claiming that Gaza's merchants are responsible, but the truth is that the Israelis are the ones who imposed the restrictions."
Following COGAT's announcement, the union met with Gaza's Ministry of Economy to raise concerns that Israel was using fees charged by the ministry as a pretext to restrict commercial supplies.
Sheheiber said the ministry had asked merchants to pay 10,000 Israeli shekels, or about $3,226, for each truck entering Gaza. During the meeting, ministry Undersecretary Khaled Al-Raqab said the payment was not a tax but a donation intended to help pay civil servants in the territory.
The competing accounts leave uncertainty over the immediate cause of the halt, while the consequences for Gaza's already fragile supply network could be severe.
Israel has long accused Hamas of imposing fees on imported goods to finance its operations. However, the suspension places the immediate burden on Gaza's residents, who rely on shipments approved by Israeli authorities for much of their food and other essential supplies.
It also remains unclear whether aid agencies will be permitted to increase deliveries to offset the loss of commercial goods.
COGAT estimates that Gaza's population of roughly 2 million requires about 250 truckloads of goods each day. That figure is substantially below the minimum of 600 trucks per day stipulated under a ceasefire agreement brokered by the United States a year ago.
The suspension comes despite signs of improvement in Gaza's food security earlier this year. The world's leading authority on food insecurity reported that conditions had improved since famine was declared in the territory in August 2025, but remained at crisis levels, with most families still unable to obtain enough food.
The assessment warned that "even small disruptions to humanitarian access could rapidly reverse recent gains," underscoring the risks posed by the interruption of commercial deliveries.
For families already struggling to secure food, the loss of another supply channel could mean higher prices, fewer choices and greater difficulty obtaining essential goods as temperatures fall.
The restrictions also highlight Gaza's dependence on access controlled by Israel. Merchants coordinate with suppliers outside the territory, but their shipments must undergo Israeli military inspections before entering. That system leaves the enclave particularly vulnerable to decisions that interrupt the movement of goods.
The broader humanitarian crisis stems from the war that began Oct. 7, 2023, following Hamas' incursion into southern Israel that killed about 1,200 people in Israel and took 251 hostages.
Israel responded with an extensive bombardment and ground invasion that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.
The ministry says more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed since the cease-fire took effect.
Women and children account for about half of those killed, according to the ministry.

Diplomats to MEMO: Colombia’s ICJ withdrawal reflects alignment with US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:51:51 UTC
17:51:51 KST

Colombia’s decision to withdraw from South Africa’s genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), followed by the opening of its embassy in occupied Jerusalem on Wednesday, has drawn criticism from former Latin American ambassadors, who see the moves as a significant shift in Bogotá’s foreign policy, particularly its stance on Palestine.
Colombia’s Foreign Ministry confirmed that it had informed the Court of its decision to withdraw the declaration of intervention filed on 5th April 2024 under Article 63 of the ICJ Statute.
The move marks a reversal of the position taken by former President Gustavo Petro, whose government cut diplomatic ties with Israel in May 2024 over its military offensive in Gaza and backed South Africa’s case at the ICJ.
The ministry explained that the decision was made under the president’s constitutional authority to manage foreign relations, while emphasising that Colombia remains committed to its obligations under the 1948 Genocide Convention.
Speaking to MEMO, Roberto Mayorga Lorca, professor of Economic Law and former Chilean ambassador to the Philippines, criticised the Colombian government’s change of position. “The shift by Colombia’s current government regarding the genocide in Gaza has been regrettable,” Mayorga said.
He argued that since President Abelardo de la Espriella took office in August, Bogotá had moved away from condemning Israel’s actions in Gaza, to adopting what he described as a position of “complicity or concealment”.
Mayorga identified four major developments behind the policy shift: the restoration of diplomatic relations with Israel, the relocation of Colombia’s embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem, the lifting of restrictions on exports to Israel, and the withdrawal of Colombia’s intervention in the ICJ proceedings.
READ: Flavio Bolsonaro’s first-round lead in Brazil alarms Palestine supporters
Mayorga said the change reflected Bogotá’s increasing alignment with US foreign policy. “The explanation for this shift appears to have been provided by the Foreign Ministry itself, which indicated that Colombia was aligning its position on this matter with Trump’s policy,” he said.

Addressing the legal implications of Colombia’s withdrawal from South Africa’s genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice (ICJ, the Professor of International Relations at the Central University of Chile (UCEN) Nelson Hadad argued that the decision would have little impact on the proceedings or the court’s eventual judgment.
“I believe Colombia’s withdrawal will have no significant legal consequences. It is simply the withdrawal of one country and does not affect in any way the outcome we expect from the court,” he said.
He also rejected the suggestion that the move constituted a diplomatic victory for Israel, stressing that it would have “no influence whatsoever on the court’s eventual ruling.” Hadad expressed confidence that the ICJ would ultimately find that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, while pointing to the deliberate deprivation of food, water and medicine as conduct relevant to the legal definition of genocide.

He further warned that Colombia’s decision formed part of broader political efforts to undermine international judicial institutions and weaken accountability for alleged violations of international law. “The objective is to destroy and dismantle the authority of international courts,” he said, accusing the United States of targeting both the ICJ and the International Criminal Court (ICC) to shield Israel from legal scrutiny.

New house sales in Türkiye rose 3.9 percent year-on-year to 51,519 in September, according to official data released on Oct. 16.

Adjusted for calendar effects, new house sales increased 3.8 percent annually. On a seasonally and calendar-adjusted basis, they rose 5.5 percent from August, while existing home sales remained unchanged.

In January-September, new house sales edged down 0.6 percent from the same period last year to 359,913, while total housing transactions declined 7.2 percent to 1.09 million.
In the first nine months of 2026, home sales to foreigners declined by 4.3 percent year-on-year to 15,308 units, according to TÜİK data.

Drone strikes in Black Sea raise fears of Russian escalation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:48:48 UTC
17:48:48 KST

Romanian warships sail during a Romanian Navy led exercise outside Constanta, Romania, on April 16, 2024. (AP Photo/Andreea Alexandru, File)
A string of drone attacks on at least seven cargo vessels in the Black Sea this month, off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria, has some members of the alliance wondering if Russian President Vladimir Putin is seeking escalation to test their support for Ukraine in its war against Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
The attacks in the two countries’ exclusive economic zones threaten a global shipping route and have left two people dead, with at least 25 still missing. They also run the risk of drawing other countries directly into the war for Ukraine.
Throughout the war, Russia has repeatedly bombarded Ukraine’s Black Sea and Danube River ports, leaving Kiev increasingly reliant on alternative routes to get its grain exports to markets in Africa and the Middle East. Russian drones have repeatedly violated Romanian airspace near some of Ukraine’s Danube ports.
In the latest incidents, fires broke out on two ships struck by drones on Oct. 14 and 15, one in Romania’s territorial waters.
Romanian President Nicusor Dan said on Oct. 15 in Brussels that “two drones” had hit the vessels but did not say whose drones they were. “There will be a reaction from the Romanian state,” he warned.
Increasingly, the suspicion falls on Russia.
“There is no logic in Ukraine attacking its own ships and crews, given that the outcome of all these attacks favors Russia, and indeed, the logic points in that direction,” Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told his country’s Parliament.
“The problem is that we cannot prove it.”
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said on X on Oct. 15 that he met Radev and Dan to discuss security in the Black Sea and “the latest attacks on commercial shipping.”
“NATO has strengthened our posture along the eastern flank including with increasing counter-drone capabilities,” he said.
“NATO will continue to work closely with our Allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defense posture as needed.”
A source in Romania’s defense sector, who was not authorized to speak publicly about the incidents, told The Associated Press that the attacks are designed to hurt Ukraine economically and that “Romania is not the target right now.”
“All summer we’ve been hunting all kinds of [drone] debris, water drones, sea drones, air drones, debris in the water, on the beaches,” they said. “If this continues, someone should do something about that.”
The source added they have heard Türkiye “would like to summon all the riparian [Black Sea] states to plan a mission to escort these convoys” through a militarized safe corridor.
“I’m not sure about Turkish, but our Romanian vessels don’t have anti-air defense systems to protect against drones,” they said. “That would be a high risk for the Navy, for military vessels to escort this.”
In July, Romania, Bulgaria and Türkiye expanded the Black Sea Mine Countermeasures Task Force naval pact to “expand the missions to the protection of critical submarine infrastructure,” according to Romania’s Defense Ministry. It would include, it said, a permanent naval presence in Romania’s exclusive economic zone.
Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Oct. 14 that the country plans to join NATO’s Drone Edge project by the end of October. Launched in July, the initiative, which Romania also joined, aims to invest over $40 billion in “counter-drone capabilities” over the next five years.

Norway wealth fund urged to ease nuclear arms ban after Gaza investment row
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:36:13 UTC
17:36:13 KST

Norway wealth fund urged to ease nuclear arms ban after Gaza investment row
Review prompted by Gaza action calls for Norway’s sovereign wealth fund to lift ethical risk limitations on its investments.
A government-appointed committee has called for Norway’s sovereign wealth fund to lift limitations on its investments based on ethical risks, including those regarding nuclear weapons and Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
In a report released on Thursday, the committee said the world’s largest sovereign wealth fund, which controls assets totalling nearly $2.3 trillion, should be allowed to invest in companies that produce nuclear weapons. With reference to Gaza, it also called for the fund to refrain from involvement in “diplomatic” issues.
Led by former Central Bank Governor Svein Gjedrem, the committee recommended easing the fund’s investment conditions as part of a broader overhaul that would give its manager, the Central Bank, greater discretion over how it addresses ethical risks.
The review was prompted in part by controversy over the fund’s disinvestment last year from United States construction giant Caterpillar. The fund said the move was prompted by Caterpillar’s purported involvement in rights violations perpetrated by Israel amid its genocidal war on Gaza and in the occupied West Bank. Washington has since pressured Oslo over the move.
“Parts of the rationale for the appointment of the Committee was the Fund’s management related to the war in Gaza,” the committee commissioned by the government said. In the report, it argued that decisions regarding “another state’s conduct” should not be made by the fund but “reserved for the ordinary diplomatic channels of the Norwegian authorities”.
The unanimous recommendations of the committee in the report, which was submitted to the Ministry of Finance, also called for a review of the fund’s exclusion of investment in companies involved in the production of nuclear weapons.
Citing Norway’s reliance on NATO’s nuclear deterrent and a worsening security environment, the report suggested that investments in companies based in the US, United Kingdom and France that are involved in the production of nuclear weapons should be allowed.
The proposals also extended to reshaping the role of the fund’s independent ethics watchdog, allowing a number of assessments of potential investments to remain confidential.
‘Pandora’s box’
The report has already provoked a backlash in Norway, with opposition politicians slamming the potential changes. Meanwhile, analysts suggested that weakening ethics considerations could have a wide impact.
“If the Norwegian sovereign wealth fund – often considered a global gold standard – changes its posture towards nuclear weapons, it will open Pandora’s box for many global investors to follow suit,” Lawrence Loh, director of the Centre for Governance and Sustainability at the National University of Singapore Business School, told Al Jazeera.
The committee framed the proposed change as an obligation to protect Norway’s national security, citing the country’s dependence on its allies’ nuclear umbrella.
“The global security situation has changed. Norway is building up its defence capabilities, and the protection provided by NATO’s nuclear umbrella has become increasingly important. The companies that would be reincluded produce weapons that Norway needs for its own defence”, the report argued.
Gareth Evans, former Australian foreign minister, told Al Jazeera the report was “an encouraging initiative in a world that has become alarmingly complacent about the risks of nuclear war, with every major nuclear arms control agreement dead, dying or on life support, and the longstanding taboo against threat or use eroding”.
Amid US President Donald Trump’s shake-up of NATO, European countries are increasingly looking to join France’s nuclear deterrent umbrella.
Trump said on Thursday that Washington is holding talks with Russia and China aimed at denuclearising the countries with the biggest stockpiles of nuclear weapons.
However, Loh warned that shifting the Norwegian fund’s investment conditions could encourage investment by others in nuclear companies “in scenarios different from the Norwegians’ condition of the invested companies being based in allied, nuclear-armed NATO countries”.

Economists warn Lithuania’s 2027 budget risks rising debt and deficit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:35:00 UTC
17:35:00 KST

Lithuania’s proposed 2027 budget will further widen the government deficit and increase public debt, while ambitious revenue targets could prove difficult to meet, economists warned Friday after the government approved the draft budget.
The spending plan reflects continued fiscal expansion, with expenditure growing faster than nominal gross domestic product, even when the impact of European Union structural funding is excluded, said Indrė Genytė-Pikčienė, an economist at Artea Bank.
“Next year will be another year of generous fiscal expansion,” she told BNS, adding that declining EU structural support and fewer one-off economic tailwinds would make the outlook more challenging.
Tadas Povilauskas, an economist at SEB Bank, said fiscal policy would again stimulate the economy through borrowing. But rising deficits and public acceptance of persistent overspending could make it more difficult to consolidate public finances in the future without slowing economic growth.
The budget deficit is set to grow mainly because of higher social benefits and public-sector wages, much of which is linked to automatic indexation of pensions, benefits and salaries, Povilauskas said.
He questioned the need for an additional 150 million euros earmarked for a proposed family support package, arguing that some spending increases went beyond what indexation required. He also criticised the lack of emphasis on improving public administration efficiency.
However, he said higher social spending could support domestic businesses by boosting consumption among lower-income households.
Revenue targets under scrutiny
Genytė-Pikčienė questioned whether the government would collect all the revenue projected in the budget. Lithuania’s economy benefited this year from increased consumption following a reform of the second-pillar pension system, but that boost is expected to fade next year.
Povilauskas also described several revenue forecasts as ambitious.
Excise tax revenue is projected to rise by 11%, while value-added tax revenue is expected to increase by about 7.2%. He questioned whether the VAT target was realistic, particularly because 158 million euros of the expected increase is attributed to improved tax administration.
Household consumption is expected to grow more slowly next year as the effect of withdrawals from second-pillar pension funds fades, he said.
He also urged caution over the plan to collect 2.1 billion euros in corporate income tax, noting that the target for this year is expected to be missed.
Debt costs and EU deficit rules
Genytė-Pikčienė said the projected deficit was significant enough to raise the possibility of an infringement procedure by the European Commission because it would exceed the EU’s Maastricht deficit limit of 3% of GDP. She noted, however, that Lithuania was not the only country exceeding the threshold.
She warned that relying on borrowing to finance public spending could create serious long-term problems as debt servicing costs rise and leave less room for future policy decisions.
Povilauskas said interest payments would increase by 370 million euros next year, adding the equivalent of 0.3 percentage points of GDP to budget expenditure.
Public debt is expected to rise by another 6.5 billion euros in 2027, following an increase of 6.8 billion euros this year, reaching 48.2% of GDP by the end of next year.
The government is financing much of the increase in defence spending – from 2% to 5% of GDP over several years – through borrowing, while also increasing other expenditure, Povilauskas said. The Finance Ministry has acknowledged the risk that public debt could approach 60% of GDP by the end of the medium-term planning period.
Genytė-Pikčienė said lawmakers should carefully scrutinise any additional spending proposals during the budget process to prevent the deficit from growing further. She stressed that national defence and security must remain priorities because they are essential to economic prosperity, attracting foreign investment and supporting business stability.
Social spending and inflation
The draft budget maintains a strong focus on social spending and raising incomes, Genytė-Pikčienė said.
The average old-age pension is set to increase at a double-digit rate, while pensions for people with the required length of service are expected to rise by 11%. Salaries for teachers, statutory officers and cultural workers are planned to increase by 7.5%, with pay for judicial assistants rising by nearly 6%.
The government is seeking to offset pressure on household purchasing power from imported inflation, including higher fuel prices and heating costs, by increasing incomes, she said.
Lithuania has refrained from introducing broad measures to counter energy price increases, unlike some neighbouring countries, instead relying more heavily on income growth to cushion the impact on households.
Economist Romas Lazutka criticised the proposed 150 million-euro family package, saying its measures were universal rather than specifically targeted at people in the greatest need.
He said much of the budget deficit was effectively predetermined by legislation and existing commitments, including social benefits, education spending and public-sector collective agreements.
Reducing the deficit would likely require cuts to social spending, a politically unpopular step that would be difficult to implement, he said.
Lazutka also pointed to what he described as a structural imbalance between the state budget and the Sodra social insurance fund. Sodra regularly records a surplus and builds up reserves, while the central government runs a large deficit and borrows at interest rates higher than the returns earned on those reserves.
The arrangement means the government is paying more to borrow than it earns by investing money accumulated in the social insurance system, he said.

Mapping sanctions against Israel: 121 measures across 61 countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:32:44 UTC
17:32:44 KST

The Jewish People Policy Institute (JPPI) has launched a new database mapping sanctions and restrictive measures imposed on Israel by countries around the world. The database identifies 121 measures across 62 countries, including 93 currently in effect, 19 classified as historical and nine proposed or planned measures.
The Foreign Ministry said the figures presented in the report do not accurately reflect the sanctions situation. Diplomatic officials added: "Ultimately, there are no substantial sanctions against Israel. Will that continue? There's no guarantee it will last forever. It's possible that, at some point, the outcome will be different."
The database allows users to examine measures by country, category and status, and to view their geographic distribution on a world map. The findings indicate that pressure on Israel is not confined to a single sector. Financial measures account for the largest category, with 40 measures, about one-third of the total. Defense and security and trade follow, with 24 measures each. The database also records 14 diplomatic measures and 12 legal measures.
According to JPPI Director General Dr. Shuki Friedman, the findings should be assessed not only by the number of sanctions but, more importantly, by their potential cumulative impact on Israel's economy and its ability to maintain international trade relationships, investment flows and supply chains.
"Anyone who thinks sanctions against ministers, individuals in the West Bank or products from the area will stop at the Green Line is mistaken," Friedman said. "Sanctions have a ripple effect. When they accumulate, they can affect banks, companies, investors and trading partners that have no connection whatsoever to the person or entity being sanctioned. The real danger is the transition from targeted sanctions to damage to the systems on which Israel's economy and security depend."
The database also identifies the countries where the highest number of measures have been recorded. Spain leads with 10 measures, followed by the United States with eight, all currently limited to the academic sphere, along with two "historical measures" and five proposals to prevent supplies of various types of weapons. Britain follows with seven measures, while Belgium and Turkey have five each.
However, the number of measures does not necessarily indicate their severity or potential impact. A single measure may be far more consequential than several others. The map is therefore intended primarily to illustrate the scope of the phenomenon and its geographic spread. Alongside European countries, where a substantial share of the measures is concentrated, the database includes measures from North America, Latin America, Asia, Africa and Oceania.
"The figure of 121 is only the starting point," Friedman said. "The important question is what will happen if this trend continues. A single sanction may be limited in scope. But 121 measures across 62 countries already warrant a systemic assessment. Israel needs to examine this risk as it would any other strategic threat: map it, prepare for it and act to prevent further deterioration.
"A national mechanism is needed to address the risk, one that examines the implications of these measures for the financial system, trade, investment, supply chains and the defense industry. The response cannot be limited to dealing with each sanction separately. It requires a comprehensive approach."
Diplomatic officials said the map contains distortions, noting, for example, that European Union sanctions are also counted at the individual country level. They also argued that entry bans imposed on certain individuals should not be equated with sanctions against Israel itself.
"Ultimately, there are no substantial sanctions against the State of Israel, and that was not a foregone conclusion," the officials said. "There was a realistic possibility of a different outcome, in which we would have ended 2026 facing EU sanctions against Israel. A great deal of the Foreign Ministry's energy was devoted to thwarting those measures."
They added: "There were sanctions that were prevented. The major threat was thwarted. If the EU had decided to undermine the trade agreement, every Israeli citizen would have felt the impact. The economic consequences would have been dramatic, but that was prevented. That diplomatic Iron Dome continued to hold.
"When you're inside an Iron Dome and a lot of missiles are fired at you, some get through. But the warhead carrying a ton of diplomatic and economic explosives did not penetrate. Ultimately, we succeed because we have friendly countries we can mobilize, such as Germany, Italy and the Czech Republic. It's not just Hungary. Hungary has changed, and the diplomatic Iron Dome remains intact."
The officials continued: "It's true that Smotrich and Ben-Gvir cannot enter the EU and that there are sanctions against settlers. But ultimately, people shopping at supermarkets in Ramat Gan and Tel Aviv are not feeling the impact of the biggest weapon, which is the trade agreement. The Horizon agreements and the Open Skies agreement have also been preserved."
However, they warned that the situation could change. "Will this continue? There's no guarantee it will last forever. It's possible that, if the trends continue in the same direction, the outcome will be different in the future."
According to the officials, "The Netherlands, Spain and Ireland are frustrated that they cannot achieve the outcome they want in Brussels. At the last meeting of European foreign ministers, there was frustration that it wasn't working. So, with no other choice, they are pursuing other channels, such as the Dutch sanctions.
"We are managing to preserve the core interests, and we have also reversed negative measures in countries such as Slovenia and Colombia. It's painstaking, thankless work because nobody sees what we have managed to prevent."
The officials nevertheless acknowledged that measures introduced by Spain, Ireland and Britain concerning trade with Israeli settlements "are not positive," adding that a concerning consequence is the shift toward action by individual countries.
The Foreign Ministry said in response: "The figures presented in the report do not accurately reflect the sanctions situation, whether political or economic. The Foreign Ministry is continuously engaged in this effort and is investing enormous resources in the fight against sanctions targeting Israel.
"For example, through a sustained effort lasting a year and a half, we prevented sanctions against Israel in the European Union and numerous other countries. We are also investing considerable efforts in reversing sanctions imposed by hostile governments following changes in leadership. We have done so with considerable success in Colombia, Slovenia and elsewhere.
"Countries that promote or impose sanctions against Israel undermine their own standing and influence in the region. As we have demonstrated in our dealings with various countries, most recently the Netherlands and Britain, Israel will respond firmly and forcefully to any country that takes such measures against it."
