Cameroon’s rising femicide toll fuels protests, calls for justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:32:23 UTC
17:32:23 KST

Geraldine Achiah had been married for barely two months when she died in September, leaving behind an 18-year-old son who is struggling to come to terms with her death and demanding justice for what relatives allege was a fatal beating by her husband.
Achiah, an elementary school teacher in her 30s, had encouraged her only child, Courage Abombi, to pursue his dream of becoming a mechanical engineer. He sat for a university entrance exam just one day after her burial.
“My mom died an unexpected and painful death,” Abombi said.
Her death has become part of a growing crisis of femicide in Cameroon, where nearly 70 women have been killed this year in gender-related killings, according to the Ministry of Women's Affairs. The figure exceeds government estimates of at least 50 cases in 2023 and 67 in 2024.
The rising toll has prompted protests in major cities, including Douala and Yaounde, with demonstrators demanding stronger legal protections, more effective investigations and accountability for perpetrators. Many cases remain unresolved, while others go unreported.
Manfred Amambua, Achiah's husband, has denied killing her, police said. He has been charged with murder and is being held in jail awaiting trial. His lawyer was unavailable for comment.
Hospital records obtained by The Associated Press (AP) documented “several bruises on her face and lips” before her death. Ndzana Bienvenu, an officer involved in the investigation, said police had also collected phone footage showing Achiah and her husband after the alleged beating, along with a blood-stained bedsheet.
Her relatives say they want justice not only for Achiah but also for other women who have died in similar circumstances.
“We want justice for our daughter who died a violent death. This was a teacher who imparted knowledge on thousands of young Cameroonians,” said Regina Ngukum, Achiah's cousin.
Activists say femicide in Cameroon is fueled by economic dependence, unequal control over family property and inadequate legal protections in a society where men traditionally hold greater authority within households.
Financial hardship can make it difficult for women to leave abusive relationships, particularly when they have children to support. Some endure violence in the hope that their partners will change, activists say, while stigma and limited resources can make seeking help even harder.
“The current economic situation in the country is not helping matters. With limited resources, many women tend to endure violence in their marriages, hoping that their men will change, which is not usually the case,” Women's Affairs Minister Marie-Thérèse Abena Ondoa recently told the state broadcaster.
Ondoa described femicide cases in Cameroon as having reached a “cruel” and “alarming” proportion and pledged further government action.
The crisis mirrors a wider global pattern. About 50,000 women and girls were killed by intimate partners or other family members in 2024, according to United Nations data.
Activists argue that Cameroon needs stronger laws and a more effective judicial system to prevent gender-related killings and ensure perpetrators face meaningful punishment.
The country's Penal Code criminalizes offenses including rape but does not explicitly define femicide as a separate crime. Cases are therefore handled under broader provisions governing homicide and other violent acts.
Similar approaches are used in many African countries, where killings motivated by gender are generally prosecuted under existing homicide laws, although some governments have taken legal or policy steps specifically addressing femicide.
Cameroon's government is preparing a bill that would establish femicide as a standalone criminal offense while strengthening broader protections against gender-based violence. The proposed legislation is expected to be submitted to parliament for consideration in November.
Activists caution, however, that changing the law alone will not resolve the problems that allow cases to stall or perpetrators to escape accountability.
Carole Grace Mbarga, a Cameroonian activist based in the United States, said investigations and court proceedings can be undermined by intimidation, corruption and procedural errors that may lead to reduced charges or acquittals.
“When investigations drag on, evidence deteriorates, witnesses lose confidence, and families become discouraged,” she said.
Even when convictions are secured, the penalties can fall short of victims' families' expectations. In 2025, a man who pleaded guilty to killing his wife received a suspended five-year sentence and a fine of 52,000 CFA francs, equivalent to about $90.
For activists, such outcomes reinforce concerns that the justice system does not adequately deter violence against women.
Family members and friends gathered in Yaounde for Achiah's burial following her death just two months after her wedding in July.
Her relatives are now waiting for the legal process to take its course while joining a broader movement demanding action against femicide. Thousands of people have taken part in protests in Douala and Yaounde, calling on authorities to strengthen protections for women and ensure that cases are properly investigated and prosecuted.
Laura Sen, one of the protest organizers, said the proposed legislation must be accompanied by efforts to address systemic barriers and improve support for victims of domestic violence.
For women facing abuse, leaving a relationship can be especially difficult when they depend financially on their partners or fear social stigma. Those raising children may face additional obstacles.
Achiah's death has left her son grieving the woman who supported his ambitions and helped him imagine a future beyond their loss.
Abombi said he continues to pray that the legal process will deliver justice for his mother.
“I pray that justice will follow its due course and that her killer will face the law,” he said.
He also described dreams in which his mother returns to comfort him.
“She keeps appearing to me in a dream, consoling me not to despair and that she is still with me,” he said.

From Hormuz to Bab el-Mandeb: Saudi Arabia’s difficult choices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:29:20 UTC
17:29:20 KST

Developments in Yemen today cannot be separated from the repercussions of the war waged by the United States and Israel against Iran. The prolonged nature of this war, and the fact that it remains unresolved, arguably compel the countries of the region to reassess their strategic realities from a perspective different from the traditional approach that has shaped their thinking for decades. The US-Israeli war against Iran has brought about significant shifts in the region’s military, economic and political calculations, confronting Tehran with serious challenges and looming threats to its security, economy and future regional standing. For its part, Iran has drawn on a range of strategic assets at its disposal across the region to mitigate these threats by raising the costs borne by its Gulf neighbours. This Iranian strategy has exposed serious challenges facing the Gulf states, particularly Saudi Arabia, the most influential among them, with direct implications for their security and economies. Examining the escalating confrontation between Yemen and Saudi Arabia offers a means of analysing the challenges confronting the Kingdom today within a broader, emerging strategic perspective on the region and its future.
Saudi Arabia is facing a renewed wave of Houthi missile and drone attacks targeting its airports and oil facilities, alongside threats to Saudi shipping in the Red Sea. These targets are not new. The Kingdom faced similar attacks during the earlier years of the war in Yemen, before the de-escalation that followed the 2022 truce. That period of relative calm began to unravel on 13 July 2026, when the coalition targeted the runway at Sanaa airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing. The Yemeni government claimed responsibility for the operation, while the Houthis attributed it to Saudi Arabia. Following this, the Houthis announced that they had targeted Abha airport, before declaring a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia on 20 July. Within Yemen, the escalation has shifted from exchanges of strikes to battles aimed at changing territorial control, particularly along the western coast. Last month, Houthi forces advanced towards Mokha and areas bordering the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Saudi-backed government forces then launched a counter-offensive at the beginning of this month, announcing that they had recaptured Mokha, Dhubab and positions overlooking the strait. Fighting between the warring parties continues.
Since the outbreak of the US-Israeli war against Iran, Saudi Arabia has faced mounting pressure on the routes through which it exports oil, the mainstay of its economy. Its eastern oil export route through the Strait of Hormuz has been hit by the turmoil in shipping arising from US-Iranian confrontations in the strait. As the Kingdom became increasingly reliant on transporting oil overland through the East-West Pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea, this alternative route was also interrupted, having assumed greater importance following the damage to its eastern maritime outlet. The East-West Pipeline was targeted in a drone attack last month, for which Riyadh held Iraqi groups close to Iran responsible, before operations resumed. The blockade declared by the Houthis against Saudi Arabia’s western maritime outlet and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait added a further, compounding burden, particularly on the passage of Saudi oil tankers through the strait. Houthi attacks on Saudi oil tankers were not confined to the waters around the strait, but extended as far as the waters off Yanbu.
These developments explain the shift in Saudi Arabia’s stance towards the Houthis. After years of seeking to consolidate the de-escalation and negotiate a political settlement, Riyadh has once again turned towards military confrontation.
Recapturing coastal positions near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has become an objective linked to protecting its economic interests and exports, particularly amid the disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. In 2023, Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman affirmed Saudi Arabia’s support for dialogue aimed at reaching a comprehensive political settlement under United Nations auspices. By contrast, Reuters reported at the beginning of this month, citing informed sources, that Riyadh was preparing a ground offensive to be carried out by Yemeni forces with Saudi air support. The agency also quoted Western diplomats and Gulf officials as saying that Riyadh could not enter into new peace negotiations while the Houthis remained in control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. This shift has been reflected in Saudi air support for the latest offensive launched by Yemeni government forces against the Houthis.
Nevertheless, a return to war offers Saudi Arabia no guarantee of a decisive outcome. The previous war, which began in 2015 and involved a Saudi-led coalition with the participation of the United Arab Emirates, failed to achieve its objective of defeating the Houthis. Nor did it restore the government that the Houthis had driven out of Sanaa, leaving the capital and most of northern Yemen under their control. Similarly, the US air campaign against the Houthis in 2025 failed to eliminate their power in Yemen, despite costing more than $1 billion, destroying weapons and facilities, and killing Houthi field commanders. The campaign ended with an agreement to halt reciprocal attacks between the United States and the Houthis, an arrangement that did not extend to Israel.
Nor will the recent Mecca Alliance between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey help the Kingdom in its fight in Yemen beyond defensive and technical support, particularly while the alliance remains in its early stages.
It is also difficult to rely on the United States, given Washington’s refusal to meet a Saudi request to participate in air strikes, limiting its involvement to providing advice, intelligence and targeting data. US strategy in the region is based on expanding the role of regional partners in defending themselves, the region and US interests within it. This explains Trump’s request to Turkey a few days ago to intervene in support of Saudi Arabia.
These developments compel the countries of the region to reassess their security calculus and strategic balances, recognising that Iran and its allies are part of the regional reality and that lasting stability cannot be built by disregarding them. Relations based on cooperation and mutual interests remain an essential foundation for such stability, alongside the need to establish a balance between the instruments of power available to the Gulf states and those possessed by Iran. Throughout the current war against it, Iran has demonstrated that it possesses significant strategic assets that have inflicted heavy costs on the countries of the region, exposing an imbalance in their ability to impose comparable costs in return. If the Gulf states possessed instruments of power that made harming their security and interests costly for Iran, the costs of escalation would become mutual, potentially encouraging the parties to seek balanced political solutions that support cooperation and future stability.

Burhan Sansarlioglu and Emir Yildirim
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Global markets traded on a positive trend on Thursday with declining government bond yields and a recovery in tech stocks that had plummeted the previous day.
US macroeconomic data continue to set the direction of global markets.
The monthly Producer Price Index (PPI) in the US rose 1.3% in September, while surging 6.3% annually, faster than expected.
US producer inflation reached its highest level since March 2022 on a monthly basis and since December 2022 year-on-year.
Hotter-than-expected consumer inflation combined with the acceleration in producer inflation, fueling growing concerns that the US Federal Reserve may hike rates.
US retail sales rose above expectations by 0.8% on a monthly basis in September, reinforcing expectations that the Fed will continue its tight monetary policy.
The negative trend in tech stocks due to concerns over artificial intelligence investment profitability reversed following statements by Fed Chair Kevin Warsh.
Lingering concerns over the broader technology sector fueling worries about economic growth prompted investors to turn to bonds, dropping bond yields.
The US 10-Year Treasury yield fell 11 basis points on Thursday to 5.08%, while it is trading flat on Friday.
The US dollar fell 0.2% to 101.9, while gold is trading just above its previous close at $4,171 per ounce on Friday.
December-delivery Brent crude is down 0.5% at $105.4 a barrel on Friday after the International Energy Agency (IEA) reached an agreement to release more than 20 million barrels of diesel into the market, in addition to the remaining oil that was released at a record level from the emergency reserve.
 
Major chipmaker stocks down
The US Treasury Department added some 16 people and 10 entities allegedly linked to Iran to its sanctions list to further block Tehran’s access to the global financial system.
Meanwhile, the New York Stock Exchange traded positively on Thursday, led by gains in healthcare sectors, which also helped offset declines in tech stocks.
Shares of chipmakers Nvidia, AMD, and Intel declined 2%, 1.5%, and 3%, respectively.
Pharmaceutical giant Eli Lily’s shares gained 3.5%, health insurer UnitedHealth shares rose 2.8%, and retail titan Walmart’s shares grew 1.5%.
At the same time, top executives at SpaceX and Tesla are reportedly considering a merger, according to a Barclays analysis, driving SpaceX shares down 2.3% and Tesla shares to drop 1.3%.
Additionally, the US initial jobless claims rose to 199,000 in the week ending Oct. 10, coming in within estimates.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 1.08%, the S&P 500 rose 0.33%, and the Nasdaq Composite was up 0.08% on Thursday. American indexes started Friday on a positive trend.
Meanwhile, European stock markets traded mostly positively with strong corporate earnings and gains in healthcare companies.
The UK’s economy grew above estimates by 0.1% month-on-month and 2.1% year-on-year, driving up the British pound/US dollar exchange rate to 1.33 on Friday, its highest since Sept. 30.
The eurozone’s industrial production fell 0.5% on a monthly basis and 1.1% year-on-year in August, above estimates.
Germany's DAX 40 gained 0.33%, the UK's FTSE 100 rose 1.08%, and France's CAC 40 was up 0.78% on Thursday, while Italy's FTSE MIB 30 fell 0.72%. European indexes started Friday on a positive note.
Near Friday’s close, Asian equity markets traded higher amid a recovery in tech stocks.
SK Hynix shares surged 3.8%, Samsung Electronics rose 4.6%, Kioxia grew 3.2%, and Sony’s shares were up 2.4%.

Israel Police, Shin Bet launch manhunt for armed man in military uniform in Kafr Kara olive grove
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:21:11 UTC
17:21:11 KST

Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine was wounded during a Friday altercation between extremist settlers and Palestinians in the West Bank, with the IDF confirming the account later on Friday.
Footage seen by The Jerusalem Post appears to show Levine kneeling on a path in a press jacket and helmet, as colleagues run over to carry her to safety.
Police launched an investigation into the incident after receiving an IDF report of the West Bank clashes, according to an Israel Police spokesperson.
Palestinian media reported that Levine was beaten, sustaining fractures and cuts in the violence near Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah. Israeli sources have not independently verified this.
Levine, speaking from a hospital bed, said that she had been kicked "about 50 times," adding that if she hadn't been wearing her black jacket and helmet, she "probably wouldn't be here at all, because they just kept kicking me again and again.
"After about 10 minutes, they tried to make me get up; they pushed me back to the ground and continued kicking me," she said. "I tried to hold on to my cameras and my side bag, but in the end they just ripped everything from me and kept kicking me."
According to the IDF, soldiers initially fired warning shots into the air in an effort to disperse the crowd upon arriving on scene, eventually targeting an individual who approached them with a sharp object.
PMO: 'Serious questions remain,' facts 'unclear'
The Prime Minister's Office (PMO) condemned the attack in an X/Twitter post later on Friday, noting that the facts "remain unclear and are under investigation."
"Israel unequivocally condemns violence against anyone - Jews, Arabs, Christians, or journalists," the statement read. "Those responsible will be held accountable."
The statement indicated that "serious questions remain" regarding who specifically was responsible for the attack on Levine, emphasizing the presence of "200 Arabs and far-left activists... (and) approximately 40 Israeli youths" at the site of the attack.
"The investigation must establish the facts, including who initiated the violence," the statement continued. "We will not allow disputed incidents to be exploited to demonize the hundreds of thousands of law-abiding Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria. The facts must determine the conclusions. Not the headlines."
Washington Post editor-in-chief Matt Murray also condemned the incident in a statement earlier on Friday, according to N12 News, accusing Israeli settlers of having attacked Levine, whom he emphasized "was wearing prominent identification marks that clearly identified her as a journalist."
"We are appalled by this unjustified attack on a journalist who was doing her job," he said. "We call on the authorities to conduct a thorough investigation and act on its findings."
In addition, the US Embassy in Jerusalem told N12 that it is aware of the incident and is "monitoring the situation."
"We condemn criminal violence and call for the investigation and prosecution of those responsible," it said.
Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot also responded to the incident in a post on X/Twitter, calling it "unacceptable" and referring to the perpetrators as "violent lawbreakers."
"This handful of rioters does not represent the public in Israel. The actions of this handful stain an entire nation and severely harm the security of all Israeli citizens and IDF fighters," he said. "I back the IDF in its sharp and clear condemnation of the incident. It is incumbent upon the Israel Police to take harsh measures against this criminal violence."
Mateh Binyamin Regional Council accuses PA of bringing terrorists to attack Israelis
The Mateh Binyamin Regional Council provided a different course of events.
According to the council, the Palestinian Authority "led hundreds of anarchists and terrorists into a direct confrontation with Israelis near Abu Falah, all under the cover of the olive harvest."
"Footage from the scene shows terrorists launching fireworks directly at people and hurling stones at Israelis, while journalists stand behind them, documenting this deliberate provocation," the council said.
"The event was orchestrated by the PA; its patrol vehicles were present and highly visible at the scene, even though it is in Area B, where Israel holds responsibility for security," it added.
"Clashes broke out between Arabs and Israelis, eventually being dispersed by Border Police officers who arrived at the location. According to reports, several activists were injured during the confrontations," the council said.
The council did not explicitly comment on Levine's reported wounds.
The event was part of four incidents of nationalist-motivated violence and clashes between Israelis and Palestinians which were reported overnight and on Friday morning at several locations across the West Bank, including several olive groves.
The incidents reportedly involved vehicles being set on fire, attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters, and attacks on Palestinian homes.
In the village of Burin, a confrontation broke out during the olive harvest. Additional incidents were reported in the village of Burqa, east of Ramallah, and in Turmus Ayya. The incidents reportedly included at least four vehicles being set on fire, one of which was a civil defense vehicle, and attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters.
In a separate incident, shortly before midnight, settlers reportedly attacked Palestinian homes in the Wadi al-Sheikh area of the town of Beit Ummar, north of Hebron.
The Palestinian Red Crescent said that two wounded Palestinians, a 63-year-old woman and a 40-year-old man, had been treated and taken to the hospital. Another Palestinian was reportedly shot in the knee.
Israeli security forces arrest fleeing suspect following manhunt
Israeli security forces arrested a suspect after he fled an olive grove near Kafr Kara, Israel Police announced later on Friday.
The police and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) conducted a manhunt for the suspect lasting several hours prior to his arrest.
An M-16 rifle was also found in the vicinity.

Egypt suspends truck traffic to Sudan after Khartoum attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:20:00 UTC
17:20:00 KST

Egypt has indefinitely suspended the passage of trucks bound for Sudan through the Qustul land port after two Egyptian drivers were killed and a third was injured in a shooting at a market south of the Sudanese capital, Khartoum.
The management of Egypt’s Qustul port, which operates under the General Authority for Land and Dry Ports at the Ministry of Transport, has ordered all trucks heading to the port to stop. Trucks will not be allowed to cross by ferry into Sudan until further instructions, citing “security developments in Sudan’s Northern State”.
The suspension does not apply to passenger traffic. Buses, private cars, minibuses and individual travellers are still allowed to cross, while the restrictions apply only to trucks.
An earlier decision by Egypt’s Land and International Transport Regulatory Authority banned Egyptian trucks from entering conflict zones in Sudan. It limited commercial transport to Wadi Halfa, Argeen and the city of Dongola in Sudan, as part of measures to protect drivers from security risks.
The authority stressed that truck drivers must comply with regulations governing transport within Sudan, exercise the utmost caution and avoid entering designated areas under any circumstances.
The instructions are based on directives issued by Egypt’s Ministry of Transport on 11th May 2025, requiring drivers to avoid conflict zones and unload goods only in safe areas of Sudan’s Northern State.
The suspension comes amid security risks affecting road transport between Egypt and Sudan as a result of the armed conflict. Two Egyptian drivers were killed and a third was injured in a shooting at a market south of Khartoum.

Türkiye’s year-end inflation expectations hold steady at 29.6 percent: Survey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:17:08 UTC
17:17:08 KST

Market participants’ expectations for inflation at the end of 2026 remained broadly unchanged in October, while forecasts for inflation over the next 12 months edged higher, according to the Central Bank’s latest Survey of Market Participants.
The survey, which monitors the expectations of decision-makers and experts in the financial and real sectors regarding key economic indicators, showed that year-end consumer price inflation (CPI) expectations rose marginally to 29.63 percent from 29.61 percent in the previous survey period.
The 12-month-ahead inflation expectation increased to 23.89 percent from 23.70 percent, while the 24-month-ahead inflation forecast declined to 17.94 percent from 18.32 percent.
According to the survey, the Central Bank is expected to set its policy rate at 36 percent at the upcoming October Monetary Policy Committee meeting.
The survey showed little change in expectations for the Turkish Lira at the end of the year. The year-end exchange rate forecast for the U.S. dollar stood at 51.55 lira, compared with 51.57 lira in the previous survey.
However, the 12-month-ahead exchange rate expectation increased to 59.26 lira per dollar from 58.60 lira in the previous survey.
Participants forecast Türkiye’s gross domestic product (GDP) to expand by 2.9 percent in 2026, down from a previous estimate of 3 percent.
The GDP growth forecast for 2027 remained unchanged at 3.9 percent, according to the survey.

MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. Radicals seek to use Afghanistan as a springboard for spreading threats to Central Asia and Russia, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said.
"We take note of the fact that, according to available data, terrorist and extremist groups maintain a significant presence in Afghanistan’s areas bordering Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, where they have training camps and strongholds. Members of these groups seek to infiltrate Central Asian countries, particularly disguised as refugees and even tourists," he pointed out, addressing a conference on security issues in Central Asia and Afghanistan involving the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO), the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO).
"According to our assessments based on intelligence data, the main threat comes from militants of the Islamic State-Khorasan Province group, a regional branch of the international terrorist organization Islamic State, which is outlawed in Russia. It openly pursues the goal of undermining the Kabul government’s ability to maintain stability in the country," Lavrov went on to say.
"Besides, radicals also seek to use Afghanistan as a kind of springboard for spreading terrorist activities to both Central Asia and Russia. The Terrorist International (I can think of no other way to describe it), which is based on the other bank of the Panj River unites militants of Central Asian, North Caucasian and Uyghur origin who gained combat experience in armed raids in the Middle East and Africa, as well as preachers of radical Islamic ideas, clandestine madrasas and propaganda resources in the information field, especially on social media," the top Russian diplomat added.
In his view, developments in Afghanistan could still negatively affect regional security, "particularly if unscrupulous external players use those processes to achieve their short-term goals, which certainly do not serve the interests of Central Asia and Russia."
"We try to remain realistic and thus realize that it will take a long time to overcome the unfortunate legacy left by the United States and other NATO countries following two decades of their inglorious occupation of Afghanistan," Lavrov concluded.

Russian drones violated Moldovan airspace five times overnight
Several Russian UAVs violated Moldovan airspace on the night of 15-16 October and on the morning of 16 October.
Source: European Pravda, citing TV8
Details: The drones crossed the border amid large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine. The incidents were recorded in northern and south-eastern Moldova. No crashes or explosions were reported.
The first violation was recorded at 23:02. An object crossed the border from the direction of Tymkove in Ukraine's Odesa Oblast and headed towards the village of Ivanovca. Eighteen minutes later, it left Moldovan airspace and headed towards the Ukrainian settlement of Bronit.
The second incident was recorded at 03:37. A drone flew from the direction of the Ukrainian village of Starokozache in Odesa Oblast towards the village of Tudora in Ștefan Vodă District. One minute later, it returned to Ukrainian territory along the same route.
At 03:46, another drone crossed the border in the north from the direction of Mohyliv-Podilskyi, heading towards the town of Otaci. Two minutes later, it left Moldovan airspace near the village of Hădărăuți in Ocnița District.
The fourth violation was recorded at 05:59. A drone entered the country's airspace from the direction of Starokozache and headed towards the village of Căplani in Ștefan Vodă District. One minute later, the drone left Moldovan territory near the village of Olănești.
At 06:09, the same drone crossed the border again near the village of Purcari in Ștefan Vodă District. One minute later, it left the country's airspace via the Dnestrovsc area in the Transnistrian region, heading towards the Ukrainian settlement of Hradenytsi.
In less than seven hours, Moldova's Defence Ministry recorded five unauthorised incursions by aircraft into the country's airspace.
Background:
- On the night of 14-15 October, a drone once again violated Moldovan airspace during a Russian attack on Ukraine. Moldova's defence minister said the drone was "definitely" Russian.
- On the morning of 30 September, a drone flew through Moldovan airspace before crashing outside the village of Hîrbovăț in Anenii Noi District and exploding.

UK and Germany strengthen defence ties in London talks
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:00:33 BST
17:00:33 KST

UK and Germany strengthen defence ties in London talks
UK and Germany deepen defence-industrial cooperation at Lancaster House talks, building on the Trinity House Agreement and Kensington Treaty.
- UK and Germany strengthened defence-industrial cooperation at the latest talks at Lancaster House.
- The talks build on the Trinity House Agreement and Kensington Treaty, reinforcing cooperation between the two nations across air, land, sea and space.
- Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard and German counterpart State Secretary Jens Plötner joined industry leaders to discuss industrial priorities for collaboration.
UK-German work on key industrial collaboration and new technology was advanced yesterday as Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard hosted his German counterpart, State Secretary for Armament and Innovation Jens Plötner, at Lancaster House in London.
The latest UK-Germany Ministerial Group on Equipment and Capability Cooperation (MECC) meeting brought together senior officials and military leaders from both nations to review progress on joint defence capability programmes and to deepen the industrial partnership between the UK and Germany, two of NATO’s leading defence powers.
Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard MP said:
  Germany is one of our closest and most valued defence partners, and today’s talks demonstrate our determination to turn that ambition into real capability for our armed forces and real opportunity for our defence industries.
As threats to our shared security evolve, the UK and Germany are standing together, strengthening our forces, our industrial bases and our resilience in lockstep.
Discussions built on the Trinity House Agreement, signed in October 2024, which set out an ambitious programme of bilateral cooperation across air, land, maritime, cyber and space domains. The agreement sits under the wider Kensington Treaty, signed in July 2025, which provides the strategic framework for the UK-Germany relationship.
Among the flagship programmes on the agenda was Deep Precision Strike, a joint UK-Germany initiative to develop long-range strike capability, reflecting the shared ambition of both nations to address critical capability gaps and strengthen NATO’s deterrence.
The talks follow the Prime Minister’s visit to Berlin on 8 October, during which the UK and Germany agreed to deepen cooperation on space and to establish a new UK-Germany Counter-Hybrid Partnership, strengthening joint resilience against grey-zone threats.
Following the MECC meeting, Minister Pollard joined State Secretary Plötner at the German Embassy in London for a panel discussion which saw senior policymakers and industry leaders take stock of defence-industrial progress and identify practical priorities for deepening cooperation.
Minister Pollard was joined on the panel by State Secretary Plötner, Dr Philipp Kerth, co-founder and chief executive of German defence technology company Hypersonica, and Alex Zino, Director Business Development & Future Programmes at Rolls-Royce.
The MECC forms part of a wider programme of UK-German engagement in the lead-up to the EU-UK summit. The UK-Germany defence relationship continues to grow as both nations work towards a more resilient Euro-Atlantic security architecture, underpinned by a modern, innovative and competitive defence industrial base at the heart of NATO’s deterrence and readiness.

Tatarstan and India exploring data center cooperation – minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:57:59 UTC
16:57:59 KST

Tatarstan and India exploring data center cooperation – minister
India and Russia’s Republic of Tatarstan are exploring joint data center and digital infrastructure projects, with Indian cloud provider Bharat AI Cloud planning to sign a cooperation agreement with the region’s IT Park. 
The plans emerged at the second Russia-India TIME Business Forum in Kazan on Thursday. A technology hub in India’s southern Telangana state has expressed interest in jointly developing infrastructure in Tatarstan, the Russian region’s deputy minister of digital development, Bulat Gabdrakhmanov, said. 
The proposed partnership could allow both sides to exchange cloud technologies and expertise. Bharat AI Cloud, which earlier announced plans to open an office in Kazan, is also looking to enter the Russian market. 
Russia has established data infrastructure providers, while India’s large domestic market offers opportunities for expanding digital services, director of the Chamber for Indo-Russian Technology Collaboration (CIRTC), Subham Sarkar, said at the forum. 
The discussions build on earlier cooperation between the two sides. At last year’s TIME forum, Tatarstan’s IT Park signed a three-year agreement with CIRTC to promote technology partnerships, investment, and market access. 
Officials also explored building an artificial intelligence data center with Indian operator CtrlS in October last year. The proposed project remains under consideration, with its progress dependent on electricity costs, market demand, and opportunities to expand in Russia, according to Tatarstan’s Digital Development Ministry.
The latest talks have also brought up the possibility of establishing a so-called data embassy, which would involve hosting data infrastructure abroad under special arrangements intended to protect data sovereignty. 
Sarkar compared the proposed arrangement to the protections afforded to diplomatic missions. He said the project was technically feasible, although questions of sovereignty and regulation would take time to resolve.
India has explored similar arrangements with other countries. In January, New Delhi and the United Arab Emirates agreed to examine the possibility of establishing digital embassies under mutually recognized sovereignty arrangements. The two countries also discussed cooperation on data centers.
The India-Tatarstan discussions extend beyond data infrastructure to healthcare, AI, cybersecurity, and digital public services.
Russia could offer Indian partners domestically developed operating systems, office software, email platforms, and messaging services, the Tatarstan Information Technology Center’s deputy director general, Kamil Gazizov, said at the Kazan forum. He also highlighted opportunities for both sides to work together against cybersecurity threats.

Ensuring security of transport corridors benefits all regional countries: Iranian minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:57:06 UTC

Ensuring security of transport corridors benefits all regional countries: Iranian minister
TEHRAN- Iran’s Minister of Transport and Urban Development, emphasizing the necessity of protecting civilian infrastructure and guaranteeing the continuity of transport and transit flows in the region, presented proposals and called for the formulation of operational and time-bound plans to remove border obstacles, develop rail cooperation, and strengthen the resilience of regional corridors.
According to an IRNA report from the Ministry of Transport and Urban Development, Farzaneh Sadegh, at the 14th Meeting of Ministers of Transport of the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO) member states in Kazakhstan, expressed appreciation for that country’s hosting and stated: Due to its privileged geographical location, the ECO region has the capacity to become an integrated network of road, rail, and sea routes—a network that can strengthen connectivity among Central Asia, West Asia, the Caucasus, and open waters.
Referring to the approvals of the 13th ECO Meeting of Ministers of Transport in Tehran, she emphasized the necessity of assessing the extent of implementation of past agreements, identifying obstacles, and determining operational priorities, and said: This meeting must lead to specific, time-bound, and measurable decisions for developing regional cooperation.
The Minister of Transport and Urban Development, referring to the damage inflicted on Iran’s transport infrastructure during the attacks by the United States and the Israeli regime, said: Disruption in any part of the region’s transport network, regardless of where it occurs, can increase the time and cost of moving goods and also affect the security of supply chains of other countries.
Sadegh emphasized: Protecting civilian infrastructure, ensuring the security of communication routes, and continuing the flow of transport and transit are common interests for all ECO member states.
She asked the organization’s secretariat to examine the effects of security disruptions on regional corridors and present practical solutions for increasing the resilience of the transport network.
Sadegh further considered facilitating the movement of the road fleet and border crossings among the priorities of regional cooperation and emphasized reducing truck dwell time, simplifying customs procedures, harmonizing transport documents, and exchanging information among border authorities.
The Minister of Transport and Urban Development, referring to the revival of the ECO train and its successful operation on the Turkey, Iran, and Turkmenistan route, considered this experience a basis for expanding rail cooperation among member states.
Noting that the damaged bridges on the aforementioned rail route were repaired by Iranian engineers within 72 hours and the route was reopened, she emphasized the importance of technical readiness and maintaining the continuity of regional rail connections.
Sadegh also considered the Almaty–Tehran–Istanbul rail connection an opportunity for developing regional trade and proposed that tariff, customs, technical, and operational obstacles on rail routes be examined and a clear mechanism be created for coordinating train movements and developing regular and competitive services.
The Minister of Transport and Urban Development listed access of landlocked countries to open waters as one of the priorities of cooperation in ECO and said: Achieving this goal requires the integrated linking of ports, rail lines, roads, and logistics services.
Referring to the capacity of Chabahar Port and other southern ports of Iran, she considered the connection of Chabahar to the country’s rail network an effective factor in strengthening the link between land and sea transport, diversifying trade routes, and reducing transport costs.
The Minister of Transport and Urban Development, further emphasizing the necessity of determining the responsibilities of countries and the secretariat in following up on approvals and presenting a progress report at the next meeting, noted: Developing transport and transit in the ECO region, in addition to increasing trade and economic growth, helps strengthen regional ties and enhance the economic resilience of member states.
Sadegh proposed that the ECO secretariat, in cooperation with member states, prepare a comprehensive report on the extent of implementation of previous approvals and remaining obstacles, formulate a time-bound plan for facilitating road transport, border and customs coordination, and developing rail and multimodal services, and place on its agenda solutions for protecting civilian infrastructure and increasing the resilience of corridors.

At least four people were killed while battling a wildfire in Mount Bromo in Indonesia's East Java province.
The death toll rose to four on Thursday after another person died while being transferred to a hospital, the state-run news agency Antara reported.
The victims included two officers from Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park and two hotel staffers.
Two other people suffered serious burns while fighting the fire and were hospitalized for treatment.
Probolinggo District Head Muhammad Haris said wildfires had occurred in the national park almost every year, but had not previously caused fatalities.
Twelve people initially joined efforts to contain the current fire under standard operating procedures, but the blaze spread and the team split up, leaving six people trapped as winds shifted rapidly, Haris said.
Indonesia faces an unusually prolonged dry season, with El Nino contributing to conditions favorable for wildfires.

New house sales in Türkiye rise 3.9% in September

Mucahithan Avcioglu
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
New house sales in Türkiye rose 3.9% year-on-year to 51,519 in September, according to official data released Friday.
New homes accounted for 36.2% of total housing transactions during the month, data from the Turkish Statistical Institute (TurkStat) showed.
Overall house sales fell 9.3% from a year earlier to 142,390, as existing home sales dropped 15.3% to 90,871.
Adjusted for calendar effects, new house sales increased 3.8% annually. On a seasonally and calendar-adjusted basis, they rose 5.5% from August, while existing home sales remained unchanged.
Mortgaged house sales climbed 5.1% year-on-year to 23,397, accounting for 16.4% of total transactions.
Sales to foreign buyers increased 9.9% to 2,167, representing 1.5% of the total. Russian citizens purchased the most homes with 388, followed by Iraqis with 166 and Germans with 162.
In January-September, new house sales edged down 0.6% from the same period last year to 359,913, while total housing transactions declined 7.2% to 1.09 million.

According to IRNA, Seyyed Ali Madanizadeh, speaking to reporters after separate meetings and talks with the Chairman of the Executive Board and the Minister of Trade of the Eurasian Economic Commission at the union's headquarters in Moscow, added: "We held very good sessions."

The Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance, referring to the efforts of the enemies of the Iranian nation to fuel economic warfare and block trade and financial channels, said: "What is evident is that, thanks to God, these countries support Iran and our economy, and that Iran has managed to maintain production and trade relations with countries under the toughest conditions." He added: "The member states of the Eurasian Economic Union are equally committed and eager to develop these relations."
Continuing his Moscow visit agenda for multilateral consultations, the Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance attended the Eurasian Economic Union's headquarters and met with the Chairman of the Executive Board and the Minister of Trade to discuss accelerating bilateral trade.

Slepnev, noting that the second meeting of the Iran-EAEU working group would be hosted by Tehran in the coming months, expressed hope that the upward trend in bilateral trade would continue.
Iran's Ambassador to Russia, Kazem Jalali, and Mehdi Heydari, Deputy Minister of Economy and head of Iran's Organization for Investment, Economic and Technical Assistance, accompanied Madanizadeh during these meetings.
The free trade agreement between Iran and the Eurasian Economic Union came into force in May 2025 after completing legal procedures in the signatory countries, subsequently eliminating customs duties on 87% of goods in bilateral trade.
Within this cooperation framework, the path has been smoothed for Iranian goods to enter the market of over 180 million people in the union's member states, and reciprocally, this opportunity is available for traders from the five signatory countries in commerce with Iran.
Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Armenia are members of the Eurasian Economic Union, and Iran holds observer status in the union.
The Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) is a regional economic integration bloc in the post-Soviet space, established by a treaty signed in 2014 and launched on January 1, 2015. Its five member states are Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Armenia, with Iran, Cuba, Moldova, and Uzbekistan holding observer status.
Modelled in part on the European Union, the EAEU aims to create a single internal market with the free movement of goods, services, capital, and labour. Its core objectives include improving living standards, ensuring sustainable economic development, and boosting the global competitiveness of member economies.
The bloc is driven by institutions such as the Supreme Eurasian Economic Council and the Eurasian Economic Commission. While the EAEU has expanded external ties—notably through a free trade agreement with Iran—internal integration remains uneven, with Russia dominating trade flows in a "hub and spoke" model. The bloc has set a long-term vision to become a self-sufficient and attractive macro-region by 2045.

University's satellite collects data on space radiation at various heights above Arctic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:46:24 UTC
16:46:24 KST

ARKHANGELSK, October 16. /TASS/. The ArcticSat-1 spacecraft of the Northern Arctic Federal University (NArFU) collected data on space radiation at different heights above the Arctic. Researchers obtained data from 500 to 200 km, and there is practically no information about radiation at low levels in the circumpolar regions, leader of the university's Space Monitoring Center Roman Alyoshko told TASS.
"The main data that we were collecting is data on space radiation," he said. "This is an urgent task exactly for the polar regions. During the spacecraft's mission, we collected data on space radiation, starting from altitudes of about 500 km when it was launched into orbit, and then it was gradually decreasing over about a year and a half, to 200 km when it already began burning up. And it is even more relevant data when it was in low orbits of about 200 kilometers. There are practically no spacecraft in such orbits, and therefore data on space radiation at these heights is very valuable."
ArcticSat-1 belongs to a group of satellites that fly in low orbits, at an altitude of 400-600 km. Strictly speaking, there is no space vacuum there, and therefore the satellite constantly touches the atmosphere molecules and gradually loses speed. It does not have an engine to compensate for this, so the satellite is slowly descending. The lower is the satellite, the denser is the air and the faster is the deceleration. The Sun also affects the descent rate: with high solar activity, the atmosphere heats up and "swells", increasing the braking effect at the orbit altitude.
ArcticSat-1's orbit is polar, with an inclination of about 97 degrees. In such an orbit, the spacecraft passes over high latitudes, where the geomagnetic field does not protect well from space particles. This coincides with the project's main topic: the impact of space weather on small spacecraft in the polar regions.
"We have focused on how this affects satellites. We were receiving data on space radiation and at the same time we were receiving information about the satellite. Our goal is to make recommendations for operators of such satellites on what to do in a certain situation. In case of a very strong surge of space radiation, it may be reasonable to put the satellite into the sleep mode, that is, not to interact with it - not to cause breakdowns," the scientist said, adding it was important to find how to "prolong the life" of such satellites.
An octopus in space
On board the satellite was an art object, an octopus, - Octo-Pax by artist Nastya Miro. This is a figurine of about ten by ten centimeters, made of a domestic metal powder composition. It was in a separate cube chamber inside the satellite. Inside the chamber was also a camera facing the art object.
The octopus, according to calculations, burned down along with the satellite. The art object ended the journey the way the artist had intended it to happen: it did not stay in orbit. Entering the atmosphere, the figure traveled the same path as the spacecraft. "This fate fits deeply the project's idea. Octo-Pax was holding in its tentacles debris that is common for the orbit, and symbolized the space's cleanup from debris. The art object did not become part of this debris, as it dissolved into the atmosphere, without leaving anything behind over there - outside the Earth," the university said.
The ArcticSat-1 satellite burned down in dense layers of the atmosphere. It had worked in orbit for about a year and a half. Scientists will be processing the data obtained by it for about a year.

Thawing rate of glaciers depends on climate as well as on their shape, scientists say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:44:03 UTC
16:44:03 KST

ST. PETERSBURG, October 16. /TASS/. Scientists of the Arctic and Antarctic Research Institute (AARI, St. Petersburg) found that the rate of glacier melting depends not only on climatic factors, but also on the ice mass' shape, the institute's press service said.
"The rate of glaciers' melting depends not only on climate warming, but also on the glaciers' shape and size," the press service said. "Without adjusting assessments to the "geometry" factor, the climate estimates, based on temperature changes data, risk being inaccurate."
The scientists came to this conclusion based on results of years-long glaciological monitoring of two mountain-valley glaciers - the Aldegonda and the West Grenfjord - on the Spitsbergen Archipelago. Between 2013 and 2025, the glaciers lost about 18-20 meters of water equivalent mass, they said.
The scientists used two ways to calculate the mass balance - based on the annual changes in the glacier's surface shape, and based on the geometry relative to that recorded in 2008. The specialists found that as a result of the glaciers' shifting to lower, warmer altitude zones, they are losing annually additional 1-2% of ice on the Aldegonde and 0.5-1% on the Western Grenfjord in addition to what may be attributed to the climate. According to the scientists, over recent two decades, this addition is still not big and does not distort the overall climate assessment. However, the longer the series of observations, and the faster the glacier is melting, the more noticeable this "addition" becomes.
"The glacier is a living, constantly changing object," the institute's senior researcher Anton Terekhov explained. "As it is melting, its surface is sinking lower and lower, and down there, the air is warmer - and as a result, the ice starts melting even faster, even if the weather has not changed by a single degree. Right now, this effect is not big, but if it is not taken into account when analyzing longer series of observations, we risk mistaking part of that "geometric" history of a glacier for a climate signal that does not actually exist."
The institute's experts suggest applying this research method to other glaciers in the world. They are confident that thanks to satellite digital terrain models covering the entire Arctic and Antarctic, such calculations could be made for almost any glaciation center.
"This way we will be able to separate more accurately the real consequences of global warming from the "internal processes" of the glaciers and, accordingly, to predict more accurately their future," the press service said in conclusion.

Syria's 2013 Baniyas massacres: What happened and who was Ali Kayali?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:42:31 UTC
16:42:31 KST

The arrest on Thursday of Ali Kayali, better known as Mihrac Ural, has renewed attention to the 2013 massacres in the village of al-Bayda and the Ras al-Nabaa neighbourhood of Baniyas, both in Syria’s western Tartus Governorate.
They involved mass killings and summary executions of hundreds of civilians, including women and children, during the tenure of ousted Syrian regime leader Bashar al Assad, who led the country from 2000 until late 2024.
The Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA) said the General Intelligence Directorate had arrested Kayali while he was attempting to flee across the border, describing him as the “main suspect” in the Baniyas massacres.
Videos circulated online showed mosques in Al-Bayda broadcasting chants of “Allahu Akbar,” with those sharing the footage saying residents were celebrating news of his arrest.
The massacres took place on May 2 and 3 2013, when Assad regime forces and allied armed groups carried out military operations in Al-Bayda and the Ras al-Nabaa neighbourhood of Baniyas that included summary executions and mass killings of civilians.
The massacres
According to an August 2013 report by the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Syria, regime forces surrounded Al-Bayda on May 2, closed access routes and shelled the town before entering alongside members of the National Defence Forces.
The commission documented arrests and summary executions of civilians as well as dozens of bodies found inside homes and in the streets. Some had been burned, while others bore signs of having been beaten with blunt objects.
The following day, the operation extended to Ras al-Nabaa, where attacking forces surrounded the area, prevented residents from leaving through the main roads, shelled the neighbourhood and then entered it. Families, including children, were among those executed.
The UN commission found that the two operations were linked and said there was no indication of armed opposition activity in either area during the killings.
It estimated that between 150 and 250 civilians were killed in Al-Bayda and between 150 and 200 in Ras al-Nabaa.
The UN investigation concluded that Assad regime forces and allied armed groups, including the National Defence Forces, were responsible for killings amounting to war crimes.
Kayali’s role
During the Syrian uprising, Kayali led an armed group known as the Syrian Resistance, which fought alongside Assad regime forces and took part in military operations in several parts of the country.
Syrian authorities linked Kayali and his group to the Al-Bayda and Ras al-Nabaa massacres and announced his arrest more than 13 years after the killings.
On October 4, Syria’s Interior Ministry announced the arrest of Jamal Trabelsi, Kayali’s deputy.
The ministry said Trabelsi had participated in combat operations in support of the former regime, including the Al-Bayda and Ras al-Nabaa massacres, as well as fighting in the countryside of Hama, Idlib and Aleppo.
Kayali’s arrest came 11 days after his deputy was detained, marking a new development in efforts to pursue those accused of violations committed during the former regime’s rule.
In May, residents of Baniyas and its countryside marked the anniversary of the massacres, demanding accountability for those responsible and answers about the fate of missing people.

Addressing the 17th Summit of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP 17), held in the Armenian capital of Yerevan on Friday, Pezeshkian emphasized that US and Israel waged an unprovoked war of aggression against the Iranian nation which produced adverse effects on the ecosystem of the regional countries.
Condemning the destructive impact of wars of aggression on nature, Iranian President Pezeshkian termed it "ecocide," or environmental genocide, stating that preserving biodiversity can be important arenas for peace diplomacy.
Iranian president called for stronger international mechanisms to assess and repair environmental damage caused by armed conflict, warning that war threatens biodiversity far beyond national borders.
Turning to the Israeli massacre of Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, he stressed, “Gaza stands as a stark testament to ecocide, with devastation whose horrific impacts will endure for generations.”
President Pezeshkian warned that war caused lasting environmental devastation, citing that Gaza's contaminated soil as proof that ecological damage crosses borders and requires international intervention.
Nations subjected to illegal sanctions and foreign-imposed wars must not be forced to pay the heavy toll of these crises, Pezeshkian warned.
Protecting biodiversity can be an important arena for peace diplomacy, he said, stressing, “Not only war is merely a threat to humans and infrastructure, but also as a direct cause of the destruction of nature.”
War burns forests, destroys wetlands, pollutes soil and water, and displaces animal species, he underlined.
“We believe that biodiversity conservation can serve as a significant arena for "peace diplomacy." In a region grappling with security crises stemming from the illegal and expansionist presence of powers, as well as climate change, water scarcity, and ecosystem degradation, environmental cooperation can build bridges between nations, the bridges that pave the way for peace and security for all, peace with nature, and a future lived in harmony with the natural world.”
Pezeshkian described the environmental devastation caused by the wars in the region, including in Gaza, as “ecocide” that must be condemned, adding that pollution and ecological damage transcend national borders.
He then called on the international community to ensure that nature is not treated as a “silent and defenseless victim” of war. He said international agencies and relevant institutions should strengthen mechanisms for assessing environmental damage, mobilizing financial resources, restoring damaged ecosystems and supporting countries affected by the environmental consequences of armed conflicts.
Highlighting Iran’s biodiversity, which spans the Hyrcanian and Arasbaran forests, the Zagros Mountains, deserts and the coasts of the Persian Gulf, Sea of Oman and Caspian Sea, Pezeshkian said nature conservation is part of the country’s cultural and civilizational heritage. He noted that Iran has adopted a national biodiversity strategy and action plan, designated its Department of Environment as the national coordinating body, and prioritized the protection of endangered species and the expansion of protected areas.
The president also stressed that developing countries need fair access to financial resources, modern technologies, scientific knowledge and capacity-building opportunities to meet their environmental commitments.
He said countries facing economic sanctions or military aggression should not be left to bear alone the environmental costs of sanctions or wars they did not initiate. Without adequate funding and equitable technology transfer, he warned, global biodiversity targets would remain little more than declarations and negotiations.
“What has happened in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ‘ecocide or environmental genocide,’ which must be condemned,” he said.
Pezeshkian also pointed to the combined effects of climate change, drought, water scarcity, desertification, economic sanctions and restricted access to technology and financial resources on Iran’s environmental protection efforts.
He said Iran has been targeted by criminal wars for two consecutive years, involving the extensive use of destructive and prohibited weapons, with attacks in many cases deliberately aimed at damaging the environment, including strikes on fuel storage facilities in the capital.
The president called for genuine international cooperation to help Iran implement environmental programs and compensate for the damage inflicted.
He said Iran’s diverse ecosystems, species and genetic resources formed a natural and cultural heritage shaped by millions of years of evolution over time. From the Hyrcanian and Arasbaran forests to the Zagros Mountains, deserts and the coasts of the Persian Gulf, Gulf of Oman and Caspian Sea, these resources underpin the country’s resilience and sustainable development, he said.
President Pezeshkian said Iran had adopted a national biodiversity strategy and action plan and designated the Department of Environment as its national coordinator. Priorities include expanding protected areas to 28 percent, monitoring key species, developing wildlife rehabilitation centers and implementing action plans for 25 vertebrate species. National task forces have been established for species including the Asiatic cheetah and Persian fallow deer, he said.
Turning to armed conflict, President Pezeshkian said war burns forests, damages wetlands, contaminates soil and water, destroys habitats and introduces pollutants and heavy metals into natural systems. Such harm can persist for years after fighting ends and affect the security and well-being of future generations.
He said the United States and the Israeli regime are causing environmental damage through military operations in the region, citing damage to industrial and energy facilities, fires, pollution and harm to protective infrastructure. He said environmental impacts crossed political borders and required solutions.
Referring to Gaza, he warned that damage to soil and ecological systems could endure for generations and described the destruction as ecocide, which he emphasized should be condemned.
President Pezeshkian also highlighted the challenges facing countries dealing with climate change, drought, water scarcity and desertification while facing economic sanctions and limited access to finance and technology. Biodiversity commitments, he said, would remain on paper without adequate funding, fair access to technology and capacity-building.
He called on United Nations agencies, international financial institutions and environmental and sustainable-development bodies to strengthen funding mechanisms, assess environmental damage, restore affected ecosystems and support countries dealing with the consequences of armed conflict. Countries under sanctions or subjected to military aggression should not be left to bear these costs alone, he said.
Pezeshkian said Iran’s commitment to biodiversity protection is rooted not only in its international obligations but also in its longstanding cultural and civilizational heritage.
He noted that Iran is a country with an ancient tradition of living in harmony with nature and has a remarkable diversity of ecosystems, species and genetic resources.
From the Hyrcanian and Arasbaran forests to the Zagros Mountains, deserts and the coasts of the Persian Gulf, the Sea of Oman and the Caspian Sea, Iran’s natural wealth provides a foundation for water and food security, public health, resilience to natural hazards and sustainable development, he said.
Respect for nature, Pezeshkian added, has long been part of Iranian cultural, religious and ritual identity. Traditional agriculture, animal husbandry, the use of medicinal plants and indigenous knowledge have also developed through centuries of interaction with the natural environment.
Protecting biodiversity, he added, could become an important arena for peace diplomacy, with environmental cooperation serving as a bridge between nations and helping advance peace with nature and a safer future for coming generations.
Pezeshkian reaffirmed Iran’s readiness to share its scientific expertise, academic capabilities and experience with other countries, describing biodiversity conservation as an important avenue for “peace diplomacy.”
Cooperation could help bridge divides between nations and contribute to peace and security, coexistence with nature, and the well-being of present and future generations, he concluded.

Carnival Cruises axes half of Australian fleet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:38:12 UTC
16:38:12 KST

In short:
Carnival Cruises will drop two of the four cruise ships in its Australian fleet.
All other major cruise lines have pulled their full-time Australian ships.
Australia is a hard market for cruises to stay profitable, according to an industry expert.
Carnival Cruises has announced it will remove two of its four Australian cruise ships from March 2028, despite more than 1.4 million Australians going on a cruise last year.
Carnival, which is the only major cruise company operating full-time in Australia, announced it was pulling the Carnival Adventure and the Carnival Luminosa.
Other major cruise operators such as Disney and Royal Caribbean no longer operate full-time in Australia.
Carnival said ship schedules were considered years in advance and it was considering "long-term certainty and globally competitive operating conditions to support itinerary planning and investment".
The decision was an economic one, according to Chris Frame, a maritime historian.
"Australia is an end-of-the-line destination, and it's a huge investment."
Mr Frame said higher levels of regulation, such as tough biosecurity rules, and little cruise infrastructure made it hard for cruises to stay profitable in Australia.
"Berthing fees are higher than other markets, refuelling is higher and provisioning the ship with food is higher, as you just don't have the economies of scale."
He said that for the company, the ships were assets and "they can always be redeployed somewhere else more profitable".
New changes to cruise laws
The moves comes after a decades-old temporary exemption, allowing cruise ships to circumvent Australian labour laws, was extended earlier this month, but with new protections added for workers for the first time.
Earlier this year, an ABC News investigation revealed that workers had accused the company of 12-hour work days for seven days a week, medical neglect, not providing safe drinking water and wages less than $3 an hour. Carnival denied the allegations.
Carnival's country manager Peter Little said in a statement the company had "greater exposure to changes in local market and operating conditions" than other cruise lines. Carnival did not respond to requests for comment.
However, Jake Field of the Maritime Union of Australia claimed this was the third time Carnival had threatened to withdraw from Australia, and that it was a negotiating tactic.
"There are 80 cruise vessels that are scheduled to come to Australia, only four of them don't have collective agreements with their crews, and those are the four Carnival ships," he said.
"We'll still be surrounded by water, and be an international cruise destination. Those 80 other cruise ships will still be coming here."

US missile defence shortages could last until 2030, ousted general warned: report

16:36:45 KST

Ousted US Army Chief of Staff General Randy George warned months before the US-Israeli war against Iran that American missile defence stockpiles were critically low and could take until 2030 to recover, CBS News reported on Thursday, citing US officials familiar with his assessment.
George raised the warning in late December, two months before the conflict began. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed him from his post in April as the war was under way.
The assessment, included in the Pentagon’s fiscal 2027 force allocation planning, identified shortages of Terminal High Altitude Area Defence (THAAD) interceptors and Patriot missiles, with supplies expected to remain at strategically low levels until 2030.
Officials attributed the shortfall to weapons transfers to Ukraine, US military support for Israel and limited defence industry production capacity, according to the report.
War further strains supplies
The conflict with Iran has added pressure on US stockpiles. A Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimate found that US forces entered 2026 with about 2,300 Patriot interceptors and used between 1,050 and 1,430 of them during the conflict.
The US had about 355 THAAD interceptors before the war, of which an estimated 190 to 290 were expended, according to the estimates.
Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel and senior adviser at CSIS, told CBS News that the systems would be crucial in a potential conflict with China.
“Air defence, missile defence, that will be huge,” he said, explaining that a major confrontation with Beijing would require substantial interceptor supplies.
Replenishing the stockpiles could take years. CSIS estimates that new THAAD interceptor contracts take more than four years to fulfil, while Patriot PAC-3 orders take an average of three and a half years.
Pentagon denies shortage
The Pentagon rejected claims that US forces face a shortage of munitions.
“Claims of US munitions shortages are false,” chief spokesperson Sean Parnell told CBS News.
He added that Washington retained “everything required to strike at the time and place of the President’s choosing”.

Australia defeats Fetu Samoa 40-0 in Rugby League World Cup
Australia's quest for a fourth consecutive Women's Rugby League World Cup has started with a bang courtesy of a 40-0 victory over Fetu Samoa.
Unbackable favourites leading into the tournament opener, the Jillaroos overcame an ill-disciplined opening 10 minutes to shut out Samoa in the seven-try rout.
Things were far from easy for Australia in the second half, but the damage was already done by half-time, with five-eighth Jocelyn Kelleher and reigning Dally M medallist Tamika Upton leading the way with two try assists apiece.
Kelleher, making her Jillaroos debut, was named player of the match, where she was dangerous in attack and her kicking game troubled Samoa.

"It's a dream come true," she said.

"We still have a lot of things to fix from today. It wasn't perfect out there," Kelleher said.

Gold Coast Titans star Jaime Chapman ended her three-year Jillaroos exodus by scoring Australia's first try in the 11th minute, beating opposite winger Freedom Crichton Ropati out wide.
Australia's greatest ever try-scorer, Julia Robinson, lived up to her reputation seven minutes later when she beat three would-be defenders for her 23rd Jillaroos try in 14 appearances.

Kernick turned playmaker in the opening five minutes of the second period when she handed the ball off for Keilee Joseph to extend the Jillaroos' lead.
Brave defence might have turned the tide for Samoa, who ground their way to more opportunities at the Jillaroos end over the final 25 minutes.
Prop Laikha Clarke went the closest to securing some consolation points for Samoa, but was ruled to have dropped the ball over the line.
Of further concern for Samoa was a suspected knee injury in the dying stages to centre Sarina Masaga.
A try in the final two minutes from Australian centre Jessica Sergis capped the Jillaroos' victory and extended their almost three-year unbeaten run.
Samoa's men thrashed France in the opening match of the day, putting on a record score to win 78-4.

REPORT: Samoa 78 def. France 4
— reporting by AAP
Samoa have opened their World Cup campaign by crushing France in a 78-4 win that gives an early boost to the Pacific nation's hopes of reaching the knockout stages.
In a 14-try-to-one victory in which centre Stephen Crichton kicked 11 goals and Melbourne flyer Sua Fa'alogo crossed four times, the Samoans barely worked up a sweat at Western Sydney Stadium in Sydney on Friday.
Taking on a French side mostly made up of Super League players, the star-studded Samoan team raced out to a 28-0 lead inside 20 minutes.
The only blemish for coach Ben Gardiner was the sight of Brisbane winger Deine Mariner going off in the first half with a suspected injury.
And while they had lapses of discipline and concentration with the result sewn up — France scored their sole try through winger Guillermo Aispuro-Bichet — the heavy win will increase Samoa's points differential and their hopes of making it to the semi-finals.
One of Samoa, England or Tonga will miss the knockout stages as a result of the new tournament format, in which the top two teams from across group B and group C make it to the last four.
Samoa face Papua New Guinea in Port Moresby next week before concluding their pool games in an all-Pacific match-up for the ages against the Tongans.
The Kumuls on home soil and Tonga in Sydney will provide a much sterner test than the French, who were left for dead in a blistering opening quarter.
Mariner scored the opening try for the Toa in the third minute soon after his father Lapi had sung the country's national anthem that brought stars including Jarome Luai and Spencer Leniu to tears.
Benaiah Ioelu, Jermaine McEwen, Fa'alogo, and Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow all crossed in the next 15 minutes as the French defence was cut to shreds.
Aispuro-Bichet briefly stemmed the bleeding before Fa'alogo went in again just before halftime to make it 34-4 at the break.
The French had little resistance in the second period, with Fa'alogo adding two more while Crichton, Chanel Harris-Tavita, Shawn Blore, Izack Tago, Francis Molo and Ioelu all went over.

Lithuania has extended military assistance to patrol its border with Russia’s Kaliningrad region until mid-November, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said.
“Assessing the potential flows of residents fleeing the Kaliningrad region and related incidents of illegal border crossings, we are extending enhanced border protection until mid-November for preventive purposes,” Kaunas said.

About 100 troops are currently deployed to assist border guards.

The deployment is linked to public reports of a planned mobilisation in Russia following parliamentary elections. Katelynas has said he expects people might try to seek asylum in Lithuania to avoid military service.
Military personnel and State Border Guard Service officers patrol areas around border checkpoints. Mobile patrols, mobile observation posts and military police units can also be deployed as needed.

Putin has signed a decree placing the assets of flooring manufacturer Tarkett under the temporary management of Management Company Center Capital LLC.

Moreover, the presidential decree placed the assets of three foreign packaging companies under the temporary management of Management Company Center Capital LLC.

ISTANBUL
A wildfire burning in the hills of Malibu in Southern California grew to about 200 acres (809 decares) by nightfall, prompting evacuation warnings and orders across a wide area as officials warned of heightened fire danger due to strong winds.
The Bryson Fire broke out in the state’s Encinal Canyon area, near the Camp Kilpatrick juvenile detention facility, according to CBS News on Thursday.
Los Angeles County issued evacuation warnings and orders covering areas stretching toward Leo Carrillo State Park, Pepperdine University, and the Pacific coast.
Pepperdine said the blaze was burning about eight miles northwest of its Malibu campus, adding that winds were blowing southwest, away from the university.

Camp Kilpatrick evacuated 38 young people from its detention facility, transferring them to Barry J. Nidorf Juvenile Hall in Sylmar.
“We understand that an evacuation can be stressful for youth and their families,” the Los Angeles County Probation Department said, adding that staff were providing support and parents and legal guardians were being notified.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said city officials were closely monitoring developments, although the fire remained outside city limits.
The Los Angeles Fire Department “is prepared to respond to any fire threat that could emerge,” Bass said.
She added that resources had been positioned across several areas, including the San Fernando Valley, Santa Monica Mountains, and West Los Angeles.
Meanwhile, Southern California Edison initiated a public safety power shutoff affecting more than 60,000 residents.
The National Weather Service issued a Red Flag Warning, citing an expected moderate-to-strong Santa Ana wind event that could increase critical fire danger through Saturday.
